Title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany
Authors: Christian Dustmann, Martin Friedrich, Carl Gergs, Uta Schönberg
Affiliations: University College London; Institute For Employment Research; Rockwool Foundation Berlin; University Of Hong Kong
Abstract: Abstract Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

Title: Competition in Markups: A Theory of the Lerner Index in Networks and General Equilibrium
Authors: Lingxuan Wu
Affiliations: NYU Stern
Abstract: Abstract What determines demand elasticities and markups in production networks, where firms' demand and pricing are interdependent? I propose competition in markups, an equilibrium concept in which firms choose markups, taking other firms' markups as given. In partial equilibrium with vertical structures, it links upstream demand elasticities to downstream characteristics without backward induction and ties pass-through to the curvature of final demand. In general equilibrium with arbitrary industry networks, it microfounds firms' demand elasticities and markups through their within-industry market shares and four industry-level network statistics---cycle, substitution in production, substitution in consumption, and consumer-price impact. Empirical analysis of Compustat firms from 1997 to 2019 confirms the predicted variation of industry demand elasticities and firm markups. Relative to an exogenous-markup benchmark, endogenous markups dampen the aggregate TFP impact of a productivity shock to an industry's largest firm by 6% for the median industry, and by up to 48% across industries.

Title: The Horizon of Investors’ Information and Corporate Investment
Authors: Olivier Dessaint, Thierry Foucault, Laurent Frésard
Affiliations: INSEAD; HEC Paris; Università della Svizzera italiana and Swiss Finance Institute
Abstract: Abstract The quality of investors’ information across different horizons has real effects. When managers care about the effect of investment on their stock price, a decline in the informativeness of investors’ signals about long-term cash flows leads firms with long-term projects to cut investment more than firms with short-term projects. Using a novel, hand-collected measure of project horizons, we confirm this hypothesis: relative to firms with short-term projects, the investment of firms with long-term projects decreases by 3.7% following a 1-standard-deviation drop in the quality of investors’ long-term information. This effect becomes larger when managers prioritize current stock prices. (JEL D84, G14, G17, M41).

Title: The Role of Supply Chains in Climate Disclosure
Authors: Pietro Bonetti, Yang (Ellen) EN, Igor Kadach, Gaizka Ormazabal
Affiliations: IESE Business School; IESE Business School, CEPR, & ECGI
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the role of supply chains in shaping the public disclosure of climate information. We leverage a unique empirical setting enabled by CDP—the leading platform for corporate climate risk reporting—which allows customers to demand climate‐related information from their suppliers. Using a large international sample of customer–supplier pairs, we find a positive association between customers’ information demand and suppliers’ public disclosure on the CDP. While the estimated association is modest on average, it exhibits substantial cross‐sectional variation reflecting the disclosure incentives of both customers and suppliers as well as their relative bargaining power. We also find descriptive evidence consistent with one potential implication of the documented association for corporate decision‐making: shifts in supply network relationships toward greener and more transparent suppliers. Overall, our findings contribute to ongoing debates on how to foster climate disclosure.

Title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Cost Asymmetry
Authors: Eti Einhorn, Efrat Shust
Affiliations: Coller School of Management Tel Aviv University Tel Aviv‐Yafo Israel; The Department of Management and Economics The Open University of Israel Ra'anana Israel
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the intertemporal dynamics of asymmetric cost behavior in a competitive setting. Our analysis delves into the primitives of cost asymmetry and explores its dynamic evolution over time. The analysis yields the result that cost behavior is asymmetric by default and path‐dependent, transpiring as cost stickiness following prior resource expansion and taking the form of cost anti‐stickiness after previous resource contraction. The analysis further suggests that the magnitude of cost asymmetry, either stickiness or anti‐stickiness, is decreasing in demand uncertainty and competition intensity, increasing in adjustment costs and time discounting, and greater for small demand shocks than for large demand shocks. By highlighting cost asymmetry as a dynamic, rather than static, phenomenon, and by providing new, testable predictions regarding the direction and magnitude of cost asymmetry across firms and over time, our results offer theoretical grounding for the empirical cost asymmetry literature and may also help investors and other stakeholders interpret cost behavior in light of firms' recent history of expansion or contraction and their competitive environment.

Title: Multimarket Contact and Long-Term Oriented Language in Competition
Authors: He Gao, Tieying Yu, Hyun-Soo Woo, Albert A. Cannella
Affiliations: University of Delaware; Boston College; The University of Mississippi; Texas A&M University
Abstract: Corporate disclosure has long served as a strategic tool for managing the perceptions of audiences that shape a firm’s access to resources. Prior research has largely focused on why firms use disclosure to engage capital-market constituents such as investors and analysts, leaving open the question of when and why firms disclose for competitive purposes. Focusing on the temporal orientation of competitive strategy communication, we examine how multimarket contact (MMC) shapes firms’ use of long-term oriented language (LTL). We argue that greater MMC raises the risk of cross-market retaliation, strengthening firms’ incentives to signal a restrained competitive posture through LTL, particularly when competitive capacity is visibly constrained by poor financial performance or analyst downgrade revisions. Using a sample of 36 U.S. manufacturing firms across six industries from 2015 to 2024, we find evidence generally consistent with our predictions.

Title: The Effect of State-Mandated Employment Certificates on Child Labor Violations in the United States
Authors: Jiacong (Fred) Bao, Ashish Kabra
Abstract: The number of minors involved in child labor violations in the United States more than tripled from 2017 to 2025. Compounding this issue, several state legislatures have recently weakened child labor protection laws. A key component of these laws is whether employers are required to obtain an employment certificate when hiring minors under 18 years of age, which typically requires a parent’s signature and is issued by a school. Proponents of loosening child labor regulations argue that there is a lack of evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of these laws in reducing child labor violations. In this study, we examine the effect of state-mandated employment certificates on reducing child labor violations. We find that the requirement leads to an average of 13.3% fewer violation cases (not statistically significant), 31.8% fewer minors involved in child labor violations, and 34.9% lower civil penalties per minor, indicating reduced severity of violations that do occur. The negative effects on the number of cases and minors persist after addressing endogeneity concerns, as assessed using two novel instrumental variables. Furthermore, we find a positive relationship between the number of unaccompanied migrant children released to a state and the incidence and severity of child labor violations, suggesting that this demographic is particularly vulnerable to labor exploitation. We identify two key mechanisms driving the effectiveness of employment certificates. First, they act as a legal deterrent for employers, as the documented acknowledgment of regulations makes it more difficult to claim ignorance. This is reflected in the higher rate of violations categorized as “willful” in certificate-mandate states. Second, they enhance stakeholder awareness and monitoring. Compliance improves for requirements explicitly documented in the certificates but not for those less visible. Moreover, among common certificate features, parental consent shows the strongest protective effect, suggesting the importance of active oversight and awareness. To our knowledge, this study is the first to provide quantitative evidence for the efficacy of mandating employment certificates in reducing child labor violations. It highlights the critical role of state policies in protecting minor workers and aims to enrich the discourse on child labor regulation and policy implementation.

Title: A General Framework for Importance Sampling with Markov Random Walks
Authors: Cheng-Der Fuh, Yanwei Jia, Steven Kou
Affiliations: Taoyuan, Taiwan; Hong Kong, China; BOSTON UNIVERSITY, Questrom School of Business, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
Abstract: Although stochastic models driven by latent Markov processes are widely used, the classical importance sampling methods based on the exponential tilting for these models suffer from difficulties in computing associated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions and the plausibility of the indirect asymptotic large deviation regime for the variance of the estimator. We propose an importance sampling framework that twists the observable and latent processes separately using a link function that directly minimizes the estimator’s variance. An optimal link function is chosen within the locally asymptotically normal family. We show the logarithmic efficiency of the estimator. As applications, we estimate an overflow probability under a pandemic model and the CoVaR, a measurement of the co-dependent financial systemic risk; both are beyond the scope of traditional importance sampling methods due to nonlinear features.

Title: Alternating Methods for Large-Scale AC Optimal Power Flow with Unit Commitment
Authors: Matthew Brun, Thomas Lee, Dirk Lauinger, Xin Chen, Xu Andy Sun
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Operations Research Center, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02139-4307, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Institute for Data, Systems, & Society, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; Texas A&M University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, College Station, Texas, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02142, United States
Abstract: Security-constrained unit commitment with alternating current optimal power flow (SCUC-ACOPF) is a central problem in power grid operations that optimizes commitment and dispatch of generators under a physically accurate power transmission model while encouraging robustness against component failures. SCUC-ACOPF requires solving large-scale problems that involve multiple time periods and networks with thousands of buses within strict time limits. In this work, we study a detailed SCUC-ACOPF model with a rich set of features of modern power grids, including price-sensitive load, reserve products, transformer controls, and energy-limited devices. We propose a decomposition scheme and a penalty alternating direction method to find high-quality solutions to this model. Our methodology leverages spatial and temporal decomposition, separating the problem into a set of mixed-integer linear programs for each bus and a set of continuous nonlinear programs for each time period. To improve the performance of the algorithm, we introduce a variety of heuristics, including restrictions of temporal linking constraints, a second-order cone relaxation, and a contingency screening algorithm. We quantify the quality of feasible solutions through a dual bound from a second-order cone program. To evaluate our algorithm, we use large-scale test cases from Challenge 3 of the U.S. Department of Energy s Grid Optimization Competition that resemble real power grid data under a variety of operating conditions and decision horizons. The experiments yield feasible solutions with an average optimality gap of 1.33%, demonstrating that this approach generates near-optimal solutions within stringent time limits.

Title: Locational marginal value of battery network
Authors: Xinjiang Chen, Puxiang Tan, Yu Yang, Guannan He
Abstract: The battery network, including stationary energy storage (SES) and mobile energy storage (MES), is gaining attention for the role in improving power system flexibility and resilience. However, most studies focus on SES or fail to evaluate the economic contributions of MES to node operations. Additionally, the impact of battery degradation caused by frequent charging and swapping on the value of MES is often overlooked. To address these gaps, we propose a framework to evaluate the locational marginal value (LMV) of a battery network, defined as the cost reduction achieved by adding one unit of battery capacity with a specific state of health (SOH) to MES at a given node. We define functions for battery energy efficiency and capacity based on SOH and develop a model to optimize battery network and power system dispatch, considering battery charging and swapping coordination. Analytical expressions for LMV are derived, capturing their dependence on system operating states and conditions. The LMV is decomposed into three components: the energy storage component, the energy transportation component, and the locational marginal price component. Using data from China's power systems, we validate the LMV theory through numerical experiments, revealing that using batteries with different SOH results in a 20 % difference in the LMV of the battery network, demonstrating its accuracy and value in guiding MES deployment.

Title: Optimal investment in an energy storage system
Authors: Marta Castellini, Chiara D’Alpaos, Fulvio Fontini, Michele Moretto
Abstract: Renewable energy production plays a crucial role in the energy transition. However, many renewable energy sources are intermittent, and there is often a mismatch between energy production and consumption, which can be partially solved by storage. In this paper we investigate the investment decision in a photovoltaic (PV) power plant coupled with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), namely an Energy Storage System (ESS). We aim to investigate the relationship between the net present value (NPV) of the investment and the technical implications related to the maximum amount of energy to be stored while also accounting for the impact of energy prices. In our setting an ESS is connected to the national power grid. Energy can be produced, purchased from the grid, stored, self-consumed, and fed into the grid. PV production and energy consumption loads evolve stochastically over time. In addition, as BESSs are costly, the energy stored has an opportunity cost, which depends on the prices of energy purchased from the grid and energy fed in and sold to the grid, respectively. However, BESS can significantly contribute to increasing ESSs’ managerial flexibility and ESSs’ value. We investigate the optimal size of a BESS that minimizes ESSs’ net operating costs. We also provide insights into the optimal operating strategy of an ESS. Our results show that the net operating costs of an ESS are relatively small. They decrease for increasing selling prices of energy, whereas they increase with increasing volatility of the stock of energy stored in the battery.

Title: The impact of ancillary services in green hydrogen investment valuation
Authors: Lars Erik Lunde Halbrendt, Maria Lavrutich, Inger Kristine Melhus, Ståle Størdal
Abstract: As the share of intermittent renewable energy sources increases, there is a growing need for flexible resources to maintain grid stability. Green hydrogen, produced by electrolysis, is recognized as a key flexible resource because of its easily adjustable production process. However, previous studies often deem investments in green hydrogen production unprofitable, largely because they tend to overlook the potential revenue from ancillary services. This paper addresses this gap by examining the impact of integrating ancillary services into the investment strategy for a green hydrogen production plant. We link a stochastic price model with an hourly resolution optimization and a real options valuation to quantify the benefits of co-optimizing hydrogen production and ancillary service participation for hydrogen plants in Norway and Germany. Our results show that optimizing the electrolyzer's daily production to include participation in ancillary services markets substantially raises the project's NPV and eliminates the value of delaying investment. In contrast, without ancillary services, spot-price volatility creates an incentive to delay investment. This effect is stronger in Germany than in Norway due to more volatile spot prices. This highlights the complementary role of real-options valuation and participation in the ancillary services markets, where ancillary service revenues act as an operational hedge, smoothing cash flows and reducing price volatility, thereby reducing the incentive to postpone investment.

Title: Integrating real options analysis with ε-constraint optimization for multi-objective decision-support: A case study on investment in offshore electrification
Authors: Olga Noshchenko, Verena Hagspiel, Maria Lavrutich
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel multi-objective real options approach for optimal investment planning, focusing on economic and environmental aspects of polluting projects’ decarbonization under market uncertainty. The approach integrates real options analysis with the multi-objective optimization method, where emissions are treated as an ε-constraint, a predefined upper limit representing an emission limit set by the company. By using such an integrated approach, the research addresses the dilemma between a project's profitability and environmental performance. The proposed methodology is applied to a case study of offshore platform electrification on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, where offshore wind power electrification is considered a key strategy to meet emissions reduction targets. The model aims to identify optimal investment decisions allowing to balance emissions constraints and project profitability while considering fluctuating commodity and CO 2 allowance prices. The results highlight the potential for decarbonization and the effectiveness of setting and committing to environmental targets at the firm level. Meanwhile, the sensitivity analysis of different renewable energy technology scenarios underscores the critical role of technological development in driving further decarbonization.

Title: Robust valuation and optimal harvesting of forestry resources in the presence of catastrophe risk and parameter uncertainty
Authors: Ankush Agarwal, Christian Oliver Ewald, Yihan Zou
Abstract: We determine forest lease value and optimal harvesting strategies under model parameter uncertainty within stochastic bio-economic models that account for catastrophe risk. Catastrophic events are modeled as a Poisson point process, with a two-factor stochastic convenience yield model capturing the lumber spot price dynamics. Using lumber futures and US wildfire data, we estimate model parameters through Kalman filtering and maximum likelihood estimation and specify the model parameter uncertainty set as the 95% confidence region. We numerically determine the forest lease value under catastrophe risk and parameter uncertainty using reflected backward stochastic differential equations (RBSDEs) and establish conservative and optimistic bounds for lease values and optimal stopping boundaries for harvesting. Numerical experiments further explore how parameter uncertainty, catastrophe intensity, and carbon sequestration impact the lease valuation and harvesting decision. In particular, we explore the costs arising from this form of uncertainty in the form of a reduction of the lease value. These are implicit costs which can be attributed to climate risk, and are likely to become more significant as forestry resources play a larger role in the energy transition. We conclude that in the presence of parameter uncertainty, it is better to lean toward a conservative strategy reflecting, to some extent, the worst case than being overly optimistic. Moreover, our results suggest that convenience yield plays a substantial role in determining optimal harvesting strategies within the two-factor model adopted in this study.

Title: Tokenizing creativity in open communities
Authors: Fernando S. Oliveira, Su Jung Jee
Abstract: Open communities, where individuals share and evaluate creative content, often face challenges in maintaining high-quality contributors over the long term. This study examines the effective governance of Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), an emerging organizational paradigm that may address this issue. Built on blockchain technology, DAOs operate through decentralized and automated decision-making, using cryptographic tokens to reward contributors transparently. Assuming that transparent and collectively determined reward mechanisms can encourage participation, we develop an agent-based model with reinforcement learning to simulate the long-run implications of diverse DAO governance structures. Our models account for the cumulative process of reward acquisition and behavioral adaptation, shaping the evolution of such communities. We juxtapose three DAO scenarios, each characterized by its approach to distributing engagement rights that shape community evolution: Egalitarian (equitable rights distribution), Merit-based (rights based on reputation), and Property-based (rights contingent on investment). These models are compared with traditional open communities that lack reward mechanisms. Our findings underscore the potential of tokenizing creativity to sustain open communities. Notably, the Merit-based DAO exhibits high engagement rates and weak concentration of governance decisions compared to other governance structures. Meanwhile, the Property-based DAO presents a viable alternative by fostering exploratory learning and inclusive reward distribution for creators, albeit with relatively low engagement.

Title: Real-time decision-support using simulation (RtS) for operational responsiveness in urgent and emergency care: Bridging the gap between conventional simulation and digital twins
Authors: Alison Harper, Navonil Mustafee, Joe Viana
Abstract: Conventional simulation models in healthcare are typically parameterised using historical data, limiting their ability to support responsive, real-time operational decision-making. They are therefore poorly suited to dynamic, high-pressure environments such as urgent and emergency care, where decisions must reflect the current system state. In this paper, we introduce real-time decision-support using simulation (RtS), a methodology that integrates real-time operational data into a discrete-event simulation model to enable context-aware, short-term decision-making. The model integrates partial real-time data feeds with historically derived distributions using a novel data fusion and model initialisation approach. By continuously aligning the simulation with the evolving system state, RtS enhances situation awareness and enables the evaluation of adaptive interventions whose implementation influences subsequent system behaviour. We implement the technical component of our RtS framework through a proof-of-concept model of an Urgent Care Network comprising multiple emergency and urgent care facilities. We evaluate resource-neutral operational policies designed to support short-term adaptation under conditions of rising demand. Our results demonstrate that, under the modelled high-demand conditions, normal emergency department operations can be restored within a 4-hour period through the implementation of two adaptive policies. By operationalising RtS in a service-based setting and demonstrating its effectiveness relative to conventional simulation, our findings provide healthcare stakeholders and OR practitioners with both the technical foundations and the scholarly framing needed to engage in mainstream discussions on deploying RtS as a step-change solution toward simulation enabled digital twins in complex sociotechnical systems.

Title: An efficient divide-and-conquer enhanced metaheuristic for operating room scheduling: A real-world case study
Authors: Marc Chouraqui, Salma Makboul, Alice Yalaoui, Farouk Yalaoui, Lionel Amodeo, Virginie Roger
Abstract: This paper proposes an efficient resolution method to solve the Operating Room (OR) allocation and scheduling problem under real-world hospital constraints using a divide-and-conquer enhanced metaheuristic approach. The objective is to assign a set of elective surgeries to appropriate ORs and intra-day time slots while satisfying practical constraints such as surgeon availability, room compatibility, setup-dependent times, and limiting surgeon idle time to a specified threshold, aiming to minimize the makespan and surgeon's overtime. The problem is modeled as an integer linear programming formulation with proven NP-hard complexity and integrated lower bound calculations. By decomposing the scheduling task into smaller, independent subproblems, the proposed divide-and-conquer strategy significantly improves the performance of the underlying Iterated Local Search metaheuristic. Extensive experiments based on real data from a partner hospital demonstrate the method's scalability and superiority over classical metaheuristics related to OR scheduling approaches in the literature, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Title: Dynamic pricing and learning with censored demand
Authors: Haitao Liu, Ping Cao, Jinpeng Liang, Wenyu Wang
Abstract: We study a single-product pricing problem where lost sales are unobservable, and prices are discrete. The demand is price-dependent, but the seller lacks prior knowledge of the demand-price relationship and demand distributions. The objective is to dynamically experiment with prices and learn from censored sales data to identify the optimal price that maximizes revenue. We propose two revenue distribution estimation methods: one is suitable for general and nonparametric demand, and the other is specifically designed for Gaussian demand. For nonparametric demand, we develop a machine learning model using artificially generated uncensored data to approximate revenue distributions. For Gaussian demand, we derive closed-form expressions for the mean and variance of censored revenue, allowing for the estimation of unknown parameters. Using the large deviations theory, we establish optimality conditions under infinite testing periods and develop a dynamic price-testing policy. Under mild assumptions, we show that the asymptotic allocation obtained by the proposed policy converges to the optimal allocation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithms outperform traditional methods, providing robust solutions under a variety of demand distributions, including Gaussian, Gamma, Weibull, and mixed distributions. Our findings reveal significant interactions between inventory levels and the number of learning rounds, offering valuable managerial insights for price optimization with censored demand.

Title: Pitfalls in radial efficiency decomposition for parallel production systems
Authors: Chiang Kao
Abstract: The data envelopment analysis (DEA) radial model is able to measure the system and division efficiencies of the parallel production system composed of several divisions at the same time. Moreover, the system efficiency can be decomposed into a weighted average of the division efficiencies. However, there is a pitfall in determining the target point for calculating radial division efficiencies, which may obtain negative values under variable returns to scale as discussed in the literature. This paper analyzes the reason that causes the decomposition to fail and develops a model to calculate the correct radial division efficiencies. It is proven that the possibly erroneous radial division efficiency decomposed from the radial system efficiency is less than or equal to the correct radial division efficiency under both constant returns to scale and variable returns to scale. Furthermore, the correct radial division efficiency is less than or equal to the division-specific radial efficiency under constant returns to scale and is equal to the division-specific radial efficiency under variable returns to scale.

Title: Pareto fronts for privacy-utility trade-offs in multi-query systems
Authors: Yi Yin, Guangquan Zhang, Hua Zuo, Jie Lu
Abstract: Multi-query systems have become a common paradigm for enabling flexible access to sensitive data. However, their openness introduces privacy risks, most especially from attribute inference attacks (AIAs), where adversaries infer sensitive attributes by analyzing strategically crafted queries. While defenses such as differential privacy (DP) and query limit help mitigate these risks, determining appropriate privacy parameters, particularly the privacy budget ϵ and the maximum query limit N , to protect privacy while maintaining data utility remains a significant challenge. To address this trade-off, we first introduce a bilevel optimization framework for multi-query systems. We construct a realistic interaction model involving a query-based system (QBS) server, users, and a QueryCheetah-based attacker to capture real-world multi-party dynamics under advanced threat scenarios. Within this framework, the upper level is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem that seeks to defend against the attacker while satisfying utility requirements by selecting appropriate privacy configurations. The lower level simulates an attacker that optimizes its attribute inference strategy under these configurations. To solve the upper-level optimization problem, we design a task-aware adaptive Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to search for Pareto-optimal configurations. The algorithm leverages the monotonicity of privacy and utility metrics, and incorporates dynamic search space pruning and direction-guided mutation to enhance search efficiency and improve solution quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework can significantly enhance search efficiency and optimization precision given advanced AIA threats.

Title: Rules for consistent aggregation: With application to cost efficiency decompositions
Authors: Bert M. Balk, José L. Zofío
Abstract: This study offers a complete discussion of existing and novel rules for consistent aggregation, here interpreted as rules ensuring that measurement scores for units can somehow be added or averaged so that their sum or mean has the same structure and interpretation as the unit-level scores. Examples are the denominator rule and the numerator rule, but there are many more, dependent on the choice of aggregation function, either the arithmetic, harmonic or geometric mean, and associated weights, either symmetric or asymmetric. Additionally, when the aggregates are decomposed, this can be done based on equal or unequal weights for the different components. Several of these general rules have appeared dispersedly in the literature to evaluate applied research in fields such as index numbers, efficiency measures, productivity analysis, cross-efficiency measures, and composite indicators. To address this fragmentation, we present a unified framework for assessing and comparing these rules, highlighting their individual characteristics. In addition, we conduct an empirical application that brings all the decompositions together and compares them using a common dataset of financial institutions. From a methodological standpoint, the overall conclusion is that for consistent decomposition a geometric mean, based on symmetric weights — so that there is no need to distinguish between denominator and numerator rules — is advisable. Consistent factorial decompositions appear then also straightforward.

Title: A best-worst method-based FlowSort approach for multi-criteria sorting problems
Authors: Xiao-Hong Pan, Shi-Fan He, Ying-Ming Wang, Jafar Rezaei
Abstract: Best-Worst Method (BWM) is a behaviorally-inspired decision-making method supporting decision-makers to evaluate and prioritize alternatives based on a set of criteria. This study introduces a novel version of BWM, incorporating concepts from the FlowSort method, which is designed to classify alternatives. Given a set of alternatives characterized with a number of criteria, first, a set of limiting profiles, as multi-criteria vectors, is defined by the decision-maker. Using these limiting profiles, pairwise comparisons are conducted between the two reference limiting profiles (best and worst), and the other limiting profiles. These pairwise comparisons form the basis to derive the priorities of the limiting profiles, which are the foundation of establishing criterion-specific value functions. Then, the criterion-wise value scores of alternatives are derived from the value functions. Subsequently, the outranking degrees between alternatives and reference limiting profiles are calculated based on a V-shape function. Following this, a min–max optimization model is established to infer classification indices. Finally, by exploring the relationships between classification indices of limiting profiles and alternatives, several assignment rules are developed to classify alternatives into different classes. The proposed method is applied to a supplier classification problem, and its performance is compared with several existing multi-criteria sorting methods. Its practical applicability is further demonstrated through a real-world case study on university assessment.

Title: How much harder are indifference adjustments? An experiment on the cognitive effort in multi-criteria decisions
Authors: Wolfgang Haidinger, Florian A.D. Burnat, Juergen Branke, Walter J. Gutjahr
Abstract: This study investigates the cognitive effort required for indifference adjustments (IAs) compared to preference statements (PSs) in multi-criteria decision analysis. While IAs provide substantially more preference information than PSs do, the empirical question of whether the additional cognitive burden is justified remains underexplored. We conducted a field experiment with 83 Austrian roofing professionals who made product decisions about roofing tiles. Participants evaluated products described by 2-4 attributes using both the PS and IA methods, with response time and subjective difficulty ratings as effort measures. Surprisingly, we found that IAs required only 10%–20% more cognitive effort than PSs despite their significantly higher information yield. The effort difference increased slightly with the number of attributes, but remained modest throughout. Our findings suggest that the majority of cognitive effort in both methods stems from comprehending the alternatives rather than making an actual preference judgment or indifference adjustment. These results have important implications for multi-criteria decision support system design, suggesting that IAs offer an attractive trade-off between information gain and cognitive burden.

Title: Non-negative autoregressive moving average models for intermittent demand: Forecast accuracy and inventory implications
Authors: Giacomo Sbrana, M. Zied Babai
Abstract: Autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models are widely used in retail demand forecasting, particularly for stationary data. However, their performance on Walmart’s demand data in the M5 competition has been low. One reason could be that ARMA models can generate negative forecasts for intermittent demand patterns, which are prevalent in the Walmart dataset used in the M5 competition. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that enables ARMA models to effectively forecast intermittent demand. Specifically, we establish conditions under which a generic ARMA model generates non-negative filters and forecasts. Additionally, we derive expressions for approximate prediction intervals, making the approach suitable for stock control applications. Through an empirical analysis of 42,686 time series from Walmart’s M5 competition data and 24,029 series from a global cosmetics retailer, we show that a simple non-negative ARMA(1,1) model significantly outperforms standard benchmarks in both point forecasts and prediction intervals. Moreover, the empirical inventory performance analysis shows that the non-negative ARMA(1,1) leads to the highest inventory efficiency as compared to all the benchmarks considered in the paper. These findings underscore the potential of ARMA models to effectively forecast intermittent demand when non-negativity is enforced.

Title: Entry of a sustainable single-category retailer in a market with multi-category retailers
Authors: H. Sebastian Heese, Eda Kemahlıoğlu-Ziya, Olga Perdikaki
Abstract: New sustainability-marketed firms have emerged in the grocery and consumer packaged-goods categories in response to consumers’ rising preferences for sustainable products. Motivated by this trend in the retail industry, we study how the entry of a new firm that sells an assortment of sustainable consumer goods in one category affects consumers’ channel choices and the existing competing retailers’ market shares across different product categories. We analytically characterize consumers’ shopping preferences in a market with a premium-price retailer and a low-price retailer that each sell two different types of product offerings—packaged goods and fresh goods. We then consider how the entry of a sustainable-product online retailer, which operates only in the packaged-goods category and offers a limited selection, affects consumer preferences, and how the sustainable entrant should price its offering. We find that the low-price retailer becomes more vulnerable after the entry of the sustainable firm, as such entry decreases the retailer’s sales at least weakly in both product categories. In contrast, a brick-and-mortar retailer that charges premium prices and offers more sustainable fresh products can benefit in both the fresh-product and packaged-goods categories from the entry of a sustainable-product competitor. Our findings suggest that the sustainable firm can gain a larger share in highly competitive markets with low price differentials between the two existing retailers in the two product categories, and when customers are not inclined to visit multiple stores to complete their shopping. We identify two pricing strategies for the entrant. When the entrant’s product offering is highly attractive, it is optimal to charge a relatively higher price to extract profit from a larger customer base; when its offering is less attractive, a lower price is optimal to ensure market penetration. Our findings highlight the importance of cross-category interactions in retail competition and provide insights for both sustainable entrants and incumbent retailers.

Title: A generalized data-driven production planning model: algorithmic foundation and simulation-based performance assessment
Authors: Tobias Völker, Lars Mönch
Abstract: Production planning models must consider the non-linear relationship between resource workload and cycle times when timing work releases to meet demand. This is particularly crucial in semiconductor manufacturing where cycle times are of the order of ten weeks and subject to fluctuations at high utilization levels. Data-driven (DD) production planning formulations have been proposed to address this issue as an alternative to clearing function (CF)-based formulations. DD models characterize a production system through a set of discrete system states representing the multivariate relationship between work in process (WIP) and throughput of all products under steady-state conditions. The cycle times are usually not negligible in relation to the period length. The WIP-throughput relationship alone does not sufficiently capture the congestion behavior of the system under these conditions. The planning model must also correctly identify the periods in which the throughput will be realized as output. We investigate the temporal relationship of WIP and output under different cycle time regimes, and propose the concept of flow patterns that specify the expected input and output quantities over several periods based on the WIP at a specific point in time, and extend the concept of system states. To accommodate these patterns, we establish a DD planning formulation that generalizes previous DD models and outperforms other DD variants and the Allocated CF (ACF) formulation in computational experiments using a large-sized wafer fab model.

Title: Selecting return insurance and online channel modes for a capital-constrained manufacturer
Authors: Kebing Chen, Qianyao Zhou, Shengbin Wang, Dong Lei
Abstract: For clothing sold online, the high return rate poses a distinct challenge compared with other product categories. A liberal return policy helps alleviate consumers’ purchase uncertainty and increase their willingness to pay, yet it also imposes a substantial financial burden on companies. To address this issue, we examine a basic supply chain system that consists of a capital-constrained manufacturer and an online platform and explore the manufacturer's online channel mode selection and return insurance strategy. First, we demonstrate that the manufacturer's financing strategy is influenced not only by the level of her initial capital but also by the return insurance cost and the sales mode. Second, we find that when the return insurance cost is sufficiently low, offering return insurance becomes viable, and doing so effectively shifts a substantial portion of the shopping cost to consumers. The choice of online channel mode then determines which party bears responsibility for providing the return insurance service. We show that when the platform's commission rate is high, the manufacturer may avoid profit loss in the agency mode, but should prioritize consumer satisfaction and effectiveness of the platform's marketing effort. Third, our analysis indicates that while the platform's marketing effort consistently increases the manufacturer's profit, it does not always benefit the platform, especially when the manufacturer has limited production capital. Finally, we examine the robustness of our results by extending the baseline model to more realistic settings and consider three key extensions: two alternative financing modes, manufacturer-bearing return costs, and marketing cost sharing.

Title: Optimizing the two-dimensional bandwidth problem under the maximum norm using exact and heuristic approaches
Authors: Sergio Cavero, Eduardo G. Pardo, Eduardo Rodriguez-Tello, Eric Monfroy, Claudia Vasconcellos-Gaete
Abstract: This paper addresses the Two-dimensional Bandwidth Minimization Problem (2D-BMP) using the L ∞ -norm distance, focusing on embedding a guest graph into a grid-like host graph to minimize the maximum edge distance. While previous research has emphasized theoretical aspects and regular graphs, practical methods for complex graphs remain underexplored. Solving 2D-BMP is crucial for applications such as VLSI design, network simulation, and scheduling, though its NP-hard nature poses significant challenges. We propose three exact Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) models—arithmetic, finite domain, and dichotomic optimization to efficiently solve the 2D-BMP. Additionally, we introduce the Convergence-Based Multi-start Algorithm (CBMA), a heuristic combining greedy construction and local search for approximate solutions. Our CSP exact methods found optimal solutions for 70 small benchmark instances from diverse standard graph topologies, including 21 previously unknown. On the other hand, the CBMA achieved new upper bounds, requiring moderate computational times, for 113 graphs extracted from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection which present larger and more complex structures.

Title: Modeling and analysis of lot streaming and lot splitting in the flexible job-shop scheduling problem
Authors: Stéphane Dauzère-Pérès, Liji Shen
Abstract: The first aim of this paper is to provide an overview on how lot streaming and lot splitting, i.e. when jobs (or lots) are divided into sublots, can be applied to the flexible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP). Lot streaming corresponds to the case where the sublots must be processed consecutively on the machines, whereas lot splitting allows sublots to be scheduled independently. The latter is particularly interesting in the FJSP, as sublots can be assigned to different machines. We investigate different variants of lot streaming and lot splitting, related to the consistency of the sublot sizes, of the sublot orders for lot streaming and of the sublot assignments for lot splitting. The differences between these variants are discussed and the associated mathematical models are proposed. Afterwards, we conduct extensive computational experiments on classical instances in the literature to analyze the impact of each variant and of some key parameters. For instances solved to optimality, lot streaming achieves significant improvements of over 20%, while lot splitting is able to provide additional savings of 8% on average. Recommendations are derived based on the numerical results and on practical considerations associated to the implementation of lot streaming and lot splitting. Finally, some conclusions and perspectives are provided.

Title: Improved approximation for min-max k-path cover with neighborhoods: Leveraging refined geometric spanning and adaptive recombination
Authors: Jun Wu, Feng Chu, Zhen Yang, Yongxi Cheng
Abstract: We study the min–max k-path cover problem with neighborhoods (min–max k-PCPN) in the Euclidean plane. Departing from classic discrete-point routing, this problem models customers as service neighborhoods (fixed-radius disks), where demand is satisfied by visiting any point within the geometric region. To address the resulting structural complexity, we propose a search-and-partition framework centered on an adaptive recombination mechanism with a refined geometric spanning strategy. Specifically, this approach hinges on (i) a tightened asymptotic bound for the generalized minimum spanning tree with neighborhoods (GMSTN), which serves as a refined geometric spanning backbone, and (ii) an adaptive recombination mechanism that dynamically partitions neighborhoods and reassembles them into cost-balanced paths based on the spanning backbone. By leveraging the synergy between these two components, our framework yields a new fixed-parameter tractable asymptotic approximation algorithm for the min–max k-PCPN. Furthermore, we generalize our methodology to several related min–max k-path and k-tree cover problems, consistently improving upon the best-known (asymptotic) approximation ratios.

Title: Prelim p. 2; First issue - Editorial Board
Quantifying undetected severe misconduct in medical research
Authors: Katrin Hussinger, Maikel Pellens

Title: Private Firm Disclosures and Public Firms' Debt Choice
Authors: Fengqin Chen, Jeffrey Pittman, Walid Saffar
Affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; Memorial University; Virginia Tech; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Abstract: ABSTRACT Analyzing a cross-country sample, we provide evidence implying that private firm disclosure transparency narrows information asymmetry, which, in turn, lowers public firms' reliance on bank debt. Channel tests help substantiate that private firm disclosure elicits this positive externality, evident in lower monitoring demand, lower borrowing costs, and higher credit rating quality. Cross-sectional results suggest that the impact of private firm transparency is larger when public firms suffer worse information opacity, private firm disclosures are more important to their public peers, and bond markets are more developed. In relying on the staggered implementation of electronic business registers as a plausibly exogenous shock and a simulated disclosure scope as the instrumental variable, we continue to find that private firm disclosures reduce public firms' bank debt reliance, helping to alleviate endogeneity threats. Data Availability Statement: The data used in this study are obtained from publicly available sources identified in the paper. JEL Classifications: G32; G21; M41.

Title: CEO environmental communication, speech acts, and firm value
Authors: Hai-Anh Tran, Stephan Ludwig, Bach Nguyen, Charles H. Noble, Dhruv Grewal
Abstract: Abstract Signaling theory predicts that communication, such as by CEOs, might complement observable environmental engagement by a firm, by reducing information asymmetry. Yet it remains unclear whether firms with stronger environmental engagement communicate more about these efforts and the potential implications for firm value. To analyze 14,523 firm-quarter earnings call Q&A sessions held by 364 publicly listed firms between 2007 and 2022, the current research measures CEO communication about firm environmental engagement and the communicative intent behind such communication by combining MSCI Environmental Pillar Scores, Compustat data, and a fine-tuned DeBERTa model. Firms with stronger environmental engagement communicate less, rather than more, about their efforts during earnings call Q&A sessions. Yet CEO communication about firm environmental engagement can be positively associated with firm value, depending on the communicative intent the CEO indicates, such that assertive and directive speech maintain this positive association, but expressive and commissive speech acts are negatively associated with firm value.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Risk budgeting under general risk measures
Authors: Vali Asimit, Liang Peng, Radu Tunaru, Feng Zhou

Title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
Authors: Parinitha Sastry, Ishita Sen, Ana-Maria Tenekedjieva
Affiliations: Wharton; Harvard Business School; Arizona State University
Abstract: Abstract This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

Title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors
Authors: Tristan Gagnon-Bartsch, Matthew Rabin, Joshua Schwartzstein
Affiliations: University of Iowa; Harvard University; HBS
Abstract: Abstract People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

Title: Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework
Authors: Hanna Wang
Affiliations: Universitat Autónoma de Barcelona, Barcelona School of Economics
Abstract: Abstract I develop and estimate a life-cycle discrete-choice model of fertility and female labour supply to study the optimal design of a range of child-related policies. First, I examine two German reforms that introduced wage-contingent parental leave payments and expanded access to low-cost public childcare. I find that both reforms raised completed fertility, with the parental leave reform having a particularly strong impact on highly educated women. Second, I solve for a budget-neutral optimal policy portfolio that maximizes either aggregate welfare or fertility, while ensuring that welfare and fertility do not decline for any education group. I consider four prominent child subsidies as well as the degree of tax jointness. My results show that optimal policy has the potential to increase welfare by 0.5% or fertility by 5.7%. While the solutions are qualitatively similar, they prioritize different policy instruments depending on the specific objective being targeted.

Title: The Effect of Non‐US Tax Authority Monitoring on Income Shifting by Affiliates of US Multinationals: Evidence From EDGAR Search Activity
Authors: Sabrina Chi, Anh V. Persson, Terry Shevlin, Oktay Urcan
Affiliations: California State University, Fullerton Fullerton California USA; University of Illinois at Urbana‐Champaign Champaign Illinois USA; University of California, Irvine Irvine California USA; University of Washington Seattle Washington USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Governments worldwide are concerned that multinational enterprises (MNEs) shift profits across borders to avoid taxes. While prior research shows that home‐country tax enforcement can reduce tax avoidance, far less is known about whether foreign tax authorities (FTAs) can constrain income shifting by MNE affiliates. We measure FTA monitoring using data on FTAs' downloads of US MNEs' annual reports filed with the SEC. We find that FTA monitoring is more intensive in higher‐tax‐rate countries with a larger MNE presence, consistent with those jurisdictions facing stronger incentives to monitor income shifting. More importantly, we find that monitoring by an affiliate's local tax authority does not systematically reduce income shifting by US MNE affiliates, whereas aggregate monitoring in the MNE group affects an affiliate even when its own local FTA is not observably monitoring it. This result is consistent with a spillover effect of FTA monitoring. This association is stronger when FTAs operate under information‐exchange treaties, when company disclosures are more detailed, and when enforcement capacity is greater. We also find positive associations between aggregate FTA monitoring and subsequent tax avoidance and tax settlements of US MNEs. Our findings suggest monitoring by multiple FTAs effectively combats MNE tax avoidance and have implications for how tax administrations design and coordinate monitoring efforts.

Title: Biological Age and its Value to Marketing Theory and Practice
Authors: Steven D. Shaw, Remi Daviet, Gideon Nave
Abstract: Aging has profound effects on how we consume, yet marketers often simplify aging to the mere passage of time (chronological age; ChronAge), overlooking biological and psychological aspects and meaningful variation within ChronAge segments. This paper highlights the need for multidimensional approaches to studying aging consumers and pioneers a framework integrating biological aging into consumer behavior theory. It introduces a measure of biological age (BioAge), derived from epigenetic data, to marketing. Using Health and Retirement Study data, the analyses demonstrate that BioAge captures distinct aspects of aging, not reflected in ChronAge, and improves prediction of consumer activities and spending. BioAge is most useful in domains where functional capacity, energy, cognition, and health-related constraints shape engagement, including technology use, social and physical activity, and discretionary entertainment spending, and is limited in more routinized or necessity-based domains. The analyses further show that BioAge mediates the impact of time on consumer behavior through objective physiological pathways, including chronic disease, cognitive functioning, and physical vitality, rather than subjective perceptions of health. The paper concludes with implications and best practices, including how BioAge can improve segmentation and customer lifetime value optimization, and the ethical and legal challenges of its use in research and practice.

Title: Causal Alignment: Augmenting Language Models with A/B Tests
Authors: Panagiotis Angelopoulos, Kevin Lee, Sanjog Misra
Abstract: We develop a framework for improving the effectiveness of marketing communications by aligning a language model to the causal signal in A/B tests. The core idea is that randomized experiments reveal not just which content performs best, but directions of improvement that can serve as supervision for a generative model. Using within-experiment comparisons, we fine-tune a language model to create an improver architecture that transforms lower-performing content into higher-performing content. The resulting model can be composed with any baseline decision-maker, e.g. a human expert, to suggest improvements to new content. We validate our framework through a large-scale field experiment in email marketing spanning 36 new campaigns and 283 million impressions. Subject lines improved by our aligned model achieve click-through rates 32% higher than those from unassisted human experts, while a general-purpose language model with 30 times as many parameters as our fine-tuned model does not improve outcomes. This suggests that alignment to experimental data adds value beyond model capabilities alone. Our findings provide the first field evidence that aligning language models to A/B tests improves outcomes in real marketing campaigns and show that integrating AI with experimentation can train systems that make better future decisions.

Title: The Implications of Generic Responses in Online Customer Service Operations
Authors: Jitsama Tanlamai, Wreetabrata Kar, Warut Khern-am-nuai, Yossiri Adulyasak
Abstract: Businesses use a range of strategies to manage online customer service, with social media serving as a popular platform. A growing practice in social-media customer service is the use of generic responses to address customer inquiries. Our study investigates the impact of these generic responses on customer engagement and satisfaction. We analyze social media data from one of the largest banks in the United States and apply machine-learning techniques to extract relevant information from textual data. We leverage a quasi-experimental setting in which a generic response to a customer’s inquiry serves as the treatment. We find that generic responses increase the likelihood that customers reply to the bank. Among customers who reply, generic responses are associated with lower satisfaction. However, our further analyses show that under certain conditions, strategic use of generic responses is associated with higher customer satisfaction. Our findings provide guidance to operation managers regarding how generic responses can be tailored and used to improve online customer service operations.

Title: Code and Data Repository for Urban Delivery with a Coordinated Fleet of Trucks and Drones

Title: Recommender Systems Under Privacy Protection
Authors: Can Küçükgül, Özalp Özer, Shouqiang Wang
Affiliations: Rutgers School of Business, Camden, New Jersey 08102; FBA Science, Selling Partner Services, Amazon, Seattle, Washington 98109; and Naveen Jindal School of Management, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080; Naveen Jindal School of Management, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080
Abstract: We examine how a profit-driven platform designs its recommender policies under varying privacy protection regimes. We demonstrate a functional equivalence between opt-out protection and unprotected privacy. Notably, granting consumers the autonomy to misrepresent personal data can compel the platform to distort recommendations, inadvertently harming both parties. When recommendations are purely informative, such privacy controls can deter personalization entirely. However, when recommendations also serve an allocative role—controlling product access—algorithmic discrimination may emerge, restricting the disadvantaged minority from valuable opportunities. These findings remain robust even with endogenous profit margins. This paper was accepted by Omar Besbes, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05007 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Omar Besbes, revenue management and market analytics.

Title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
Authors: Adeline Delavande, Jayant Ganguli, Friederike Mengel
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Technology Sydney, Ultimo, New South Wales 2007, Australia; Department of Economics, University of Essex, Colchester CO4 3SQ, United Kingdom; and Department of Applied Economics, Erasmus University Rotterdam, Burgemeester Oudlaan 50, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands
Abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A. Delavande acknowledges funding from the Economic and Social Research Council Research Centre on Micro-Social Change [Grants ES/L009153/1 and ES/S012486/1] and the National Institute on Aging [Grant P01AG008291]. Ethical approval was obtained by the Ethics Social Sciences subcommittee at the University of Essex in August 2015. Title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
Authors: Sumit Agarwal, Pengsheng Lin, Yupeng Lin, Ruichang Lu, Xiaojun Zhang
Affiliations: NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore; School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China; Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China
Abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. Y. Lin gratefully acknowledges financial support from the NUS Research Grant [Grants A-8001725 and A-8004426]. R. Lu and X. Zhang acknowledge the financial support of the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 71903005, 72402005, and 72472001].
