Title: Editorial Board
Balancing Efficiency and Safety: How and When Algorithmic Management Induces Gig Workers' Unsafe Behavior
Authors: Yanghao Zhu, Lirong Long, Shiyingzi Huang, Yannan Zhang, Zejie Huang
Affiliations: School of Management Huazhong University of Science and Technology Wuhan Hubei China; School of Business Administration Southwestern University of Finance and Economics Chengdu Sichuan China
Abstract: ABSTRACT As the gig economy expands, millions of food delivery riders rely on gig platforms for their livelihoods, yet this growth has also been accompanied by rising traffic violations and accidents, posing risks to both rider and public safety. It is therefore critical to understand not only the mechanisms driving gig workers' unsafe behavior but also the factors that may mitigate it. Drawing on goal conflict theory and the job demands–resources model, we examine the mediating role of performance–safety goal conflict in the relationship between algorithmic goal setting and unsafe behavior, and further test a dual‐stage moderated mediation model in which algorithmic monitoring and conscientiousness function as boundary conditions. To test our hypotheses, we conducted four interrelated studies using a multi‐method approach: Study 1 employed LLM‐based text analysis ( N = 657), Study 2 adopted a video‐based scenario experiment ( N = 140), Study 3 implemented a three‐wave survey ( N = 242), and Study 4 incorporated objective behavioral data of unsafe behavior ( N = 151). Across these studies, the findings consistently demonstrate that algorithmic goal setting intensifies gig workers' performance–safety goal conflict, which in turn increases unsafe behavior. Moreover, algorithmic monitoring amplifies the effect of algorithmic goal setting on performance–safety goal conflict, whereas conscientiousness serves as a critical personal resource that mitigates the impact of performance–safety goal conflict on unsafe behavior. This study advances existing research by revealing how algorithmic management contributes to gig workers' unsafe behavior and offers practical implications for reducing such risks through both the optimization of algorithmic systems and the cultivation of gig workers' conscientiousness.

Title: Micro‐Foundations of “ Doing Well by Doing Good ”: Multilevel Effects of Work‐Life Policies on Employee Well‐Being and Sales Growth
Authors: Margarita Mayo, Laura Guillén, Jie Cao, Shainaz Firfiray, Juan I. Sanchez
Affiliations: IE Business School IE University Madrid Spain; Universitat Ramon Llull ESADE Business School Barcelona Spain; College of Business Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Zhongshan Beiyi Campus China; Business School University of Aberdeen Aberdeen UK; Florida International University Miami Florida USA; EGADE/Tecnologico de Monterrey Business School Mexico City Mexico
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study unravels how the effects of work‐life policies (WLPs) on individual employees' perceived control over their work schedule have cumulative effects across employees, ultimately crossing levels to enhance organizational outcomes like sales. We tested a multilevel mediating model comprising two cross‐level mechanisms: a top‐down link between the organization's availability of WLPs and individual‐level variables like control over work schedule and job satisfaction, and a bottom‐up link between job satisfaction (aggregated within the organization) and sales growth. Analyses of multilevel, multisource data from 3262 employees in 70 organizations supported the top–down hypotheses predicting that gains in employee control over their work schedule mediate the positive relationship between WLPs availability and job satisfaction. Furthermore, analyses of sales growth data using a matched subsample of 39 organizations and 1872 employees supported the bottom–up hypothesis that organization‐level job satisfaction is positively associated with sales growth over a three‐year span. Our results begin to shed light on the micro‐foundations of doing well (i.e., increasing sales) by doing good (i.e., increasing employees' control over their work schedules through WLP).

Title: From Static Fit to Dynamic Alignment: The Emergence and Evolution of HR Ecosystems in Fragmented Workplaces
Authors: Can Ouyang, Xianwei Shi, Hao Zhang
Affiliations: Antai College of Economics and Management Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China; School of Labor and Human Resources Renmin University of China Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Fragmented work arrangements increasingly challenge conventional firm‐centric approaches to human resource management (HRM), as HR activities become distributed across multiple actors. The concept of HR ecosystem offers a powerful lens for understanding this shift, yet we know little about how such ecosystems emerge and evolve over time. Drawing on 178 in‐depth qualitative interviews from China's online food delivery sector, we find that HR ecosystems evolve through four stages: pre‐emergence static alignment, misalignment, realignment, and dynamic alignment. A defining feature of this process is the emergence of functional shared governance, in which HR responsibilities are distributed out of operational necessity rather than consensual power sharing. As this diffusion disrupts previously established static alignment, organizations respond through maintenance and adaptation strategies, with digital technologies enabling coordination and responsiveness across dispersed participants. These efforts produce dynamic alignment—an ongoing process through which HRM is continually recalibrated to maintain coherence while accommodating variation and change. Our findings contribute to the literature by theorizing how HR ecosystems emerge, how functional shared governance develops, and how dynamic alignment is achieved over time.

Title: Cross‐Border Acquisitions and Firm Financial Performance: The Overlooked Role of Training Investments
Authors: Abubakr Saeed, Kalin D. Kolev, Tanveer Hussain, Shaun Pichler, Omer Farooq Malik
Affiliations: Department of Management Sciences COMSATS University Islamabad Islamabad Pakistan; Department of Management Marquette University Milwaukee Wisconsin USA; Essex Business School University of Essex, Southend Campus Southend‐on‐Sea UK; School of Accounting & Finance University of Vaasa Vaasa Finland; Department of Management California State University Fullerton California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Cross‐border acquisitions involving developed and emerging economies serve as an important source of organizational learning and performance renewal. Yet, how these cross‐border learning opportunities are internalized through human capital investment and how such investments influence post‐acquisition outcomes remain a theoretically rich but empirically underexplored question. Based on the resource‐based view of the firm and, in conjunction, the absorptive capacity literature, we propose that acquisitions between firms from different economic categories (developed vs. emerging economies) have a positive effect on the training investments, which, in turn, positively mediates the effect of cross‐border acquisitions on post‐acquisition firm performance. We further propose firm‐specific contingencies that bound the relationships between cross‐border acquisitions, training investments, and firm performance. Specifically, we argue that acquirers with prior experience are less reliant on training investments, and R&D of the acquired firm plays a complementary role to training investments in generating higher returns from the acquisition. We test these propositions using data on 1759 acquisition deals during the period 2004–2023. Our results provide support for our theoretical arguments. The findings advance the human resource management literature by highlighting the capability‐building role of training in leveraging human capital to enhance firm performance in cross‐border acquisitions. The study also has practical implications for multinational acquirers aiming to strengthen organizational capabilities and build post‐acquisition resilience through targeted training investments.

Title: Line Managers as Conduits of Corporate Standards: Evidence From Human Resource Practices in Fast Food Franchise Chains
Authors: Tashlin Lakhani, Can Ouyang, Hyesook Chung, Rosemary Batt
Affiliations: Nolan School of Hotel Administration, SC Johnson College of Business Cornell University Ithaca New York USA; Antai College of Economics and Management Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China; Naveen Jindal School of Management University of Texas at Dallas Richardson Texas USA; ILR School Cornell University Ithaca New York USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study integrates organizational theory and strategic human resource management research to examine how corporate standards for managing frontline employees shape human resource (HR) implementation at the unit level. While prior research has recognized the role of line managers, less is known about how HR investments directed at line managers influence their implementation of HR practices. We argue that more extensive HR‐related corporate standards, embedded in chain training and technology systems, lead franchisees to invest in line manager training and compensation. These investments enhance line managers' ability and motivation to implement HR practices for frontline employees in line with corporate standards. We further propose that corporate enforcement mechanisms, in the form of contract terminations, strengthen these relationships. Using a nationally stratified random sample of 908 franchisee‐owned units across 143 U.S. fast food chains, we combine survey data on unit‐level HR practices with independent measures of corporate standards from franchise disclosure documents. Results reveal that corporate standards do not simply flow through to frontline employee HR practices but are instead transmitted through line manager HR investments, with stronger effects under greater enforcement. These findings identify line managers as key conduits through which corporate standards are enacted in unit‐level practices and highlight the importance of aligning standards, managerial investments, and enforcement in decentralized organizations.

Title: Issue Information
Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
Authors: Ilias Filippou, David E. Rapach, Mark P. Taylor, Guofu Zhou
Affiliations: Florida State University; Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta; Washington University in St. Louis and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR); Washington University in St. Louis
Abstract: Abstract The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Housing Yields
Authors: Stefano Colonnello, Roberto Marfè, Qizhou Xiong
Affiliations: Ca’ Foscari University of Venice; University of Turin, and Collegio Carlo Alberto; University of Oxford
Abstract: Abstract We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
Authors: Miao Liu, Wanrong Xu, Rachel Xi Zhang
Affiliations: Boston College; Southern University of Science and Technology; National University of Singapore
Abstract: ABSTRACT Although extensive research examines the costs and benefits of adopting new disclosure regulations, little addresses the consequences of regulatory inaction. We investigate whether firms in nonadopting countries incur additional information losses, beyond the forgone benefits, when their foreign peers adopt International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Nonadopters bear an absolute liquidity cost as foreign peers adopt IFRS, consistent with negative externalities from IFRS and accompanying reforms. Exploiting heterogeneity across nonadopting countries, we observe more pronounced liquidity declines among firms with greater institutional ownership overlap with IFRS peers. This effect appears more pronounced when IFRS peers are domiciled in countries with concurrent enforcement reforms or greater comparability improvements. Further evidence shows shared intermediaries—investors and analysts—reduce information production for nonadopters as other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Overall, regulatory inaction degrades information environments: resources shift to the new regime, worsening liquidity for firms in the old regime. Title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
Authors: James J. Blann, Phillip T. Lamoreaux, Beverly J. Larson
Affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology; Arizona State University; University of Florida
Abstract: ABSTRACT Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Title: Rethinking Supplier Integration in Humanitarian Supply Chains: Feasibility and Constraints From an International Humanitarian Organization Perspective
Authors: Jihee Kim, Nezih Altay, Stephen Pettit, Anthony Beresford
Affiliations: School of Management Anglia Ruskin University Cambridge UK; Department of Management and Entrepreneurship DePaul University Chicago Illinois USA; Logistics and Operations Management Cardiff University Cardiff UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the widely recognized importance of integrative practices in commercial supply chain operations, their application in humanitarian supply chains (HSCs) remains underexplored. HSCs differ from commercial supply chains in their relational dynamics and integration processes, operating under extreme uncertainty, demand volatility, infrastructural disruption, and resource scarcity across a complex web of actors. Using an embedded single‐case design, this study assesses supplier integration (SI) in humanitarian operations in a leading international humanitarian organization (IHO), as well as the IHO's relationships with eight key suppliers. Drawing on the relational lenses of power, trust, and commitment, distinct integration patterns were identified across different supplier types. The findings highlight humanitarian‐specific contextual constraints and are used to inform a typology of SI feasibility encompassing feasible, selectively feasible, and low‐feasibility integration. This typology provides a foundation for guiding supplier relationship management in complex humanitarian contexts. This study offers a framework for understanding how relational and structural conditions shape integration in humanitarian settings and underscores the need for IHOs to adopt context‐appropriate supplier management approaches that reflect the unique dynamics of humanitarian operations.

Title: Optimal portfolio execution strategies under chance constraints on the capital adequacy ratio
Authors: Ruijing Yang, Zachary Feinstein, Somayeh Moazeni

Title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
Authors: Nathan Lassance, Alberto Martín-Utrera
Affiliations: LFIN/LIDAM, UCLouvain; Iowa State University
Abstract: Abstract We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. JEL Classification: G11, G12.

Title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
Authors: Ferhat Akbas, Minjie Huang, Felix Meschke
Abstract: ABSTRACT We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

Title: Beyond Leaderism: Recentering Leadership Science Towards Relationships in Action
Authors: Janaki Gooty, Chou‐Yu (Joey) Tsai, Tiffany Keller Hansbrough, Peter D. Harms, Sean N. Walsh
Affiliations: UNC Charlotte; Binghamton University; University of Alabama
Abstract: Abstract The historical origins of ‘Great Man’ theories of leadership, and their contemporary offshoots, have produced an accumulated literature in which the leader's behaviours are the focal unit of analysis. This Point article surfaces five theoretical assumptions underlying the leader behavioural paradigm: leaderism, individualistic attribution, behavioural universalism, democratization of leadership, and individual‐level ontology. We discuss theoretical counterfactuals to each assumption and call for a shift in the scene of scholarly conversation, from individual leaders to relationships that incorporate context and stakeholders. This shift in the focal unit of analysis from individual leader behaviour to relationships represents a foundational theoretical pivot built on multidisciplinary foundations, attention to levels of analysis, and a deep grounding in context. By questioning the assumptions underlying 85 years of leader behaviour research, we argue that the science (episteme), skill development (techné), and contextual judgement (phronesis) of leadership could be more tightly coupled by directing the spotlight towards relationships in context rather than individual leaders. In doing so, we move the focus from leaders in action to leadership as relationships in action .

Title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
Authors: Tiantian Yang, Jiayi Bao, Tianna Barnes, Ming D. Leung
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania; Texas A&M University; Dartmouth College; University of California, Irvine
Abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that manipulates attire within candidates, using two photos of each candidate: one in professional attire, one in casual. The results converge across field and experimental data. Professional attire improves hiring prospects overall but yields substantially smaller returns for Black candidates. Moderated mediation tests confirm that perceived professionalism drives this disparity, such that race discounts how attire translates into perceived professionalism and how perceived professionalism translates into hiring. The racial gap attenuates in customer-facing roles in which appearance is task relevant. These findings challenge supply-side accounts of hiring inequality and reveal how a demand-side interpretation of equivalent signals perpetuates racial disadvantages.

Title: Book Review: Heimer, C. A. Governing the global clinic: HIV and the legal transformation of medicine HeimerC. A. (2025). Governing the global clinic: HIV and the legal transformation of medicine. University of Chicago Press. 424 pp. ISBN 9780226838649
Authors: Silvia Dorado

Title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects
Authors: Cláudia Custódio, Miguel A. Ferreira, Emilia Garcia-Appendini, Adrian Lam
Affiliations: Imperial College Business School; Nova School of Business and Economics; University of St. Gallen; University of Pittsburgh
Abstract: Abstract We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?
Authors: Cloé Garnache
Affiliations: Oslo Metropolitan University Housing Lab and Center for Energy Policy and Economics (CEPE), ETH Zürich
Abstract: Abstract Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Order batching and sequencing in robotic mobile fulfillment systems
Authors: Yanling Zhuang, Yun Zhou, Xiangpei Hu

Title: The Cross-section of Subjective Expectations: Understanding Prices and Anomalies
Authors: Ricardo Delao, Xiao Han, Sean Myers
Affiliations: University of Southern California Marshall School of Business; Bayes Business School, City University London; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: Abstract We decompose cross-sectional differences in the level of price-earnings ratios using professional forecasts. High price-earnings ratios are accounted for by both low expected returns and overly high expected earnings growth. The magnitudes and timing of the comovements between prices, earnings growth, and returns are consistent with gradual learning rather than expectations being highly sensitive to recent realizations. Earnings growth surprises do not translate 1-1 into one-period returns but instead are gradually reflected in returns over time. A structural risk-premium model incorporating constant-gain learning about mean earnings growth replicates our findings and generates realistic dispersion and persistence in price-earnings ratios. (JEL G11, G12, G14, G40)

Title: Forward Return Expectations
Authors: Mihir Gandhi, Niels Joachim Gormsen, Eben Lazarus
Affiliations: Copenhagen Business School and the Danish Finance Institute; Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, and NBER; Haas School of Business, University of California, Berkeley, and NBER
Abstract: Abstract We measure investors’ short- and long-term stock-return expectations using both options and survey data. These expectations at different horizons reveal what investors think their own short-term expectations will be in the future, or forward return expectations. Across data sources, investors’ forward return expectations are countercyclical, especially when measured as forward risk premiums. This countercyclical variation is, however, excessive, as changes in forward return expectations are too large relative to subsequent realized short-term expectations. The excess variation in forward return expectations can help account for a meaningful share of the stock-price declines during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 crisis. (JEL G10, G12, G40)

Title: Local Returns and Beliefs about the Stock Market
Authors: Tobin Hanspal, Clemens Wagner
Affiliations: WU Vienna University of Economics and Business, Vienna Graduate School of Finance (VGSF), and CEPR , Department of Finance, Accounting and Statistics, Welthandelsplatz 1, A-1020 Vienna
Abstract: Abstract We show that investors extrapolate from recent stock returns of locally headquartered firms when forming beliefs about aggregate stock market outcomes. While it may be optimal to rely on local information, these effects are unrelated to how informative local returns are on predictions of aggregate outcomes. Evidence from a sample of retail investors suggests this belief extrapolation is driven by investors’ own holdings of local firms. Our findings suggest that beliefs about information contained in public signals vary systematically with geography, and are an important component of local biases in equity markets.

Title: From Slack to Staff: Managers' Allocation of Slack Resources to Hiring
Authors: Veroniek Collewaert, Ine Paeleman, Tom Vanacker, Frederik Anseel, Dries Bourgois
Affiliations: Vlerick Business School; KU Leuven; University of Antwerp; Ghent University; University of Exeter; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Abstract: Abstract Prior research views cash holdings, or high‐discretionary slack, as a buffer against shocks or a catalyst for strategic change. Drawing on stakeholder salience theory, we argue that cash can also reshape managers' interpretation and prioritization of employee hiring‐related claims, thereby increasing hiring, and that this effect is more pronounced when structural influences heighten the salience of those claims. Study 1, a large‐scale field study of Belgian firms, finds a positive but diminishing relationship between cash and hiring. This relationship strengthens under conditions of greater firm dependence on specific employee groups or following an exogenous legal reform, both of which are hypothesized to make the salience of specific employee groups more apparent. In Study 2, a vignette experiment offers causal support for the hypothesized mechanism, with employee salience cues strengthening how managers translate cash into hiring allocations. Combined, our findings contribute to research on slack resources and stakeholder salience by showing that managers use high‐discretionary cash not only for buffering or strategic change but also to respond to salient stakeholders.

Title: When Marketers Get the Top Job: How Marketing CEOs Influence Firms’ Product-Market Strategy
Authors: Shekhar Misra, Ben Lee, Christophe Haon
Abstract: Research on upper echelons in marketing has primarily focused on the CMO, yet the CEO ultimately bears responsibility for key strategic decisions, including those related to marketing. This study examines how CEOs with marketing experience (i.e., “marketing CEOs”) influence firm stock market performance by shaping product portfolio decisions. Drawing on upper echelon theory and in-depth interviews with business practitioners, we argue that marketing CEOs are more effective at selecting customer segments and implementing competitive strategies, leading to more differentiated portfolios and, consequently, higher shareholder returns. Our analysis of the main research question combines a qualitative study, a natural experiment involving CEO turnovers, large-scale panel data analysis, and an experiment with executives. Our results show that marketing CEOs positively impact shareholder returns through portfolio differentiation. Furthermore, the positive effect of marketing CEOs on portfolio differentiation is strengthened by their larger professional networks and a strong customer orientation within the firm but is diminished by CEO overconfidence and high firm financial leverage. Our findings highlight the distinctive value of CEOs with marketing experience and provide insight into the conditions that enhance or constrain their ability to generate firm value.

Title: Impatient for Impact: Intertemporal Preferences for Earlier Donation Impact Timing
Authors: Jieyi Chen, Oleg Urminsky
Abstract: Impatience when choosing for oneself has been widely documented, but are people also impatient when making prosocial decisions about benefits to unknown others? The authors study whether and why people care about a donation’s “impact timing,” the time when the benefits of the donation would reach the beneficiaries. In seven pre-registered experiments (N = 2,462) and an analysis of GoFundMe secondary data, they show that people consistently prefer to donate to a charitable program with an earlier impact timing, across different causes, donation amounts, timeframes, charity sizes and tradeoffs between impact timing and other considerations (impact magnitude, number of prior donors, remaining cost to complete, quality rating, and overhead). They find that decreased perceived benefits of delayed donation impact provides an incomplete explanation of the impact timing preference. Beyond less discounting of less delayed benefits, people also infer greater donation efficacy-based trust from earlier impact timing, increasing donation preferences. Together, the strong preference for earlier impact timing is an important and largely overlooked aspect of prosocial decision-making, with implications for building trust in prosocial organizations.

Title: Customer-to-Manufacturer: Should a Platform Cooperate with More Manufacturers?
Authors: Tonghuan Shi, Lin Tian, Zhen Xu
Abstract: The traditional top-down relationship between manufacturers and consumers has led to persistently high failure rates in new product development. In response, the emerging customer-to-manufacturer (C2M) model leverages online platforms as intermediaries to directly transmit consumer feedback to manufacturers, thereby improving decision-making in product innovation and increasing the likelihood of product success. This paper develops an analytical model to study the strategic adoption of the C2M model in an online marketplace with one platform and two competing manufacturers. We focus on the role of platform information and examine how its trade-offs shape market outcomes. Our analysis shows that the impact of platform information on manufacturers' expected profits is non-monotonic. Moreover, manufacturers' cooperation decisions in C2M depend on the information price and are moderated by the amount of information. For the platform, unexpectedly, involving more manufacturers in C2M cooperation is not always optimal, especially when information is sufficient. We further show that the C2M model benefits the platform and consumers and improves social welfare, while potentially reducing manufacturers' profits. Overall, our results provide managerial and regulatory implications for platform-based C2M practices.

Title: Optimizing Size-Based Bundle Promotions: Balancing Customer Appeal and Product Costs
Authors: Ruijiu Mao, Shuai Jia, Chung-Piaw Teo
Abstract: Size-based bundle promotions (“ p -for- s ”) are widely used in retail to increase basket size, but designing them is challenging when product costs and customer preferences are heterogeneous. Customers favor high-value products; however, including such items increases the bundle’s cost and may require a higher price to sustain profitability. Existing models typically assume identical costs or uniform preferences and therefore largely overlook the interaction between cost heterogeneity and customer preferences. To examine this interaction, we begin with the “ p -for-1” case under classical MNL and mixed MNL models and provide clear structural insights: (i) cost heterogeneity makes assortment selection nontrivial, motivating joint optimization of assortment and pricing; (ii) preference heterogeneity makes optimization under mixed MNL models computationally difficult; and (iii) extending MNL to “ p -for- s ” settings requires approximations and becomes intractable as s grows. Building on these insights, we develop an optimization framework for general “ p -for- s ” promotions with multiple concurrent offers. Our approach uses sample average approximation (SAA) to approximate the valuation distribution with a finite sample of customer valuations and reformulates the resulting problem as a discrete bilevel program that captures surplus-maximizing customer behavior. To improve computational tractability, we combine the SAA-based mixed-integer reformulation with low-rank completion, customer clustering, and consideration-set construction. Finally, a large-scale case study using data from a major e-commerce retailer shows that our framework yields substantially higher model-implied profit than the cost-threshold heuristic and outperforms other bundle-promotion benchmarks.

Title: Partial or full doses first? Vaccine allocation under limited supply
Authors: Ming Hu, Chaoyu Zhang, Yun Zhou
Affiliations: University of Toronto; City University of Hong Kong; McMaster University
Abstract: Vaccines have proven highly effective in curbing disease spread in the face of sudden large-scale infectious diseases. However, the challenge of limited vaccine supplies during initial mass production or in certain regions such as Africa poses a significant hurdle. To address this issue, one potential solution is the implementation of a fractional dosing approach, whereby individuals receive partial doses of the vaccine to achieve partial immunity. In this article, we investigate the optimal vaccine allocation policy in scenarios where the vaccine supply is scarce. By exploring the trade-offs between administering fractional and full dosages, we formulate the problem as an optimal control problem under disease transmission dynamics to minimize the total number of infections over a planning horizon. Specifically, we extend the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model by introducing two new compartments for partially and fully vaccinated individuals. Under mild conditions, we demonstrate that an attainable optimal vaccine allocation policy exhibits a bang-bang structure, suggesting that either the Partial Doses First (PDF) or the Full Doses First (FDF) allocation policy achieves optimality at any time. Furthermore, we compare the committed PDF and FDF policies for the entire planning horizon and identify a critical threshold on the fractional-dose vaccine efficacy, such that when the efficacy is above (resp., below) this threshold, choosing the committed PDF (resp., FDF) policy is better. Using COVID-19 vaccination data, we calculate thresholds for different countries in January 2021 to recommend to governments whether the priority should be given to allocating the first dose or to prioritizing the allocation of both first and second doses to the population. We also illustrate the versatility of our proposed scarce capacity allocation model in addressing a broad spectrum of resource allocation problems under diffusion dynamics, for which partial resource allocation can still yield some, though not full, benefits and the optimal allocation decision involves balancing the coverage and protection level.

Title: Democratizing Optimization with Generative AI
Authors: David Simchi-Levi, Tinglong Dai, Ishai Menache, Michelle Xiao Wu
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; Johns Hopkins University Carey Business School, Baltimore, Maryland, United States; Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, United States; Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, United States
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have captured the public imagination, whereas mathematical optimization remains little recognized beyond specialists. In this article, we argue that GenAI can bridge the persistent gap between optimization's technical capabilities and its limited real-world uptake. We present the 4I framework (Insight, Interpretability, Interactivity, Improvisation) as a set of design principles for combining GenAI with mathematical optimization. Insight establishes a trusted, up-to-date view of current operations; Interpretability explains model logic and trade-offs; Interactivity enables conversational what-if analysis; Improvisation supports model updates and event-driven re-optimization. By making optimization tools more intuitive, explainable, interactive, and adaptable, we envision a future in which frontline decision-makers can base their choices on rigorous, iterative analysis. We discuss how GenAI complements, rather than replaces, optimization: GenAI lowers barriers to modeling and interpretation; mathematical optimization reliably enforces the business goals, rules, and hard constraints encoded in the model. We also address emerging concerns, from hallucinations to the risk of over-reliance, and outline research directions for integrating GenAI and optimization responsibly. The GenAI boom gives the optimization community an opportunity to expand its impact by making optimization more accessible and trustworthy to a wider audience.

Title: Synergistic gains between high skilled labor and workplace automation: The case of corporate innovation
Authors: Shiu-Yik Au, Gunchang Kim, Andréanne Tremblay
Abstract: Though corporate automation has boosted labor productivity over the past few decades, oddly research productivity has fallen over the same period. This research explores this inconsistency by examining how automation can boost research productivity, but only within firms that reallocate their skilled labor effectively. This study shows that firms more prone to automation, as proxied by firm-level Substitutability of Labor with Automated Capital (SLAC), generate significantly more patents in the future. The underlying mechanism appears to be complementary reorganization of skilled employees. Using the intensity with which firms disclose their dependence on high-skilled labor as a key moderator, we find evidence consistent with the possibility that firms that reallocate their critical high-skilled employees to creative and highly cognitive tasks file more patents. The patents filed by firms with high automation potential are more cited, more explorative and more valuable than patents filed by firms with low automation potential.

Title: The coevolution of trust and behavioral uncertainty: Toward a theory of vulnerability acceptance in entrepreneurial ventures
Authors: Lars Huemer, Jan Ketil Arnulf
Affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School Oslo Norway
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary This conceptual study develops a process theory of vulnerability acceptance explaining how trust and behavioral uncertainty coevolve as entrepreneurial actors form, interpret, and realize opportunities. Trust is frequently invoked to explain creativity, exploration, and opportunity formation, yet remains theorized through predictability and evaluability, which entrepreneurial opportunities often lack ex ante. We distinguish three forms of vulnerability acceptance: uncertainty creating, releasing, and decreasing trust. Each transforms the uncertainty it engages, which in turn reinforces or unsettles that form, so no form is terminal. Their salience shifts across opportunity formation, interpretive recombination, and realization, and misalignment between a form and the conditions it confronts impairs entrepreneurial progress. Trust thereby becomes a means through which epistemic conditions are produced, not only a response to them. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurship exposes forms of vulnerability that cannot be explained by risk‐based models of trust alone. Entrepreneurs often face the practical question: “Trust them to do what?” The answer depends on the kind of agency they are willing to be vulnerable to, and it changes as an opportunity takes shape. That may mean backing people to take the work somewhere no one can yet specify, relying on others' expertise to make sense of what is emerging, or counting on them to deliver what was agreed. Trust is therefore not only a way of reducing uncertainty but a means of transforming it, and progress depends on recognizing when the prevailing form fits the conditions and when it does not.

Title: Rethinking sector-specific bankruptcy prediction: Leveraging cross-sector failure patterns through distance-based company representations
Authors: Philippe du Jardin, Koen W. De Bock

Title: Dynamic pricing and contract choice in a review-driven supply chain under market growth
Authors: Jian Song, Haijie Zhou, Mark Goh

Title: What do we know about job knowledge tests? A 30-year update of validity evidence.
Authors: Sara J. Bianco, Chad H. Van Iddekinge, Jake T. Harrison, Philip L. Roth, Huy Le

Title: Unintended Consequences of Holding Dollar Assets
Authors: Robert Czech, Shiyang Huang, Dong Lou, Tianyu Wang
Abstract: ABSTRACT We propose and examine a novel mechanism whereby holdings of dollar assets by foreign institutions can have a large, unexpected impact on foreign Treasury yields in crisis periods. Non‐U.S. institutions hold substantial dollar assets and hedge dollar exposures by selling dollars forward. In crisis periods, the dollar appreciates against other currencies. To meet margin calls on foreign exchange (FX) hedging positions, traditionally passive institutions liquidate domestic safe assets to raise cash. We show that during the recent COVID crisis, U.K. institutions with substantial dollar holdings and FX hedging positions sold large amounts of gilts, contributing significantly to the observed gilt yield spike.

Title: From Contested Endogenization to Regulatory Unravelling of Mandatory Human Rights Due Diligence: Extending the Endogeneity of Law Framework
Authors: Nora Lohmeyer, Elke Schüßler, Sarah Ashwin
Affiliations: Radboud University; Leuphana University Lüneburg; Johannes Kepler University; London School of Economics and Political Science
Abstract: Abstract Drawing on the endogeneity of law framework, this study examines how business, legal, public, and civil society actors constructed the meaning and practice of mandatory human rights due diligence in the context of the German garment industry and the German Supply Chain Act. Using interview, document, and observation data spanning the period 2019 to 2026, our findings reveal a two‐stage process: an initial phase of contested endogenization in which actors experienced with private regulation prevented convergence on a managerialized interpretation of the law, followed by regulatory unravelling in which changes in the political‐economic climate provided avenues for substantively weakening the law and preventing its implementation. We discuss how the dual processes of managerializing a law and legalizing of organizations is complicated by three boundary conditions: the complexity of the regulatory issue, the field's regulatory maturity, and the degree of regulatory uncertainty. Connecting the endogeneity of law framework with research on the public and private governance of global supply chains allows us to theorize refinements to this framework when applied to contested, complex governance fields, and to derive a set of theoretical and practical implications for public supply chain regulation.

Title: Crossing the Design–Use Divide: How Organizations Select Innovations to Adopt
Authors: Rebecca Karp
Affiliations: Harvard Business School
Abstract: Prior scholarship on technology and organizations has focused either on how innovations are designed or how they are used, often assuming that successful selection stems from successful design. But this assumption has limited our understanding of patterns of resistance and advocacy that can influence how and whether innovations reach organizations in the first place. To explore these patterns, this study asks, how does selection unfold within organizations, and what are the consequences of this process for the design and use of innovations? Drawing on a two-year ethnographic study, I examine how entrepreneurs piloted their AI-based innovations with potential adopting organizations. Rather than testing for learning or generalizability, organizations set up committees that engaged in process manipulation by narrowing the scope of pilots, controlling conversations, assigning pilot responsibility, and using goal claiming to align pilot outcomes with committees’ majority preferences. Committees with more adversarial members designed pilots that tested advanced aspects of entrepreneurs’ innovations, hoping for failure. Committees with a majority that championed the innovations tested basic aspects, ensuring success. While pilots run by champions mostly succeeded, these innovations faced more resistance later, during implementation, than did innovations piloted successfully by adversaries. This study shows that innovation is endogenous to selection, and reveals that champions can temper innovation, while adversaries can enable it.

Title: Navigating the Family Support Dilemma in Female Entrepreneurship: An Embeddedness Perspective
Authors: Mulu Hundera, Stefanie Habersang, Mona Mensmann
Affiliations: Department of Corporate Development, Faculty of Management, Economics, and Social Sciences, University of Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany; Institute of Management and Organization, Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Lower Saxony, Germany
Abstract: Drawing on family embeddedness and gender performativity, we examine how family support is enacted and governed through gendered norms, and how female entrepreneurs navigate these dynamics. Based on indepth interviews with female entrepreneurs and family members in Ethiopia, we introduce the family support dilemma: a process in which support enabling female entrepreneurship simultaneously generates explicit or internalized obligations that constrain sustained engagement and growth over time. Our findings show that family support is embedded in gendered social structures, functioning as a site of norm enforcement where support is granted or withdrawn based on women’s enactment of gender role expectations.

Title: Robust Meta-Graph Learning: Exploring Multilevel Feature Interrelationships To Enhance Multimodal Time Series Prediction
Authors: Zongxi Liu, Gang Chen, Shuaiyong Xiao, Huimin Zhao
Affiliations: School of Management, Missouri State University, Springfield, Missouri 65897; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, People’s Republic of China; School of Economics and Management, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, People’s Republic of China; and Laboratory of High Quality Urban Development and Strategic Decision, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, People’s Republic of China; Sheldon B. Lubar College of Business, University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee, Milwaukee, Wisconsin 53201
Abstract: The booming digital economy has provided unprecedented opportunities for enhancing prediction performance with multimodal time series data in a broad range of business analytics scenarios. In this study, we explore multilevel, asynchronous feature interrelationships in multimodal time series data and disentangle the intricate interrelationships with a design artifact named RMGL (for robust meta-graph learning). The design of RMGL is rooted in graph convolutional networks. The core of RMGL is a meta-graph composed of three hierarchically interconnected graphs, representing feature-, modality-, and timestep-wise interrelationships, respectively. The interconnections across the graphs allow feature representations to propagate simultaneously through a graph attention mechanism, thereby quantifying multilevel feature interrelationships with graph structures synchronously and efficiently. Furthermore, capitalizing on the low-pass nature of graph convolutional filters, RMGL introduces a weight regularization scheme to effectively learn the meta-graph for prediction. RMGL outperformed state-of-the-art alternatives in our empirical evaluation involving both regression (financial risk prediction) and classification (sentiment analysis, humor detection, and intent recognition) tasks. Ablation experiments, exploratory analyses, and economic value analysis indicate the utility of every design component in RMGL. The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

Title: Code and Data Repository for Optimization techniques for modeling with piecewise-linear functions
Authors: Peter Dobrovoczki, Tamás Kis
Abstract: This repository contains the source code, benchmark instances, and computational experiments accompanying the paper Optimization techniques for modeling with piecewise-linear functions by Péter Dobrovoczki and Tamás Kis.

Title: Swap and Save: How a Button Shapes Lasting Online Grocery Shopping Behavior
Authors: Rubén Gonzálvez, Xiaolin Li, Sarit Weisburd, Xinrong Zhu
Affiliations: Complutense University of Madrid, 28040 Madrid, Spain; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Kowloon, Hong Kong; The Hebrew University, Jerusalem 9190501, Israel; and Centre for Economic Policy Research, London EC1V ODX, United Kingdom; Imperial College London, London SW7 2AZ, United Kingdom
Abstract: Using data from the mineral water category on a price comparison platform that delivers real-time prompts of cheaper alternatives through “swap and save” buttons, this study examines whether and how these prompts influence persistent product choices in online grocery shopping.

Title: Online Reusable Resource Allocations with Multi-class Arrivals
Authors: Tianming Huo, Wang Chi Cheung
Affiliations: Singapore Management University, College of Integrative Studies, Singapore, Singapore; National University of Singapore, Department of Industrial Systems and Management, Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: In this paper, we study an adversarial online reusable resource allocation problem with multi-class arrivals, where each class is associated with its price per unit time and usage duration. Each unit of resource will be returned after the usage duration of the class of customer that the unit has been allocated to. We propose a simple online algorithm which achieve the best possible competitive ratio among all online policies when the usage durations of any two classes are divisible. Its competitive ratio is proved using a novel Auxiliary Algorithm that constructs a feasible solution to a linear program that upper bounds the optimum. We show that our policy can be extended to the case of general durations and the advance booking problem where each usage duration only starts after an arbitrary period. We show that our policy achieves at least half of the optimal when the durations are general, and for advance booking with equal usage durations.

Title: Online Decision Making with Local Differential Privacy
Authors: Yuxuan Han, Zhipeng Liang, Yang Wang, Jiheng Zhang
Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science of Technology, Mathematics, Clear Water Bay, Hong Kong; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Department of Industrial Engineering and Logistics Management, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Hong Kong University of Science of Technology, Clear Water Bay, Hong Kong
Abstract: Contextual bandit algorithms are useful in personalized online decision-making. However, many applications, such as personalized medicine and online advertising, require the utilization of user-specific information for effective learning while maintaining user privacy due to privacy concerns. This motivates the introduction of local differential privacy (LDP), a stringent notion of privacy, to contextual bandits. In this paper, we design LDP algorithms for stochastic generalized linear bandits to achieve the same regret bound as in non-privacy settings. Our main idea is to develop a stochastic gradient-based estimator and an update mechanism to ensure LDP. We then exploit the flexibility of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), whose theoretical guarantee for bandit problems is rarely explored, to address generalized linear bandits. We further conduct experiments using both simulated and real-world datasets to demonstrate the consistently superior performance of our algorithms under LDP constraints, with reasonably small LDP parameters (ε, δ) to ensure strong privacy protection.

Title: Joint Assortment Planning and Inventory Control under General Choice Models
Authors: Qiaochu Fu, Woonghee Tim Huh, Yanzhi Li, Tongwen Wu
Affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, Department of Decision Analytics and Operations, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; The University of British Columbia, Sauder School of Business, Vancouver, Canada; City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon, Hong Kong; University of Toronto, Rotman School of Management, Toronto, Canada
Abstract: We propose a constant-factor approximation framework for the joint assortment planning and inventory management problem, where customers substitute to less preferred in-stock products if more preferred products are out of stock. The customer arrivals follow an increasing-failure-rate (IFR) distribution, and customer purchasing behavior is governed by a discrete choice model with dynamic inventory availability. Our decision involves determining the initial inventory vector, subject to a capacity constraint. Our algorithm begins with a novel fluid relaxation that identifies at most two candidate assortments with the highest potential profitability. For each assortment, we construct a static-allocation-based lower bound on the expected total revenue for an inventory vector that stocks only the products in the assortment. The final inventory decision is the vector that maximizes the stronger of these two lower bounds. We establish a (κ/4−ε)-approximation guarantee for a broad class of substitutable choice models, in which adding products weakly decreases the choice probabilities of existing items, and for which the cardinality-constrained assortment optimization problem admits a κ-approximation algorithm. Our result provides the first constant-factor approximation ratios for this problem under several important choice models, including the Markov chain choice model and the mixture of MNL models. Moreover, our framework also achieves the state-of-the-art approximation ratio of 0.25 for the MNL choice model. Our guarantees can be further strengthened when the capacity constraint is relatively loose or when the demand distribution is deterministic or Poisson.

Title: Restaurant Density and Delivery Speed in Food Delivery Platforms
Authors: Wenchang Zhang, Zhanzhi Zheng, Ruomeng Cui
Affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington Kelley School of Business, Operations & Decision Technologies, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Kenan-Flagler Business School, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States; Emory University Goizueta Business School, Atlanta, Georgia, United States
Abstract: Food delivery platforms (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Meituan) are racing to expand by signing as many restaurants as possible. Such expansion directly translates into changes in restaurant density on the platform, making it crucial to understand how density affects restaurant outcomes. This paper examines the impact of restaurant density on incumbent restaurants and compares three key externalities induced by increased density: customer expansion and cannibalization, which are well documented in the literature, and delivery pooling (i.e., drivers being closer to restaurants and bundling multiple orders before delivery), which has received much less attention. Using a queueing-theoretical model, we develop testable hypotheses on how these externalities influence delivery speed, sales, revenues, and customer spending. Employing two-way fixed effects and instrumental variable estimation with data from a major Chinese food delivery platform, we find that higher restaurant density improves delivery speed and sales for partnered restaurants but reduces order size; heterogeneous-effects estimation further reveals that fast-food and high-volume restaurants benefit more from increased density, while made-to-order and thermally sensitive cuisines see weaker gains. Combining the empirical evidence with our theoretical predictions, our evidence is most consistent with delivery pooling playing a more pivotal role than customer expansion or cannibalization in shaping density effects. Furthermore, nonlinear least squares estimation of our theoretical model reveals that driver arrival speed at restaurants rises with density, shortening customers' wait times and inducing them to place more—but smaller—orders. However, this effect follows an inverted-U-shaped pattern, indicating diminishing delivery pooling benefits—and even adverse effects—at very high density. Finally, we extend our theoretical framework to develop a simulation model, estimated using data, which allows us to isolate the effect of each externality and identify restaurant-specific optimal densities through counterfactual simulations. Results show substantial heterogeneity in sales-maximizing densities across restaurants, with most operating below their optima. Our findings also suggest that platforms should prioritize expansion in low- to moderate-density regions to maximize delivery efficiency and restaurant sales, while carefully managing congestion and tailoring support based on restaurant type in denser markets.

Title: Corrigendum to “The moderating effects of management's Non-GAAP treatment of a CAM item and investors' position on investors' management credibility judgments” [Accounting, Organizations and Society 116 (2026) 101629]>
Authors: Wei Chen, Kirsten Fanning, Ken T. Trotman, Jun Wang
Abstract: The authors would like to add the following abstract to the published paper. ABSTRACT: The reporting of non-GAAP earnings allows management discretion to depict earnings that are often more favorable than audited GAAP earnings. Audit standards now require auditors to include critical audit matters (CAMs) in audit reports, which highlight areas of subjectivity and complexity, and may or may not be included in non-GAAP earnings numbers. In an experiment, we predict and find that when management's treatment of an impairment loss, which auditors identify as a CAM item, reveals a non-GAAP profit instead of a non-GAAP loss, long investors increase, but short investors decrease, their judgments of management credibility. We find evidence supporting theory suggesting that the joint effect on investors' management credibility judgments is explained by a different information search process for long compared to short investors. Our study documents that investors' responses to non-GAAP earnings and CAM disclosures jointly depend on management's disclosure choices and investors' position (long vs. short). Keywords: non-GAAP earnings; critical audit matters (CAMs); information search; management credibility; investor judgments

Title: A New Wave of Talent: Big 4 Response to New Partner Qualification Requirements in China
Authors: Pietro A. Bianchi, Lin Liao, Miguel Minutti-Meza, Yini Wang
Affiliations: Bocconi University; Nanjing Audit University; University of Miami; Loyola Marymount University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine how the Big 4 responded to evolving partner qualification requirements in China. By 2017, at least 80 percent of the Big 4 partners were required to hold CICPA qualifications, a requirement that did not apply to local firms. Using data from a 14-year window around the reform, we document that the Big 4 expanded their partnership and primarily complied through internal promotion of locally licensed auditors, often into junior signing roles and serving new clients. Our analyses of audit outcomes yield mixed and time-varying evidence: although we observe relative increases in restatements in selected periods, the triangulated evidence does not suggest a pervasive deterioration in audit quality. However, we find a decline in the Big 4’s market share and audit fee premium. Overall, our findings shed light on how regulatory interventions targeting auditor qualifications reshape audit firms and market competition. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M4; M40; M41; M42; M49.

Title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
Authors: Yong Li, Ming Zeng, Alexis Li
Affiliations: Department of Management & Entrepreneurship University of Nevada, Las Vegas Las Vegas Nevada USA; Hupan School of Entrepreneurship Hangzhou Zhejiang China; Brown University Providence Rhode Island USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.

Title: Materiality and investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility : A replication and extension of Flammer (2013)
Authors: Steven D. Kofford, Ben W. Lewis, Myles Melancon
Affiliations: Department of Management, College of Business Colorado State University Fort Collins Colorado USA; Department of Management, Marriott School of Business Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA; School of Business Mississippi Christian University Clinton Mississippi USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We replicate and extend Flammer's (2013) event study of investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility. Flammer found that investors react positively to eco‐friendly events and negatively to eco‐harmful events, with positive reactions diminishing and negative reactions intensifying from 1980 to 2009. We confirm her results in a narrow replication and find that these time trends persist in a quasi‐replication extending the sample through 2019, despite major shifts in the institutional environment for sustainability investing. We then extend Flammer by incorporating financial materiality and find that the investor reactions and time trends Flammer observed are primarily concentrated in material events. Notably, investors drew this distinction throughout the 40‐year window we study, predating the institutionalization of materiality‐based sustainability analysis. Managerial Summary We examine how investors respond to companies' environmental actions. Analyzing 40 years of data on US‐listed public firms, we find that investors reward companies for eco‐friendly actions and penalize them for harmful ones. Over time, these reactions have shifted: investors have grown less enthusiastic about eco‐friendly actions and more critical of harmful ones. Importantly, investors react primarily to environmental actions that are financially relevant, or “material,” to the business and were doing so well before formal standards existed. Within material actions, positive reactions to eco‐friendly initiatives have weakened while negative reactions to eco‐harmful ones have grown stronger. These findings suggest that managers should prioritize environmental initiatives closely tied to their company's financial performance.

Title: Cluster-based Benders decomposition for multistage appointment scheduling
Authors: Tianwei Zhou, Yulong Zhang, Jinhua Gan, Ben Niu, Qiaoxuan Wu, Xusheng Wu

Title: Stochastic Quadratic Dynamic Programming
Authors: Vincent Guigues, Adriana Washington
Abstract: We introduce an algorithm called SQDP (Stochastic Quadratic Dynamic Programming) to solve some multistage stochastic optimization problems having strongly convex recourse functions. The algorithm extends the classical Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming (SDDP) method replacing affine cuts by quadratic cuts. We provide conditions ensuring strong convexity of the recourse functions and prove the convergence of SQDP. In the special case of a single stage deterministic problem, we call QCSC (Quadratic Cuts for Strongly Convex optimization) the method and prove its complexity. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance and correctness of SQDP, with SQDP being much quicker than SDDP for large values of the constants of strong convexity both for a multistage problem and a two-stage assembly recourse model. We also present the results of numerical experiments on deterministic problems where QCSC is much quicker than several popular competing optimizers for solving 6 strongly convex optimization problems from the literature.

Title: Leveraging social legitimacy to navigate geopolitical fragmentation and populist polarization
Authors: Izzet Sidki Darendeli, TL Hill
Abstract: Abstract Although earning political legitimacy helps MNEs manage political risk, association with governments and political elites can become liabilities when regimes, alliances, and public sentiment shift. Reflecting on our study of MNE survival during abrupt regime change, we revisit social legitimacy as a complement to, and sometimes a substitute for, political legitimacy. We distinguish two foundations of social legitimacy: relational legitimacy, built through broad ties across societal constituencies, and material legitimacy, earned by providing products, services, and investments perceived as valuable by non-elite society. Although long recognized as a part of earning and maintaining a license to operate in any country, social legitimacy has become an increasingly important hedge against the ebbs and flows of political power driven by geopolitical fragmentation, populism, and polarization. Indeed, as geopolitics and populism make political affiliations more noticeable and more volatile, we suggest that efforts to earn social legitimacy play an increasingly important role in MNE nonmarket strategy. We identify theoretical and empirical questions concerning the sources, usefulness, and limits of earning social legitimacy; urge researchers and leaders to learn from and connect to non-elite sectors of society; and suggest ways that investment in social legitimacy can help MNEs navigate political turbulence worldwide.

Title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
Authors: Hunt Allcott, Jason Baron, Thomas Dee, Angela L Duckworth, Matthew Gentzkow, Brian Jacob
Affiliations: Stanford University and NBER; Duke University and NBER; University of Pennsylvania; University of Michigan and NBER
Abstract: Abstract Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

Title: Correction to: The Financial Channel of the Exchange Rate and Global Trade
The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
Authors: Mike Burkart, Samuel Lee, Paul Voss
Abstract: ABSTRACT We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

Title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
Authors: Yan Leng, Yunxin Sang, Ashish Agarwal
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure human preferences and opinions, but their outputs can diverge from human responses. We introduce human mimicry calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc, model-agnostic method that uses aggregate human benchmark data to learn how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, and model checkpoints. In applications to consumer transaction data and public opinion surveys, HuMCal improves agreement with human benchmarks over standard aggregation rules, and the calibrated weights often remain useful across time, geography, industry, and question clusters.

Title: Experimental Evidence on Structural State Dependence in Demand
Authors: Sebastian Gabel, Daniel Guhl, Günter J. Hitsch, Kyoung Hwan (Joe) Kook
Affiliations: Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands; School of Business and Economics, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Berlin, 10178, Germany; Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
Abstract: The paper provides nonparametric estimates of structural state dependence from a natural field experiment for 223 brands.

Title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
Authors: Seung Hyun Kim, On Amir, Kenneth C. Wilbur
Affiliations: Spears School of Business, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, Oklahoma 74078; Rady School of Management, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, California 92093
Abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments testing how three appeals based on tipping motivations—injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity—affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. Overall, the norms message increased tipping the most, and did so without reducing returning demand, showing that tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers.

Title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
Authors: Diego R. Känzig
Affiliations: Northwestern University, CEPR, and NBER (email: )
Abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

Title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
Authors: David M. Ritzwoller, Joseph P. Romano
Affiliations: Stanford University (email: )
Abstract: Statistical inference is often simplified by sample splitting. This simplification comes at the cost of the introduction of randomness not native to the data. We propose a simple procedure for sequentially aggregating statistics constructed with multiple splits of the same sample. The user specifies a bound and a nominal error rate. If the procedure is implemented twice on the same data, the nominal error rate approximates the chance that the results differ by more than the bound. We illustrate the application of the procedure to several widely applied econometric methods. (JEL C20, C30, C52)

Title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
Authors: Andrew J. Fieldhouse, Karel Mertens
Affiliations: Mays Business School, Texas A&M University (email: ); Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, CEPR (email: )
Abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

Title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
Authors: Sam Asher, Kritarth Jha, Paul Novosad, Anjali Adukia, Brandon Tan
Affiliations: Imperial College London (email: ); Development Data Lab (email: ); Dartmouth College (email: )
Abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India.
