Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

Title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
Authors: Nathan Zorzi, Martin Beraja
Affiliations: Dartmouth (email: ); UC Berkeley and NBER (email: )
Abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

Title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
Authors: Lorenzo Lagos
Affiliations: Brown University, NBER, and IZA (email: )
Abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

Title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
Authors: Clare Balboni, Johannes Boehm, Mazhar Waseem
Affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science (email: ); University of Geneva (email: )
Abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

Title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
Authors: Eric Chyn, Kareem Haggag, Bryan A. Stuart
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Texas-Austin, and NBER (email: ); Anderson School of Management, University of California-Los Angeles, and NBER (email: ); Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and IZA (email: )
Abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

Title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
Authors: Oliver Pfäuti
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin (email: )
Abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

Title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
Authors: Xiwen Bai, Jesús Fernández-Villaverde, Yiliang Li, Francesco Zanetti
Affiliations: Tsinghua University (email: ); University of Pennsylvania (email: ); Peking University HSBC Business School and UIBE (email: ); University of Oxford (email: )
Abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

Title: Front Matter
Launching for the “Greater Good”: Spillover Effect of ESG Funds
Authors: Fangyuan Ma, Linlin Ma, Yuan Wang, Bo Xu
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Market Return Decomposition and Equity Risk Premium Predictability
Authors: Yanyan Lin, Chongfeng Wu, Guofu Zhou, Shunwei Zhu
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Strategy as a theory of change
Authors: Sergio G. Lazzarini, Todd R. Zenger, Teppo Felin
Affiliations: Insper São Paulo Brazil; David Eccles School of Business University of Utah Salt Lake City Utah USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.

Title: Cost allocation in collaborative maintenance clustering with common set-up costs: A cooperative game theory approach
Authors: Andries van Beek, Marco Slikker, Loe Schlicher
Abstract: In this paper, we analyze a setting in which multiple different players (e.g., firms) have to carry out preventive maintenance jobs. Each player is responsible for one job, with a job-specific minimal frequency and with maintenance costs, consisting of a job-specific variable component and a fixed component, which is the same for all jobs and independent of the set of jobs executed. Players can collaborate by clustering jobs, where maintenance in such a cluster is performed at the frequency of the job with highest minimal frequency. Players can benefit from such clusters if savings in fixed costs outweigh the increase in maintenance costs of those jobs that are forced to execute maintenance at a higher frequency. We investigate how to allocate the cost savings resulting from an optimal clustering of collaborating players. By analyzing axiomatic properties of such allocation methods, we conclude that certain intuitive methods may be met with resistance in practice. To address this, we focus on cost allocation methods such that no subgroup of players has a financial incentive to ‘split off’ and not cooperate with other players. Using insights from cooperative game theory, we identify and characterize such allocation methods.

Title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
Authors: Matthew J Baker, Jonathan Conning
Affiliations: Hunter College and the Graduate Center, CUNY
Abstract: Abstract Economists and historians have long debated how open-access areas, frontier regions, and customary landholding regimes transformed into private property. This paper analyses decentralized enclosure processes using the theory of aggregative games, examining how population density, enclosure costs, potential productivity gains, and local governance capacity, including the power to demand compensation, jointly determine the mix of property regimes. Depending on these fundamentals, private decisions to enclose may be strategic complements or substitutes. Strategic complements generate tipping points and socially destructive property races, whereas strategic substitutes produce smoother transitions and may leave enclosure below the social optimum. While policies to strengthen customary governance or compensate displaced stakeholders can realign incentives, addressing one distortion while neglecting others can worsen welfare.

Title: Who Do You Vote For? Same-Race Voting Preferences in Director Elections
Authors: Johan Sulaeman, Qiaozhi Ye
Affiliations: National University of Singapore, Sustainable and Green Finance Institute and NUS Business School , 15 Kent Ridge Dr, 119245; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Dishui Lake Advanced Finance Institute
Abstract: Abstract This paper highlights racial and ethnic preferences in corporate director elections. Using a comprehensive dataset of mutual fund voting records, we discover that mutual fund managers are more likely to vote for director nominees who share their racial or ethnic identity. Funds managed by White-dominated teams exhibit the strongest same-race preferences, particularly those in fund families with scarce minority representation. Same-race voting preferences have detrimental implications for the career outcomes of minority director candidates, and are associated with worse fund performance primarily when fund managers operate under weaker accountability. We investigate various potential mechanisms—including statistical discrimination, value maximization, conflicts of interest, social networks, and taste-based biases—and find that the evidence aligns most closely with a taste-based explanation for same-race preferential voting. JEL Classification: G23, G34, G41, J71

Title: Mandatory Disclosure and Peer Firms' Learning From Stock Prices
Authors: Jaewoo Kim, Hunter Pearson, Brady Twedt
Affiliations: Lundquist College of Business University of Oregon Eugene Oregon USA; C. T. Bauer College of Business University of Houston Houston Texas USA; Mays Business School Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Theory posits that mandatory disclosure influences peer firms' learning from stock prices in two non‐mutually exclusive ways: intra‐industry information transfers and the reallocation of information acquisition efforts. Using mandatory segment disclosure as our setting, we document a decrease in investment‐ q sensitivity for peers of disclosing firms. This effect is stronger among peers with greater economic links to disclosing firms and peers with the greatest incentives to glean information from prices. Our findings provide novel evidence that mandatory disclosure can have significant negative externalities on peer firms' investment efficiency via a managerial learning from the stock price channel. These insights inform regulators assessing the economic consequences of mandatory disclosure, while also assisting managers who rely on information from stock prices to guide investment decisions.

Title: Whose Job Is It, Anyway? The Effect of the Review Process on Employee Performance
Authors: Adam Bross, Ryan D. Sommerfeldt
Affiliations: Auburn University Auburn Alabama USA; Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Companies have widely adopted a system of work‐product reviews whereby the work of one individual is subsequently reviewed by another to ensure its quality. We examine how managers can effectively implement a review of employee work to improve performance. Organizations review employees' work to identify mistakes and improve work quality. However, reviews may also reduce employees' effort and initiative if they expect reviewers to identify and correct their errors for them. We use an experiment to examine how employee performance depends on who conducts the review and how feedback is provided. Specifically, participants' work was reviewed by either a superior or a peer, and the reviewer provided either general, high‐level guidance (autonomy‐oriented) or specific corrective information about errors (dependency‐oriented). Employees performed best when superiors provided high‐level guidance or when peers provided specific corrective feedback, with these benefits emerging over time. Guidance from a superior increased employees' sense of responsibility, whereas corrective help from a peer strengthened feelings of teamwork and cohesion. Review approaches that did not fit these combinations offered no clear performance benefit relative to having no review. The findings show that review effectiveness depends on matching the feedback approach to the reviewer's organizational rank. These results have important implications for managers, accountants responsible for internal controls, and audit professionals involved in designing and implementing the review process.

Title: Who Benefits from Citizenship? Varying Effects of Naturalization Decisions in the Early-Twentieth-Century United States
Authors: Peter Catron, Nathan I. Hoffmann, Mingze Li
Affiliations: University of Washington, USA; Emory University, USA
Abstract: Citizenship acquisition is widely viewed as a mechanism for improving economic outcomes, yet little is known about whether its benefits are distributed evenly. This article examines the varied returns to naturalization in the early-twentieth-century United States, assessing whether naturalization uniformly benefits all immigrants or is especially impactful for those already positioned to profit. Using naturalization records from New York City’s Southern District in the early 1900s, we construct a novel historical dataset for 1,947 immigrants who declared their intent to naturalize. By linking these records to U.S. census data from 1920, 1930, and 1940, we are able to observe immigrants’ characteristics at the point when they make naturalization decisions and to track their outcomes over time. Our findings reveal that immigrants who completed the naturalization process attained significantly higher occupational status than those who initiated but did not complete naturalization. In addition, citizenship is most transformative for those facing the greatest disadvantages. Additional analyses corroborate these findings in linked full-count census data for the entire United States. Citizenship confers occupational advantages not only through formal rights but as a resource that enables claims-making in the labor market, with greater returns to less advantaged immigrants.

Title: A Moral Foundations Perspective on CEO Political Ideology
Authors: Moritz Appels, Marc Kowalzick, Michael Woywode
Affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Mannheim
Abstract: As a reflection of their fundamental value systems, CEOs’ political ideology has come to be regarded as a major predictor of their strategic decision-making. Among the most persistent characterizations in this literature, liberal-leaning CEOs are considered to exhibit a distinct preference for evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices due to their ideological endorsement of equality—an association derived from the conceptualization of political ideologies along the motivated cognition perspective and routinely used to differentiate them from their more conservative peers. Yet, moral psychologists increasingly call for a broader understanding of the moral values differentiating liberals and conservatives. We therefore introduce moral foundations theory to the study of CEO political ideology, according to which liberal- and conservative-leaning CEOs differ in their focus on individual- versus group-centric concerns but, contrary to the existing consensus, should both endorse evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices. We find evidence for corresponding U-shaped rather than linear effects of CEOs’ political ideology in a sample of over 1,600 S&P 1500 CEOs. As such, we offer a novel theoretical perspective on CEOs’ political ideology and its organizational ramifications.

Title: Competitive Dormancy in Interfirm Rivalry: Consequences for Rival Actions
Authors: Tianxu Chen, Jianhong Chen, Lingling Pan, Wenpin Tsai, Ming-Jer Chen
Affiliations: West Virginia University; University of New Hampshire; University of Pittsburgh; Pennsylvania State University; University of Virginia
Abstract: In this study, we examine the implications of competitive dormancy, defined as a situation in which a focal firm’s observed time span of inaction following its prior action has exceeded the firm’s typical duration between successive actions. We argue that competitive dormancy may be perceived as inconsistent with a rival’s expectations and may be associated with an interpretive process concerning the rival’s subsequent actions. Integrating expectancy violation theory (EVT) and competitive dynamics research, we propose that the relationship between a focal firm’s competitive dormancy and the likelihood of rivals’ subsequent actions varies with their relative market standing and strategic resource commitment. Using a sample of 78,055 daily observations from 28 firms across 14 industries from 2000 to 2017, we find support for our hypotheses.

Title: Context Matters, Doesn’t It? The Role of Context in Everyday Emotion Regulation Strategy Use
Authors: Anh Tran, Rachel Freeman-Robinson, Peter Koval, Katharine H. Greenaway, Elise K. Kalokerinos
Affiliations: Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences, The University of Melbourne; School of Psychology, University of Queensland
Abstract: A common maxim holds that “context is everything.” This perspective transformed the field of emotion regulation, which evolved from understanding which regulation strategies people use, to understanding how strategy use varies by context (i.e., strategy–situation fit). Theoretical accounts suggest contextual features are crucial in guiding strategy use. However, empirical evidence is isolated in piecemeal studies with inconclusive results. To comprehensively explore context-dependent emotion regulation, we need data on emotion regulation across many contexts, at scale. Combining up to 11 experience-sampling data sets collected from Belgian and Australian samples in an integrative analysis ( N ID = 500–1,696, N observations = 27,023–101,114, M age = 25.38 years, 71% women), we examined how regulation-strategy use varies as a function of three theory-derived contextual features— intensity , controllability , and social features (i.e., the presence and closeness of others). We found limited support that context matters for daily emotion-regulation strategy use. Our study provides a well-powered foundational step to test a theory central to emotion-regulation research and highlights the complexity of capturing strategy–situation fit in daily life.

Title: Coevolution of trader similarity networks and follower dynamics in social trading
Authors: Ye Liu, Mingwen Yang, Yong Tan
Affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology; University of Washington
Abstract: Social trading platforms have been gaining popularity against traditional brokerages over the past few years. Compared with traders on traditional financial markets, those on social trading platforms often exhibit more similar trading strategies. In this article, we examine the impact of strategy similarity patterns on traders’ popularity. We identify two competing effects of similarity: a substitution effect, whereby traders with similar strategies become interchangeable and compete for followers; and a social proof effect, whereby similarity signals credibility in an environment characterized by high uncertainty and limited verifiable credentials, thereby attracting followers. To empirically examine these effects, we construct a dynamic similarity network and develop a coevolution model that captures the joint evolution of network structure and follower dynamics. Using data from a leading social trading platform, we find that, on average, greater similarity leads to a decline in a trader’s followers over time, indicating that the substitution effect dominates. Importantly, this relationship is heterogeneous. For more established traders, the substitution effect is stronger, such that greater similarity reduces their popularity. In contrast, for less established traders, the social proof effect dominates, and similarity increases their popularity. Using counterfactual simulations, we show that reducing the density of the similarity network and promoting a more balanced distribution of followers can mitigate the negative substitution effect, thereby increasing the total number of followers on the platform and, consequently, the platform revenue. Our study identifies several managerial and operational implications for the social trading platforms.

Title: The Role of Ease-of-Return Experience on Contingent Free Shipping Policies
Authors: Ashish Kabra, Wedad J. Elmaghraby, Nitish Jain
Abstract: Contingent free shipping (CFS) policies, whereby consumers get free shipping if their orders exceed a certain amount, are commonplace. Such a policy aims to nudge customers to place larger orders by adding additional items and/or buying more expensive items ( order-swelling ). A less desirable possible outcome is that customers pad their orders to avoid paying the shipping fee but later return the opportunistic or impulse-purchase items ( return-swelling ). A retailer designing the CFS policy’s terms—threshold and shipping fee—should balance these competing effects. We study how the retailer's return environment, specifically the ease-of-return experience (EOR) for customers, moderates order-swelling or return-swelling behavior induced by a CFS policy. We collaborate with an online fashion retailer that switched across multiple CFS policies over time and offered home pickup of returns in some markets but not in others. Our difference-in-differences empirical strategy builds on these policy switches and the location-based variation in the EOR. We find that the EOR can considerably impact the relative profit performance of the CFS policies and that it moderates both the order-swelling and the return-swelling responses. Our counterfactual analysis reveals that return-swelling is the key driver of the observed difference in the relative profit performance of CFS policies across the two EOR market types. Our study documents a novel determinant of the financial performance of a CFS policy: the ease-of-return experience. Our analysis indicates that our collaborating retailer would be better off selecting a (relatively) lenient CFS policy in more convenient EOR markets and a (relatively) stringent CFS policy in less convenient EOR markets.

Title: Revitalizing the grocery store experience: An empirical study on the spillover effects of experiential services
Authors: Bengü Nur Özdemir, Stanley Frederick W T Lim
Affiliations: College of Business and Economics, University of Wisconsin-Whitewater, Whitewater, WI, USA; Michigan State University
Abstract: Grocery retailers increasingly use experiential services to attract customers to their stores. However, it remains unclear whether these services generate positive spillover effects to core grocery sales or cannibalize existing demand. We provide the first empirical evidence by studying a grocery retailer that introduced a taphouse as its first experiential service and examining the underlying mechanisms. We combine store transaction records with SafeGraph’s point-of-interest data and survey data on product attributes. Using a quasi-experimental design, we specify a synthetic difference-in-differences estimator with staggered treatment timings. Our results show significant positive spillover effects. On average, stores that feature a taphouse experienced a 5.97% increase in daily sales volume, a 6.82% rise in sales revenue, a 5.76% increase in transactions, and a 6.18% expansion in product variety compared to stores without a taphouse. Our mechanism analyses suggest that these results are associated with activity through both extensive (newly observed customers) and intensive (greater purchasing activity among existing customers) margins. We find that an average order contains fewer but relatively higher-priced items, leaving average order value statistically unchanged. Newly acquired customers make relatively smaller purchases than existing customers, whose order size does not change significantly following the taphouse introduction. We also find that products complementary to the taphouse and those with a greater propensity for impulse purchasing account for larger shares of grocery sales following taphouse introduction. Finally, nearby competing supermarkets experience reductions in both total visits and unique visitors, suggesting that local competitive substitution may contribute to the observed customer expansion. To assess generalizability, we replicate the analysis with another grocery chain in a different region that introduced a full restaurant and obtain qualitatively similar results. Overall, the findings indicate that adding a taphouse can effectively increase grocery sales volume and revenue. Although high setup costs may deter adoption, our break-even analysis projects recovery in approximately 34 to 39 weeks from grocery-side gross-margin contributions alone, or 27 to 44 weeks when alternative assumptions about taphouse profitability, including operating losses, are incorporated.

Title: Bridging the Gap: The Impact of Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments Service
Authors: Liuyi He, Jifeng Luo, Panpan Wang, Zhiyan Wu, Han Zhang
Abstract: Online healthcare communities (OHCs) play an important role in transforming healthcare delivery. While existing literature has primarily focused on the impact of teleconsultation services on offline demand, the influence of integrating offline access into OHCs on teleconsultation remains largely unexplored. This study addresses the gap by investigating how the integration of offline access into OHCs affects the utilization of teleconsultation services. We leverage a natural experiment in an OHC involving the implementation of the Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments (OBHA) feature, which allows patients to secure in-person visit appointments in the OHC. Using difference-in-differences (DID) models, we find a significant increase in new demand for adopter physicians’ teleconsultation services following the integration of OBHA, without deterioration in service quality. Notably, the increased demand largely comes from patients in remote and underserved areas seeking consultations with high-quality physicians, exhibiting a cascading effect. Furthermore, we find that OBHA adoption extends the geographic reach of physicians’ teleconsultation services and promotes a more equitable distribution of teleconsultation utilization across regions. Our findings indicate that integrating offline access into OHCs not only boosts the utilization of teleconsultation services but also helps reduce health disparities by facilitating access to high-quality resources. This study contributes to the literature on healthcare operations management, healthcare information technology, and health disparities. The insights gleaned from the study also offer practical suggestions to policymakers, OHC operators, physicians, and patients.

Title: Simplifying the Madness of Multiple Entries in March Madness
Authors: Jeff Decary, David Bergman, Carlos Cardonha, Jason Imbrogno, Andrea Lodi
Abstract: Multi-entry betting pools for single-elimination tournaments create a portfolio-design problem: a participant may submit several brackets whose scores are highly dependent, while payouts are typically concentrated on the best-performing entry. Motivated by March Madness pools, we study the problem of selecting a portfolio of brackets that maximizes the expected maximum score (EMS) across entries. This objective captures the top-heavy nature of such contests without requiring a model of opponents' bracket choices, which is difficult to estimate reliably in a tournament played only once per year. We first establish computational and structural properties of the EMS objective. Exact EMS evaluation is #P-hard in general, although it is polynomial-time computable for any fixed number of entries with an exponent that grows with the portfolio size. For two entries, EMS decomposes into single-entry expected-score terms and an expected absolute score-gap term, making explicit the trade-off between selecting individually strong brackets and diversifying across outcomes. These insights motivate two sample average approximation algorithms: an entry-by-entry method based on marginal EMS contributions and a round-by-round method that exploits the geometrically increasing scoring weights in March Madness by emphasizing late-round diversification. Computational experiments using historical tournament data show that the round-by-round method scales reliably and outperforms direct SAA and an entropy-based benchmark for larger portfolios. In a real high-stakes DraftKings pool from the 2023 tournament, our 100-entry portfolio would have achieved a 2.54% probability of attaining a maximum-scoring entry, with higher expected profit than the portfolios submitted by several elite professional bettors.

Title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
Authors: Liben Chen, Meizi Zhou, Yicheng Song, Gediminas Adomavicius
Affiliations: University of Minnesota, Information and Decision Sciences, Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States; Boston University, Information Systems, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; university of minnesota, carlson school of management, minneapolis, Minnesota, United States
Abstract: Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. Furthermore, building upon the comprehensive findings from our computational experiments, we propose flexible, parameterizable data privacy practice designs based on the notion of revelation protection. The proposed approach is designed to provide an effective balance between personalization performance and privacy considerations, as demonstrated using extensive simulation experiments. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of privacy-aware recommender systems in the context of contemporary data protection regulations. The findings can also be informative to policymakers for understanding the practical implications of various data privacy practices and for designing future policies.

Title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
Authors: Omid Rafieian
Affiliations: Cornell Tech, New York, New York 10044; and Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14850
Abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

Title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
Authors: Jason Chan, Jiahui Mo, Tingting Nian, Nila Zhang
Affiliations: Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota 55455; Poole College of Management, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina 27695; The Paul Merage School of Business, University of California, Irvine, California 92697; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China
Abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07082 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management.

Title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
Authors: Hui Ou-Yang, Weili Wu, Xingtan Zhang
Affiliations: Department of Finance, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, Beijing 100010, China; School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics, Beijing 100081, China
Abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72472171 and 72372011]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08463 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance.

Title: Inflexibility and Leverage
Authors: Lifeng Gu, Dirk Hackbarth, Yuxin Luo
Affiliations: Sy Syms School of Business, Yeshiva University, New York 10033; Questrom School of Business, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215; and European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI), 1000 Brussels, Belgium; School of Finance, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100872, China
Abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08672 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance.

Title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
Authors: Thomas Buser, Sahar Sangi
Affiliations: University of Amsterdam and Tinbergen Institute, 1018WB Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01218 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis.

Title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
Authors: Jino Lu
Affiliations: Washington University in St Louis, Olin Business School, St. Louis, Missouri, United States
Abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research.

Title: Actualizing entrepreneurial futures: Imaginaries, Visions, and the Olivetti Corporation
Authors: Vittoria Magrelli, Roy Suddaby, Trevor Israelsen, Emanuela Rondi, Alfredo De Massis
Abstract: Entrepreneurship is often understood as the pursuit of opportunities or the creation of new ventures, yet these perspectives offer limited insight into how entrepreneurs sustain coherence between imagined futures and feasible action over extended periods of time. Entrepreneurs commit resources and coordinate others around desired futures they believe can be brought into being. Emerging work reconceptualizes entrepreneurship as a process of actualization, yet we still know little about how actualization unfolds over time, particularly when entrepreneurs pursue morally and culturally meaningful futures that must be reconciled with shifting conditions of feasibility. Drawing on a historical process analysis of Adriano Olivetti and the Olivetti Corporation, we theorize entrepreneurial actualization as a recursive relationship between entrepreneurial imaginaries (historically situated, value-laden conceptions of desirable futures) and entrepreneurial visions (pathways that are feasible in the present and translate those aspirations into commitments and actualization practices). While imaginaries articulate what ought to be realized, visions specify what can be realized under existing constraints. Our process model explains actualization coherence: the extent to which evolving action remains connected to the desired future that gives it purpose and direction. We show that such coherence erodes when the capacity to recalibrate visions is lost, as occurred after Olivetti's death. We contribute to research on entrepreneurship as actualization, on entrepreneurial process, and on the extended temporal horizons across which entrepreneurial futures unfold, persist, and sometimes outlive the ventures that pursued them.

Title: Analysts’ Perspectives on Climate Change: An Examination of Analyst Reports
Authors: Jesse Chan
Affiliations: Boston University
Abstract: ABSTRACT I explore the nature of analysts’ climate-related discussion in their reports. Focusing on industries most exposed to climate change, I find very few reports (less than 2 percent) and a minority of analysts (less than 11 percent) discuss climate-related topics. Analysts concentrate climate-related discussion among utilities, mostly discussing renewable energy and regulatory issues. These discussions exhibit no significant association with short-term earnings forecasts and a weak association with more pessimistic long-term growth forecast revisions. Climate-related discussion is also associated with more optimistic target prices when analysts do not issue long-term growth forecasts, suggesting the development of a long-term perspective correlates with views on climate-related issues. Discussions of solar-, emissions-, and automotive-related topics are associated with this greater target price optimism. These findings highlight how analysts’ climate-related discussion relates to long-term expectations and concentrates among highly exposed firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. A detailed listing of how each large language model (LLM) classified each climate-related report, a document describing the details of this listing, a firm-year summary of climate-related discussion and subtopical classifications, and a description document of this firm-year summary are available upon request. JEL Classifications: Q56; G24; M41.

Title: Sales-Based CEO Incentives and Their Effect Across the Supply Chain
Authors: Jen Choi
Affiliations: Korea University Business School
Abstract: ABSTRACT I examine how the use of sales performance measures in CEO incentive contracts affects the operations of a firm and its suppliers. A growing number of firms are evaluating and compensating their CEOs based on sales performance. However, because sales performance measures are narrow measures that do not incentivize cost control, they can influence operational decisions that affect not only the firm but also its suppliers. I show that the use of sales performance measures in CEO bonus contracts is associated with inventory fluctuations that increase the bullwhip effect, a phenomenon in which a firm exhibits greater volatility in production than in demand, thereby increasing the order volatility faced by its suppliers. Instrumental variable tests using the firm’s network connections through compensation consultants mitigate concerns that the results are driven by omitted factors. Collectively, my findings illuminate spillover effects of CEO incentive contracts on economically linked firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M10; M12; M40; M41; M52.

Title: Audit Quality and Audit Partner Ownership of Non-Audit Businesses: Evidence from China
Authors: Clive S. Lennox, Zanyue Qi, Xi Wu
Affiliations: University of Southern California; Central University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether audit partners’ ownership stakes in affiliated non-audit businesses are related to audit quality. We argue that non-audit ownership is a relatively sharp measure of auditor-client economic bonding, which can impair auditor independence. Using a unique setting in China where we observe partners’ equity stakes in both audit and non-audit businesses, we find that audit adjustments are significantly smaller when engagement partners hold larger ownership stakes in non-audit businesses. Audit adjustments are further reduced when the entire audit partnership holds greater ownership in affiliated non-audit businesses, suggesting that non-audit ownership matters at the audit firm level as well. Additional analyses suggest that these results are driven by impaired independence, rather than partner distraction or endogenous partner-client matching. Our study informs ongoing policy debates on the structuring of audit and non-audit businesses as well as the investments of non-audit entities in accounting practices. Data Availability: The authors have nondisclosure and confidentiality agreements for their use of proprietary data, which were provided to the authors for independent academic research only. Nonproprietary data are available from sources identified in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; M48; M52.

Title: When People Management Backfires: A Qualitative Study of Unintended Consequences of Line Managers' Support for Employees
Authors: Roos Mulder, Eva Knies, Jasmijn van Harten, Maria Peeters
Affiliations: Utrecht University School of Governance Utrecht University Utrecht the Netherlands; Faculty of Social and Behavioral Sciences Utrecht University Utrecht the Netherlands
Abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how and why well‐intended people management can backfire, resulting in unintended consequences such as reduced well‐being and performance. Although people management—the combination of line managers' implementation of HR practices and their leadership behavior in supporting employees—is generally assumed to result in positive outcomes, emerging evidence suggests that benevolent line manager behavior may have adverse effects. However, insight into the underlying mechanisms through which such backfire occurs remains limited. To address this gap, we utilized a multi‐actor qualitative approach by conducting 55 interviews among line managers and employees in the Dutch hospital sector using the Critical Incident Technique. We identify three mechanisms through which backfire unfolds: (1) constrained communication in the context of policies and regulations, (2) overcompensation in the context of performance pressure, and (3) accountability in the context of conflicting fairness perceptions. Across these mechanisms, we show that backfire emerges not from poor managerial intent but from the interaction between line managers' intentions and behaviors, employees' interpretations, and structural constraints. By conceptualizing backfire as a structurally constrained and interactional process, this study advances people management research beyond dominant explanations focused on implementation quality or outcome trade‐offs, and highlights the importance of context in shaping employee responses.

Title: Close-enough general routing problem for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles in monitoring missions
Authors: Huan Liu, Michel Gendreau, Binjie Xu, Guohua Wu, Yi Gu
Abstract: We introduce a close-enough multi-UAV general routing problem (CEMUAVGRP) where a fleet of homogeneous UAVs conduct monitoring tasks involving both nodes, each of which has its disk neighborhood, and edges, aiming to minimize the total distance. To solve the problem, we develop a two-phase iterative matheuristic, partitioning the CEMUAVGRP into a general routing phase where a satisfactory route including required nodes and edges for each UAV is obtained without considering the disk neighborhoods of required nodes, and a close-enough routing phase where representative points are improved for each required node in the determined route. To be specific, a variable neighborhood descent (VND) heuristic is proposed for the general routing phase, while a second-order cone programming (SOCP) procedure is applied in the close-enough routing phase. These two phases are performed in an iterative fashion under the framework of an adaptive iterated local search (AILS) algorithm until the predefined termination criteria are satisfied. Extensive experiments and comparative studies are conducted, demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed AILS-VND-SOCP algorithm.

Title: Dynamic location-routing with decentralized modular production facilities and resource collection: A Variable Neighborhood Search approach
Authors: Julia Erdmann, Stefan Lier, Tristan Becker
Abstract: Hydrogen is emerging as a sustainable fuel, relevant for heavy-duty vehicles such as agricultural machinery, which are prevalent in rural areas. While utilizing residual biomass, such as straw or wood, is a promising option for local bio-hydrogen production, both the residues and the hydrogen demand are typically small-scale and geographically dispersed. Coupled with limited local infrastructure, the resulting high transportation costs threaten the economic viability of bio-hydrogen. To address this challenge, we propose a flexible, decentralized bio-hydrogen supply chain network, allowing hydrogen production close to both rural customers and residues, and thereby reducing transportation costs. We formulate this concept as the Dynamic Modular Location-Routing Problem with Resource Collection and Customer Delivery (DMLRP-RCCD). Our model simultaneously optimizes production site selection, the dynamic allocation of mobile production units, resource selection, and both resource collection and customer delivery route generation over a multi-period planning horizon. To solve this highly complex problem, we develop a tailored, nested Variable Neighborhood Search metaheuristic. Extensive computational experiments across 288 instances demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of our solution approach, which achieves highly competitive and stable results compared to a state-of-the-art exact solver. Furthermore, a real-world case study confirms the practical applicability of our concept and demonstrates that dynamic, decentralized production can successfully meet local hydrogen demand. These outcomes underscore the potential of our work for the future decarbonization of heavy-duty transport in rural areas.

Title: Strategic selection of remanufacturing business models: A consumer perception perspective
Authors: Zhongxin Hu, Christina Imdahl, Zümbül Atan
Abstract: As a key circular economy strategy, remanufacturing allows original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to reduce waste by restoring used products to ``as-new''conditions. This paper investigates an OEM's optimal remanufacturing business model by incorporating consumer perceptions into price and production quantity decisions. We analyze three alternative models: no remanufacturing, OEM in-house remanufacturing, and third-party remanufacturer (TPR) authorized remanufacturing. We extend the authorization with a two-part tariff contract and consider a stochastic market size. Through a numerical approach, we optimize price and quantity decisions based on consumer perceptions and develop a hierarchical decision roadmap to guide model selection. Our findings show that when consumer's perceived value of remanufactured products is high, OEM in-house remanufacturing is most profitable and reduces environmental impacts, but generally leads to a market dominated by remanufactured products. In contrast, when consumer's perceived value of remanufactured products is moderate and TPR remanufacturing significantly increases the perceived value of new products, the TPR-authorized remanufacturing is most profitable. It typically boosts total market sales, but accordingly increases environmental impacts. In addition, sensitivity analysis indicates that two-part authorization contracts are more advanced in meeting stringent environmental requirements than one-part contracts. Incorporating market size stochasticity enhances system profitability while keeping environmental impacts within a limited scope.

Title: Supplemental Material for What Do We Know About Job Knowledge Tests? A 30-Year Update of Validity Evidence
Correlated Demand Shocks and Asset Pricing
Authors: Byungwook Kim
Affiliations: University of California , Irvine
Abstract: Abstract I propose a mechanism through which institutional investors’ correlated demand shocks provide a source of market risk in asset pricing. Institutional investors have mandates to beat a similar market index. During periods of strong stock market performance, their incentive to outperform intensifies as more of them fall short of the market index. This incentive induces procyclical risk-taking behavior, generating correlated demand that elevates the market betas and risk premia of exposed stocks. Quasi-experiments using exogenous changes in index membership support a causal interpretation of the mechanism. Elevated betas are associated with a higher perceived cost of capital and reduced firm investment.

Title: Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
Authors: Christoph Huber, Felix Holzmeister, Magnus Johannesson, Christian König‐Kersting, Anna Dreber, Jürgen Huber, Michael Kirchler
Abstract: ABSTRACT Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

Title: The Future of Entrepreneurship Research Includes Online Panel Data—If Used Correctly
Authors: Jeffrey M. Pollack, J. Jeffrey Gish, Timothy L. Michaelis, Jeni L. Burnette, David J. Scheaf, Jon C. Carr, Nicholas A. Smith
Affiliations: Management, Innovation, and Entrepreneurship, NC State University, Raleigh, NC, USA; Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, NY, USA; Department of Psychology, NC State University, Raleigh, NC, USA; Hankamer School of Business, Baylor University, Waco, TX, USA; Northern Illinois University, DeKalb, IL, USA
Abstract: As online panel data (OPD) become more widely used across the behavioral sciences, editors, reviewers, and researchers in entrepreneurship are asking whether it has a legitimate place in our field. We believe the answer is yes—provided three conditions are met. First, the online panel’s participants and definition of entrepreneur must match the research question. Second, studies must incorporate best practices for sample verification. Third, generalizability must be explicitly addressed as part of the study (or set of studies). If researchers do these things, OPD can meaningfully advance both theory and practice in entrepreneurship research. That said, real questions remain. What kinds of studies are suitable for OPD? Who are these respondents, and are they who they say they are? Are they human, and are they entrepreneurs as commonly defined in the literature? Our recommendations and checklist aim to enable entrepreneurship researchers to answer these questions and make informed choices when collecting data and publishing results using OPD.

Title: A learning and searching method for integrated process planning and scheduling
Authors: Hongpei Li, Han Zhang, Ziyan He, Jiaqi Hu, Hongsong Yuan
Affiliations: Northwestern University; National University of Singapore; University of British Columbia; The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, Shanghai, China
Abstract: The integrated process planning and scheduling problem combines process route planning and shop scheduling to achieve high efficiency in manufacturing and maximize resource utilization, which is crucial for modern manufacturing systems. Traditional approaches, such as mixed-integer linear programming and heuristic algorithms, often struggle to balance solution quality and computational efficiency, particularly in large-scale scenarios. To address this, we propose learning-then-searching, an efficient framework combining deep reinforcement learning with heuristic search to solve integrated process planning and scheduling problems. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and develop a deep reinforcement learning method tailored to capture the complex relationships among operations, machines, and jobs. With the learned policy distributions, Monte Carlo tree search employs learned priors and problem-specific rollouts to further refine scheduling strategies, effectively balancing exploration and exploitation to achieve better solutions. Experimental results show that the proposed framework improves solution efficiency and quality over traditional methods across benchmark and large-scale instances, with pronounced advantages when route ambiguity is high. It also offers practitioners a flexible tradeoff between rapid policy-based decisions and further refinement through tree search when additional computation time is available.

Title: Code and Data Repository for Branch-Price-and-Cut for the Workforce Scheduling and Routing Problem with Delivery and Pickup at Dispatch Points
Authors: Haocheng Zhuang, Hu Qin, Jiliu Li, Rui Zhang

Title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
Authors: Jerry Anunrojwong, Santiago R. Balseiro, Omar Besbes
Affiliations: Yale School of Management, New Haven, Connecticut 06511; Graduate School of Business, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics.

Title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
Authors: Yanan Li, Yu Qin, Wenjun Wang
Affiliations: Business School, Beijing Normal University, Beijing 100875, China; Department of Applied Economics, Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China; Carbon Neutrality and Climate Change Thrust, Society Hub, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), Guangzhou 511453, China
Abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
Authors: Bin Luo, Guofu Zhou, Ti Zhou
Affiliations: College of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China; Olin School of Business, Washington University in St. Louis, St. Louis, Missouri 63130; School of Economics and Management, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China
Abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance.
