Title: Bots with Empathy: Reactance Against Emotion-Aware AI Agents in Customer Service
Authors: Elizabeth Han, Dezhi Yin, Han Zhang
Affiliations: McGill University; University of South Florida; Hong Kong Baptist University
Abstract: The advance of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has enabled chatbots to be emotionally responsive. In customer service, expressing empathy is a critical component of employee emotional responsiveness and a popular recovery strategy following service failure. However, the impact of empathy expressed by a chatbot is less clear. In this research, we investigate how and why chatbot-expressed empathy after service failure may influence customers’ service evaluations differently. Extending the psychological reactance literature, we propose that an empathetic chatbot may trigger customer reactance due to the unique nature of AI chatbots (vs. humans). We further propose that the triggered reactance can undermine perceptions of a chatbot’s competence and warmth, ultimately hurting service evaluations. We conducted three laboratory experiments to test these predictions. Our theoretical framework and findings illuminate the more nuanced and distinct role of empathy expressed by AI chatbots, and they suggest a critical need for chatbot developers and companies deploying chatbots to be aware of user reactance in customer service.

Title: Affect-Infused Reflective Process in Responding to Burdensome Role Expectations: An Affect-Cognition Theory Extension of Yagil’s “I Don’t Want To”
Authors: Chang Su, Xiaoran Hu
Affiliations: University of Oxford; London School of Economics

Title: Building Digital Resilience against Major Shocks
Authors: Waifong Boh, Panos Constantinides, Balaji Padmanabhan, Siva Viswanathan
Affiliations: Nanyang Technological University; University of Manchester; University of South Florida; University of Maryland
Abstract: Major shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic create unique and exceptional challenges for different entities, including individuals, groups, and organizations. In this special issue editorial, we introduce the concept of digital resilience, which refers to the capabilities developed through the use of digital technologies to absorb major shocks, adapt to disruptions caused by the shocks, and transform to a new stable state, where entities are more prepared to deal with major shocks. The individual papers in this special issue offer compelling examples of how digital resilience is exhibited and how the process of digital resilience can unfold in response to specific major shocks. Drawing upon and extending these papers, we present an integrated framework of how digital technology can help build resilience capabilities, which is missing in past research but needed to mitigate and manage future major shocks, including financial recessions and climate change. We conclude with four important themes for future IS research.

Title: The effects of national security assessments in public procurement on competition, sustainability, innovation, and critical technology procurement
Authors: Pelle Berkhout, Anne Rainville, Matthijs Janssen, Koen Frenken
Abstract: By strategically leveraging public procurement, governments can harness market competition to drive business innovation and sustainable development. It remains unclear, however, how this premise is affected by heightened security awareness due to increasing geopolitical tensions. Focusing on European Union (EU) member states, we examine how security-oriented practices in public procurement affect tender outcomes. Using data from a recent pan-European survey of 1613 procurement projects, coupled with data from the EU's tender platform Tender Electronic Daily, we test the effect of using national security assessments (NSAs) during tender preparation on competition, innovation, sustainability, and critical technology procurement. We find that conducting such assessments has positive effects on innovation and on critical technology procurement, but only for tenders won by domestic suppliers. NSAs can thus create urgency and mobilize resources to innovate through public procurement, but possibly in a way that reinforces national rather than EU-wide technological development. We identify a tension between the need for research and coordination of NSA development at the EU level to avoid market distortions arising from uncontrolled NSA proliferation versus a heightened bureaucratic burden for suppliers. We also argue that stimulating joint cross-border innovation procurement, particularly of critical technologies, is key to fully leveraging the benefits of the EU internal market when pursuing strategic policy goals.

Title: Decoupling voting and cash flow rights
Authors: Andre Speit, Paul Voss, András Danis
Abstract: The equity lending and option market both allow investors to decouple voting and cash flow rights of common shares. We provide a theory of this decoupling. While either market enables investors to acquire voting rights without cash flow exposure, empirical studies demonstrate a substantial difference in implied vote prices. Our model explains this surprising difference by uncovering the mechanism by which vote prices in the equity lending market are endogenously lower than those implied by the option market. We show that even though votes are cheaper in the equity lending market, activists endogenously choose to purchase votes in both markets.

Title: Diversification versus Consumption Motives for Early Exercise of Employee Stock Options
Authors: Kevin J. Murphy, Marshall Vance

Title: The Signaling Role of Seemingly Myopic Investment Behavior
Authors: Cyrus Aghamolla, Vivian W. Fang, Renhui Fu
Affiliations: Rice University; Indiana University Bloomington; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper analytically and empirically investigates managerial investment responses to negative shocks in firm value. In the model, managers are privately informed about the shocks’ persistence, and those facing transitory shocks strategically underinvest to boost earnings and signal financial strength to investors. The model also predicts counter-signaling: firms with strong fundamentals do not need to cut investment to convey strength. We exploit the 2003 mutual fund trading scandal as a plausibly exogenous source of price pressure. Consistent with signaling, we find that firms with greater tainted-fund ownership are more likely to meet or narrowly beat analyst forecasts by cutting R&D, and that this behavior is associated with more favorable earnings announcement returns and better long-run performance. Consistent with counter-signaling, these firms are less likely to cut R&D when they beat analyst forecasts by a wide margin. Cross-sectional tests also support the model’s comparative statics. Data Availability: All data used in the study are publicly available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: C73; D82; G23; G31; G34.

Title: Iterated local search for coverage path planning with imperfect extended detection
Authors: Dominik Richard, Michael Morin, Claude-Guy Quimper
Abstract: Naval mines, many of which are remnants of past conflicts, still threaten ships, wildlife, and the environment. To detect these underwater mines, autonomous minesweepers can be used, e.g. a REMUS 100 autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) equipped with sidescan sonars. We frame the minesweeping task as a combinatorial optimization problem called coverage path planning with imperfect extended detection (CPPIED). An efficient solution to the CPPIED minimizes both the path length and the number of turns (in that order), while satisfying stochastic coverage constraints in a grid environment. The current state of the art is a hybrid heuristic called DpSweeper. We show that, although this algorithm rapidly produces feasible solutions, the path quality is limited by its greedy nature. Since local search algorithms are known for their capacity to improve feasible solutions to large-scale combinatorial problems, such as vehicle routing problems with spatial coverage, we propose an iterated local search heuristic to enhance the solutions generated by DpSweeper. Our heuristic reduces the path length of solutions provided by DpSweeper by 9% to 28%, and the number of turns by 19% to 42%, hence improving the planning methods for minesweeping operations and bridging vehicle routing and coverage path planning problems.

Title: Adaptive threshold iterated local search: An adaptive self-parameterizing algorithm for solving sports timetabling problems of the international timetabling competition 2021
Authors: Ahmad Muklason, I Gusti Agung Premananda
Abstract: The International Timetabling Competition 2021 (ITC 2021) has established a rigorous benchmark for sports timetabling; however, the most effective solvers reported in the literature often rely on complex, instance-specific parameter tuning. This dependency limits their practical applicability in real-world scenarios where algorithmic expertise is limited. To address this trade-off between algorithmic performance and generality, in this study, we propose an adaptive threshold iterated local search (AT-ILS). Unlike conventional metaheuristics that utilize static cooling schedules or fixed memory lengths, AT-ILS employs a novel self-parameterizing mechanism that dynamically tunes acceptance thresholds by sampling the local solution landscape during execution. We evaluated the approach on the entire 45-instance ITC 2021 benchmark, optimizing soft-constraint penalties from precomputed feasible solutions. The experimental results demonstrate that AT-ILS achieves competitive performance without requiring the algorithmic expertise typically needed to configure sensitive parameters. Furthermore, the algorithm establishes new best-known solutions for four benchmark instances: Middle 2 and Middle 3, obtained from unoptimized feasible solutions, and Early 1 and Late 11, obtained by warm-starting the unmodified algorithm from the previously best-known solutions. These findings demonstrate that a self-parameterizing local search method can achieve competitive performance, offering a practical alternative to solvers that require extensive tuning.

Title: Traffic service provision and pricing with consumer segmentation in online retail platform
Authors: Zheng Luo, Xu Chen
Abstract: This study investigates the strategic provision of traffic services by online retail platforms operating under an agency selling mode, examining the interplay between two prevalent performance-based pricing mechanisms: cost-per-click (CPC) and cost-per-action (CPA). We develop a game-theoretic framework incorporating consumer heterogeneity—segmented into exploratory and non-exploratory types—and power dynamics. Within an online retail supply chain structure, the platform selects traffic service strategies and pricing models while the supplier determines retail pricing. We analyze two distinct governance structures: an online retail platform-Stackelberg model and a generalized Nash Bargaining model on traffic service fee. We find the effect of traffic services on sales volume and consumer surplus is not uniformly positive, depending on the pricing mechanisms. Key findings reveal that traffic service provision is contingent on operational costs, with the traffic operating cost emerging as a critical implementation barrier. The choice between CPC and CPA hinges on three strategic dimensions: market-specific consumer composition (exploratory vs. non-exploratory ratios), relationship-specific bargaining power distribution, and internal platform economics (agency selling fee). CPC proves superior more in markets dominated by a low agency selling fee and online retail platform-centric power structures. Conversely, CPA outperforms in environments characterized by non-exploratory consumer majorities, high agency selling fee, and supplier-leading bargaining dynamics. Our analysis demonstrates how these factors interactively shape platform revenue models, providing insights for traffic service implementation decisions. The strategic guidance assists platforms in strategically selecting pricing mechanisms based on market conditions and operational parameters.

Title: Unpacking the micro–macro transmission mechanism: how home-country culture selectively shapes cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial internationalization
Authors: Razieh Rosie Sadraei, Vahid J. Sadeghi, Andrew Delios
Abstract: Abstract International business accounts treat national culture as a country-level antecedent that shifts average export propensity uniformly, leaving the individual-level mechanisms producing within-country heterogeneity in internationalization intensity unspecified. We address this micro–macro transmission gap using social cognitive theory, examining how individualism versus collectivism and risk avoidance versus tolerance selectively recalibrate three cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial export decisions: perceived self-efficacy, perceived opportunity availability, and fear of failure. Our multilevel analysis of 40,529 observations across 41 countries spanning 2010–2019 reveals divergent rather than uniform moderation: individualism amplifies self-efficacy and opportunity availability beliefs through the social validation pathway, while risk avoidance constrains opportunity availability beliefs and fear of failure through the anticipatory self-regulation and outcome expectancy pathways. Fear of failure’s directional relationship with internationalization is contingent on the expectations of failure costs that the home-country cultural environment establishes through the outcome expectancy pathway, rather than being uniformly inhibitory as prior frameworks assume. These findings advance international business microfoundations theory by specifying the observable transmission pathways through which national cultural dimensions produce heterogeneous export intensity outcomes within the same national context. For policymakers, the findings imply that interventions to strengthen self-efficacy or opportunity awareness work best when calibrated to a country’s cultural profile.

Title: Correction: National identity rhetoric under bilateral geopolitical tensions: evidence from Taiwanese MNEs
Authors: Jin-Su Kang, Sunghoon Kim, Chuan-Kai Lee

Title: Winning at Defense by Playing Offense: Discrediting by Target Firms in Activist Hedge Fund Campaigns
Authors: Matthias Brauer, Marc J. Mertens, Louis Vandepoele
Affiliations: University of Mannheim; Copenhagen Business School
Abstract: Prior research highlights the far-reaching strategic and governance consequences for firms targeted in activist hedge fund (AHF) campaigns. Yet, how target firm executives and directors can effectively defend against these campaigns remains underexplored. Drawing on impression management (IM) theory, we reason that executives and directors use discrediting in their public rebuttal letters to negatively influence shareholders’ evaluations of AHFs’ reputation. To nuance this prediction, we develop a taxonomy distinguishing between source-focused discrediting, which directly attacks AHFs’ reputation, and message-focused discrediting, which challenges the validity of AHFs’ claims to indirectly tarnish their reputation. We theorize that both discrediting subtypes enhance target firms’ defense success, particularly when deployed in combination. Adopting a temporal perspective on IM theory, we further argue that the effectiveness of discrediting diminishes as more time elapses between an AHF’s public attack and executives and directors’ rebuttal. A manual content analysis of 841 rebuttal letters issued during U.S. AHF campaigns (2000–2023) provides robust support for these predictions. Beyond contributing to shareholder activism research by offering new insights into the determinants of campaign outcomes, our study advances IM theory by conceptualizing discrediting as a multidimensional influence tactic and exploring its effectiveness and temporal dynamics in adversarial contexts.

Title: Machine Learning Instrument Variables for Causal Inference
Authors: Amandeep Singh, Kartik Hosanagar, Amit Gandhi
Affiliations: University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: A machine learning framework for constructing strong instrumental variables from weak exogenous data achieves semiparametric efficiency with applications to advertising and demand estimation.

Title: Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
Authors: Soomi Kim
Affiliations: Columbia Business School, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

Title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
Authors: Irina Gemmo, Pierre-Carl Michaud, Olivia S. Mitchell
Affiliations: Department of Finance, HEC Montréal, Montréal, Quebec H3T 2A7, Canada; Department of Applied Economics, HEC Montréal, Montréal, Quebec H3T 2A7, Canada; and National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; and Business Economics and Public Policy Department, the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: We study the impact of a financial education program on portfolio choices in a setting that allows us to examine both participation decisions and differences in program benefits across individuals. We directly elicit willingness to pay for financial education and show that individuals with higher financial literacy, greater confidence in applying new knowledge, and higher expected returns are willing to pay more. Using incentivized portfolio allocation tasks, we develop outcome measures tailored to individual risk preferences and show that financial education improves decision quality along these dimensions. The program increases the share of participants who experience an improvement by 20 percentage points, corresponding to average gains of 3.2 percentage points of initial wealth. Individuals with the highest willingness to participate benefit disproportionately from the program, with important implications for the design and evaluation of financial education initiatives. By isolating a specific investment skill in a setting with voluntary participation, our design sheds light on how selection into financial education shapes measured program effects and informs the assessment of broader workplace and public training programs. Title: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power
Authors: Amandeep Singh, Jiding Zhang, Senthil Veeraraghavan
Affiliations: Foster School of Business, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; W. P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona 85281; Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104
Abstract: Fulfillment by Platform: Competition and Upstream Market Power E-commerce platforms increasingly offer fulfillment services that promise faster delivery and easier access to customers. This study shows that these services create a trade-off. Using transaction-level data from a major online marketplace, the authors find that platform fulfillment improves the customer experience and raises consumer welfare, but it also changes competition among sellers. Because fulfillment through the platform adds costs for merchants, smaller sellers with thinner margins must raise prices more than larger sellers. As a result, large merchants gain share while smaller merchants lose ground, increasing upstream market concentration. The findings matter for regulators, platforms, and merchants because they show that a service that benefits consumers can still weaken competition on the seller side. The paper provides rare empirical evidence from both sides of an e-commerce marketplace and highlights why platform policies should be evaluated not only by customer benefits, but also by their effects on market structure.

Title: Location-Allocation of Emergency Service Systems in Light Traffic
Authors: Xin Wang, Weiliang Liu, Loon Ching Tang, Zhisheng Ye
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Systems Engineering and Management, National University of Singapore, Singapore 117576; Department of Systems Engineering and Engineering Management, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong

Title: Innovation booms, easy financing, and human capital accumulation
Authors: Johan Hombert, Adrien Matray
Abstract: Innovation booms are often fueled by easy financing, allowing new technology firms to pay high wages that attract skilled labor. Studying the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) boom in the late 1990s, we show that high-skill workers who joined the ICT sector during the boom experienced sizeable long-term earnings losses. These earnings patterns stem from accelerated skill obsolescence rather than worker selection or the subsequent bust in the ICT sector. Moreover, during the boom, financing disproportionately flowed to firms whose workers would later experience the largest productivity declines, amplifying the negative effect of labor reallocation on aggregate human capital accumulation.

Title: Are direct lenders more like banks or arm’s-length investors?
Authors: Young Soo Jang
Abstract: Using novel data on loans to private equity (PE) sponsored firms, I examine whether direct lenders lend more like banks or arm’s-length investors. Financial covenants are ubiquitous in direct lending. Borrowers face more covenants, and violate them more often, than in bank loans. Direct lenders actively intervene post-violation, prompting firms to adopt conservative policies. During the COVID pandemic, they showed greater flexibility than banks, facilitated by more frequent PE sponsor equity injections. Prior sponsor relationships also predict higher credit supply for distressed borrowers. Overall, similar to banks, direct lenders engage in active monitoring and relationship lending.

Title: Defending the Hoax: A Commentary on Willmott’s “Management Theory: Jungle, Myth, or Hoax?”
Authors: Stefan Schwarzkopf

Title: Asymmetric Jeopardy through Dissonant Ties: An Extension of Brands and Kilduff’s “Multiplex Jeopardy”

Title: The Value of Resource Redeployability in the Face of Committed Rivals
Authors: Phebo D. Wibbens, Teresa A. Dickler, Timothy B. Folta
Affiliations: INSEAD; Marburg University and IE University Madrid; University of Connecticut
Abstract: The ability of multi-business firms to redeploy resources across businesses is a principal source of corporate advantage, as evidenced by a plethora of theoretical and empirical research. However, extant theory is silent in clarifying how resource redeployability might impact competitive behavior of rivals. Redeployability reduces irreversible commitments, which have long been recognized to deter rivalry, allow privileged access to scarce resources, and sustain a valuable strategic position. This raises a tension between the flexibility advantages and potential commitment disadvantages of redeployability. Using a dynamic computational model, we explore the competitive conditions under which redeployability can be advantageous or detrimental to long-term value. In addition to enhancing our understanding of the boundary conditions around the value of resource redeployability, this study also has implications for real option models and the broader dynamic capabilities literature.

Title: “MOB” Mentality? On the Formation and Consequences of Moralized Opinion-Based Intergroup Conflict in Organizations
Authors: Michael G. Pratt, Luke N. Hedden, Hamza Khan
Affiliations: Boston College; University of Miami; University of Illinois Chicago
Abstract: Organizations and their employees are increasingly engaging publicly with social issues, such as climate change, systemic racism, and LGBTQIA+ rights. Why does such engagement sometimes result in conflict and dysfunction in organizations? To build a theoretical foundation for answering this question, we bridge insights from research on opinion-based groups and psychological research on moralization to theorize a novel type of group—a moralized opinion-based (MOB) group—defined as an identity group that forms around a shared opinion that has been moralized by group members. We explain how the emotion of disgust affects opinion moralization, and why this makes MOB intergroup conflict uniquely dehumanizing, contagious, and difficult to resolve. We also explain how distinct configurations of MOB groups and formal groups in organizations can foster unique patterns of conflict—ultimately affecting members’ strength of identification foci, as well as their productivity. We offer practical suggestions for more productively engaging with social issues, and suggest a research agenda for better understanding the process and outcomes of MOB intergroup conflict in organizations.

Title: From an Uncoordinated Cacophony to a Coordinated Harmony: An Integrative Theory of Collective Voice
Authors: Nathan A. Black, Daniel W. Newton, Jennifer D. Nahrgang
Affiliations: University of Oklahoma; University of Iowa
Abstract: Scholars have exhibited enduring enthusiasm for voice and increasingly recognize the value of collective effort in the voice process. Despite this attention, research on collective voice remains fragmented across the organizational behavior and industrial relations traditions of voice, resulting in a problematic theoretical landscape marked by significant divergence regarding the nature, predictors, and outcomes of collective voice compared to aggregated forms of individual voice. To distinguish the coordinated nature of collective voice from aggregated individual voice, we leverage resource mobilization theory to propose an integrative theory of collective voice. Our integrative theory delineates open corporate opportunity structure, structural interdependence, and psychological safety as antecedents that drive employees’ opportunity, motivation, and ability to coordinate collective voice, respectively. Our theory then addresses a key trade-off of collective voice, which, compared to aggregated individual voice, is more likely to increase organizational effectiveness as well as organizational factionalism. Finally, we specify structural (i.e., centralization) and content (i.e., promotive voice and prohibitive voice) contingencies that shift these paradoxical effects. Our integrative theory has important implications for voice research and resource mobilization theory, unlocking future research directions to further expand our understanding of collective voice.

Title: How Underdogs Succeed and Fail: An Integrated Model of the Workplace Underdog’s Trajectories
Authors: Liuxin Yan, Daniel J. McAllister, Grace J. H. Lim, Kai Chi Yam
Affiliations: Tsinghua University; National University of Singapore; Nanyang Technological University
Abstract: Despite the widespread appeal of underdog characters in popular culture, being labeled a workplace underdog can be both stressful and challenging. Drawing on the literature on emotion, the challenge–threat framework, and emotion regulation, we propose a comprehensive theory that unpacks the double-edged nature of underdog expectations. Specifically, we explain how individuals respond differently based on how they interpret and manage the negative emotions elicited by these expectations. We introduce four distinct underdog narratives, each characterized by a unique configuration of emotional activation (i.e., low or high) and cognitive appraisals (i.e., challenge or threat): (1) strategic underdogs, (2) paranoid underdogs, (3) deluded underdogs, and (4) resigned underdogs. Our framework illustrates how individuals within each configuration regulate their emotions and cope with underdog expectations. Furthermore, rather than viewing success or failure as static endpoints, we adopt a process-oriented and temporal perspective to examine the enduring effects of underdog expectations, exploring how interpretive schemas shape behavior differently for “overcomers,” who successfully defy underdog expectations, and “succumbers,” who fail to do so. Our theory sheds new light on underdog dynamics in the workplace and offers a systematic framework for future research.

Title: The Impact of Learning Mode and Speed on Mutual Learning
Authors: Jerker Denrell, Michael Christensen, Thorbjørn Knudsen, Chengwei Liu
Affiliations: University of Warwick; University of Southern Denmark; Frankfurt School of Finance & Management; Imperial College London
Abstract: Research on organizational learning emphasizes that slow learning fosters exploration and encourages recombination of knowledge and practices. However, the role that slow learning plays in the spread of knowledge in organizations remains underexplored. This gap is important because the learning mode that actors apply to select practices is critical for organizational performance gained through mutual learning. We identify two key learning modes: success-based (learning from successful peers) and norm-based (conforming to majority views). We analytically distill our insights into six propositions that explore how variations in learning modes, learning speeds, and network centrality shape organizational learning outcomes. Our findings reveal a critical coupling between learning modes and speed: Norm-based learners should adopt slow learning, while success-based learners should always learn faster. Contrary to prior studies emphasizing organizational structure, we show that effective knowledge utilization is primarily driven by the interaction of learning modes and speeds. Hierarchy emerges as a factor only when mixed learning modes interact with varying speeds. These insights enrich our understanding of slow learning by highlighting its contingent value in knowledge selection and assimilation. Our study offers testable predictions and practical guidance for organizational design in contexts such as multinational retail chains, manufacturing firms, and franchise organizations.

Title: Management Theory: Jungle, Myth, or Hoax?
Authors: Hugh Willmott
Affiliations: Bayes Business School and Cardiff Business School
Abstract: Two stories, revolving around the metaphors of jungle and myth, dominate accounts of mainstream management theory (MMT). An alternative metaphor, the hoax, is proposed as an alternative. Drawing parallels with the fable of the Emperor’s New Clothes, the analysis revives an explicit engagement of metaphors to theorize MMT as a phenomenon of interest. Four features of hoaxes relevant for theorizing MMT are proposed and explicated: mendacity; fantasies of control; stifling critical reflection; and normalized cynicism. The relevance of the hoax metaphor is further demonstrated by addressing its status as theory; its relevance to the study of “grand challenges”; the possibility of reconciling MMT and critical management studies (CMS); and the future of management education.

Title: Multiplex Jeopardy: Dissonant Ties Promote Gender Bias in Workplace Social Networks
Authors: Raina A. Brands, Martin Kilduff
Affiliations: University College London
Abstract: This paper develops new theory on how dissonant ties—work relationships characterized by positive and negative valence—shape gender inequality in organizational networks. We introduce the concept of multiplex jeopardy to explain how dissonant ties disproportionately harm women, due to their overlap with gender stereotypes. Specifically, we argue that like–disrespect ties reinforce perceptions of women as warm but incompetent, whereas dislike–respect ties reinforce perceptions of women as cold but competent, leading to both passive harm and active backlash. We further theorize that these effects extend beyond direct relationships to shape women’s experiences and outcomes through indirect gender bias. This bias distorts reputations, stifles information flow, limits career advancement, and contributes to structural inequality by reinforcing gendered network positions. We offer three theoretical contributions: (1) a novel lens on gendered outcomes in informal networks, (2) a social psychological account of how stereotypes become embedded in everyday work relationships, and (3) insight into how informal dynamics sustain gender inequality in organizations.

Title: The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
Authors: Şenay Ağca, Pablo Slutzky, Stefan Zeume
Affiliations: George Washington University School of Business; Temple University Fox School of Business; University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign Gies College of Business
Abstract: Abstract We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: The Efficiency Trap of Agentic AI in Human Resource Management
Authors: Miles M. Yang
Affiliations: Department of Management, Health at Work Research Centre, Innovation, Strategy and Entrepreneurship Research Centre Macquarie Business School, Macquarie University Sydney New South Wales Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT Agentic AI transforms HRM from data‐driven support to autonomous execution. Organizations deploy these recursive workflows to eliminate human implementation variance, yet we challenge the assumption that such alignment remains optimal. Drawing on Weick's theory of loose coupling, we argue that delegating HR execution to agentic AI creates algorithmic tight coupling. While this generates immediate hyper‐fit, the removal of strategic slack leads to structural calcification, compromising organizational resilience during polycrises. Human line managers provide a critical buffer, enabling the sensemaking necessary to absorb systemic shocks. In contrast, agentic AI workflows governed by instrumental rationality lack the value rationality required for complex organizing. We propose a governance framework to reconcile machine‐driven consistency with the human stewardship required to preserve long‐term organizational adaptability.

Title: Generative AI use in entrepreneurship: An integrative review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
Authors: Jackson G. Lu, Gerui Gloria Zhao, Anna Manyi Zheng
Affiliations: MIT Sloan School of Management Massachusetts Institute of Technology Cambridge Massachusetts USA; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. The future of entrepreneurship will depend less on whether entrepreneurs use GenAI than on how they use it. Used thoughtfully, GenAI may empower entrepreneurs by expanding their capabilities to engage in entrepreneurial activities. Used uncritically, GenAI may entrap entrepreneurs by restricting or eroding those capabilities. Entrepreneurs should therefore verify what GenAI produces, calibrate GenAI use to their expertise and task demands, and decide which tasks to delegate to GenAI while retaining human judgment for consequential decisions.

Title: Numerical gap effect in multigenerational brand names: The role of perceived innovation momentum
Authors: Yanfei Tang, Liangyan Wang, Zhiyong Yang
Abstract: Consumers frequently encounter multigenerational products labeled with numerical sequences (e.g., A1→A2→A3 vs. B10→B20→B30). Although such naming structures may appear superficial, they systematically shape consumers’ upgrade decisions. We define the numerical gap as the difference between numerical values across product generations and demonstrate that large (vs. small) numerical gaps increase upgrade preferences. This effect arises because large (vs. small) numerical gaps lead consumers to infer stronger innovation momentum. However, this inference depends on context: it weakens or reverses when large numerical gaps conflict with consumers’ expectations about how innovation unfolds, when innovation is less central to the product category, or when the implied innovation is incongruent with the brand’s positioning. By highlighting how peripheral numerical structures convey innovation signals, this research advances our understanding of how consumers interpret multigenerational brand names and offers guidance to firms designing naming strategies that encourage product upgrades.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
Authors: Nadeesha H. Bandara, Elizabeth G. Miller, George R. Milne, Lauren I. Labrecque
Abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Spoiler alert! Watch movies before they are spoiled
Authors: Byungwan Koh, Sohyun Bang
Abstract: With the rise of video-sharing platforms, user-generated videos that reveal the ending of a movie—so-called spoiler videos—have become increasingly popular. While some movie studios and industry experts view these videos as copyright infringement and advocate for their removal, other industry experts and movie fans speculate that studios may use them strategically to increase early viewership. The threat of encountering spoilers may prompt people to watch movies earlier, particularly during the opening week, when studios earn a larger share of ticket sales than in later weeks. Motivated by these speculations and based on regret theory and prospect theory, this study investigates the role of spoiler videos in the movie industry. Using data from 324 wide-release movies in Korea from 2018 to 2021, we find that compared with movies without spoiler videos in their opening week, movies with spoiler videos have higher box office revenue in their opening week and a greater subsequent rate of decline in box office revenue; that is, the existence of spoiler videos in the opening week may indeed motivate people to watch a movie earlier. Additionally, we find that when spoiler videos are available for some movies, the overall market box office revenue is estimated to be 18% higher than when no spoiler videos are available for any movie. This study complements the literature on the role of user-generated content in the movie industry and provides valuable insights into movie windowing strategies for both academia and the industry in the presence of spoiler videos.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Sustainability in marketing: A systematic analysis and future research agenda
Authors: Jonathan M. Beck, Riley T. Krotz, Francisco Zuloaga Cosme, Terry Ye Tian
Abstract: Interest in sustainability research is growing, yet fragmented definitions and piecemeal knowledge generation limit academic understanding and real-world impact. To address this confusion and advance sustainability research, this study employs a systematic literature review, science mapping, and topic modeling to analyze the history of research across academic disciplines, drawing from a final corpus of 947 articles. Through this analysis, the authors propose a holistic definition of sustainability, formally define it, and map nine distinct research topics within it, organized into three overarching themes. They then synthesize and reflect on past findings, identify key gaps, and develop a robust research agenda for the future. This research also proposes an integrative framework that reveals the interplay of seemingly disparate research areas. Ultimately, by clarifying definitions, identifying relevant topics, developing themes, and outlining a future research agenda, this work provides actionable insights for scholars, practitioners, and policymakers aiming to align marketing strategies with evolving sustainability imperatives.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: The undirected circular facility layout problem
Authors: Anja Fischer, Louisa Semrau
Abstract: In the Undirected Circular Facility Layout Problem (UDCFLP) one has given a set of departments, their lengths and pairwise weights between the departments. The goal is to find an arrangement on a circle that minimizes the total sum of the weighted center-to-center distances, either measured in clockwise or in counter-clockwise direction, depending on which distance is shorter. Despite the advantages of circular manufacturing systems in comparison to row layout systems, the UDCFLP with arbitrary lengths has not been considered in the literature before. We present two new mixed-integer linear programming models for the UDCFLP by adapting two well-known models from well-studied facility layout problems from the literature and exploiting their connection with the UDCFLP. To strengthen our models, we study the structure of the associated polytopes. We derive different classes of cutting planes and prove their correctness. In a computational study we compare our stand-alone models and their strengthened variants regarding the deviation between their lower bounds and heuristically determined upper bounds and their computational times.

Title: Designing fulfilling and productive workdays: Effects of task meaningfulness sequences on daily engagement and performance.
Authors: Soohyun Yoon, Eunjeong Kwon, Jeffery A. LePine, S. R. Aurora, Daniel W. Newton, Ned Wellman

Title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-Led Interviews
Authors: Friedrich Geiecke, Xavier Jaravel
Affiliations: LSE , United Kingdom; LSE & CEPR
Abstract: Abstract The advent of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to conduct qualitative interviews at scale, with thousands of respondents, thereby bridging qualitative and quantitative methods. We develop a simple, versatile approach for researchers to run AI-led qualitative interviews, including voice interviews. We assess its robustness by drawing comparisons to human experts and with several respondent-based quality metrics. The versatility of the approach is illustrated through four broad classes of applications: eliciting key factors in decision making, political views, subjective mental states, and mental models of the effects of public policies. High performance ratings are obtained in all of these domains. Our applications highlight the potential of AI-led interviews as a tool for measurement, hypothesis generation, and discovering mechanisms.

Title: Do PCAOB Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
Authors: Kenneth L. Bills, Chris E. Hogan, Jennifer E. Puccia
Affiliations: Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA; Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

Title: Book Review: James S. Fishkin. Can Deliberation Cure the Ills of Democracy? FishkinJ. S. (2025). Can deliberation cure the ills of democracy?Oxford University Press, 2025. 192 pp. ISBN 9780198944416
Authors: Ilana Redstone
Affiliations: Department of Sociology, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL

Title: Simply a Sign of the Season? Christmas Trees as Cultural Ciphers in Local Government Management of Diversity
Authors: Gary J. Adler, Damon Mayrl, Eric Plutzer, Jonathan S. Coley, Rebecca Sager, Elise Wolff
Affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; Colby College; Oklahoma State University; Loyola Marymount University
Abstract: How do local governments symbolically manage the diversity of their residents? Drawing from an original representative sample of local government officials, we use a novel survey experiment with open-ended survey responses to examine preferences for cultural objects that symbolically manage religious diversity, an axis of difference that is increasingly salient to social conflict. Our experiment randomly varies the content of holiday displays on government property to measure diversity management strategies. Results show that government officials prefer the assimilationist strategy of a Christmas tree—by itself—over multiculturalist and exclusivist strategies, which both include sectarian religious content. Officials also evaluate Christmas trees as the content least likely to signal government endorsement of religion, compared to other holiday displays. We argue that these patterns can be explained by conceiving of a Christmas tree as a cultural cipher, a well-known cultural object that affords a range of meanings and resonates across social identities as innocuous. We argue that cultural ciphers are useful for an assimilationist approach to managing diversity because their ambiguity allows them to act as a vehicle of symbolic inclusion while also sustaining the meanings of majority groups. We also consider how cultural ciphers may lose their power for civic solidarity.

Title: Incentivizing Equality? How Work-Family Policies Affect Parenthood Penalties in 27 Countries
Authors: Allison Dunatchik, Pilar Gonalons-Pons
Affiliations: University of South Carolina, USA; University of Pennsylvania, USA
Abstract: Work-family policies are theorized to shape the division of paid labor after parenthood, but recent studies have cast doubt on their importance. Leveraging harmonized longitudinal data spanning 27 countries and an analytic focus on couples and couple dynamics, our study shows that work-family policies do shape how divisions of paid labor change with parenthood, and that they also moderate the importance of couples’ relative resources as a determinant of the division of labor. We find that moderate-length paid maternal leave and greater childcare availability reduce parenthood penalties in couples’ division of paid work time, while prolonged leave exacerbates penalties. Furthermore, by focusing on couples, we provide novel evidence that partners’ relative resources do not operate uniformly across work-family policy contexts, showing that policies can incentivize couples to divide paid work in ways their relative resource profiles would not otherwise predict. We find that moderate-length paid leave and greater childcare availability encourage egalitarianism among male-breadwinner couples, although extended leave encourages greater gender traditionalism among female-breadwinner couples. These findings reveal that classic theories of household specialization and bargaining are not universal, and highlight the need for greater theoretical attention to how country- and couple-level forces interact to shape gender inequality.

Title: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
Authors: Aritra Bhattacharya, Raghu Bommaraju, Rob Waiser
Abstract: Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales managers . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an aggregate target ( Aggregate Target Scheme , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each individual territory or salesperson ( Individual Target Scheme , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition improved performance , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the reallocation of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a sales star bias —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased joint fieldwork , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

Title: Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment with Timing Coordination Requirements
Authors: Gang Li, Anantaram Balakrishnan
Abstract: We address a tactical planning problem facing organizations that must perform geographically dispersed jobs with timing dependencies using appropriate teams of workers and equipment. This Tactical Workforce Planning and Deployment (TWPD) problem, which is motivated by the annual planning and budgeting activity for rail infrastructure maintenance and upgrades, requires making simultaneous decisions on resource sizing and selection, resource-to-job assignment, and resource repositioning to complete all jobs while minimizing resource and transportation costs. Key challenges include timing coordination among jobs, varying resource capabilities, and sequence-dependent changeover costs. Prior scheduling and routing models often focus on short-term decisions, assuming a given set of resources, and do not incorporate complex timing coordination requirements. We propose a large-scale optimization model, with strong timing coordination constraints, that integrates all the features of the TWPD problem. To solve this difficult problem, we propose three new families of valid inequalities to further strengthen the model and develop problem reduction procedures as well as an optimization-based multi-stage algorithm to identify good initial feasible solutions. Our Composite method applies these acceleration strategies before initiating an exact branch-and-bound solution procedure. To test the effectiveness of this method, we first apply it to real data sets for track maintenance from a leading railroad company and compare its performance with a method that uses a standard solver without our enhancements. We find that our method dramatically outperforms the standard method. We also test our method on many randomly generated problems to validate its superior performance and identify problem features that make this problem difficult to solve. When compared to a manual tactical plan, our method quickly generates a near-optimal solution that saves over 15% in annual total cost, demonstrating the practical value and viability of our model and method. We conclude by discussing some managerial implications and insights from our results.

Title: Optimal return policies with heterogeneous search rewards
Authors: Fangruo Chen, Weitao Ren, Wenqiang Xiao
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Central University of Finance and Economics; New York University
Abstract: This paper studies return policy design for an online seller serving consumers who can resolve product-fit uncertainty through costly pre-purchase search, with search rewards varying across consumers. Return policies shape not only post-purchase return behavior but also ex-ante search and purchase decisions, thereby generating endogenous consumer segmentation. One might expect that inexpensive search would reduce the seller’s incentive to offer a generous refund. In our baseline model, however, we show that full refund outperforms no refund when search costs are sufficiently low. We trace this result to a fundamental trade-off in implementing a full-refund policy: the search-relief effect versus the return-inducing effect. Full refund substitutes for search by allowing consumers who would otherwise search to purchase directly and evaluate fit after purchase, thereby removing their search-based information advantage and restoring the seller’s pricing power. However, it also induces returns from consumers who would otherwise purchase without search and keep the product, sacrificing the revenue generated by their tolerance for misfit. When search costs are sufficiently low, most consumers would otherwise search, and the search-relief effect therefore dominates the return-inducing effect. As search costs fall further, full refund can also achieve a win-win outcome, indicating that pre-purchase search may be socially inefficient. These findings explain when and why sellers may optimally discourage ex-ante search in favor of ex-post product evaluation.

Title: Design and pricing of online dating subscriptions
Authors: Titing Cui, Michael L Hamilton
Affiliations: University of Tulsa; City University of New York
Abstract: Online dating is now the most common way for new couples in the United States to meet, with more than 30% of U.S. adults having used a dating app and with global industry revenues exceeding three billion dollars annually. Most dating apps monetize primarily through subscription pricing, offering users fixed periods of access to paid features for recurring fees. However, applying subscription pricing to online dating apps presents some unique challenges. Unlike other digital services, users’ valuations of dating app services typically decline with use, as continued participation can be costly in terms of both time and emotional effort, and repeated renewals signal unsuccessful app-mediated searches. Moreover, users who achieve their goal of finding a partner subsequently exit the platform, creating an apparent tension between providing value by successfully matching users and a dating app’s goal of generating profit and sustaining a large userbase of paying subscribers. Given these unique challenges and the transient nature of user engagement with dating apps, it is interesting to note that leading U.S. dating apps, such as Hinge and Bumble, have begun offering increasingly long subscription options, including lifetime subscriptions. In this article, we analyze the performance of subscription pricing strategies with varying period lengths for online dating platforms. We propose a natural model of dating app monetization and use it to evaluate how subscription length affects both profit and steady-state userbase size. We find that suitably priced lifetime subscriptions can Pareto-dominate all finite-period subscriptions over both objectives, providing a compelling explanation for their emerging use. We then extend our analysis to subscription menus with two options and show that offering one short-term subscription option and one lifetime option guarantees approximately 59.4% of the optimal two-option menu performance.

Title: Corporate Pension Risk-Taking in a Low Interest Rate Environment
Authors: Vasso Ioannidou, Roberto Pinto, Zexi Wang
Affiliations: Bayes Business School, City St George’s, University of London, London EC1Y 8TZ, United Kingdom; and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), London, United Kingdom; Luiss University, Viale Romania 32, Rome, 00197 Italy; and Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster LA1 4YX, United Kingdom; Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster LA1 4YX, United Kingdom; and Dishui Lake Advanced Finance Institute, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai 200433, China
Abstract: We examine how funding deficit pressures shape the risk-taking of U.S. corporate defined-benefit pension plans and how targeted regulatory relief can mitigate these incentives. Using the 2012 Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act reform, which temporarily eased funding pressure by revising discount rate calculations, we show that plans receiving greater relief significantly reduced their equity allocations and shifted toward safer assets. This derisking was most pronounced among active plans and those sponsored by more financially constrained firms. Our findings demonstrate that targeted regulatory relief can curb risk-taking incentives even without altering underlying economic conditions or financial reporting standards and shed light on the likely (and unlikely) frictions driving such behavior. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Pinto acknowledges financial support from the Lancaster University Management School Pump Prime Program. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02928 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance.

Title: The Equity Market Implications of the Retail Investment Boom
Authors: Philippe van der Beck, Cameron Cohen, Coralie Jaunin
Affiliations: Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163; Université de Lausanne, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland; and cSwiss Finance Institute, 8006 Zürich, Switzerland
Abstract: We quantify the equilibrium impact of retail traders on the U.S. equity market within a structural model of asset demand. Estimating investor-specific demand curves, we find that Robinhood traders are fundamentally distinct from all other investors, including other households: their demand is the most elastic and tilts most strongly toward volatile and microcap stocks. Each dollar invested through Robinhood generates more than five dollars in aggregate equity repricing, exceeding hedge funds, other households, and all other investor types. We decompose the cross-sectional variation in stock returns during Robinhood’s growth surge in 2020 into investor-specific components and find that shifts in Robinhood traders’ latent demand drove 11% of small-cap return volatility despite their negligible aggregate wealth share. To explain these demand shifts, we show that Robinhood traders are the only investor group whose latent demand is well explained by attention proxies: their demand exhibits a V-shaped response to past returns and rises sharply with trading volume. Our findings suggest that the growth of retail trading platforms represents a fundamental shift in the composition of equity demand with equilibrium consequences disproportionate to retail investors’ share of aggregate wealth. Title: Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms
Authors: Omar El Housni, Ulysse Hennebelle, Alfredo Torrico
Affiliations: School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14850; and Cornell Tech, Cornell University, New York, New York 10044; Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, USC Viterbi School of Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089
Abstract: On the Power of Adaptivity in Choice-Based Matching Platforms Online labor, lodging, and carpooling platforms decide not only whom users can choose but also when those options are shown. Simultaneity can crowd attention around a few popular users and leave many good matches unrealized. In the forthcoming Operations Research paper, “Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms,” the authors study how much platforms gain by updating assortments after observing earlier choices. They compare four policy classes, ranging from showing all assortments at once to fully adaptive policies that process users one by one. They prove that adaptivity within one side improves performance by at most a factor of [Formula: see text], whereas fully adaptive policies improve on one-sided adaptive policies by at most a factor of two; both bounds are tight. They also develop efficient approximation algorithms, extend their results to constrained settings, and empirically show that their methods perform far better than their worst-case guarantees.

Title: Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting
Authors: Yilun Chen, Jiaqi Lu
Affiliations: School of Data Science, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China; and School of Management and Economics, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China

Title: Qualitative Research in the Age of AI: Considerations, Critiques, and Craft
Authors: Andrew Nelson, Anne-Laure Fayard, Alex Murray
Affiliations: Lundquist College of Business, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oregon 97403; Nova School of Business and Economics, 2775-405 Carcavelos, Portugal

Title: Problem of locating and allocating charging equipment for battery electric buses under stochastic charging demand
Authors: Sadjad Bazarnovi, Taner Cokyasar, Omer Verbas, Abolfazl (Kouros) Mohammadian
Abstract: Bus electrification plays a crucial role in advancing urban transportation sustainability. Battery Electric Buses (BEBs), however, often need recharging, making the Problem of Locating and Allocating Charging Equipment for BEBs (PLACE-BEB) essential for efficient operations. This study proposes an optimization framework to solve the PLACE-BEB by determining the optimal placement of charger types at potential locations under the stochastic charging demand. Leveraging the existing stochastic location literature, we develop a Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Program (MINLP) to model the problem. To solve this problem, we develop an exact solution method that minimizes the costs related to building charging stations, charger allocation, travel to stations, and average queueing and charging times. Queueing dynamics are modeled using an M/M/s queue, with the number of servers at each location treated as a decision variable. To improve scalability, we implement a Simulated Annealing (SA) and a Genetic Algorithm (GA) allowing for efficient solutions to large-scale problems. The computational performance of the methods was thoroughly evaluated, revealing that SA was effective for small-scale problems, while GA outperformed others for large-scale instances. A case study comparing garage-only, other-only, and mixed scenarios, along with joint deployment, highlighted the cost benefits of a collaborative and a comprehensive approach. Sensitivity analyses showed that the waiting time is a key factor to consider in the decision-making.

Title: A prudent framework for understanding risk-awareness in demand response
Authors: Liudong Chen, Bolun Xu
Abstract: We show that risk-aware behaviors in demand response originate from superquadratic state-dependent cost functions and price uncertainty with skewed distributions. We obtain such results through developing a novel theoretical demand response framework that combines non-anticipatory multi-stage decision-making with superquadratic cost functions. We introduce the concept of prudent demand, defined by a positive third-order derivative of the cost function, which is the first principle for risk-averse behavior despite a risk-neutral objective. Our analysis establishes that future price uncertainty affects immediate consumption decisions, and the extent of this response scales proportionally with the skewness of the price distribution. We visualize our theoretical findings through numerical simulations and illustrate their practical implications using a real-world case study.

Title: Strategic investment in electricity markets: Robust optimization versus stochastic programming
Authors: Álvaro García-Cerezo, Afzal S. Siddiqui, Trine K. Boomsma, Raquel García-Bertrand, Luis Baringo
Abstract: Decarbonization policies have spurred the adoption of variable renewable energy (VRE) technologies such as wind and solar power. To enable flexible resources and accommodate VRE’s intermittency, electricity markets are shifting toward renewable-aware dispatch based on stochastic optimization. However, strategic firms may exploit such market structures to manipulate prices to their advantage. To complement the extant literature, we compare investment decisions as well as worst-case profits and losses in the context of generation expansion by a strategic firm that uses either risk-averse stochastic programming or robust optimization. The former is a bi-level optimization problem, whereas the latter is a tri-level problem. Our contributions are threefold in addressing policy and methodological challenges. First, we demonstrate that using robust optimization instead of stochastic programming generally leads to investment plans with a higher share of VRE because it serves as a hedge during undesirable realizations with low consumer willingness to pay and high marginal costs for conventional generation. Second, a regret analysis shows that the worst-case profit is significantly reduced if an investor uses expansion decisions from stochastic programming, highlighting the importance of selecting a methodology aligned with the main objective of the investor. The effect is especially pronounced if decisions stem from a social planner, thereby indicating how a conventional, centralized perspective may fail to reflect private incentives for generation expansion in evolving electricity markets. Third, the analysis of strategic behavior necessitates state-of-the-art decomposition techniques such as the constraint generation-based algorithm and the column-and-constraint generation algorithm for the bi- and tri-level problems, respectively.

Title: Power-gas infrastructure planning under weather-induced supply and demand uncertainties
Authors: Rahman Khorramfar, Dharik Mallapragada, Saurabh Amin
Abstract: Implementing economy-wide decarbonization strategies based on decarbonizing the power grid via variable renewable energy (VRE) expansion and electrification of end-uses requires new approaches for energy infrastructure planning that consider, among other factors, weather-induced uncertainty in demand and VRE supply. An energy planning model that fails to account for these uncertainties can hinder the intended transition efforts to a low-carbon grid and increase the risk of supply shortage especially during extreme weather conditions. Here, we consider the generation and transmission expansion problem of joint power-gas infrastructure and operations planning under the uncertainty of both demand and renewable supply. We propose two distributionally robust optimization approaches based on moment (MDRO) and Wasserstein distance (WDRO) ambiguity sets to endogenize these uncertainties and account for the change in the underlying distribution of these parameters that is caused by the climate change, among other factors. Furthermore, our model considers the risk-aversion of the energy planners in the modeling framework via the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) metric. An equivalent mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of both modeling frameworks is presented, and a computationally efficient approximation scheme to obtain near-optimal solutions is proposed. We demonstrate the resulting DRO planning models and solution strategy via a New England case study under different levels of end-use electrification and decarbonization targets. Our experiments systematically explore different modeling aspects and compare the DRO models with stochastic programming (SP) results.

Title: Robust collaborative routing problem with time-dependent travel times and uncertain service durations for home services
Authors: Li Jiang, Xiaoning Zang, Changyong Liang, Xiang Fang
Abstract: Balancing cost efficiency with high service quality has become a challenge for service providers in the rapidly growing home service sector, where tasks are time-sensitive and affected by traffic conditions and uncertain service durations. To address this, we propose a robust collaborative routing model that integrates time-dependent travel times and uncertain service durations, enabling multiple providers to optimize routes jointly, reduce costs, and improve service reliability. The proposed model captures two major sources of uncertainty: (i) time-dependent travel times arising from urban traffic congestion and (ii) stochastic service durations due to personalized task requirements. To handle these complexities, we propose a route-based robust optimization framework with a master problem and multiple pricing problems and incorporate individual rationality constraints to ensure sustainable long-term collaboration. A robust branch-price-and-cut algorithm is developed to solve the model, integrating column generation for the master problem with a tailored robust labeling algorithm for the pricing problems. Computational experiments on benchmark and real-world instances validate the efficiency and effectiveness of our method in handling uncertainty. Results also reveal a key trade-off: while collaboration considerably reduces total cost and fleet size, it may increase the risk of service delays. Our approach addresses this by incorporating tunable robustness parameters, which offer decision-makers a practical means to balance cost efficiency with service reliability.

Title: Geometric optimization of wildlife corridors on grid-based landscapes using integer programming
Authors: Chao Wang, Jorge A. Sefair, Robert J. Fletcher
Abstract: Conservation corridors play a critical role in mitigating biodiversity loss by linking fragmented habitats. A central challenge in designing these corridors lies in satisfying ecological requirements through geometric constraints such as connectivity, redundancy, width, and size. In this study, we propose a mixed-integer programming model that integrates these geometric features into the corridor design process, with the objective of maximizing corridor utility over a grid-based landscape. To enhance computational performance, we develop a Branch-and-Cut algorithm supported by a bound-improving heuristic, valid inequalities, and a variable reduction preprocessing routine. We evaluate our approach on a real-world landscape aimed at protecting the Florida panther, as well as on a suite of computer-generated landscapes. Results show that the algorithm can efficiently produce near-optimal solutions for instances with up to 3000 patches within a two-hour time limit.

Title: Taxing emissions and de-risking investments in renewables: Insights from electricity markets
Authors: Ibrahim Abada
Abstract: We investigate the optimal design of CO 2 taxation policies along with renewable energy de-risking instruments in the context of decarbonizing power sectors that are subject to investment risk. We develop a two-stage multi-period stochastic equilibrium model that captures endogenous investment decisions regarding production and storage assets. Some market fundamentals, such as demand, prices, and production profiles, are risky. Furthermore, investors are risk-averse and the financial market is incomplete inasmuch as it lacks sufficient risk-sharing instruments. The model integrates economic and environmental incentives through a multi-objective framework based on social welfare and emissions, allowing for the characterization of the Pareto-optimal frontier for de-risking/emissions-taxation policies. As a proof of concept, we apply the model to a stylized representation of the French power system, considering a diverse mix of generation and storage technologies. Our results show that de-risking instruments and CO 2 taxes are imperfect substitutes and must be optimized jointly to avoid suboptimal outcomes—such as over-investment in renewable production, market distortions induced by excessive de-risking, or insufficient emissions reductions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that commonly used de-risking instruments in Europe may lead to spot-market inefficiencies and welfare losses. Our findings provide actionable policy guidance by identifying optimal de-risking/emissions-taxation combinations and quantifying the performance gap in current European policies relative to the Pareto frontier.

Title: From the ivory tower to the field: The impact of humanitarian operations research on humanitarian practice
Authors: Erica Gralla, Maria Besiou
Abstract: Since the first publications on humanitarian operations, researchers have been concerned about the impact of our research on humanitarian practice. This paper seeks to better understand the gap between research and practice and, thus, how to narrow it. We incorporate not only the research perspective, through a review of 640 abstracts in humanitarian operations and a survey of the author community, but also the practitioner perspective, through 18 interviews with experienced humanitarian practitioners and a review of 131 practitioner conference proceedings. We assess the extent of practice impact, and find limited but important instances. We identify new barriers to achieving practice impact from the practitioner perspective. Finally, we develop a framework for describing the depth and reach of practice impact achieved by a research project, with a description of many ways in which such impact may be (and has been) achieved. We hope these efforts enable greater researcher accountability to practitioners and clearer paths to practice impact for the field.

Title: Dynamic incentive mechanisms on renewable power consumption with generators’ competition
Authors: Shuqin Xu, Qi Xu, Devika Kannan, Kannan Govindan
Abstract: The growing penetration of renewable energy into the power grid has heightened competition between renewable and conventional generators. To facilitate renewable power consumption and carbon emissions reduction, and to ensure a higher quality of power supply, this paper considers that the energy trading platform incentivizes competitive power generators to improve electricity supply quality by offering dynamic incentive contracts. This study examines how to formulate dynamic incentive contracts with considering competition between power generators over electricity supply quality. It compares dynamic contracts with and without competition, as well as static contracts under competition. Additionally, case studies from China and Australia's power sectors are analysed. The results demonstrate that dynamic contracts enhance renewable energy consumption as competition intensity increases. Compared to the non-competitive scenario, dynamic contracts incorporating competition incentivize power generators to deliver higher electricity supply quality. When the potential share of green electricity demand exceeds a certain threshold, Australia achieves higher renewable electricity trading volumes and consumption levels than China.
