As competition intensifies, China must more promptly take measures to meet the required share of green electricity demand to achieve its 2030 renewable energy targets. Furthermore, the study contributes to the revenue management field and finds that dynamic contracts outperform static contracts, supporting the United Nations 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. Renewable energy consumption performs significantly better under dynamic contracts.

Title: Do social relationships lead to bias in group decision-making? A simulation analysis based on screening-selection model
Authors: Xue Feng, Shifeng Liu, Yuan Xu, Xiaopu Shang
Abstract: In the group decision-making (GDM) process, social networks play a crucial role in facilitating communication and information exchange among decision-makers (DMs). However, most existing GDM models primarily focus on interactions among DMs, while neglecting the social relationships between DMs and the alternatives being evaluated (named “reviewees”). As decision-making environments grow more complex and involve numerous alternatives, traditional single-stage GDM models often struggle to balance efficiency and accuracy. To address the above limitations, we propose a screening-selection GDM (SS-GDM) model, which integrates both the social trust network among DMs and the social relationships between DMs and reviewees, thereby capturing how social factors influence opinion dynamics and consensus formation across two distinct yet interconnected stages: the screening stage and the selection stage. A numerical case and comparative analyses demonstrate the practical application and advantages of the proposed SS-GDM method. Simulation experiments further indicate that social trust and opinion similarity are the key drivers in shaping group opinions and promoting consensus. However, the social relationships between DMs and reviewees can lead to bias during the screening stage. In contrast, the selection stage characterized by open communication can weaken such bias. Additionally, when reviewees exhibit high capability, such bias tends to diminish. Overall, this model enhances our understanding of how social networks influence GDM processes and provides actionable strategies to improve fairness and reduce bias in real-world GDM scenarios, such as excluding DMs with close social ties to reviewees, anonymizing reviewee information during the screening stage, and encouraging open communication during the selection stage.

Title: Substitute recommendations and in-transit order cancellations
Authors: Guangyong Yang, Yunhuan Zhang
Abstract: Online retail platforms are implementing in-transit order cancellations (ITOC) through digital logistics such as delivery interception. Although originally designed to reduce return losses for sellers and enhance consumer experience, platforms have repurposed ITOC into a marketing tool that creates additional revenue by using substitute recommendations to induce consumers to cancel initial orders and purchase substitutes. This study analytically examines how the interplay of substitute recommendations and ITOC affects the profits of downstream platform and upstream seller in an agency-based supply chain. Our findings show that platforms benefit from ITOC even when recommending inferior substitutes, while sellers benefit under conditions of high value losses from returns and low consumer return hassle costs. Furthermore, when premium substitutes are recommended, ITOC may create a conflict of interest between platforms and sellers, whereas recommending inferior substitutes better aligns their interests. Our study highlights that substitute recommendations and ITOC can be complementary, enabling platforms to balance seller interests and their profits.

Title: An active three-way concept-cognitive computing system for dynamic financial fraud detection
Authors: Yun-Long Mi, Yi Qu, Huan Zhu, Zongrun Wang, Gang Kou, Yong Shi
Abstract: Fraud detection is a popular topic in financial services, and has been extensively studied in different areas such as accounting and finance, information systems, business intelligence, and data mining. However, most machine learning methods rely on supervised learning and assume a balanced class distribution within the data. This ignores the problems of evolving data over time, between-class imbalance, and label scarcity in the fraud detection process. Crucially, these methods cannot obtain outstanding detection prediction performance due to their failure to address the dynamic data with limited labels and class imbalance. Therefore, we propose a novel dynamic fraud detection method: active three-way concept-cognitive computing system (atC3S). It comprises constructing an initial learning model, making fraud predictions, active three-way concept learning, and updating the learning model. The atC3S leverages an active three-way concept learning method, concept-center neighborhood, and concept-dynamic optimization strategies to improve the effectiveness of dynamic fraud detection. Experimental results on several real-world financial fraud datasets show that atC3S can demonstrate excellent performance on discriminating between fraudulent and nonfraudulent detections under label scarcity and class imbalance scenarios. Finally, excessive requests for label information from experts are not the most cost-effective strategy considering the label acquisition cost.

Title: The impact of technology spillover and diffusion on competing manufacturers’ market expansion strategies
Authors: Hui Huang, Bin Liu, Naimeng Liu
Abstract: In technology-asymmetric markets, technology upgrading may help weak manufacturers expand, but it can also intensify rivalry with powerful incumbents. Weak manufacturers may rely on passive technology spillover, whereas powerful manufacturers may respond through deliberate technology diffusion under profit sharing. This paper develops a two-stage Stackelberg game to examine how these two upgrading paths jointly shape market encroachment and firms’ strategic incentives. A distinctive feature of our framework is that competition intensity is endogenous to the technology gap, so technology upgrading affects not only perceived product quality but also the intensity of rivalry. We show that technology spillover does not uniformly improve the weak manufacturer's market expansion outcome. Although spillover improves product appeal, it can also intensify competition enough to reduce the profitability of substantial encroachment. However, we also find that technology spillover may broaden the boundary of substantial encroachment when the spillover level remains relatively low. Technology diffusion is sustained under a narrower set of conditions. It becomes attractive when the weak manufacturer's cost disadvantage is limited, and the technology gap is sufficiently small, and it may arise either as a jointly preferred arrangement or as a defensive response to unmanaged spillover. We further characterize the implementable range of profit-sharing terms and show that technology diffusion may be strategically desirable yet contractually infeasible when technological or cost asymmetry is too large. These findings clarify how alternative upgrading paths reshape market encroachment and when rival upgrading can be sustained through contract-based governance.

Title: Chance-constrained battery management for electric bus scheduling
Authors: Léa Ricard, Guy Desaulniers, Andrea Lodi, Louis-Martin Rousseau
Abstract: The adoption of electric buses introduces challenges related to limited driving range, extended charging times, and strict battery management requirements. These requirements — often set by battery leasing companies or warranty providers — typically include recommended ranges for the battery's state-of-charge (SoC). This study addresses these challenges by proposing a novel chance-constrained model for the electric vehicle scheduling problem that accounts for stochastic energy consumption and battery management guidelines. The model ensures compliance with recommended SoC ranges while optimizing operational costs. A tailored branch-and-price heuristic with stochastic pricing problems is developed. Computational experiments on realistic instances show that the stochastic approach offers good trade-offs between operational costs and compliance with battery management guidelines, reducing costs by up to 10% compared to a deterministic worst-case benchmark. In contrast, we show that relying on expected energy consumption yields solutions with a near-certain probability of violating SoC guidelines, rendering such an approach unsuitable for practical use.

Title: Two approaches for real-time robust rolling stock rescheduling given disruption duration uncertainty
Authors: Joris Wagenaar, Evelien van der Hurk, Richard Lusby, Marie Schmidt
Abstract: In railway planning, effective disruption management tools can limit the impact of a disruption. A key challenge is that disruption durations are typically uncertain, leading to inefficiencies such as unnecessary shunting, seat-shortages, end-of-day inventory mismatches, and trip cancellations. To address this challenge, we propose two different approaches for incorporating robustness in real-time rolling stock rescheduling under uncertain disruption duration, an aspect that is typically assumed to be known in existing rescheduling models. The first approach, Light trip robustness (LTR) requires that a pre-specified percentage of critical trips are robust with respect to their incoming composition across different disruption durations. The second approach, Strict composition robustness (STR), ensures feasibility across all possible disruption durations without further changes to compositions or shunting operations. Both methods extend a well-known rolling stock rescheduling model by explicitly accounting for multiple possible disruption durations. We develop an online evaluation framework and conduct a computational study using real-world data from the Dutch railway network. Our results demonstrate that explicitly accounting for disruption duration uncertainty can significantly reduce rescheduling costs when disruptions last longer than initially expected. For instance, the STR model achieves up to 21% lower total costs compared to models that do not consider robustness, while the LTR model offers flexibility and performs well under moderate uncertainty. However, these benefits can come at a cost when the initially expected disruption duration is accurate. Overall, our results show that robust rolling stock rescheduling can significantly improve operational resilience and reduces the need for reactive updates. The appropriate level of robustness should be chosen based on the likelihood of disruption duration extensions.

Title: The collect-and-process vehicle routing problem with completion time minimization: An application in home healthcare
Authors: Leandro C. Coelho, Simona Mancini
Abstract: Home healthcare (or simply homecare) refers to providing medical services to individuals in their homes rather than in a hospital or in outpatient clinics. This system is convenient for the public authorities, which reduces the operational costs of medical facilities, is beneficial for the environment because it prevents patients from going to a hospital, and is comfortable for patients who can receive medical assistance without leaving their houses. In this work, we deal with clinical exams such as blood sampling, which requires collecting a sample from the patient and delivering it to a laboratory where it must be processed and analyzed. Currently, healthcare professionals collect all the samples and then deliver them to the labs at the end of the day. This results in an inefficiency in the processing system, in which labs are overloaded in the late afternoon and are not working during the first part of the day. To better balance lab workload and provide timely results to the patients, we introduce the Collect-and-Process Vehicle Routing Problem with Completion Time minimization, in which each lab has a maximum processing capacity for each time slot, and samples exceeding this capacity are postponed to the next slot. The goal is to provide a routing and scheduling plan that minimizes a sample’s average completion time. We provide a formulation of the problem and a fast procedure to compute tight lower bounds. To efficiently and effectively handle large-sized instances, we develop a multi-neighborhood local search matheuristic. Results show the high-quality performance of the proposed method. Insights indicate that it is more convenient to visit labs at the end of the time slot than to visit them at the beginning and exploit the residual time to collect further samples. Another insight is that solutions containing well-balanced routes in terms of route duration are preferable with respect to unbalanced ones.

Title: Exact methods and a scalable heuristic for a hierarchical bi-objective two-agent scheduling problem
Authors: Shijin Wang, Ruihe Liu, Yihong Hu, Feng Chu
Abstract: This paper studies a hierarchical bi-objective two-agent scheduling problem motivated by a practical Print-on-Demand (POD) production setting. The primary objective is to minimize the total number of tardy jobs, and the secondary objective is to minimize the absolute difference in average weighted tardiness between the two agents, thereby capturing an efficiency–fairness trade-off. We formulate two mixed integer programming (MIP) models using position-based and time-indexed decision variables, and strengthen them with five valid inequalities (VIs). To solve medium-scale instances to optimality, we develop a tailored decomposition-based cutting-plane (CP) method enhanced with three infeasibility cuts and one no-good cut. For larger instances, we design a two-stage heuristic combining tardy-pattern search and sequence refinement. Computational experiments evaluate the valid inequalities, the efficiency–fairness trade-off, the limits of the exact methods, the dispatching-rule baselines, and the heuristic scalability. The results show that the position-based MIP formulation enhanced with all VIs reduces average solution times for small instances by about 97%. They further reveal that allowing only one or two additional tardy jobs can reduce the fairness imbalance. The exact CP method solves most instances with up to 50 jobs within one hour and can prove optimality for many tested instances with 80 and 100 jobs, although with more variable runtimes. The heuristic outperforms baseline dispatching rules andobtains high-quality solutions for instances with up to 1000 jobs within seconds. These results provide a scalable solution framework for fairness-aware real-world POD scheduling.

Title: Scheduling in distributed two-machine permutation flow shops for maximizing the total early work subject to arbitrary due dates
Authors: Xin Chen, Yongkang Zhao, Xinbo Liu, Bertrand M.T. Lin, Jacek Blazewicz
Abstract: This study addresses the problem of maximizing total early work in distributed flow shops that are composed of multiple identical distributed two-stage flow shops. The total early work criterion quantifies the cumulative benefit of scheduling jobs relative to their arbitrary due dates. To tackle this challenge, we first present a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) model to formalize the problem. We establish that the general problem is computationally intractable and prove that even a simplified scenario involving a single flow shop remains strongly NP-hard. However, for the special case where the number of due dates is constant, we introduce a pseudo-polynomial time dynamic programming algorithm, demonstrating that the problem is then weakly NP-hard. Furthermore, we design two meta-heuristic approaches, a genetic algorithm and an ejection chain algorithm, to generate high-quality scheduling solutions. Computational experiments reveal that the genetic algorithm outperforms the ejection chain algorithm in terms of scheduling quality, though it requires a longer running time.

Title: Minimizing maximum regret in two-stage facility location with site preparation costs
Authors: Ronald G. McGarvey, Andreas Thorsen
Abstract: This paper introduces the two-stage capacitated facility location problem under demand and facility construction cost uncertainty with site preparation costs. In the first stage, the decision maker decides whether to pay site preparation costs to obtain an option for potential future utilization of a facility at each candidate site. In the second stage, after demand and facility construction costs are known, the decision maker decides whether to execute each option and construct a facility at each prepared site, and simultaneously allocates demands across the utilized facilities. We use a robust optimization framework with budgeted uncertainty sets to formulate a mixed-integer linear program and develop a column-and-constraint generation algorithm, incorporating a Benders decomposition approach, to solve the resulting minimax regret problem. We conduct numerical tests to identify the relationship between problem conditions and the optimal solution’s properties. We further examine the performance of the minimax regret solution evaluated against the minimax cost objective (and vice versa), and find that minimax cost solutions exhibit higher worst-case regret for instances with a large percentage of fixed cost associated with the first-stage decision and one of the following conditions: (a) small transportation cost, (b) large total facility cost, or (c) a large number of potential facilities. The minimax regret model appears to hedge against the potential regret of overinvestment in the first stage by preparing fewer facilities and increasing capacity utilization, at the expense of larger travel distances.

Title: Editorial Board
Science-Industry Collaborations over the Business Cycle: Evidence from European Regions
Authors: Aurelien Quignon
Abstract: Business cycles shape the innovation incentives and search strategies of science and industry. Using a novel dataset of collaborative patents across 218 European regions from 1990 to 2018, this paper examines the association between recessions and regional science-industry collaborations. I find that science-industry collaborations decrease during economic recessions and increase during expansions. Further analyses suggest that business cycles are associated with shifts in science-industry collaborations' innovation search strategies, with the exploitation of technologies already known to the region increasing during expansion. In contrast, the exploration of new technologies is acyclical. Results contribute to our understanding of collaborative innovation dynamics over the business cycle and offer new insights into the negative effects of recessions.

Title: Beyond the clock: Submission timing and research impact
Authors: Guangyao Zhang, Lili Wang, Wencan Tian, Xianwen Wang
Abstract: In today's hypercompetitive scientific environment, researchers increasingly face strong incentives to secure priority in discovery. This paper investigates the relationship between the timing of scholarly paper submissions and their subsequent impact. Using over 600,000 arXiv submission records linked to citation counts, journal placement, editorial recognition, and online attention, we find positive pooled associations across all four measures, while the within-submitter evidence is strongest for citations and top-journal placement. Moreover, the association is stronger in more recent years and for submissions made by female scientists, scientists with greater academic influence, and researchers located in countries with a stronger long-term orientation. Taken together, the findings suggest that non-standard submission timing may serve as a revealed-preference signal of the relative priority assigned to a project. They do not imply that submitting or working outside standard hours causes higher-quality research.

Title: What Interruptions Say About Your Organizational Culture
Authors: Ghulam Murtaza, Benjamin Laker, Rahman Khan, Athar Hameed
Abstract: Recent research suggests that interruptions when meeting attendees are speaking are significant moments that affect how employees experience workplace culture and can lead to self-censoring. Taking a different approach to meeting facilitation can help leaders become more aware of when this is occurring so that they can improve participant dynamics, encourage meeting attendees to contribute, and more effectively respond to interruptions.

Title: Synthesizing Information-Driven Insider Trade Signals
Authors: Jens Heckmann, Heiko Jacobs, Patrick Schwarz
Affiliations: University of Duisburg-Essen; University of Liège HEC Liège
Abstract: Abstract We propose a novel approach to synthesize presumably information-driven insider trading signals for the cross section of stocks. We find that the resulting straightforward composite strategy can often forecast returns in a global sample. This predictability is strongest in equal-weighted portfolios, short holding periods, and insider-buying signals, and it improves further with global diversification. Cross-country analysis reveals that varying insider trading restrictions between countries have limited explanatory power for the performance of the composite strategy. Overall, the results are consistent with a short-term informational advantage of insiders, which might be due to the skillful interpretation of non-private news.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Conceptual search: A generative view of entrepreneurial imagination
Authors: Felipe A. Csaszar
Affiliations: Ross School of Business University of Michigan Ann Arbor Michigan USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs cannot pursue ventures they never imagine. This article develops a generative view of entrepreneurial imagination as the construction of an evolving candidate set through generation, provisional evaluation, and revision. Conceptual search represents venture concepts as text, transforms them through interpretable operations, and compares their promise. A large language model prototype demonstrates complementary modes: local refinement lifts a concept from sixteenth to third among 30 ventures under a validated evaluator, while global recombination reaches distant possibilities that refinement makes competitive. The framework shows how search architecture determines what enters, survives, and develops, and how AI may broaden imagination within firms while producing correlated imagination across firms. By making imagination programmable, auditable, and experimentally tractable, conceptual search opens a research program on how entrepreneurial possibilities are constructed. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs can pursue only the ventures they imagine, and valuable ideas routinely go unbuilt because nobody thinks of them. AI makes imagining cheap: it can draft, critique, and rewrite venture concepts in seconds, so developing ideas becomes a process that can be designed, run, and audited. I demonstrate a system that evolves real venture concepts: step‐by‐step refinement lifted a middling concept to third place among 30 real ventures, as ranked by an AI judge shown to predict fundraising, while recombining distant ideas created novel concepts that refinement made competitive. The entrepreneur's job shifts from generating a few ideas to governing many: choosing what to search, keep, and test in the market. One caution: rivals using the same AI will imagine similar ventures; advantage comes from proprietary problems, data, and evidence.

Title: Common ownership and consumer welfare
Authors: Saeed Janani, Sina Aghaie, Darima Fotheringham, Mark B. Houston
Abstract: Abstract Rival firms with shared institutional investors (i.e., common owners) may compete less aggressively, potentially harming consumer welfare. Yet, research on common ownership has primarily focused on firm performance, often overlooking welfare outcomes or revealing contradictory results. This paper adopts a strategic network perspective to examine how common ownership affects firms’ service quality and pricing levels, which directly impact consumer welfare, and how customer and competitor factors that alter the focus of competitive strategy moderate these effects. To test the hypotheses, the authors analyze a rich, multi-market dataset of U.S. airline firms from 1995 to 2025. Findings reveal that competing firms with higher common ownership tend to have lower service quality and set higher prices. However, this effect is attenuated for firms with high customer-asset value and amplified among rivals competing across multiple markets. The findings demonstrate common ownership’s influence on firms’ marketing mix strategies and offer actionable insights for managers, policymakers, and investors.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Pairwise comparisons meet optimal transport theory
Authors: Matteo Brunelli, Silvia Lorenzini
Abstract: In this paper, we reinterpret pairwise comparison theory through the lens of optimal transport. The main contribution is the connection established between pairwise comparison matrices, doubly stochastic scaling, and entropy-regularized transport problems. Using Sinkhorn scaling, we show how consistency, priority derivation, and inconsistency assessment can be studied within a common optimal-transport framework. As methodological consequences of this connection, we obtain a new characterization of consistency, a Sinkhorn-based prioritization method, and an entropy-based inconsistency index. We study these proposals both analytically and numerically, and compare them with established methods from the literature.

Title: Competition and refurbishing strategy in closed-loop supply chains considering collection priority
Authors: Dongfeng Jia, Sijie Li
Abstract: When a brand manufacturer and an independent refurbisher (IR) both refurbish and compete, this paper introduces collection priority to allocate the limited used products (cores) between them, a mechanism that couples asymmetric collection caps with asymmetric refurbishing costs. We model this competition in a closed-loop supply chain where the manufacturer supplies both new and refurbished products while the IR supplies only refurbished products, and analyze five scenarios representing different refurbisher configurations and priority regimes. Four equilibrium regions arise under each collection-priority regime, with six distinct refurbishing strategy patterns across the two regimes. Within the partial-refurbishing region analyzed, we obtain the following findings. Adding more refurbishers does not necessarily improve profitability or reduce environmental impact. Under manufacturer priority, the IR's refurbishing-entry decision is independent of the new-product cost; under certain conditions, the priority-holding manufacturer may have a stronger incentive to refurbish alongside an active IR than alone. We also examine several extensions: the main qualitative insights largely remain robust under uncertain refurbishable yield, sequential decision making, and a two-part refurbishing-cost structure, while endogenizing the acquisition of priority reveals that competing for it is not always worthwhile; under some conditions, acquiring collection priority is payoff-irrelevant.

Title: Models for the assessment of partial scale characteristics in polyhedral technologies
Authors: Grammatoula Papaioannou, Victor V. Podinovski
Abstract: Partial scale characteristics of efficient frontiers include the notions of partial scale efficiency, most productive scale size and returns to scale that are evaluated with respect to some selected subsets of inputs and outputs, while keeping the remaining inputs and outputs fixed. We show that, in any polyhedral technology, all such partial characteristics can be assessed by solving linear programs based on the appropriately specified partial cone extension of the technology. We obtain a general operational statement of such cone extensions and illustrate our results by an example.

Title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
Authors: Samuel Häfner, Curtis R Taylor
Affiliations: University of St. Gallen; Duke University
Abstract: Abstract We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.

Title: Craft and Industrialization: Uncovering the Plasticity and Frontier of Craft
Authors: Mirva Peltoniemi, Antti Sihvonen
Affiliations: Tampere University; University of Helsinki
Abstract: Abstract Craft as an approach to work has been proposed as an alternative to industrial mass production. While industrialization has led to the replacement of craft logic with industrial logic to create uniformity and scale operations, the role of craft in industrialization remains ambiguous. Building on the analysis of engineering work performed at an R&D laboratory in the pulp and paper industry, we explore how and why craft enables industrialization. Our findings reveal how elements of craft manifest in engineering work by helping to transform ideas into useful objects, balancing scientific accuracy with practical usefulness, and fostering a sense of community and identity within the engineering field. These findings point to the plasticity of craft logic , suggesting that elements of craft can be transferred into new contexts and reinterpreted to address new objectives. Considering that these activities took place in an R&D laboratory that drove industrialization, they also reveal the existence of a craft frontier that escapes standardization by providing a context for crafting candidates for future standards. Craft frontier enables the coexistence of craft and industrial logics, where craft can contribute to industrialization by establishing foundations for managerial control without being absorbed into it.

Title: “The Minimum Wage Is the Maximum Wage”: How Goal Replacement Perpetuates Means–Ends Decoupling
Authors: Satwant Dahiya, Christian Busse
Affiliations: Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg
Abstract: This research examines how organizations contribute to the perpetuation of means–ends decoupling (MED) within issue-based fields organized around societal problems, under conditions of heightened field scrutiny. In such settings, organizations often profess commitment to field goals and visibly comply with institutionally prescribed practices to satisfy monitoring, reporting, and public evaluation requirements. However, many adopted goals remain underachieved, raising questions about how compliance without progress endures and how claims of commitment remain credible under transparency regimes intended to spur substantive goal pursuit. Our data came from 75 interviews with 68 brands, suppliers, and third-party organizations pursuing worker well-being in global fashion supply chains. We unveil auditability-based goal replacement as an organizational-level mechanism through which actors rhetorically foreground compliance as public evidence of commitment while narrowing internal goal pursuit to auditable thresholds that serve their core goals, thereby allowing shortfalls to persist. Self-silencing about this substitution and the instrumentalizing of shortfalls close the configuration into a self-reinforcing loop. The study advances MED scholarship by (i) showing how organizations leverage field conditions and appropriate the existing scrutiny infrastructures to advance their core goals while reproducing the means–ends gap, (ii) problematizing the authenticity of commitment claims, and (iii) explaining how goal-ineffective compliance prevails as a credible substitute for adopted goals. It also extends research on organizational responses to institutional complexity and calls for greater attention to institutional impact—that is, the realized advancement of the societal aim an institution emerged to address.

Title: Hybrid Kidney Allocation: Improving Equity by Fair Integration of Deceased Donor-Initiated Chains in Kidney Exchange
Authors: Roby Cremers, Twan Dollevoet, Joris van de Klundert, Michal Andrzej A. Mankowski
Affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam Erasmus School of Economics, Econometric Institute, Rotterdam, ZH, Netherlands; Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez Escuela de Negocios, Department of Operations and Analytics, Viña del Mar, Valparaiso, Chile; NYU Grossman School of Medicine, Department of Surgery, New York, New York, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Living donor kidney exchange programs (KEPs) expand access to transplants by enabling exchanges among patient-donor pairs. However, highly sensitized patients are disproportionately hard to match and face long waits. Deceased donor–initiated chains (DDICs) have been proposed to enable more transplants by diverting an occasional deceased donor kidney from the waitlist to start a KEP chain, which ends by returning a kidney to the waitlist. Yet, DDICs have seen virtually no implementation. In the U.S., this is largely due to concerns that the kidneys returned may differ in blood-type distribution from those diverted, disadvantaging waitlist patients of certain blood types. We study how DDICs can be integrated into KEPs while explicitly protecting blood-type-specific waitlist access. Methodology/results: We develop two forward-looking optimization approaches: one that solves a stochastic model using Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and one that solves a static model with forward-looking constraints. Through simulation, we show that forward-looking models are needed to preserve the blood-type distribution of donations to the waitlist. Under both models, even limited use of DDICs significantly increases transplant rates for highly sensitized patients. While the static approach requires only modest extensions to models as currently used in practice, the more complex and time consuming SAA-based approach yields larger equity gains. Managerial implications: DDICs can improve access to life-saving transplants for the most disadvantaged KEP patients without reducing access for any blood type on the waitlist. By explicitly controlling the blood-type distribution of waitlist donations, matching policies can address objections that have hindered DDIC adoption, calling for renewed policy evaluation.

Title: The effect of prime brokers’ balance sheet constraints on hedge fund performance: Evidence from the GSIB surcharge
Authors: Yueting Jiang, Yiwen Shen
Abstract: Hedge funds often use leverage provided by prime brokers to enhance their investment returns. We investigate how prime brokers’ capital constraints impact the performance of connected hedge funds. At the hedge fund level, we construct a measure for prime brokers’ balance sheet constraints using the capital requirements under the Basel III framework. We document that tighter balance sheet constraints of prime brokers lead to lower future return, alpha, volatility, Sharpe ratio, and information ratio of the hedge funds. These findings are consistent with an analytical model in which prime brokers respond to balance sheet constraints by increasing leverage cost or decreasing leverage provision to hedge funds. We show that the estimated effects are more pronounced for hedge funds with higher leverage demand elasticities and during more capital-binding periods. Our results reveal the real effects of bank regulation on connected financial institutions via the services of prime brokers. We conduct empirical tests for our identification strategy and support our findings via multiple robustness checks.

Title: What Do “Most People” Believe? Race, Gender, and the Generalized Other
Authors: Natasha Quadlin, Trenton D. Mize, Long Doan, Bianca Manago
Affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles; Purdue University; University of Maryland; Vanderbilt University
Abstract: When people form beliefs in social life, they often calibrate their own thinking against what they anticipate “most people” think. Although prior research demonstrates the importance of these inferences, scholars have yet to examine who is best proxied by “most people.” Given persistent inequalities in U.S. society that advantage White men, as well as theories of cultural hegemony, we hypothesize that “most people’s” imagined beliefs are closely proxied by those of White men. We test these ideas using an original survey experiment conducted with a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults ( N = 2,089) in which we adapt 64 core items from the General Social Survey. Respondents were randomly assigned to answer these questions either from the perspective of most people, or from the perspective of designated race-gender groups. Contrary to our hypothesis, we find strong and consistent evidence that White men are not seen as standard-bearers for most social issues. Instead, perceptions of what most people believe are highly aligned with the imagined beliefs of White women. Importantly, this pattern emerges not because White women are seen as influential, but because White women are perceived as less extreme than other groups. We also observe variation across respondents, such that respondents tend to center their own race-gender group in conceptualizing most people’s beliefs (with White women typically close behind).

Title: Peer benchmarking and digital upgrading: Field experiments on business websites
Authors: Anwar Adem, Richard Kneller, Qian Cher Li
Abstract: Can low-cost comparative information trigger firms to improve the performance of a digital asset they already own? Using two large-scale randomised controlled trials with approximately 7000 UK firms in the distilling and retail sectors, we study whether peer benchmarking of website performance prompts measurable improvement. Firms receiving benchmarked website metrics and targeted recommendations exhibit modest average improvements, with more favourable effects among initially underperforming firms, consistent with partial convergence towards the industry frontier. The catch-up dynamic is strongest on mobile metrics, including as a spillover in the first experiment, in which reports contained desktop metrics only, a pattern consistent with firms focusing improvement efforts where performance gaps are greatest. Treated firms also show suggestive report-aligned increases in the adoption of mobile-optimisation and content-delivery technologies. These patterns are consistent with comparative performance information helping firms identify and respond to performance shortfalls. The findings position peer benchmarking as a scalable, low-cost instrument for narrowing the digital divide among SMEs: informational aspiration cues generate more favourable responses among firms furthest behind than among firms nearer the frontier.

Title: Capital Market Pressure and Racial Inequality in Labor Violations
Authors: Seth S. Carnahan, Sarah E. McVay, MaryJane R. Rabier
Affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis; University of Washington
Abstract: ABSTRACT Managers can boost reported earnings to meet capital market expectations by pursuing aggressive cost-minimization strategies that violate labor laws, such as pressuring frontline employees to forgo safety protocols or work off the clock. We investigate whether labor law violations, which benefit the firm at the expense of employees, fall disproportionately on nonwhite frontline employees. Across similar locations (e.g., stores or plants) within the same firm, we predict and find that locations with a higher share of nonwhite frontline employees are more likely to experience a labor law violation. This racial inequality in labor violations is especially pronounced in settings more prone to racial discrimination and during periods of acute capital market pressure to meet earnings benchmarks, providing insight into the mechanisms underlying the observed disparity. Our evidence suggests that capital market pressure is associated not only with labor violations but also with racial inequality in exposure to those violations. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text.

Title: Enabling Employee Adaptability to Change: The Joint Effect of Compensation Contract and Process Accountability
Authors: Marte Abts, Martine Cools, Sabra Khajehnejad, Alexandra Van den Abbeele
Affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; KU Leuven
Abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations increasingly operate in uncertain environments, requiring employees to revise task strategies to remain effective. We examine how pay for performance (PFP) influences adaptive performance following unanticipated change and argue that process accountability moderates this effect. Although PFP increases effort, it hinders adaptation by reinforcing persistence with an existing task strategy. Process accountability channels PFP-induced motivation into deeper strategic deliberation, enabling adaptation. We test our predictions in an experiment manipulating compensation (PFP versus flat wage) and process accountability (absent, reflection-only, and present), with participants in the reflection-only condition privately reflecting on their decision-making to isolate the social-evaluative component. Results show that PFP, relative to a flat wage, decreases adaptive performance when process accountability is absent, has no significant effect under reflection-only, and increases it when process accountability is present. Additional analyses suggest that strategic deliberation partially explains this effect. The findings underscore pairing PFP with process accountability to foster adaptation. Data Availability: Data are available upon request. JEL Classifications: D91; M21; M41; M52.

Title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
Authors: Georg von Krogh, Ann‐Kristin Weiser, Patrick Nicolas Tinguely
Affiliations: Department of Management, Technology, and Economics ETH Zurich Zürich Switzerland
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

Title: Managing the dual nature of customer engagement in product innovation: A sensegiving and sensemaking perspective
Authors: Zhenghao Michael Xia, Xiaodong Marcus Li, Kang Xie, Jinghua Xiao, Wanghua Cao
Abstract: Customer engagement can both facilitate and complicate continuous incremental product innovation. Customer contributions may deepen a firm’s market understanding, yet they can also fragment product direction or reinforce familiar solution paths. Although these competing effects have been widely documented, less is known about how firms interpret customer contributions and translate them into actionable product direction. This study addresses this gap through an inductive, comparative case study of four video game firms, drawing on sensegiving and sensemaking as analytical lenses to examine firm activity at the customer interface. The analysis identifies two recurring risks of customer engagement, cognitive misalignment and cognitive redundancy, and two recurring benefits, expertise deepening and scalable feedback. Firms manage these risks and benefits through two strategies: directive guidance preserves the usefulness of customer input when such input threatens product coherence, whereas integrative collaboration enables learning from customer contributions when engagement creates genuine opportunities for product development. Building on these findings, this study develops a process model showing how firms sustain product coherence while continuing to learn from customer input within continuous incremental innovation.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
Authors: Jonathan Gruber, Adam Solomon
Affiliations: MIT, and NBER; NYU Stern
Abstract: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

Title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
Authors: David Argente, Esteban Méndez, Diana Van Patten
Affiliations: Yale University and NBER; Central Bank of Costa Rica
Abstract: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

Title: The Rise of Alternatives
Authors: Juliane Begenau, Pauline Liang, Emil Siriwardane
Affiliations: Stanford GSB, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, NBER, and CEPR; Georgia Tech; Harvard Business School and NBER
Abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data.

Title: The economics of data unions: optimal data sharing and coordination
Authors: Lin William Cong, Simon Mayer
Affiliations: Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University, 91 Nanyang Avenue, Wee Cho Yaw Plaza, Singapore 639956; Fanhai International School of Finance (FISF), Fudan University, Building E, 311 Bishui Road, Yangpu District, Shanghai 200433, China; PBC School of Finance (PBCSF), Tsinghua University, 43 Chengfu Road, Haidian District, Beijing 100083, China; Tepper School of Business, Carnegie Mellon University, 4765 Forbes Avenue, Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA
Abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

Title: Measurement Error, Manipulation, and the Value of Short‐Term Performance in Job Retention
Authors: Naomi Rothenberg
Affiliations: Department of Accounting and Business Analytics University of Alberta Edmonton Alberta Canada
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how the accuracy of a short‐term performance measure affects its value when a principal decides whether to retain or fire an agent, who can manipulate that measure. Compared with ignoring performance and never firing the agent, the performance measure is valuable when the savings in the expected cost of the retention error is more than the expected cost of the firing error. A more accurate performance measure can have a non‐monotonic effect on its value: Greater accuracy improves the principal's ability to correctly identify the agent, which increases efficient firing, but it causes the incompetent agent to increase manipulation to avoid being fired, which increases inefficient retention. With a less accurate performance measure, the incompetent agent has weaker incentives for manipulation, and an increase in accuracy increases its value due to the identification effect. With a more accurate performance measure, the manipulation effect dominates, and an increase in accuracy decreases its value. The results imply that the principal prefers an imperfect performance measure when the agent can choose the level of manipulation.

Title: Book Review: Joel Gehman, Paula Jarzabkowski, Ann Langley, and Haridimos Tsoukas (Eds). Organizing beyond Organizations for the Common Good: Confronting Societal Challenges through Process Studies GehmanJ.JarzabkowskiP.LangleyA.TsoukasH. (Eds.). (2025). Organizing beyond organizations for the common good: Confronting societal challenges through process studies. Oxford University Press. 272 pp. ISBN 9780198956648
Authors: Fannie Couture, Jean-François Soublière
Affiliations: HEC Montréal, Montréal (QC), Canada

Title: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
Authors: Lars Kaiser, Alexander Edeling, Marc Fischer
Abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.

Title: From chit-chat to conversion: Cost-efficient conversational recommendation via retrospective learning and isolated reflection
Authors: Jiahui Wang, Hongke Zhao, Likang Wu, Bing Lv, Ning Jia
Affiliations: Tianjin University
Abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

Title: Do you lose when you sell loose? Impact of unpackaged sales on profit and waste
Authors: Ismail Kirci, Dorothee Honhon, Alp Muharremoglu
Affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign; University of Texas at Dallas; Amazon.com
Abstract: Loose sales—the sale of unpackaged products by unit or weight—are frequently promoted as a way to reduce waste because they allow consumers to purchase exactly the quantity they want, rather than being constrained by the fixed quantities dictated by the pre-packaged format. We study a retailer selling a highly perishable product under two possible formats: fixed-size packages and/or loose. The retailer chooses prices and package size to maximize profit. Consumers perceive loose products as fresher, but they also incur an inconvenience cost arising from the additional time and effort required. For the retailer, loose sales carry a higher unit variable cost due to increased labor requirements. In a homogeneous market, we show that, if consumers place substantially higher value on the loose option and its cost is not significantly greater than that of packaged sale, the retailer can make more profit selling only loose at a high price to consumers who buy the quantity they desire. Otherwise, the retailer is better off selling packages of large size, forcing consumers to buy more than they desire to purchase. Interestingly, consumer waste can actually be greater when the product is sold exclusively in loose format. In a heterogeneous market with two consumer segments which differ in the magnitude of their consumption needs, three possible optimal strategies emerge: selling only loose to both segments, selling only (relatively small) packages to both segments, or selling (relatively large) packages to high-consumption needs consumers and selling loose to the low-consumption needs consumers. Our results also demonstrate that selling loose instead of or alongside packages can often be a win-win strategy, simultaneously boosting retailer profits and reducing consumer waste compared to selling only packages. However, in some cases, introducing loose sales may increase waste. These findings indicate that retailers may derive financial gains from offering products in loose form; however, they should ensure that the associated sustainability benefits are genuine before positioning it as a green strategy. Likewise, policymakers seeking to reduce food waste should carefully consider product-and market-specific conditions rather than promoting loose sales as a universally effective waste-reduction measure.

Title: When good practices go too far: Overshooting in organizational culture
Authors: Francisco Brahm, Christoph Loch, Joaquin Poblete
Affiliations: London Business School; University of Navarra; Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile
Abstract: Business research has examined how useful practices can be made to spread and develop in organizations. However, practices have been observed “overshooting”: either over-diffusing—too many employees adopt them, including some whose usage is unproductive; or becoming over-sophisticated—the practice becomes too elaborate, reducing organizational performance. Independent models of over-diffusion and over-sophistication have been proposed; this article integrates both aspects in a simple, unified model of overshooting. We offer a cultural evolution model that studies how interaction dynamics among employees are able to diffuse and stabilize an equilibrium of underperforming cultural practices, at the same time over-developing the practice so its sophistication goes beyond productive levels. People adopt practices from others based on information about the practice’s productive value, but also influenced by social dynamics with other employees, such as status. Our model clarifies the circumstances in which over-diffusion and over-sophistication can arise, and how these two elements of overshooting relate to each other. We map our model in detail to two cases—process management practices (e.g., six sigma) and Uber’s aggressive culture—and discuss the managerial implications.

Title: Interoperability Meets Accountability: How Data Interoperability and Experiential Quality Influence Malpractice Lawsuits
Authors: Sukrit Pal, David E. Cantor, Anand Nair
Abstract: A persistent challenge that many patients continue to face is substandard care including errors in their medical records (Sharma et al., 2019). To address this situation, health information exchanges (HIE) have been established to seamlessly share patient data across organizations. In this study, we examine whether policy-driven support for data interoperability—operationalized through health information exchange (HIE) systems—is associated with increased malpractice liability. Drawing on the empowerment literature, we argue that greater operational transparency enabled by data sharing may empower patients to scrutinize care quality, thereby elevating the risk of litigation. Using an eight-year panel data set covering 952 U.S. hospitals from 2010 to 2017 and over 24,000 malpractice case filings, we find that HIE adoption is associated with a statistically significant 10.5% increase in malpractice lawsuits. However, this effect is moderated by hospitals’ experiential quality, as measured by patient-reported experiences of communication, empathy, and responsiveness. In hospitals with high experiential quality, the effect of HIE adoption on malpractice lawsuits is reduced by 20.4%, suggesting that positive patient interactions can reduce the legal risks associated with HIE adoption. Our findings highlight a critical trade-off. While data interoperability improves operational coordination and patient engagement, it can also elevate legal exposure. This research contributes to the operations management and public policy literature by reframing interoperability not just as a backend coordination tool but also as a patient-facing technological development with reputational and legal implications.

Title: Participation governance in consumer and AI co-creation: Whether to intervene and how to design it
Authors: Mengxia Zhang, Brian Rongqing Han, Tianshu Sun, Lan Luo, Joseph M. Golden
Affiliations: Western University; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business; University of Southern California; Paper2Audio, Seattle, WA, USA<?pag \vspace*{-1.6pc}?>
Abstract: Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

Title: Harnessing renewable portfolio standards for sustainable futures: An empirical examination of spillover effects
Authors: Chunjie Zhao, Anqi Wu, Ramanath Subramanyam
Affiliations: Denison University; Florida International University; Gies College of Business, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Abstract: Given the importance of managing industrial energy consumption, setting standards and implementing policies that encourage renewable energy use is crucial for incentivizing sustainable firm practices. Public policy designs must align closely with firms’ environmental policies to help mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support a sustainable future. While research on policy impacts on firm environmental performance and the supply chain's role in sustainability is growing, a critical, understudied effect is the spillover of government rules to supply chain partners and peer firms, especially those outside the direct purview of environmental regulations. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates data from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS). The latter refers to state-driven initiatives that incentivize electricity consumption from eligible renewable resources. We examine the causal effects of state-level policies on firm-level GHG emission intensity, with particular emphasis on the spillover effects of policies on unregulated firms across markets. We break down emission intensity into Scope 1 and Scope 2 and capture facility-level data to analyze spillover effects in granular detail. Using a staggered difference-in-differences methodology, our analysis finds a promising negative association between RPS introduction and GHG emission intensity among unregulated firms across industries. Interestingly, firms headquartered in states with more conservative initial targets during RPS adoption and progressive, milestone-based implementation strategies have significantly lower GHG emission intensity than those headquartered in states with more aggressive initial targets or long-term absolute targets. Our findings have significant implications for developing environmental regulations and public policies aimed at reducing GHG emission intensity.

Title: What drives physician efficiency? Evidence from emergency department operations
Authors: Raha Imanirad, Soroush Saghafian, Stephen J Traub, Nicole R Hodgson
Affiliations: York University; University of Maryland; Optum Arizona and New Mexico; Mayo Clinic Arizona
Abstract: Emergency department (ED) physicians play a critical role in healthcare. Yet increasing demand, resource constraints, and growing patient complexity pose significant challenges to physician efficiency. In this study, we investigate the determinants of ED physician efficiency using a multi-stage framework. First, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis to measure physician efficiency based on data from 110,325 patient visits at a leading U.S. hospital. Second, we use Tobit regression to analyze how physician experience, shift familiarity, and patient severity influence physician efficiency. Third, we conduct robustness checks, including omitted variable bias sensitivity analyses, permutation tests, and machine learning-based classification analyses, to address concerns regarding endogeneity and model misspecification. Our results show that physician efficiency increases with experience at a diminishing rate. Efficiency also varies with shift familiarity, with the estimated association weakening as physician experience increases. Higher patient severity is associated with lower physician efficiency, consistent with greater resource demands for higher-severity patients. This negative association is attenuated for more experienced physicians, suggesting that they are better able to maintain efficiency when managing more demanding clinical conditions. Accordingly, staffing strategies that assign relatively more experienced physicians to higher-severity patients may help maintain physician efficiency, while shift familiarity may inform a scheduling strategy that emphasizes greater scheduling consistency for relatively less experienced physicians and greater flexibility for relatively more experienced physicians. Simulation results illustrate the potential reductions in physician resource use associated with these strategies. Together, these findings highlight the value of evidence-based physician staffing and scheduling to improve physician efficiency in EDs.

Title: Exact Algorithms for Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problems: A Unified Framework with New Benchmark Results
Authors: Sunkanghong Wang, Roberto Baldacci, Fabio Furini, Lijun Wei, Qiang Liu
Affiliations: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Computer Integrated Manufacturing System, School of Electromechanical Engineering, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou 510000, China; and Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, Faculty of Business, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China; College of Science and Engineering, Hamad Bin Khalifa University, Doha, Qatar; Department of Computer, Control, and Management Engineering “Antonio Ruberti”, Sapienza University of Rome, 00185 Rome, Italy
Abstract: This paper investigates two-dimensional knapsack problems modeled as the Generalized Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problem (G2KP), a variant not previously studied in the literature. The importance of the G2KP lies in its crucial role in designing Branch-Price-and-Cut (BPC) algorithms for the classical Two-Dimensional Bin-Packing Problem. We propose a novel and effective exact solution framework that incorporates both nonnumerically exact and numerically exact algorithms tailored to G2KP. The framework also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the well-known Two-Dimensional Knapsack Problem (with and without item conflicts) and the Two-Dimensional Orthogonal Packing Problem, solving several previously unsolved instances and establishing new benchmark results. These findings highlight the framework’s potential to inspire algorithmic developments for pricing problems in related BPC methods and higher-dimensional packing problems. To support future research, we make the algorithm code, instance data, and detailed results publicly available.
