Title: “Generate” the Future of Work through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
Authors: Jin Liu, Xingchen Xu, Xi Nan, Yongjun Li, Yong Tan
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China School of Management, Department of Management Science, Hefei, Anhui, China; University of Washington, Information Systems and Operations Management, Seattle, Washington, 98195-0005, United States; University of Washington, Michael G. Foster School of Business, Seattle, Washington, 98195, United States; USTC, management science, Hefei, 230026, China; University of Washington, Michael G. Foster School of Business, Seattle, Washington, 98195-3200, United States
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.

Title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
Authors: Zhuping Liu, Bicheng Yang, Subodha Kumar
Affiliations: Baruch College Zicklin School of Business, Marketing and International Business, New York, New York, United States; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Faculty of Business, management and marketing, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Temple University, Supply Chain, Information Systems, Marketing, and Statistics, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
Abstract: As mobile apps increasingly mediate digital engagement, push notifications have emerged as a key tool for directing user attention, yet systematic evidence on their behavioral and ecosystem-level effects remains limited. Using data from over 200 push campaigns and 60 million user-campaign observations on a leading U.S. mobile-offer marketplace, we combine large-scale observational analyses with controlled experiments to study how push notifications shape user engagement. We find that push notifications significantly increase same-day click-throughs to advertised merchants, with substantial heterogeneity across merchant characteristics, user characteristics, message design, and delivery timing. Beyond focal-merchant responses, notifications are associated with increased engagement with non-advertised merchants both within and across categories, suggesting that push notifications reshape attention across the marketplace ecosystem. Both the large-scale empirical analysis and controlled experiments yield evidence consistent with two complementary mechanisms—content-driven processing of notification information and reminder-based attention activation. The results also identify attentional saturation as a key boundary condition—repeated exposure produces diminishing responsiveness and may even reduce engagement at high notification frequencies. These findings position push notifications as a mobile-native attention-allocation lever that platforms can strategically deploy, while underscoring the need to balance engagement gains against user fatigue and attention costs.

Title: Mobile Location-based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
Authors: Jin Soo Han, Gunwoong Lee, Keongtae Kim
Affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology College of Business, IT Management, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Korea University, Management Information Systems, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decisions, Operations and Technology, Shatin, Hong Kong
Abstract: We investigate the impact of mobile location-based recommendation systems (MLBRS) on the performance of local businesses. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 16,720 restaurants and quasi-experimental variation generated by the official launch of a leading MLBRS, we employ a 2-Stage Least Squares instrumental-variable framework to estimate the effect of algorithmic exposure on consumer engagement. Our analysis reveals that a 1% increase in exposure is associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks; separately, a 1% increase in clicks is associated with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Importantly, the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks). This pattern highlights a boundary condition of MLBRS: algorithmic visibility can aid, but it does not by itself resolve the uncertainty involved in acting on a recommendation. Downstream conversion is stronger when restaurants provide richer digital information and reputation signals, including consumer reviews and owner-curated information such as photos and menus. Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample provide consistent evidence of a positive association between algorithmic exposure and revenue, suggesting that MLBRS can shape the connection of online recommendations to offline economic outcomes.

Title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
Authors: Zhi (Aaron) Cheng, Ting Li, Paul A. Pavlou
Affiliations: Department of Management, London School of Economics, London WC2A 2AE, United Kingdom; Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands; University of Miami Business School, Miami, Florida 33146
Abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. These findings reconceptualize transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters decisional assurance and stabilizes retention under quality uncertainty. Title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
Authors: Alexandre Jeanneret, Valeri Sokolovski
Affiliations: School of Banking and Finance, UNSW Business School, Kensington, New South Wales 2033, Australia; Alberta School of Business, University of Alberta, Edmonton AB T6G 2R3, Canada
Abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
Authors: Shan Liu, Fan Zhang, Jing Wang, Baojun Gao
Affiliations: School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China; Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics, and Operations Management, School of Business and Management, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China; Business School of Science and Technology, Wuhan University, Wuhan 430072, China
Abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions. Further analyses reveal that winners with previous competition medals are more likely to favor contributing content over competing again, whereas winners with more prior contribution medals are less inclined to further increase contributions. Moreover, team winners exhibit a lower tendency than solo winners to shift their efforts from competition to contribution. We add to the symbolic awards literature by uncovering a novel goal-shifting effect induced by contest medals, where award receipt redirects user effort from the focal rewarded domain to other forms of platform engagement. Title: From Bytes to Bites: Examining the Online and Offline Spillover Impacts of Online Food Delivery Platform Subscriptions
Authors: Jaeho Myeong, Yongjin Park, Francis Joseph Costello, Keongtae Kim, Jae-Hyeon Ahn
Affiliations: College of Business and Economics, Hanyang University ERICA, Ansan 15588, Republic of Korea; College of Business, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Nova School of Business and Economics, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, Campus de Carcavelos, 2775-405 Carcavelos, Portugal; Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Seoul 02455, Republic of Korea; and Seoul Business School, Seoul School of Integrated Sciences & Technologies (aSSIST) University, Seoul 03767, Republic of Korea
Abstract: With the rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms, subscription models have emerged as a strategic tool to retain users and shape consumption behavior. Despite their growing prevalence, the broader impacts of these subscriptions—both within the OFD sector and across downstream consumer activities—remain underexplored. Leveraging a difference-in-differences approach and a large-scale individual-level transaction data set, we identify a significant shift in consumption from a competing platform to the focal platform following the introduction of a subscription service. This shift did not result in cannibalization; instead, overall food consumption within the OFD market increased. Geospatial analysis shows that subscribers were more likely to engage in offline spillovers, including increased local dining and activity in nearby noncompeting economic sectors. These patterns suggest that subscriptions in physical services, like OFD, not only reshape digital engagement, but also, they influence consumer mobility and stimulate localized economic ecosystems. Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster crosschannel engagement, and generate positive spillovers in adjacent sectors. The findings offer actionable guidance for platform designers and policymakers to enhance consumer welfare and support local economic vitality. They also provide new evidence for restaurants that additional platform usage costs may be offset by latent economic benefits from heightened consumer engagement. This paper was accepted by D. J. Title: Why Zoning Is Too Restrictive
Authors: Jack Favilukis, Jaehee Song
Affiliations: Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia V6T 1Z2, Canada; Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado, Boulder, Colorado 80309
Abstract: Economists estimate that zoning regulations raise house prices, lower productivity, and reduce aggregate welfare, yet regulations remain widespread. We develop and solve a model in which fragmented zoning authority leads to overly strict regulations: Homeowners impose stricter regulations to mitigate local congestion but fail to internalize the broader impact on metro-wide affordability. Empirically, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of local governments explains 12% of the variation in zoning restrictiveness. Using an instrument based on 19th-century municipal fragmentation, we show that greater fragmentation leads to stricter zoning and higher housing costs. These findings suggest that centralizing zoning decisions could alleviate housing affordability challenges. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
Authors: Øystein Foros, Hans Jarle Kind, Greg Shaffer
Affiliations: Norwegian School of Economics (NHH), 5045 Bergen, Norway; and CESifo, 81679 Munich, Germany; University of Rochester, Rochester, New York 14627
Abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. Title: Optimize-via-Estimate: How to Make Finite-Sample Corrections for Sampling Uncertainty in Data-Driven Optimization
Authors: Gar Goei Loke, Taozeng Zhu, Ruiting Zuo
Affiliations: Durham University Business School, Department of Management and Marketing, Durham, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, Institute of Supply Chain Analytics, Dalian, China; National University of Singapore, Analytics & Operations, Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: We propose a novel procedure for correcting for the effects of sampling and parameter uncertainty in data-driven convex optimization. We consider the data-driven setting wherein the distribution lies in a parametric family with unknown parameter. The decision-maker possesses a historical data set, from which solves a prescriptive solution as a function mapping such a data set to decisions, and measures its out-of-sample performance as an average over data sets of the same size under the sampling distribution. As the parameter is unknown to the decision-maker, we argue that this problem is ill-defined and further prove that there cannot exist solutions generalizably optimal over all parameters. As such, we formulate the problem as a weighted multi-criteria optimization with weights defined by a density (termed ‘prior’) over the uncertain parameter, and call its optimal solution prior optimal. We prove that sufficient conditions for prior optimality reduces to functions of the sufficient statistic of the parametric family, and this function can be solved as a point-wise optima of a corrected function of the original objective, with terms accounting for parameter uncertainty and sampling uncertainty respectively. The correction for sampling interpretation is verified by a close to (but not) zero ex-ante regret against a perfect information oracle in numerical illustrations on the newsvendor and portfolio optimization problems.

Title: Real-Time Solution of Quadratic Optimization Problems with Banded Matrices and Indicator Variables
Authors: Andres Gomez, Shaoning Han, Leonardo Lozano
Affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States; University of Southern California, The Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, 90089-0001, United States; University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, United States
Abstract: We consider mixed-integer quadratic optimization problems with banded matrices and indicator variables. These problems arise pervasively in statistical inference problems with time-series data, where the banded matrix captures the temporal relationship of the underlying process. In particular, the problem studied arises in monitoring problems, where the decision-maker wants to detect changes or anomalies. We propose to solve these problems using decision diagrams. In particular we show how to exploit the temporal dependencies to construct exact and approximate decision diagrams. For problems over matrices with bandwidth equal to one, the proposed method runs in polynomial time. Moreover, if the bandwidth and condition number of the matrix is fixed, then we show that the proposed method can be modified to run into an additive approximation scheme. We also describe how to construct the convex hull of the set under study from the decision diagrams, and how to deploy the method online to solve the problems via a shortest path algorithm. Computational experiments show that, for problems with bandwidths less or equal than three, our proposed algorithm compares favorably to a state-of-the-art off-the-shelf solver in the offline setting, and that we are able to solve problems in milliseconds for the online setting.

Title: Online Allocation with Heterogeneous Supply and Minimum Workload Guarantees
Authors: Garud Iyengar, Raghav Singal
Affiliations: Department of IEOR, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Tuck School of Business, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire 03755

Title: On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
Authors: Li Xia, Zhihui Yu, Haoran Wu
Affiliations: School of Business, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou 510275, China
Abstract: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.

Title: “We’re Not Handling Cases, We’re Shaping Lives”: How Lawyers Preserve Professional Authority and Advance Social Responsibility via Moral Identity-Based Client Persuasion
Authors: Siyin Chen, Qiusi Yan
Affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Abstract: Professionals are increasingly expected to deliver socially responsible services that protect vulnerable third parties, yet their authority may be threatened when such recommendations appear to conflict with clients’ perceived self-interests and desired end goals. Drawing on a qualitative study of 91 legal cases in China, we examine how lawyers navigate this tension when persuading initially resistant clients to accept socially responsible counsel. We develop a process model of “moral identity-based client persuasion,” a form of relational expertise that enables lawyers to preserve professional authority by reconstructing clients’ desired end goals to incorporate third-party welfare. The process begins with client moral identity discernment, through which lawyers determine whether a client’s moral identity is situationally salient. It unfolds through three linked practices: (1) articulating moral identity threats, (2) providing moral identity affirmations, and (3) legitimizing moral identity enactments. Together, these practices render socially responsible counsel both self-relevant and technically defensible to clients. We further identify three client-level inhibitors of success: insufficient moral identity salience, entangled decision locus, and limited emotional resilience. These findings augment research on professional work by identifying a novel form of relational expertise that mobilizes clients’ personal identities to secure compliance, and extend moral persuasion research into professional service contexts.

Title: Breaking the Silence: Developing an Organizational Mental Health Capability
Authors: Abbie Griffith Oliver, Jeffrey B. Lovelace
Affiliations: University of Virginia; University of Georgia

Title: Industrial policy in times of market power
Authors: Domenico Delli Gatti, Roberta Terranova, Enrico Maria Turco
Abstract: We explore the effects of different industrial policies in a macroeconomic agent-based model calibrated to reproduce the decline in US business dynamism over the last half-century. R&D subsidies to innovators raise GDP growth but exacerbate the trend toward rising market power, while financial subsidies to adopters and standard capital-replacement schemes have negligible aggregate effects. A meaningful reversal of market power emerges only when innovation support is paired with adoption-oriented measures that relax the knowledge constraints of small adopters, e.g. the establishment of a National Competence Center providing technology transfer and knowledge upgrading. The effectiveness of each policy is dependent on the underlying technological regime: the growth–dynamism trade-off is sharpest in science-based regimes and attenuated in scale-intensive and supplier-dominated ones.

Title: Do long-term yields help to estimate short-term risk premia?
Authors: Andrea Berardi, Roger Brown, Stephen M. Schaefer
Abstract: We identify a new and important property of affine term structure models: at long maturities, the slope of the term structure of risk premia becomes “almost observable”. Exploiting this property by fitting models to long-maturity data dramatically improves the precision of estimates of risk premia and expected short rates across the term structure. In a Monte Carlo experiment we show that using rates with maturities up to 25 years, rather than 10 years as is standard in the literature, reduces the standard deviation of estimation errors in risk premia, expected short rates and term premia by over 70%. Applying this approach to US Treasury data, we find that variation in expected short rates accounts for a much larger share of variation in yields (and variation in term premia a correspondingly smaller fraction) than in the widely used estimates reported by the Federal Reserve. Accounting for time-variation in yield volatility is key to successful extraction of the risk premium information in long rates. Our approach therefore departs from much of the empirical literature in two important respects: it incorporates long-maturity yields and allows for time-varying yield volatility, whereas most existing studies ignore long-term yields and rely on constant volatility models.

Title: Silencing Pollution: The Environmental Consequences of Anti-SLAPP Laws
Authors: Xikai Chen, Jinjun (Ricky) Ke, Yu Flora Kuang
Affiliations: California State University Fresno; Xiamen University; University of Technology Sydney; The University of Melbourne; Tilburg University
Abstract: Abstract We examine whether free-speech protections influence corporate environmental performance. Using the staggered enactment of U.S. anti-SLAPP statutes in a stacked difference-in-differences design from 1990 to 2019, we find that these laws significantly reduce firms’ toxic emissions without curbing economic activity. Anti-SLAPP enactments also promote environmental investment through green innovation, abatement spending, and waste reduction management, and strengthen governance via improved sustainability oversight, ESG-linked executive pay, employee training, and supply chain management. The effects are stronger when stakeholder monitoring is stronger and when managerial incentives embed sustainability goals. Overall, free-speech protections generate powerful environmental benefits.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: A Shared Interest: Do Bonds Strengthen Equity Monitoring?
Authors: Todd A. Gormley, Manish Jha
Affiliations: Washington University in Saint Louis and National Bureau of Economic Research; Georgia State University
Abstract: Abstract Institutional investors conduct more governance research and are less likely to follow proxy advisor vote recommendations when a company’s bonds comprise a larger share of their assets. These findings are driven by bond holdings, shareholder proposals, and companies where fixed-income managers are more likely to be attentive and share an interest with equity investors in improving governance. The findings do not concentrate on companies or shareholder proposals where creditor–shareholder conflicts are likely. Overall, the findings suggest that corporate bond holdings influence how actively institutions monitor their equity positions and contribute to institutions’ overall incentive to be engaged stewards.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde: Feedback and Welfare When Hedgers Can Acquire Information
Authors: Jacques Olivier
Affiliations: HEC Paris
Abstract: Abstract I ask whether hedgers who speculate should be regulated differently from other speculators in a model where information acquisition is endogenous, and information has real effects. Hedging benefits and feedback effects generate strategic complementarities between market-maker, firm manager, and trader, which causes multiple equilibria. Gains from trade are lower when hedgers acquire information, while speculators may produce less information than socially desirable. A “Volcker rule” separating hedging and speculative activities may help select the higher welfare equilibrium. When too little information is produced, contracts whereby a firm subsidizes losses of designated market-makers (DMM) to make prices more informative increase welfare.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Expected and Realized Returns on Volatility
Authors: Guanglian Hu, Kris Jacobs
Affiliations: The University of Sydney Business School; University of Houston
Abstract: Abstract Expected returns on market volatility, which can be obtained from VIX futures prices in closed form using standard models, positively predict subsequent realized volatility returns. Volatility returns are negative on average. Following increases in volatility, expected volatility returns and subsequent realized volatility returns become more negative. Because realized volatility returns are negatively correlated with index returns, expected volatility returns also negatively predict S&P 500 index returns, but these results are less significant. The results are robust to a wide range of variations in the empirical setup and to small-sample biases.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Investment Functions with q in the Presence of Unobserved Persistent Shocks
Authors: Kyoo il Kim, Suyong Song, Jiawei (Brooke) Wang
Affiliations: Michigan State University; University of Iowa; Miami University
Abstract: Abstract We study the classical relationship between a firm’s investment and q , for which an unobserved persistent shock is an important factor in the investment decision. In our setting, besides the potential measurement problem of q , controlling for the unobserved shock becomes a new challenge. We develop an estimation method that addresses both econometric issues given timing and information set assumptions. Using 16,256 unique public firms in the United States from 1975 to 2021, we find that q remains a significant factor of investment even after controlling for the unobserved shock and measurement error.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Real Disinvestments and the Distress Anomaly: Evidence from Stocks, Bonds, and Loans
Authors: Shuwen Yang, Kevin Aretz, Yafei Zhang
Affiliations: USTB: University of Science and Technology Beijing; The University of Manchester Alliance Manchester Business School; American University of Sharjah
Abstract: Abstract We argue that firms’ ability to disinvest real assets helps rationalize the negative distress premiums in stocks, bonds, and, as we show, loans and firm assets. Using a real options model in which shareholders and debtholders share disinvestment proceeds, the model suggests that the stock (debt) distress premium becomes more negative with the proceeds paid out to that class, and that both premiums can be negative when debtholders receive most of the proceeds. Using hard-asset disinvestment-ability proxies, the stock (bond or loan) distress premium becomes less (more) negative with those proxies, possibly suggesting that shareholders benefit more strongly from nonsecured-asset disinvestments.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Credibility of Mandatory Disclosure by Credit Rating Agencies and Market Feedback
Authors: Jaewoo Kim, Seyoung Park, Ryan Wilson
Affiliations: University of Oregon Lundquist College of Business; Georgetown University McDonough School of Business; University of Iowa Tippie College of Business
Abstract: Abstract Using the Credit Rating Agency Reform Act of 2006, we examine the effect of the credibility of mandatory disclosure by credit rating agencies (CRAs) on market feedback. We find an increase in investment-price sensitivity for firms affected by the act, and the increase is enhanced when managers have greater incentives to glean information from prices—when firms are exposed to multiple dimensions of uncertainty, have higher growth options, face more competition, have less informed managers, or have higher accounting fraud risk. Our findings suggest that the greater credibility of CRA mandatory disclosure improves managerial learning from stock prices.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Swimming Against the Current: Contrarian Retail Trading
Authors: Brad Cannon, Hannes Mohrschladt
Affiliations: Binghamton University; University of Potsdam Faculty of Economics and Social Sciences and University of Münster Finance Center Münster
Abstract: Abstract Retail investor contrarian selling depends on whether a position is at a gain or a loss. Selling propensity increases in daily returns for positions with unrealized gains (contrarian selling) and decreases in returns for loss positions (trend-following selling). This pattern is consistent with behavioral arguments that investors update their beliefs when stock prices move away from their purchase prices. In line with increased liquidity from contrarian selling, illiquid stocks exhibit weaker short-term reversals when investors have higher unrealized capital gains. Our findings diminish following stock splits, suggesting that unrealized capital gains are central to contrarian behavior, particularly when investors perceive them clearly.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Careers in Finance
Authors: Andrew Ellul, Marco Pagano, Annalisa Scognamiglio
Affiliations: Indiana University Kelley School of Business; University of Naples Federico II
Abstract: Abstract Past research has documented a substantial finance wage premium. We examine whether this premium reflects differences in lifetime career opportunities. Using resume data, we reconstruct career trajectories in finance and nonfinance sectors and build synthetic measures of career attractiveness that account for compensation levels, growth, and risk. We find that asset management and investment banking provide a sizable risk-adjusted career premium relative to banking, insurance, and other sectors. This premium has declined across cohorts, particularly relative to high tech. Labor-market entry patterns respond to these premia: potential entrants treat finance and high-tech careers as substitutes when choosing where to start.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Financial Consequences of the Belt and Road Initiative
Authors: Mehmet Ihsan Canayaz
Affiliations: Pennsylvania State University Smeal College of Business and University of Cincinnati Carl H. Lindner College of Business
Abstract: Abstract China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) aims to create economic corridors encompassing two-thirds of the world’s population and 40% of global GDP. Using the inauguration of a railway tunnel between Europe and Asia as a quasi-natural experiment, I demonstrate that countries gaining access to BRI’s freight routes issue significant amounts of high-yield debt. This debt is largely absorbed domestically, reallocating capital away from firms without translating into infrastructure investment. State-owned enterprises appear insulated from tightening financial conditions. I document mechanisms involving political alignment with China, exposure to trade policy uncertainty, and topographic fit based on historical Orient Express routes.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Rewriting CRSP’s History: Impact of Altered Monthly Returns on Asset Pricing
Authors: Patrick Schwarz, Dominik Walter, Patrick Weiss
Affiliations: University of Liège HEC Liège; University of Konstanz; Reykjavik University
Abstract: Abstract In January 2025, CRSP discontinued the existing stock tape used in many published papers. This transition rewrites 9.62% of monthly returns by more than 1 basis point (bp), primarily due to a change in the dividend reinvestment assumption. Analyzing the impact for a comprehensive set of premia in several thousand sorting specifications reveals that, on average, 11.43% of all monthly long-short returns differ by more than 10 bp—especially in early periods, NBER recessions, and return-based sorts. Reassuringly, average premia and their significance remain largely unaffected, suggesting CRSP changes mainly introduce unsystematic variation without altering key asset pricing conclusions.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: M&As Efficiency Gains: Evidence from Branch-Level Data
Authors: Lucas Argentieri Mariani, Bernardo Ricca
Affiliations: Bocconi University, BAFFI and IGIER; Insper
Abstract: Abstract We examine how banks reallocate employees following mergers and acquisitions (M&As) and the resulting effects on productivity. Using matched employee–branch data combined with branch-level financial information, we show that M&As expand internal labor markets and trigger substantial worker redeployment. Newly consolidated banks reassign high-ability loan officers to acquirer branches, increasing productivity. Target branches also experience productivity improvements, primarily driven by restructuring and cost reductions. These effects are strongest in municipalities where the combined pre-merger internal labor markets of the target and acquirer were larger, highlighting the central role of internal labor markets in generating efficiency gains from consolidation.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Shaped by Confucius: The Cultural Origin of Corporate Behavior
Authors: Zhihui Gu, Hao Liang, Hanyu Zhang
Affiliations: Nankai University Business School; Singapore Management University
Abstract: Abstract We examine how Confucian culture operates as an informal institution by fostering relational contracts that substitute for formal legal frameworks in shaping corporate behavior. Using data on historical Confucian academies near firms’ headquarters in China, we find that greater cultural exposure is associated with higher investment in stakeholder relationships—measured by social contribution, stakeholder protection, courtesy expenses, patenting, and trade credit. These effects persist after controlling for human capital and alternative cultural influences, and weaken in regions with stronger formal institutions. Our findings highlight the enduring role of culture in supporting trust-based governance when formal contracting is limited.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Optimal Retirement Saving and Dissaving
Authors: Claus Munk
Affiliations: Copenhagen Business School
Abstract: Abstract Applying a rich model of individuals’ life-cycle utility maximization, I comprehensively evaluate retirement saving plans. Across a range of individual characteristics, access to basic plans with constant expected payouts and no or full annuitization leads to individual utility gains of up to 5.07% of initial wealth and lifetime income ($43,800 in present value terms), and almost all individuals prefer full annuitization and a target-date fund investment strategy. With flexible plans allowing for partial annuitization and non-constant expected payouts, utility gains go up to 5.81%, and most individuals prefer a high degree of annuitization and expected payouts being increasing through retirement.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Political Affiliation and Media Distrust: Evidence from Stock Market Investors
Authors: Mancy Luo, Alberto Manconi, Massimo Massa
Affiliations: City University of London Bayes Business School; Bocconi University; INSEAD
Abstract: Abstract Does distrust in politically affiliated media induce a bias in investor beliefs? We study the acquisition of Dow Jones & Co. by News Corporation in 2007 as a shock to the political affiliation of Dow Jones outlets. Following the acquisition, the prices of Republican- (Democrat-) aligned stocks become less sensitive to favorable (unfavorable) Dow Jones Newswires (DJNW) sentiment, consistent with the market attaching less credibility to a politically affiliated source. There is, however, no evidence of change in DJNW sentiment, coverage, or language about Republican/Democrat stocks, suggesting a loss of stock price informativeness. Consistent with this view, a portfolio exploiting the attenuated reaction to DJNW news earns abnormal returns following 2007.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Connectivity infrastructure and innovation: The effects of headquarters versus subsidiary management
Authors: Catherine Magelssen, Luis Ballesteros, Casidhe Troyer
Abstract: Improvements in connectivity infrastructure can stimulate innovation by reducing information frictions across locations, yet firms benefit unevenly, and the organizational sources of this heterogeneity remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on information processing theory, this study examines how the locus of managerial authority within multinational enterprises (MNEs)—specifically, whether R&D subsidiaries are managed by headquarters or by another subsidiary—influences the change in innovation from improved connectivity. We use a novel longitudinal dataset covering 1004 R&D subsidiaries from 78 MNEs and exploit the staggered global rollout of broadband as a quasi-exogenous shock to connectivity. Triple-difference analyses using matched samples indicate that broadband increases subsidiary innovation on average, but the effects are driven by R&D subsidiaries managed by other subsidiaries. These subsidiaries experience substantially larger post-broadband increases in innovation productivity, knowledge flows from their managing entity, and co-inventions with their managing entity than headquarters-managed subsidiaries. Additional analyses are consistent with a widening gap when headquarters face greater information complexity, associated with larger MNE size, more extensive international operations, and broader roles, suggesting that headquarters' heavier information load constrains its ability to leverage improved connectivity. Consistent with information processing under constraints, we find suggestive evidence that headquarters prioritize their most important and technologically proximate subsidiaries. In contrast, subsidiary-managed units achieve innovation gains more broadly. The findings show that the innovation benefits of connectivity infrastructure hinge on organizational structure, highlighting the pivotal role of subsidiaries in managing innovation and the conditions that can impede or enhance these effects, advancing understanding of both connectivity-enabled innovation and MNE management.

Title: Editorial Board
Serial or Parallel? Sublexical Scanpath Analysis of Eye-movement Sequences in Single Word Reading
Authors: Hend Lahoud, Adi Shechter, Titus von der Malsburg, David L. Share
Affiliations: Department of Learning Disabilities, Faculty of Education, University of Haifa; Edmond J. Safra Brain Research Center for the Study of Learning Disabilities, University of Haifa; Faculty of Education, Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee; Institute of Linguistics, University of Stuttgart
Abstract: Are the letters of a written word processed sequentially or in parallel? Despite an abundance of research on visual word recognition, the evidence in this longstanding debate rests almost entirely on indirect inferences from word-length effects and conventional whole-word eye-movement measures. We sought direct evidence on the serial-parallel question by investigating sublexical gaze-fixation sequences—so-called scanpaths . This study is the first to apply scanpath analysis to fixation sequences within single words. Thirty-four Hebrew-speaking adult university students read aloud three-letter and five-letter real words and pseudowords while their eye movements were tracked. As expected, real words showed more parallel processing, whereas pseudowords displayed more sequential, letter-by-letter scanpaths. Surprisingly, longer words tended to elicit serial processing regardless of word familiarity. Our findings support the applicability of scanpath analysis in visual word recognition and its potential to open up new perspectives on word-recognition processes.

Title: Secretary problems with random number of candidates: How prior distributional information helps
Authors: Junhui Zhang, Patrick Jaillet

Title: Strategic introduction of manufacturer’s suggested retail price in a dual-channel supply chain
Authors: Can Liu, Dafei Wang, Shuguang Zhang
Abstract: Motivated by the widespread use of manufacturer's suggested retail prices across industries and the growing prevalence of dual-channel supply chains, this paper investigates the strategic introduction of suggested retail price by a manufacturer supplying a traditional retailer and an e-retailer. Using a static game-theoretic model, we analyze when and why the manufacturer introduces a suggested retail price and its impact on channel members and consumers. We identify the suggested retail price as a strategic tool regulating inter-retailer competition and reshaping the basic market size, requiring the manufacturer to balance these opposing forces. Key findings reveal that: (1) Strong brand competitiveness makes the adoption of suggested retail price optimal, as it effectively mitigates price competition and supports price markups. (2) The suggested retail price asymmetrically influences the retailers. In particular, it protects the e-retailer's market presence even when its competitive position is weak, but cannot prevent the exit of a sufficiently disadvantaged traditional retailer. (3) The e-retailer benefits from the suggested retail price in most cases, whereas the traditional retailer does so only in a limited regime. Crucially, under certain conditions, the introduction of the suggested retail price achieves a win-win-win-win outcome, simultaneously improving profits of the manufacturer and the retailers, and consumer surpluses.

Title: Accepting returns from competing e-tailer: The role of selling mode
Authors: Yi Chen, Qin Su, Gang Li, Fangkezi Zhou
Abstract: Cooperative-return-to-store (CRS) programs, where brick-and-mortar retailers (BMRs) accept returns of products sold on e-tailer platforms, are gaining traction as a strategy to boost store traffic. However, BMRs are often constrained by competitive concerns. This study examines how a competing e-tailer's selling mode (reseller, marketplace, or dual) influences the viability of CRS for a BMR in a supply chain context. We find that the reseller (marketplace) mode is more favorable to the adoption of CRS by the BMR when the positive externalities of the store traffic are strong (weak). This distinction comes from the BMR's varying reliance on wholesale price reductions from its supplier. We further show that the dual mode surpasses single modes in enhancing CRS agreements and social value because the e-tailer and third-party seller can share demand shifts. These findings offer actionable insights for BMR managers in partner selection and policymakers to evaluate e-commerce regulations. Our results remain robust across diverse consumer return behaviors, cost structures, decision frameworks, and CRS formats.

Title: Do entrepreneurs live longer? A Cox survival analysis of entrepreneurship and lifespan
Authors: Yanying Chen, Zijie Song, Hanqing Fang, Cristiano Bellavitis
Abstract: Empirical evidence on whether entrepreneurship benefits or harms health is mixed, in part because prior work emphasizes short-run symptoms and medical diagnoses rather than cumulative outcomes. We shift attention to lifespan, the total years lived, as an integrative, life-course endpoint and theorize entrepreneurship as a time-embedded career experience whose health outcomes depend on agency (opportunity-driven vs. necessity-driven entrepreneurship), cumulative exposure (duration and frequency), and timing (current vs. past engagement). Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (1998–2020; 137,542 person-waves from 27,501 individuals), we estimate Cox proportional hazards models, supplemented by robustness checks including monozygotic twin analysis. Entrepreneurship is positively associated with a longer lifespan relative to wage employment. Mediation analyses suggest that this association is partly accounted for by differences in mental health, whereas aggregate physical health does not appear to meaningfully explain the relationship. The positive association with lifespan is concentrated among opportunity-driven entrepreneurs and is stronger among individuals with greater cumulative entrepreneurial exposure. The findings also reveal a temporal pattern: better physical health is primarily associated with current entrepreneurial engagement, whereas better mental health is more closely linked to prior entrepreneurial experience. Further analyses indicate that the positive association between entrepreneurship and lifespan may be more pronounced among women and among entrepreneurs with higher incomes or larger firms. Collectively, these findings advance research on entrepreneurial health by reframing entrepreneurship as a life-course experience and specifying who benefits, through what mechanisms, and when .

Title: Generative AI and the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantages
Authors: Haiyang Zhang, Robert Wuebker, Jay B. Barney
Affiliations: Harvard Business School Boston Massachusetts USA; University of Utah Salt Lake City Utah USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects the ability of entrepreneurial opportunities to generate sustained competitive advantage. We argue that GenAI's impact is conditional on how those opportunities are formed. Discovery opportunities originate from exogenous industry shocks. However, widely available GenAI tools are likely to commoditize opportunity recognition in these settings and thus reduce advantages that might have been generated by exploiting these opportunities. Creation opportunities emerge endogenously, under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, through entrepreneurial action and interaction with the environment. However, GenAI cannot fully resolve the Knightian uncertainty inherent in creation settings, so sustained advantage here depends on whether resources and capabilities developed through creating an opportunity are inimitable. Unawareness opportunities rely on competitive neglect. GenAI may reduce the advantages of firms in these settings when it makes rents legible to potential competitors and when search is directed toward these invisible markets. Managerial Summary Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT and Claude help entrepreneurs spot opportunities, but every competitor can potentially access the same tools. Whether GenAI can create sustained competitive advantages, this paper argues, depends on how an opportunity is formed. When opportunities arise from entrepreneurs noticing an external market shift, GenAI levels the playing field by commoditizing recognition and pushes entrepreneurs to win through execution and hard‐to‐copy complements. When opportunities are created through actions and interactions of entrepreneurs with their environments, GenAI does not fully remove the uncertainty that makes these efforts entrepreneurial but can speed up experimentation. When opportunities emerge from entrepreneurs operating in markets neglected by competitors, GenAI may have a limited effect on advantage unless it makes invisible markets publicly known.

Title: Everything everywhere all‐at‐once? AI , expertise–output decoupling, and new entrepreneurial strategy trade‐offs in the age of abundance
Authors: Jen Gennai, Riitta Katila, Minu Kumar, Ian Sinapuelas
Affiliations: T3 Consultants New York New York USA; Microsoft Redmond Washington USA; Google Mountain View California USA; Stanford University Stanford California USA; San Francisco State University San Francisco California USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

Title: Pay‐for‐prominence: The (un)intended consequences of monetary incentives on employees' networks and attrition
Authors: Alessandro Iorio, Giuseppe Soda, Brandy Aven
Affiliations: Department of Management and Technology Bocconi University Milan Italy; ICRIOS Bocconi University Milan Italy; Tepper School of Business Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We introduce the concept of pay‐for‐prominence , a system where employees are monetarily incentivized to become knowledge hubs in the intrafirm network and examine its effects on employees' networks and attrition. Integrating social network theory with relational incentives theory, we argue that pay‐for‐prominence motivates strategic networking behaviors that lead to the emergence of prominent connectors. However, these changes are associated with higher attrition as employees are preoccupied with networking, thus suggesting a trade‐off between enhanced connectivity in the short term and the risk of network fragmentation in the long term. Using a field quasi‐experiment in a multinational firm, we show that organizations can successfully incentivize employees' network prominence, but doing so may produce unintended consequences. Managerial Summary We examine the impact of using monetary incentives to encourage employees to become knowledge hubs in the workplace informal network—a term we label pay‐for‐prominence. We find that offering monetary rewards based on network metrics encourages employees to broaden their connections, enhancing knowledge flows within the firm. However, employees who become more socially prominent experience higher attrition than those who do not, as they become preoccupied with networking. Therefore, while incentivizing networking can improve knowledge sharing, it also requires careful management to avoid unintended consequences, such as the exit of key players that could cause fragmentation of the social network. Managers should weigh the benefits of increased connectivity against the risks of fragmentation when designing incentive programs aimed at fostering informal networks.

Title: Identifying and managing milestones in consumers’ goal journeys
Authors: Amanda Ann Garrison, Linda L. Price
Abstract: Abstract Understanding consumers’ holistic journeys as unfolding events is paramount for managing service design and delivery. Touchpoints, “moments of truth” and critical incident research primarily focus on firm-facing events and consumers’ evaluations of firm encounters, rather than critical events in consumers’ own goal pursuit. This article introduces and uncovers the significance of milestone events in consumers’ journeys. Milestones are significant events that mark a major step or turning point in a consumer’s journey. Multi-stage, multi-context qualitative consumer journey research is used to inductively identify the key features and implications of milestones. They are distinct from other service events and consequential for consumers’ lives. This research fills a significant research gap in understanding consumer goal journeys. Identifying and understanding consumers’ milestone events enables service firms to support and improve goal progression; increase confidence in success; help consumers prepare for and interpret milestone outcomes; and manage risk by adjusting or pivoting from the goal.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Return on AI (RoAI): A framework for assessing AI investments in the marketing organization
Authors: Vamsi K. Kanuri, Adithya Pattabhiramaiah, Shrihari Sridhar
Abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing as firms increasingly delegate activities and decisions previously performed by marketers to AI systems. As AI assumes a greater role in market-facing decisions, understanding the value firms realize from these investments becomes increasingly important. Building on marketing accountability and resource-based theory, we develop a Return on AI (RoAI) framework that conceptualizes AI investment through the people, processes, and capabilities that enable its deployment and governance. RoAI evaluates incremental benefit while accounting for value retention, evidence durability, and the full costs of deployment over time. The framework identifies a distinctive consequence of delegated judgment, wherein AI can improve current performance while reducing the experiential practice through which marketers develop and maintain the judgment required to evaluate and redirect the AI solution. This mechanism helps explain heterogeneity in AI returns across firms and over time. We develop seven testable predictions and an agenda for research on creating, appropriating, and sustaining value from AI.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Buffering institutional erosion: organizational ties and SME exports under populism
Authors: Xiaolong Shui, Luyang Chen, Michael A. Witt
Abstract: Abstract We argue that pre-existing organizational ties can partially buffer against the adverse effects of populist deinstitutionalization. In contrast with the chronic institutional weakness emphasized in prior literature, populist deinstitutionalization reflects a politically driven weakening of institutions that firms had previously relied on. This disrupts established routines and increases the transaction costs of cross-border exchange. For SMEs, which are highly dependent on external institutional support for internationalization, pre-existing ties to government actors, international suppliers, and foreign owners can provide partial buffering by replacing some of the coordination, information, and enforcement functions lost through institutional erosion. We test these arguments using data on 10,399 SMEs across 29 economies in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The results support our theoretical expectations: while populism is negatively associated with SME exporting, pre-existing organizational ties attenuate this adverse association, with foreign ownership providing the strongest buffering effect. Our findings extend institution-based research by identifying politically driven institutional erosion as a distinct challenge for international business and by showing that organizational ties can function as selective, imperfect buffers rather than substitutes for formal institutions.

Title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
Authors: Tymon Słoczyński
Affiliations: Brandeis University
Abstract: Abstract In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. I show that the weights on some conditional LATEs are negative and the IV estimand is no longer interpretable as a causal effect under a weaker version of monotonicity, i.e. when there are compliers but no defiers at some covariate values and defiers but no compliers elsewhere. The problem of negative weights disappears in the interacted specification of Angrist and Imbens (I1995), which avoids misspecification and seems to be underused in applied work. I illustrate my findings in an application to the causal effects of pretrial detention on case outcomes. In this setting, I reject the stronger version of monotonicity, demonstrate that the interacted instruments are sufficiently strong for consistent estimation using the jackknife methodology, and present several estimates that are economically and statistically different, depending on whether the interacted instruments are used.

Title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
Authors: Henrique de Oliveira, Yuhta Ishii, Xiao Lin
Affiliations: São Paulo School of Economics - FGV; Pennsylvania State University; University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: Abstract Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies—those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. With more actions, a robustly optimal strategy decomposes the problem into local comparisons and assigns each comparison to the source that is best at that comparison. With more states, the same specialization logic survives through a concavification characterization: the decision problem is decomposed into payoff-relevant components, and each component is assigned to its best source. These results offer a new rationale for why ignoring information can be optimal and highlight the benefit of using specialized information sources when correlations are ambiguous.

Title: Auditors' Response to Clients' Cyber Breaches: A Human‐Capital Perspective
Authors: Bing Li, Yifu Li, Jeffrey Pittman, Wenfeng Wang
Affiliations: Department of Accountancy City University of Hong Kong Kowloon Hong Kong; Department of Accounting Renmin University of China Beijing China; Faculty of Business Administration, Memorial University St. John's Newfoundland and Labrador Canada; Department of Accounting and Information Systems Virginia Tech Blacksburg Virginia USA; Department of Accounting Southern University of Science and Technology Shenzhen China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Using online job postings data, we explore whether auditors adjust their human capital in response to clients' cyber breach incidents. We find that audit offices increase their demand for cybersecurity specialists after their clients' cyber breaches, implying that cyber breaches change not only client risk but also their auditor's production function. Consistent with expectations, we document that this impact is larger when breaches involve their own clients (rather than those of peer offices within the same audit firm) and when breaches directly involve financial information. Our evidence holds for both cyber‐focused and non‐cyber‐focused offices, highlighting the broad impact of cybersecurity risks on audit practices. Additionally, we find that audit offices with relatively high investment in cybersecurity human capital are better able to preserve their market share among clients in high‐cyber‐risk industries after a client's cyber breach.

Title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
Authors: Ned Augenblick, Eben Lazarus
Abstract: ABSTRACT We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

Title: It's in the Small Steps: Navigating Knotted Change‐Stability Tensions in Complex Collaborations
Authors: Lea Stadtler, Luk N. Van Wassenhove
Affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management; INSEAD
Abstract: Abstract Addressing societal challenges requires collaborative arrangements that can adapt to changing environments while maintaining coherence. Existing research highlights collaborative responses to change, yet the processes through which such responses emerge remain poorly understood. Notably, collaborative change involves not only balancing change and stability but also navigating knotted collective‐individual tensions that arise in realigning interests, coordination structures, and operations. To advance understanding of these dynamics, we conduct an in‐depth longitudinal study of collaborative change in a cross‐sector disaster relief partnership. Across successive change stages, we identify stability drivers emerging from collective‐individual tensions that prompted the partners to adopt specific balancing practices. These practices enabled a change process that was incremental and fragile in progression, yet resilient in its cumulative pattern. We develop a process model that explains the dynamics of collaborative change and shows how balancing change and stability enables partners to progressively broaden and occasionally transcend collective‐individual alignment as trust and mutual understanding deepen. This study advances collaboration and paradox theory by exposing balancing practices tailored to collaborative settings that enable adaptation in dynamic environments and by proposing a gradual approach to navigating knotted paradoxes.

Title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
Authors: Philip Bond, Yue Yuan, Hongda Zhong
Affiliations: Foster School of Business, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195; and Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Finance Theory Group, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; and School of Management and Department of Economics, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; and University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080; and The Centre for Economic Policy Research, London, EC1R 5HL, United Kingdom
Abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. We show that this asymmetry in the diversity of transaction methods in issuances and repurchases and the size-method relation in issuances are natural consequences of the single informational friction of a firm having superior information to investors. Moreover, although this friction always leads firms to issue inefficiently little, it leads firms to repurchase too little if they maximize long-term shareholder value but too much if the primary goal is to boost short-term share prices. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: Y.
