Title: Differentiation from mentors and the gender productivity gap in research: Evidence from electrical engineering
Authors: Denis Trapido
Abstract: The gender productivity gap — women's persistently lower research output relative to men — is a primary driver of gender inequality in science and technology careers, yet its causal origins remain incompletely understood. This study proposes a novel mechanism underlying the gender productivity gap: female researchers' greater differentiation from their academic mentors. Drawing on theories of creative atypicality among underrepresented minorities, I argue that in male-dominated fields, women diverge more from mentors' research agendas due to both discriminatory treatment and being less constrained by fields' mainstream paradigms. Because differentiation from mentors impedes research productivity, this divergence contributes to the gender productivity gap. An analysis of careers in information theory, a subfield of electrical engineering, showed that female researchers differentiated more from mentors than male researchers: a significantly larger share of their work was not co-authored with academic advisers, was published in different research domains, cited different antecedent work, and had co-authors outside the adviser's co-authorship network. Multivariate regression decomposition showed that all of these differences except the last accounted for a significant portion of the gender productivity gap. These findings hold after controlling for parenthood and domestic partnership. The study advances understanding of the relational origins of gender inequality in research careers and suggests targeted interventions to better integrate female doctoral students into mentors' research programs.

Title: Closer to the leader, above the coworkers? How leader gratitude expression shapes employee responses across relational targets
Authors: Hun Whee Lee, Yahua Cai, Yuanmeng Wang, Seo-Young Byun, Sang Hoon Han, Timothy Judge
Abstract: Leader gratitude expression is widely regarded as a beneficial leadership practice. Integrating social exchange theory with social comparison theory, we not only affirm this view but also show that leader gratitude can carry unintended consequences under specific conditions. We argue that for employees higher in prosocial motivation, leader gratitude strengthens employees’ relational attachment to the leader and, in turn, increases organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs) directed toward the leader. For employees higher in Machiavellianism, it instead heightens a sense of superiority over coworkers, promoting counterproductive work behaviors (CWBs) directed at peers. We tested this dual-pathway model across four studies: two multi-wave field studies conducted in China (N = 524) and the United States (N = 180), and two experimental studies, including a vignette-based experiment (N = 138) and a critical incident technique study (N = 142). Results consistently supported the positive pathway from leader gratitude expression through relational attachment to leader-directed OCB. The negative pathway from leader gratitude expression through sense of superiority to coworker-directed CWB emerged specifically when employees were high in Machiavellianism. These findings advance a target-specific view of leader gratitude, showing that a single positive act can deepen the focal relationship while, for some employees, undermining those outside it.
Journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

Title: Editorial Board
Why Is Intermediating Houses So Difficult? Evidence from iBuyers
Authors: Greg Buchak, Gregor Matvos, Tomasz Piskorski, Amit Seru
Affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, and National Bureau of Economic Research; Northwestern University and National Bureau of Economic Research; Columbia University and National Bureau of Economic Research; Stanford Graduate School of Business, Hoover Institution, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, and National Bureau of Economic Research
Abstract: We study the frictions in dealer-intermediation in residential real estate through the lens of "iBuyers," technology entrants, who purchase and sell residential real estate through online platforms. iBuyers supply liquidity to households by allowing them to avoid a lengthy sale process. They sell houses quickly and earn a 5% spread. Their prices are well explained by a simple hedonic model, consistent with their use of algorithmic pricing. iBuyers choose to intermediate in markets that are liquid, and in which automated valuation models have low pricing error. These facts suggest that iBuyers' speedy offers may come at the cost of information loss concerning house attributes that are difficult to capture in an algorithm, resulting in adverse selection. We calibrate a dynamic structural search model with adverse selection to understand and quantify the economic forces underlying the tradeoffs of dealer intermediation in this market.

Title: The Impact of Unions on Nonunion Wage Setting: Threats and Bargaining
Authors: David A. Green, Ben M. Sand, Iain G. Snoddy, Jeanne Tschopp
Affiliations: University of British Columbia and Institute for Fiscal Studies; York University; Analysis Group; University of Bern
Abstract: In this paper we provide new estimates of the impact of unions on nonunion wage setting. We allow the presence of unions to affect nonunion wages both through the typically discussed channel of nonunion firms emulating union wages in order to fend off the threat of unionisation and through a bargaining channel in which nonunion workers use the presence of union jobs as part of their outside option. We specify these channels in a search and bargaining model that includes union formation and, in our most complete model, the possibility of nonunion firm responses to the threat of unionisation. Our results indicate an important role played by union wage spillovers in lowering wages over the 1980-2010 period. We find de-unionisation can account for 38% of the decline in the mean hourly wage between 1980 and 2010, with two-thirds of that effect being due to spillovers. Both the traditional threat and bargaining channels are operational, with the bargaining channel being more important.

Title: Environmental Consequences of Hydrocarbon Infrastructure Policy
Authors: Thomas R. Covert, Ryan Kellogg
Affiliations: Airbnb; Harris School of Public Policy, University of Chicago, and National Bureau of Economic Research
Abstract: The U.S. shale boom has profoundly increased crude oil movements by both pipelines-the traditional mode of transportation-and railroads. This paper develops a model of how pipeline investment and railroad use are determined in equilibrium, emphasizing how railroads' flexibility allows them to compete with pipelines. We show that policies that address crude-by-rail's environmental externalities by increasing its costs should lead to large increases in pipeline investment and substitution of oil flows from rail to pipe. Similarly, we find that policies enjoining pipeline construction would cause 80-90% of the displaced oil to flow by rail instead.

Title: Peer Effects and Rank Concerns in the Classroom
Authors: Michela M. Tincani
Affiliations: University College London (UCL), Institute for Fiscal Studies, Stone Centre at UCL, CESifo, Human Capital and Economic Opportunity Global Working Group, and INSPIRE
Abstract: I examine how disruptions to students' environments propagate to their classmates to understand the mechanisms behind peer interactions in the classroom.I combine administrative and survey data from Chile with detailed measures of housing damages from the 2010 earthquake, one of the most violent ever recorded.Damages to a student's own home reduced achievement and raised self-reported cost of study effort.Average damages among classmates induced schools to reallocate resources towards student support and increased achievement.In contrast, dispersion in classmates' damages had heterogeneous achievement effects across the prior performance distribution, which schools did not appear to mitigate, pointing to peer interactions.Motivated by evidence suggesting students value classroom rank, I show that a game-of-status model of competition for grades rationalizes the findings.The results suggest that, beyond production complementarities and a desire to conform, a desire to compete could shape peer effects on learning.2 Examples of studies using naturally occurring exogenous variation in peer characteristics to account for confounding effects are Hoxby (2000); Angrist and Lang (2004); Hoxby and Weingarth (2005); Lavy, Paserman, and Schlosser (2012); Imberman, Kugler, and Sacerdote (2012).3 I gratefully acknowledge Prof. Sergio Ruiz of the Geology Department at the University of Chile, a leading expert on the seismic vulnerability of Chilean buildings, for feedback on the damage measure.The measure falls within Deterministic Earthquake Loss Estimation, which aims to estimate losses from a specific seismic event.It stands in contrast to Probabilistic Earthquake Loss Estimation, which aims to predict potential losses from many possible seismic events (McGuire (2004)).

Title: Online Business Models, Digital Ads, and User Welfare
Authors: Daron Acemoglu, Daniel Huttenlocher, Asuman Ozdaglar, James Siderius
Affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth
Abstract: We present a model where social media platforms offer plans that intermix entertaining content with digital advertising (“ads”). Users derive utility from entertainment and learn about their valuation for a product from ads. While some users are fully rational, others naïvely perceive digital ads as more informative than they actually are. We characterize the profit-maximizing business model of the platform and show that welfare is lower when the platform monetizes through advertising instead of subscription both for naïfs (because they are targeted by intense digital advertising, which makes them over-optimistic about product quality and over-purchase the product) and for sophisticates (because the inflated demand from naïfs increases the firm’s price). This negative welfare effect is intensified when the platform can offer mixed business models that separate the naïve and sophisticated users into different plans. Our results are robust to firm-level and platform-level competition, because digital ads soften competition between both firms and platforms. We also show how digital ad taxes can improve welfare. Real Effects of Subjectivity in Measuring Fair Values
Authors: Verena Braun, Robert F. Göx, Felix P. Niggemann, Ulrich Schäfer
Affiliations: Department of Business Administration University of Zurich; Department of Accounting, Innovation, and Strategy University of Vienna
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how the subjectivity in measuring fair values of assets without readily observable market prices affects investment efficiency and shareholder value. When fair values are objective measures of asset value, they facilitate efficient investment decisions that align with shareholder interests. In contrast, firms' reliance on subjective valuation inputs causes underinvestment in long‐term projects. If fair values are highly subjective, they may lead firms to favor less profitable short‐term projects with objectively measurable fair values. When project returns are positively correlated, subjectivity in valuing long‐term projects induces overinvestment in short‐term projects with objective fair values. Regardless of these distortions, fair value measurement can add shareholder value. Not measuring fair values altogether leads to underinvestment, which moderately subjective fair values can alleviate.

Title: Fixed Pay for Output or Time? Implications for Work Speed and Quality
Authors: Carolyn Deller, Santiago Gallino
Affiliations: The Wharton School University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper explores the influence of two fixed payment arrangements—time‐based and output‐based wages—on worker behavior and performance in a multidimensional task setting. We examine how these wages affect the time workers spend on individual units of a task and their work quality. We contend that fixed compensation schemes can implicitly communicate standards of acceptable work. Our empirical evidence from MTurk experiments and a laboratory experiment indicates that workers on output‐based wages deliver higher quality and spend more time on individual units than their time‐based counterparts. These findings are consistent with output‐based wages, implying a standard of acceptable quality—without a conflicting standard of speed—to which workers respond. Our results emphasize the power of implicit cues from fixed compensation schemes and offer insights for employers, suggesting the choice between output‐ and time‐based wages should be informed by whether quality or turnaround time is valued more.

Title: Monitoring Quality of Mafia‐Connected Accountants
Authors: Pietro A. Bianchi, Jere R. Francis, Antonio Marra, Nicola Pecchiari
Affiliations: Bocconi University; University of Missouri (Emeritus)
Abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate the monitoring quality of accountants with ties to the Mafia in their role as auditors for “clean” firms—those with no known ties to organized crime. Using a proprietary government database, we identify Italian firms with alleged ties to the Mafia through their executives, directors, or shareholders. We define “suspect accountants” as those who serve as auditors for these Mafia‐connected firms, acknowledging their potential associations with criminal entities. We predict and find evidence that “clean” clients (treatment group) monitored by suspect accountants are more likely to engage in earnings management practices that reduce taxable income, compared with a control sample of “clean” firms monitored by accountants with no known Mafia ties (control group). Our findings suggest that accountants with ties to the Mafia act as low‐quality monitors in the “clean” economy.

Title: The Impact of Financial Reporting Mandates on Labor Unions
Authors: Qingkai Dong, Anthony Le
Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Booth School of Business University of Chicago
Abstract: ABSTRACT Labor unions in the United States are subject to financial reporting mandates. This study examines how these mandates affect unions and their members. Using several regulation‐based empirical designs, we document that more granular reporting requirements adversely affect unions' election outcomes. Supplemental analyses suggest that these findings are consistent with the strategic use of unions' disclosed information by parties such as employers and their consultants. We find mixed evidence on whether the mandates materially improve oversight of unions. Lastly, we find that the mandate reduces employees' average pay without clear benefits for employers, aside from reallocating investment from labor to capital. Collectively, our results suggest that more fine‐grained financial reporting requirements impose costs on unions and weaken their ability to represent employees, resulting in worse employment outcomes.

Title: Quid Pro Quo? Private Information Flows in Shareholder Activism: Evidence from Mutual Fund Families
Authors: Eunjee Kim, Hai Pham
Affiliations: Texas A&M University; Towson University
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper hypothesizes that information flows from target firms to large shareholders during activist campaigns and that these flows have governance consequences. Focusing on actively managed mutual fund families, we find that informed trading by large‐holding fund families increases during activist campaigns relative to smaller‐holding fund families invested in the same firms. The effect is stronger for firms that attend more invitation‐only investor events, face greater threats from activist campaigns, and are harder to value. Consistent with information flowing from management to large‐holding fund families, the effect strengthens when Regulation Fair Disclosure enforcement is lax and when the information is favorable to the firm. Furthermore, the increased information advantage is associated with more management‐friendly voting behavior by these investors and a higher likelihood of target firms winning activist campaigns and retaining board seats. Overall, our findings are consistent with a potential quid pro quo in which investors’ access to information from management is associated with more pro‐management behavior.

Title: Do Engagement Quality Reviewers’ Workplace Ties with Engagement Partners Influence Audit Quality?
Authors: Yue Qi, Timothy A. Seidel, Joseph H. Zhang, Junsheng Zhang
Affiliations: School of Management University of Science and Technology of China; BYU Marriott School of Business Brigham Young University; Schmidthorst College of Business Bowling Green State University Bowling Green; School of Business Sun Yat‐sen University
Abstract: ABSTRACT The engagement quality review is a key component of an audit firm's quality control system. This study leverages unique data on individual engagement quality reviewers (EQRs) to examine how previous shared working experience between EQRs and engagement partners affects audit quality. While prior research suggests that within‐firm network ties between predecessor and successor partners facilitate knowledge transfer, we find that prior shared working experience between EQRs and engagement partners is associated with lower audit quality. Mechanism tests indicate that such experience is associated with a higher likelihood of regulatory enforcement actions related to deficiencies in audit procedures, insufficient evidence, and a lack of professional skepticism. We also find that such experience corresponds with higher materiality thresholds, suggesting reduced scrutiny during audit planning and execution. Additional analyses reveal that these adverse effects primarily arise when previous shared working relationships did not produce adverse outcomes, when EQRs are not audit industry leaders, and when they face lower reputational risk. These findings are especially salient given that EQRs’ previous shared working experience with engagement partners appears to weigh heavily in EQR assignments. Overall, our study provides important insights into the implications of EQR independence and the determinants of engagement quality review effectiveness.

Title: Using Unconscious Thought to Improve Evaluations of Complex Accounting Estimates
Authors: Blake Holman, Benjamin P. Commerford, Finn Kinserdal
Affiliations: University of South Carolina; University of Kentucky, NHH Norwegian School of Economics; NHH Norwegian School of Economics
Abstract: ABSTRACT Complex accounting estimates are becoming increasingly important to financial statements. Yet, such estimates create ample opportunities for bias. Although both management and independent auditors are tasked with ensuring these estimates are free from error and bias, evaluating the appropriateness of these measures can be quite difficult. Drawing on unconscious thought theory, we predict and find across three experiments that engaging in unconscious thought can improve accounting practitioners’ evaluations of accounting estimates. In Experiment 1, we use practicing auditors as participants and find that unconscious thought improves less‐experienced auditors’ ability to recognize income‐decreasing patterns of bias. In contrast, more‐experienced auditors respond similarly to both incoming‐increasing and income‐decreasing bias, regardless of whether they use conscious or unconscious processing. In Experiments 2 and 3, we provide evidence that prompting managers to engage in unconscious thought also improves their recognition of patterns of bias within estimates. Overall, our findings demonstrate how unconscious processing can be intentionally prompted to improve accounting professionals’ ability to recognize subtle patterns of bias that they might otherwise overlook.

Title: Do Investors Value Auditor Involvement in Non‐GAAP Reporting?
Authors: Phillip T. Lamoreaux, Lauren Matkaluk, Amy G. Sheneman
Affiliations: Arizona State University; University of San Diego; The Ohio State University
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines investors’ perceptions of auditor involvement in non‐GAAP reporting as captured by non‐GAAP disclosures in 10‐K filings. We find that firm‐years with auditor involvement in non‐GAAP reporting have higher CARs, lower bid–ask spreads, lower stock volatility, and lower abnormal trading volume on 10‐K filing dates. To sharpen identification of auditor involvement, we hand‐collect non‐GAAP measures and reconciliations for S&P 500 firms and identify which exclusions reconcile directly to the audited financial statements. As the percentage of exclusions that reconcile directly to the audited financial statements increases, bid–ask spreads and stock volatility on 10‐K filing dates decrease. We find that the results are not driven by strategic reporting or managers’ responses to perceived litigation risk. This study provides new insights into non‐GAAP disclosures outside of earnings announcements, which have been largely ignored in prior literature. Collectively, our results suggest investors value auditor involvement in non‐GAAP reporting and inform policymakers and standard setters considering the usefulness of assurance over non‐GAAP measures.

Title: Revenue Recognition Comparability and Analysts’ Disclosure Processing Costs
Authors: Andrea Tillet
Affiliations: Wisconsin School of Business University of Wisconsin–Madison
Abstract: ABSTRACT I examine whether the FASB's revenue recognition guidance under ASC 606 influences revenue comparability across firms and industries and whether revenue comparability reduces analysts’ disclosure processing costs. I extract firms’ revenue policy disclosures from 10‐K filings to measure their textual similarity and compare revenue policies across firms and industries. I find an increase in revenue comparability for firms in different industries with similar revenue‐generating transactions upon adoption of ASC 606. In contrast, I find a decrease in revenue comparability for firms in the same industry with similar revenue‐generating transactions. Further, though I find that analysts are more likely to forecast revenues when firms have higher revenue comparability, this benefit of revenue comparability is less pronounced under ASC 606. This finding suggests the ASC 606‐related changes to revenue comparability impose disclosure processing costs on analysts.

Title: A Tale of Two Market Disciplines: How Does Bank Financial Misconduct Affect Peer Banks in the Local Deposit Market
Authors: Ya Kang, Yupeng Lin, Yang Qiu
Affiliations: CUHK Business School, Chinese University of Hong Kong; NUS Business School, National University of Singapore; School of Management, Zhejiang University
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the spillover effect of bank financial misconduct on the uninsured deposits of peer banks within local markets. We first validate that misconduct banks experience an increase in deposit spreads and a corresponding outflow of deposits following the misconduct. We then show local peer banks exhibit divergent deposit responses, contingent on how misconduct is perceived by information recipients in different economic contexts. During normal periods, depositors receiving a negative signal about bank misconduct reallocate their funds from misconduct banks to local peers, a local reallocation effect that decreases deposit spreads and increases deposit inflows for peer banks. Cross‐sectional analysis further reveals that this local reallocation effect is more pronounced for financially sophisticated depositors, amplified when peer banks have strong fundamentals, but attenuated when misconduct banks are financially sound. During financial crisis periods, however, bank misconduct leads to withdrawals from both misconduct banks and their peer banks, a local contagion effect whereby local peer banks face increased deposit spreads and deposit outflows following the misconduct.

Title: The Value of a Loss: The Impact of Restricting Tax Loss Transfers
Authors: Theresa Bührle, Elisa Casi, Barbara Stage, Johannes Voget
Affiliations: NHH Norwegian School of Economics; NHH Norwegian School of Economics and Skatteforsk; WHU ‐ Otto Beisheim School of Management; University of Mannheim
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the economic consequences of anti‐loss trafficking rules, which disallow the use of loss carryforwards as a tax shield after a substantial ownership change. We use staggered changes to these rules in the EU27 Member States, Norway, and the United Kingdom from 1998 to 2019 and find that limiting the transfer of tax losses is related to the number of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) declining by 18%, driven by loss‐making targets. Turning to broader industry dynamics, we find decreases in survival rates of young companies after tighter regulations. Loosening of regulation is associated with increased firm survival. Tightening (loosening) anti‐loss trafficking rules is related to decreased (increased) industry productivity, especially in R&D‐intensive industries that are more prone to loss‐making. Finally, tighter anti‐loss trafficking rules are associated with lower deal synergies and risk‐taking. All effects concentrate in strict regimes.

Title: Incidence, Risk, and Disclosure of Corporate Litigation: Insights from Federal Court Filings
Authors: Mary Brooke Billings, Robert W. Holthausen, Christine Petrovits, Danye Wang
Affiliations: New York University; University of Pennsylvania; College of William and Mary; University of Iowa
Abstract: ABSTRACT We assemble and describe a sample of 174,782 lawsuits filed against 218,437 public‐company lawsuit‐defendants in federal district court from 2006 to 2021. These lawsuits involve an array of allegations, including product liability, civil rights discrimination, contract breaches, improper compensation and labor practices, antitrust violations, corruption, securities violations, pollution, and intellectual property infringement. The sample exhibits rich variation across firms, industries, time, suit type, plaintiffs, and outcomes—reflecting not only firm activities but also social, political, and regulatory trends. Although many claims matter very little, some are important individually or in aggregate. We observe 23% of defendants experience a market value decline exceeding 10% of current assets around the lawsuit filing. Consistent with the notion that even low‐stakes claims, when numerous or persistent, can introduce frictions or reflect underlying issues, we find that aggregate legal exposure is associated with increased return volatility and decreased profitability. Subsequent tests indicate that materiality, public and private enforcement, and firms’ information environments (as well as other firm traits) are associated with managers’ decisions to disclose these claims. Collectively, our descriptive evidence establishes a foundation for further research into underexplored types of corporate litigation that represent a broad range of alleged wrongdoing and socially irresponsible behavior.

Title: Issue Information ‐ Request for Papers

Issue Information
Unaffiliated component auditors and audit fee models: The case of lowballing
Authors: Angela K. Pettinicchio, Peter F. Pope, Alessandra Scimeca
Abstract: Disclosure rules in many countries require public companies to report fees paid to the principal audit firm and its affiliates, but not to unaffiliated component auditors (UCAs). Reported fees thus depend on component auditor affiliation. We show that UCA involvement is significant in many countries. Using Italian private companies’ public filings, we find that UCA involvement is a statistically and economically significant source of bias in audit fee models. This bias is particularly relevant around principal auditor changes, when some subsidiaries temporarily retain UCAs before switching to auditors affiliated with the new principal auditor. The exclusion of fees paid to temporary UCAs explains the initial-year audit fee discount (lowballing) previously documented, which disappears once these omitted fees are accounted for. Our results suggest that lowballing reflects measurement bias rather than systematic strategic pricing. Because UCAs are common internationally and disclosure rules similarly exclude these fees, this bias extends beyond Italy.

Title: IPOs and Foreign Tax Structures
Authors: Christine L. Dobridge, Rebecca Lester, Andrew Whitten
Affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; Stanford University; U.S. Department of the Treasury
Abstract: ABSTRACT Does going public affect the amount and type of corporate international tax planning? Using a panel of U.S. corporate tax return data from 2004 to 2018, we show that IPO completion is associated with the rapid implementation of multinational foreign tax structures. Specifically, within three years after filing for an IPO, firms (1) expand their presence in low-tax jurisdictions, (2) enter into cross-border agreements that accompany intangible asset transfers to foreign subsidiaries, and (3) increase the likelihood and level of foreign related-party income-shifting payments. Effects are strongest among firms with strong capital market pressure to hit post-IPO earnings targets, firms with high R&D spending pre-IPO, and firms with limited ability to use net operating loss carryforwards. We contribute to the nascent literature studying tax implications of IPOs by documenting the types and timing of specific tax strategies that enable public firms to remain lightly taxed in the post-IPO period. JEL Classifications: F23; H25; H26.

Title: Balancing Act: How Unaffiliated Analysts Navigate Private Information Disadvantages
Authors: Leila Peyravan, Brian Rountree, Konduru Sivaramakrishnan
Affiliations: Rice University
Abstract: ABSTRACT Using analyst-lender affiliation in syndicated loans as a proxy for differential access to private information, we examine how unaffiliated analysts respond to this disadvantage. We find that unaffiliated analysts are more likely to herd toward affiliated analysts following loan origination, leading to improved forecast accuracy but weaker market reactions, consistent with reduced information content. In addition, herding analysts improve their forecast accuracy for other firms in their portfolios relative to nonherding analysts, suggesting a reallocation of effort. To capture information acquisition directly, we analyze IP address data from SEC EDGAR log files and find that unaffiliated analysts increase search activity, driven primarily by those not designated as herding. Although herding behavior wanes after the first year post-loan, elevated EDGAR searches persist for three years. Overall, our study provides novel evidence on how selective access to private information influences analysts’ competitive behavior. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the text, subject to the terms and conditions of those sources. JEL Classifications: G24; G14; G29.

Title: The Paternity Leave Ripple Effect in the Finance Industry: Shaping Norms and Social Cohesion
Authors: Almudena Cañibano, Marion Festing, Stefanie Titze
Affiliations: ESCP Business School Paris France; ESCP Business School Berlin Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT Paternity leave shifts work‐life policy from accommodating women's caregiving to legitimizing men's involvement in care. We examine how this is experienced in male‐dominated workplaces and interpreted by those around leave‐takers through interviews with fathers who took extended paternity leave in French finance organizations, and other stakeholders at work (colleagues, HR representatives, top managers) and at home (life partners). Following an interpretivist, context‐dependent approach, we find that participants associated paternity leave with changes in social relations, connectedness, and concern for collective well‐being. We theorize that, under certain conditions, these changes may coalesce into relational and collective experiences aligned with social cohesion beyond the workplace. We further theorize two pathways. In a transformative cycle, paternity leave may disrupt descriptive and injunctive gender norms, and experiences aligned with social cohesion occur. In a maintenance cycle, established norms persist, and such experiences largely do not arise. These divergent pathways depend on the favorability of nested contextual conditions: meso‐ (policy design, top management engagement, organizational climate) and micro‐ (manager, peer support), within the macro‐context of a male‐dominated industry. The study extends work‐life policy research beyond individual and organizational outcomes and identifies conditions under which paternity leave may challenge gendered divisions of labor within and beyond organizations.

Title: Framing the unknowable: The role of language and frame multiplicity in early‐stage startup pitches
Authors: Ann‐Sophie Kowalewski
Affiliations: Entrepreneurship Department IE University Madrid Spain
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Early‐stage startup pitches must make largely unknowable futures plausible. As such, they bear a rhetorical burden. This study theorizes how multiple frames jointly shape this burden and, consequently, affect investor evaluations. Specifically, it considers how future growth frames interact with concreteness and novelty frames. Evidence from 618 startup pitches and ad‐hoc investor evaluations reveals that growth frames relying more on entrepreneurs' own assertions than on established grounds tend to receive lower investor evaluations. This evaluative discount is alleviated when growth is expressed concretely but becomes more pronounced when the pitch emphasizes novelty. These findings extend framing theory by explaining the relevance and possible implications of frame multiplicity in pitches and entrepreneurial communication more broadly. Managerial Summary Mobilizing support for a new venture is difficult because founders must often describe a future that does not yet exist. This study of 618 startup pitches shows that growth‐related messages can shape investor evaluations even at the earliest stage, but only if configured well. Because growth frames must appear plausible amid the uncertainty surrounding new startups, framing early‐stage startups around growth is rhetorically burdensome. Findings show that pitches are evaluated less favorably when they rely more on founders' own projections and reasoning than on established grounds such as market analyses. Concrete language can alleviate this burden, while novelty framing intensifies it. As such, this study reveals intricate and potentially unintended interactions among multiple frames within a single pitch.

Title: When machines learn with organizations: AI ‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
Authors: Linhui Wu, Shaker A. Zahra, Niron Hashai
Affiliations: Management and Organizations Department Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University Evanston Illinois USA; Strategic Management and Entrepreneurship Department Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota Minneapolis Minnesota USA; Arison School of Business Reichman University (IDC Herzliya) Herzliya Israel
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

Title: A problem-based scenario reduction approach for stochastic chemotherapy planning
Authors: Günsu Dağıstanlı Çallı, Serhat Gul, Melih Çelik
Abstract: The rising global demand for chemotherapy, combined with the limited capacity of chemotherapy units, highlights the need for efficient treatment planning. We address the problem of assigning multiple treatments of each patient to specific days and chairs over a fixed planning horizon, while accounting for uncertainty in treatment durations. The model incorporates time window constraints and nurse workload limitations, and is formulated as a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program. Deviations such as earliness, tardiness, within-window delays, deferrals to the next planning period, and overtime are penalized in the objective function. To address the computational burden of large scenario sets, we develop problem-based scenario reduction algorithms by extending a recent method from the stochastic programming literature. Using real data from an outpatient chemotherapy center, we evaluate our approach against alternative problem-based scenario reduction techniques and practical benchmark heuristics. To better reflect practice, we implement the approach within a rolling horizon framework. Finally, we perform sensitivity analyses and assess the value of stochastic solution.

Title: The project scheduling interdiction problem with delay groups
Authors: Fei Wu, Erik Demeulemeester, Jannik Matuschke
Abstract: Large-scale projects are frequently delayed by correlated disruptions: when a shared input such as a common supplier, a specialized team, or a supporting platform degrades, all dependent activities are slowed down simultaneously. This paper introduces delay groups to capture such disruptions: a delay group is a set of activities whose delays stem from a common cause, described jointly by an uncertainty set. Our model takes the perspective of an interdictor that, subject to a budget of $k$ groups, selects which groups to disrupt so as to maximize the project makespan. The interdictor can extend activity durations within each disrupted group by delays from a group-specific uncertainty set, while non-disrupted activities keep their nominal duration. We study the complexity of the resulting Project Scheduling Interdiction Problem with Delay Groups (PSIP-DG), which provides a worst-case stress test of the schedule. The problem is computationally intractable ($N\!P$-hard) for general polyhedral uncertainty sets, even for a single delay group with a continuous knapsack constraint. For budgeted uncertainty sets, we prove $N\!P$-hardness both when all activities of a disrupted group are delayed and when only one activity per group may be delayed, and derive an inapproximability bound of $1-1/e+\epsilon$ for the former case. We further develop a greedy heuristic with approximation guarantee $k$ and two structure-based heuristics with initializations and neighborhoods from tractable special cases. Experiments on $5{,}000$-activity networks show that the heuristics match the solution quality of an exact solver at substantially lower running times, in some cases finding strictly better solutions.

Title: Belief Traps Hinder Small Business Climate Action
Authors: Jeffrey Lees, Sara M. Constantino, Jean Cushen, Frederik Dahlmann, Frank G. A. de Bakker, Edoardo Della Torre, Maria Laura Frigotto, Mario Hackenbuchner, Nico Heuvinck, Emmanuel Kypraios, Anastasia Ri, Stephen Roper, Elke Schuessler, Christoph Ungemach, Dror Etzion
Affiliations: Department of Human Resource Management and Organizational Behavior, University of Groningen, The Netherlands; Department of Environmental Social Sciences, Doerr School of Sustainability, Stanford University, USA; School of Public and International Affairs, Princeton University, USA; School of Business, Maynooth University, Ireland; Warwick Business School, University of Warwick, UK; IESEG School of Management, University of Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 - LEM- Lille Economie Management, Lille, France; Department of Economics, Management and Quantitative Methods, University of Milan, Italy; Department of Economics and Management, University of Trento, Italy; Institute of Organization Science, Johannes Kepler University, Linz, Austria; Institute of Management and Organization, Leuphana University, Lüneburg, Germany; Linz Institute of Transformative Change, Johannes Kepler University, Linz, Austria; Nuremberg Institute of Market Decisions, Germany; Grossman School of Business, University of Vermont, USA
Abstract: Climate (in)action by small business owners is not driven only by policy or economic considerations but also by sociological and psychological factors, as leaders mimic the behaviors they perceive among their peers. We find that these social inferences about what others believe are often incorrect. In this registered report of 4,432 small-to-medium business owners and leaders across seven countries, we observe a persistent gap between perceived and actual beliefs. And this gap matters: small-to-medium enterprise owners exhibiting a larger gap have fewer sustainability policies in place. These results highlight how peer effects can spur climate action among business leaders.

Title: Machine Learning Measure-Supported Empirical Studies: A Survey
Authors: Wei Hu, Wenjie Huang, Yidi Liu, Bingqing Song, Mengfan Xuan, Sijia Zhou, Xin Li
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China; and Laboratory of High Quality Urban Development and Strategic Decision, Tongji University, Shanghai 200092, China; Department of Economics, Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Shenzhen 518172, China; School of Management and Economics and Shenzhen Finance Institute, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China; School of Economics and Management, Beijing Jiaotong University, Beijing 100044, China; Department of Electronic Commerce, Southeast University, Nanjing 211189, China; Department of Management and Marketing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong
Abstract: Machine learning and data science techniques have been widely used in practice and have received significant attention. In research settings, business scholars have begun to adopt machine learning as methodological tools. This paper reviews the literature that leverages machine learning-generated measurements to support empirical analysis and yield business insights, where machine learning can reduce reliance on human coding or enable new theoretical perspectives. We summarize the workflow, constructs, and measure structures in these machine learning measure-supported empirical studies. We believe machine learning holds substantial potential to advance business research. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science & Machine Learning. Title: Scalable Multistage Stochastic Optimization for Freight Procurement in Transportation-Inventory Systems
Authors: Lingxiao Wu, Wenxuan Shan, Yossiri Adulyasak, Jean-François Cordeau
Affiliations: Department of Aeronautical and Aviation Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; School of Systems Science, Beijing Jiaotong University, Beijing 100044, China; Department of Logistics and Operations Management, HEC Montréal, Montréal, Quebec H3T 2A7, Canada; and GERAD, Montréal, Quebec H3T 1J4, Canada
Abstract: The procurement of freight services is an important element for the supply chain management of a shipper (i.e., a manufacturer or retailer) that sources transportation services from the third-party logistics market. Motivated by a practical freight procurement problem faced by shippers, we provide a holistic approach to designing freight procurement strategies for transportation-inventory systems that captures the interconnections among freight procurement, transportation, and inventory management. In view of supply and demand uncertainties, we consider the problem on the basis of a multistage decision process with uncertain data. To handle instances of realistic size, we propose an enhanced stochastic dual dynamic programming solution approach. We conduct extensive numerical experiments to test the performance of the approach. The results demonstrate that our approach scales to very large instances with up to [Formula: see text] scenarios and that the proposed enhancement strategies significantly improve its performance. Compared with methods commonly adopted to solve similar problems, our approach achieves significant cost improvements based on generated instances calibrated from established benchmark instances and stochastic simulations. The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

Title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
Authors: Jia Liu, Olivier Toubia
Affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Business School, Marketing, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Columbia University, Columbia Business School, New York, New York, 10025, United States
Abstract: While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

Title: Cross-Cluster Referrals and Subsidy Schemes in Multi-Cluster Healthcare Systems
Authors: Liming Liu, Weixin Shang, Xiuli Chao, Shaohui Zheng
Affiliations: Lingnan University, Faculty of Business, Hong Kong; University of Michigan, Dept. of Industrial & Operations Engineering, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, School of Business and Management, Hong Kong
Abstract: Problem definition: Excessive and highly variable waiting times for specialty services are a long-standing problem for public healthcare systems. Healthcare authorities in some jurisdictions have begun to experiment with schemes to improve system performance, including cross-cluster referrals which allow patients to switch from their home cluster to other clusters with shorter waiting times, and opt-out subsidies which help patients seeking services from private providers outside the public system. However, few studies in the literature have examined the structure of the problem or offered analytical insights to the design of such schemes. Methodology/results: We construct a multi-cluster service network model to study optimal routing policies under both individual and system optimization. We define externalities in a network setting and establish their properties, and further identify conditions under which referrals are effective or counterproductive in reducing system costs. We also show that lowering the switching cost could inadvertently degrade overall system performance. In contrast to the classic result for single-cluster systems (e.g. Naor 1969), our analysis of opt-out and switching incentives reveals that fixed subsidies generally cannot fully coordinate a multi-cluster system due to the cross-cluster effect of externalities. However, they can effectively reduce system costs in wide ranges of system parameter values. We further show that dynamic (state-dependent) subsidies can achieve perfect alignment between individual and system optimization. Managerial implications: Our study suggests that cross-cluster referrals are effective when there is a substantial workload imbalance but without excessive system congestion. They should be implemented with proper operational control: referrals should be promoted when the workload imbalance is high, but discouraged when the overall system workload is very high while the imbalance is insubstantial. Furthermore, fixed opt-out and switching subsidies can effectively improve system performance under different demand conditions and should be applied strategically: focusing on switching subsidies when the system workload is moderate and the imbalance is substantial, but shifting the focus to opt-out subsidies when the overall system workload is high.

Title: A Decision-Support Framework for Food Bank Operations: Overcoming Waste and Uncertainty in Food Distribution
Authors: Xianjia Gao, Xin Chen
Affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Gies College of Business, Urbana, Illinois, United States; Georgia Institute of Technology, H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Atlanta, Georgia, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Food banks face the complex operational challenge of allocating uncertain and per- ishable food donations to maximize community benefit. This requires navigating difficult trade-offs between effectiveness (delivering nutritious and fresh food relative to need), efficiency (maximizing food distributed and minimizing waste), and equity (ensuring fair distribution), a task for which traditional myopic poli- cies are often ill-equipped. Our research addresses how food banks can design practical, forward-looking allocation strategies in this dynamic and challenging environment. Methodology/results: We develop a comprehensive dynamic programming framework to model the food bank allocation problem. From this, we derive two practical and implementable policies: a simple, static Scaled Fluid (SF) policy and an adaptive Re-Optimized (ReOPT) policy. We provide rigorous theoretical proofs that both policies are asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, extensive simulations using both synthetic and real data show that our proposed strategies yield significant utility gains. Managerial implications: This research provides food bank man- agers and decision-makers with theoretically sound and empirically validated tools to improve their opera- tions. Our framework offers a clear path to enhance the impact and sustainability of food distribution efforts, enabling organizations to better serve their communities by making more efficient, effective, and equitable decisions with the resources they have.

Title: Humanitarian Aid Management under Corruptible Distribution and Oversight Agents
Authors: Paola Martin, Owen Q. Wu, Larysa Yakymova
Affiliations: Indiana University, ODT, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; Indiana University Bloomington Kelley School of Business, Department of Operations & Decision Technologies, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; Yuriy Fedkovych Chernivtsi National University, Department of Economic and Mathematical Modelling, Cernivici, Černìvec′kа, Ukraine
Abstract: Problem Definition: In many crisis contexts, such as armed conflicts, natural disasters, or refugee emergencies, one of the most pressing challenges is to regulate the delivery of humanitarian aid to the final beneficiaries in the presence of both corruptible agents (those responsible for delivering aid) and corruptible inspectors (who may be bribed not to report uncovered misappropriations). Strengthening anti-corruption efforts by hiring more inspectors and/or rewarding inspectors’ truthful reporting can reduce corruption but draws on the finite humanitarian aid financing, reducing the aid delivered to the beneficiaries. Methodology/Results: We develop a three-stage game-theoretic model in which a government agency chooses inspection intensity and the reward rate for inspectors’ truthful reporting, managers decide how much aid to misappropriate, and inspectors decide whether to report detected misconduct or accept a bribe to conceal misappropriation. The government agency aims to maximize the amount of humanitarian aid reaching the beneficiaries. We find that the role of inspectors depends on the financing available. When the financing is low, inspectors serve to detect misconduct; when the financing is sufficiently high, inspectors also affect managers' behavior and deter misappropriation. The reward can also serve two purposes. It can either induce truthful reporting and eliminate bribery, or increase the bribe that managers must pay, thereby reducing their incentive to misappropriate. We characterize the impact of key parameters on the optimal anti-corruption levers. Managerial Implications: Our results provide guidance for agencies and donors on how to balance aid provision with anti-corruption measures, and how to adjust inspection intensity and incentive for truthful reporting to maximize the amount of aid reaching its intended recipients. As financing changes, resources should be allocated toward adjusting inspection intensity. In contrast, the reward rate for truthful reporting should be calibrated to the enforcement environment, and not be mechanically increased with the amount of financing.

Title: Taking a Note from Music: Conceptual Sampling and the Creative Logic of Theory Development

Title: The Hidden Upside of Tech Challenges
Authors: Stefan Tams, Ofir Turel, Kevin Hill
Abstract: The stresses of technological roadblocks and challenges can result in employee ambivalence and easily lead to disengagement. But tech stress isn’t always bad. New research shows that increasing constructive technology challenges offers employees engaging growth opportunities — if annoying tech hindrances have already been mitigated. The researchers share a three-part approach for creating a stimulating work environment while minimizing tech hurdles and employee ambivalence.

Title: Does Free Speech Law Contribute to Corporate Social Responsibility Behavior? Empirical Evidence
Authors: Paul A. Griffin, Hyun Hong, Boochun Jung, S. Katie Moon, Jiwoo Ryou
Affiliations: University of California, Davis; University of California, Riverside; University of Hawaii at Manoa; Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology; West Virginia University
Abstract: ABSTRACT People’s right to free speech can have profound effects on how firms discharge their social and environmental responsibilities. We examine these effects by analyzing the impact of the staggered enactment of anti-SLAPP free speech laws across U.S. states on firms’ corporate social responsibility (CSR) behavior. We theorize that, following the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, firms enhance their CSR activities as an economically effective means to counter negative publicity from stakeholders. Supporting this idea, we find that firm CSR activity increases after the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, accompanied by an increase in stakeholder criticism of firms’ social and environmental practices. Further, we observe an increase in the level of CSR disclosure. The link between anti-SLAPP law enactment and subsequent CSR engagement is stronger in states with more comprehensive anti-SLAPP protections than in those with weaker protections. Title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
Authors: Yiwei Dou, Danye Wang, Xi Wu
Affiliations: New York University; The University of Iowa; University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: ABSTRACT Mortgage fraud was a leading force behind the 2008 financial crisis. We measure the fraudulent income overstatement at the bank-ZIP Code-year level as the difference in the local growth between reported income in mortgage applications and the income based on IRS data. We find that overstated income is positively associated with banks’ internal control weaknesses over financial reporting and negatively associated with subsequent remediation of such weaknesses. The associations are concentrated among banks that integrate their accounting and operation processes, as proxied by the adoption of an Enterprise Resource Planning system. Finally, using the removal of internal control provisions in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act in 2005 as a shock to internal control quality, we find that affected banks experience increased income overstatement on mortgage applications. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from the public and proprietary sources identified in the article. Access to proprietary data is subject to the relevant providers’ licensing restrictions. JEL Classifications: G01; G21; G28; G51; M41.

Title: How Black Accounting Faculty Exercise Agency to Navigate Career Advancement within Institutional Structures
Authors: Michelle K. Harding, Jennifer R. Joe, Kerri-Ann Sanderson
Affiliations: Virginia Tech; Bentley University
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how tenured BAF experience and navigate institutional structures while advancing their careers. Leveraging a qualitative approach, we find BAF encounter recurring forms of marginalization embedded in organizational structures that lead to social identity threats that destabilize their identities as scholars and teachers. BAF respond to these threats by employing agentic and self-preserving coping responses designed to affirm identity and negotiate career advancement. Although coping responses can be effective on an individual level, they do not transform institutional structures and can provoke pushback that reinscribes marginalization. The findings unsettle common assumptions that effort in conditions marked by objectivity and neutrality drives career advancement and highlight the institutional structures and invisible labor that BAF navigate to achieve career advancement. We fill the void in the literature examining how career advancement unfolds within racialized conditions of academic institutions and advance research on minoritized group status in accounting academia.

Title: Productivity versus Efficiency: The Effect of Incentive Focus on Target Setting in Participative Budgets
Authors: Jake Andrassy, Jason L. Brown, Timothy Mallon, Ashley K. Sauciuc
Affiliations: Texas State University; Indiana University Bloomington; Portland State University
Abstract: ABSTRACT Firms typically design incentive systems to motivate employees and advance firm objectives, including productivity (i.e., maximizing output) and efficiency (i.e., minimizing input). However, there remains little empirical research on the potential psychological effects of adopting a productivity versus efficiency focus on employee risk perceptions and decision-making. To address this important gap, we examine how these different incentive foci affect employee target setting under participative budgets. We predict and find that employees perceive efficiency incentives as riskier than productivity incentives, leading to lower target setting. Moreover, consistent with our theory, this effect disappears in the absence of outcome uncertainty. We also find employees are less likely to achieve their target and have higher error rates under efficiency incentives, despite setting easier targets. Overall, our findings suggest that efficiency incentives, relative to productivity incentives, can have detrimental effects on target setting and subsequent performance in participative budgeting settings. Data Availability: Contact the authors. JEL Classifications: M41; M52; J33.

Title: Innovation Orientation in New Product A Unified Framework of Backward-Looking and Forward-Looking Perspectives
Authors: Yueyue Zhang, Xia Zhao, Ling Xue, Cheng Zhang
Affiliations: University of Nottingham Ningbo China Ningbo, PR China; Terry College of Business, University of Georgia Athens, GA U.S.A.; School of Management, Fudan University Shanghai, PR China
Abstract: This study develops an integrated framework to reconcile different theoretical lenses on how firms respond to expected competitive threats with different innovation orientations in new product development. The framework unifies both the forward-looking and backward-looking perspectives of organizational decision-making. We theorize how a firm’s past performance feedback (a key backward-looking factor) shapes the relationship between expected competitive threats (a key forward-looking factor) and product innovation orientation by influencing the firm’s sense of controllability, and how this effect is influenced by the firm’s information technology (IT) investment and alliance network structure. Based on an empirical analysis of 1,571 public US firms, we find that past performance feedback has a positive moderating effect on the relationship between expected competitive threats and product exploration orientation. Specifically, when the firm has unfavorable past performance feedback, the relationship between expected competitive threats and product exploration orientation is significantly negative, as predicted by the threat-rigidity theory. However, when the firm has favorable past performance feedback, this relationship becomes positive, as predicted by the Behavioral Theory of the Firm. We theorize and empirically verify that the sense of controllability derived from past performance feedback explains firms’ divergence in the framing of competitive threats and subsequent production innovation decision-making. Moreover, we find that the positive moderating effect of past performance feedback is alleviated when the firm has higher information processing capabilities (proxied by higher IT investment) or more external information access (proxied by a higher level of structural holes in its alliance network). Further examination suggests that greater information processing capabilities and information access allow firms to maintain a sense of control when expecting heightened competitive threats. These findings highlight the importance of information within the unified theoretical framework of both the backward-looking and forward-looking perspectives for product innovation.

Title: Digital Resilience as a Process of Relational Resourcing1
Authors: Angelos Kostis, Jonny Holmström, Stefan Haefliger
Affiliations: Umeå School of Business, Economics and Statistics, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden; Management Science and Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, U.S.A.; Swedish Center for Digital Innovation, Department of Informatics, Umeå University Umeå, Sweden; House of Innovation, Stockholm School of Economics, Stockholm, SWEDEN, and Bayes Business School, City St. George’s University of London, London, UK
Abstract: Digital resilience has become increasingly crucial for organizations and professionals in times of major exogenous shocks and escalating crises. Complementing capability-oriented accounts of digital resilience, we examined how resources are created through evolving relations, offering a process view of digital resilience. Through a longitudinal, qualitative study of Greek primary school teachers, we explored how digital resilience emerges through evolving relations despite limited organizational support. Drawing on a resourcing lens, our study establishes that digital resilience emerges and is sustained when professionals, motivated by value-laden beliefs that make them assume responsibility for turning potential resources into resources-in-use to respond to a shock, engage in a process we call relational resourcing. Our model of relational resourcing shows how resourcing convictions are enacted through processes including appropriating personal digital technologies, enlarging relational functionalities, and routinizing new enactments of resourcing convictions. Our findings expand resourcing theory by showing how resourcing activities entail new ways of relating from which resource value derives. Furthermore, the findings add to the relational view of technology by theorizing how and why entities or professionals learn to relate.

Title: Collective Attention Configurations in Open-Source Software Development: Interlacing for High Performance1
Authors: Yanran Liu, Arun Rai
Affiliations: Department of Operations, Business Analytics, and Information Systems, Lindner College of Business, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, OH, U.S.A.; Center for Digital Innovation and Computer Information Systems Department, Robinson College of Business, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, U.S.A.
Abstract: Coordinating open-source software (OSS) development requires both the division and integration of developers’ attention. How to combine these contradictory logics effectively, however, remains unclear. Adopting a configurational lens, we distinguish between developers’ primary attention, or their top-priority focus, and secondary attention, or their spare capacity. Along these two lines, division and integration take on different forms. Recombining these forms yields two new coordination logics: interlacing, which combines primary division with secondary integration, and interlocking, which combines primary integration with secondary division. Applying the same or different logics across OSS’s two key work types—discursive and technical—produces a broader set of coordination configurations. Analyzing 4,291 release cycles from 1,004 GitHub machine-learning projects, we find that isomorphic interlacing—applying interlacing in both work types—delivers the strongest performance of development speed, novelty, and quality. Configurations pairing interlacing with division or integration also perform well under particular contingencies of task interdependence, project ownership, and release-cycle length. By contrast, configurations involving interlocking consistently underperform. Our study advances OSS coordination theory by identifying a high-performing configuration that systematically combines division and integration and clarifying when alternative configurations can substitute for it.

Title: Reconceptualizing Patient Engagement with Mobile Healthcare Apps: A Computationally Intensive Theory Development for Patient Engagement Networks
Authors: Inkyoung Hur, Chul Woo Yoo, Jahyun Goo, Weidong Xia
Affiliations: Department of Information Technology and Operations Management, College of Business, Florida Atlantic University, Baca Raton, FL, USA; Department of Information Systems and Business Analytics, College of Business, Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
Abstract: Mobile healthcare apps are increasingly used to enhance patient engagement, yet research has rarely examined the underlying mechanisms that shape this engagement. Addressing this gap, the present study adopts a computationally intensive theory development approach to explore how mobile healthcare apps afford patient engagement. To this end, rather than focusing on isolated app affordances, we examine affordance networks – interconnected patterns of app usage by patients and clinicians – and their association with diverse engagement goals. Through empirical analysis and an abductive reasoning process, we reconceptualize patient engagement with mobile healthcare apps as Patient Engagement Networks (PENs): linked sets of collaborative digital actions between patients and/or clinicians, enacted by mobile healthcare apps, that support the pursuit of healthcare goals. We propose four distinct modes of PENs, such as emergent, time-deliberate, supportive, and self-service, each reflecting a unique configuration of engagement. These findings offer valuable theoretical and practical insights into the evolving nature of digital healthcare interactions.

Title: A Generalist Activity Paradox: Individual Performance and Collective Production Efficiency on Open Innovation Platforms
Authors: Lusi Yang, Zhiyi Wang, Steven L. Johnson
Affiliations: J. Mark Robinson College of Business, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA U.S.A.; Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO U.S.A.; McIntire School of Commerce, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA U.S.A.
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between generalist activity and multilevel performance on open innovation platforms for new product development. In such settings, task decomposition allows contributors to engage flexibly across multiple task types, giving rise to generalist activity, defined as the distribution of engagement across a wide variety of task types. Drawing on the generalist literature and the theory of collective production, we theorize how generalist activity relates to both individual and collective performance of crowds. Our multilevel framework and empirical findings indicate that generalist activity is positively associated with individual performance. However, due to the emergent nature of collaboration, a higher level of generalist activity within a crowd is associated with lower collective production efficiency, revealing a multilevel tension. This tension is attenuated as the crowd size increases. Mechanism analysis further shows that valuable contributions are more likely to emerge when contributors with generalist activity build upon task-focused inputs from preceding contributors with low levels of generalist activity. Overall, this study provides theoretical implications for open innovation platform research, generalist literature, and the theory of collective production.

Title: Outcome Over Process: Advancing Both Fairness and Performance in Crowdfunding Through ML-Assisted Promotion
Authors: Lauren Rhue, Jessica Clark
Affiliations: Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland – College Park College Park, MD U.S.A.
Abstract: Crowdfunding platforms can influence project success through their promotion policy, which determines which projects receive enhanced visibility. Promotion policies can directly influence inclusivity on the platform and potentially address well-documented disparities across creators. This study examines how alternative machine learning (ML) problem framings for promotion policy affect fairness and business performance. Using data from 118,780 Kickstarter projects, we compare three ML framings: a process framing that learns to reproduce historical employee promotion decisions, a success framing that predicts whether projects will meet their funding goals, and a backers framing that predicts whether projects will attract a large number of backers. We evaluate the resulting counterfactual promotion sets using multiple fairness and performance measures. In our context, the success framing produces promotion sets with more favorable fairness outcomes and business performance outcomes than the other framings, possibly because it applies more consistent promotion decisions across similar projects. These findings demonstrate that alternative ML problem framings can produce meaningfully different promotion policies, even when trained on the same underlying data. While the success framing prioritizes practical projects, the backers framing favors projects with higher funding goals. Importantly, carefully designing the ML problem framing for promotion policies can align fairness and performance objectives, countering concerns that inclusivity necessarily comes at the expense of performance. This research contributes to the information systems literature by demonstrating that ML problem framing is a consequential choice in platform governance. It offers practical guidance for digital platforms seeking to improve fairness and business performance through ML-assisted promotion policies.

Title: Immersion in Online Interaction Rituals: The Paradoxical Role of Time-Synchronized Comments on Video Platforms
Authors: Yijing Li, Kai H. Lim, Fei Liu, Yao Li
Affiliations: Faculty of Business, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, SAR, China
Abstract: Many video platforms promote time-synchronized comments (TSCs), comments overlaid on videos in sync with specific timestamps, to facilitate social interaction and enhance video engagement. Yet TSCs can both enrich viewing experiences and distract viewers, thereby reducing engagement. Because TSCs appear as continuous overlaid streams that offer viewers little control over pacing or selection, their structural features may shape interaction in opposing ways. Drawing on interaction ritual theory, we identify two such features, comment density and word density, and examine their effects on video engagement, together with the moderating roles of content characteristics of both TSCs and videos. We test our framework through a field study using panel data from a leading TSC-enabled platform and a psychophysiological experiment that captures viewers’ real-time attentional, emotional, and behavioral responses. The results show that higher comment density strengthens perceived assembly, mutual focus of attention, and emotional entrainment, thereby increasing engagement. By contrast, greater word density disrupts mutual focus and emotional entrainment, thereby reducing engagement. Emotional entrainment emerges as the central mechanism. We also find that these effects vary with TSC emotional polarization and video genre. In addition, we test a reduced visual overlay design that mitigates the negative effects of TSCs. By clarifying how, when, and why TSCs enhance or disrupt engagement, this study extends understanding of micro-level social interaction in mediated contexts and offers guidance for improving TSC-enabled video experiences.

Title: “Phygital” Experiences: Optimization, Tailoring, and Pricing Contract Strategies on Online Platforms1
Authors: Hongseok Jang, Kyung Sung Jung, Young Kwark
Affiliations: Freeman School of Business, Tulane University New Orleans, LA, U.S.A.; Department of Information Systems, Korea University Business School (KUBS), Korea University Seoul, Republic of Korea; Department of Business Information and Analytics, Daniels College of Business, University of Denver, Denver, CO, U.S.A.
Abstract: Technology-driven tools, such as augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), bring products to life in a virtual space for online consumers and are poised to become the new standard. With more effective tools, consumers are more likely to find the products that best meet their needs. While these tools enhance online purchasing decisions, consumers vary in their ability to use them effectively. As e-shopping continues to grow, firms must carefully consider whether and how to offer these tools. In this paper, we analytically study the firm’s (1) tool provision, (2) the optimization of a tool that brings a physical experience to e-shopping, and how they differ depending on (3) the heterogeneity of consumer expertise in using the tool. We also consider (4) pricing decisions, different channel contracts, and (5) the alignment of profits with the platform through which the firm sells its products with respect to tool optimization and tailoring incentives. We find that a tool need not always be perfect; experienced users can be given an imperfect tool. Although optimal effectiveness can be higher when a tool is tailored to inexperienced users, sellers do not pursue this strategy, as it primarily benefits the platform. While the platform does not always have the same incentives as the seller in dimensions such as tool provision, pricing contracts, and tailoring preferences, we find that this misalignment in tailoring preferences can be mitigated for certain product categories. Additionally, our results show that optimal tool effectiveness is always higher under a sell-on contract, making it a potential win-win solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that tool provision can shift the platform’s preference from a sell-to to a sell-on contract, which generally benefits the seller. Altogether, we show that tool provision should be considered jointly with tailoring to different consumer experience levels. Our results remain robust when accounting for a mix of inexperienced and experienced consumers, product returns, risk-averse consumers, and cost barriers.

Title: Quo Vadis (IT) Strategy? Rethinking Strategy Within Digital Logic
Authors: Gabriele Piccoli, Kalle Lyytinen, Varun Grover
Affiliations: Stephenson Department of Entrepreneurship & Information Systems, E. J. Ourso College of Business, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, LA, USA; Department of Economics and Management, University of Pavia, Pavia, Italy; Department of Design & Innovation, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH, USA; Stockholm School of Economics, House of Innovation, Stockholm, Sweden; Department of Information Systems, Walton College of Business, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, AR, USA
Abstract: A growing consensus holds that digital strategy is business strategy. Yet, scholarship on the digital-strategy nexus lacks a first-principled definition of digital strategy, one grounded in the unique ontology of digital objects and a framework to conceptualize it in a manner that captures the novel realities of today's pervasive digital operations and the organizing logic that governs them. This paper addresses the gap by offering a foundational reframing of firm-level strategy guided by the principles of digital logic – the economic regime of value creation and capture predicated on the primacy of digital objects and their runtime orchestration into digital service stacks.
