We draw on the core guidance view of strategy and define digital strategy as the smallest set of scope, value proposition, and functional choices that, subordinate to the primacy of digital objects, optimally guides all other firm decisions. Based on the definition, we advance a framework for digital strategy formulation and execution comprising three recursive, interdependent activities: digital visioning, digital service stack architecting, and leverage point recognition and manipulation. These activities guide the coherent configuration and deployment of digital service stacks, including their operational, virtual, and contextual embeddings. We use the illustrative case of a century-old, global heavy equipment manufacturer to demonstrate how the firm reframed its strategy under digital logic. The proposed theory advances scholarship on digital strategy by foregrounding the ontology of digital objects and establishes a metatheoretical foundation for future research on digital strategy.

Title: From Monologue to Dialogue: Remaking Public Service Communication with Celebrity-as-a-Service
Authors: Antino Kim, Lingyao (Ivy) Yuan, Mike Seymour, Alan R. Dennis
Affiliations: Operations & Decision Technologies Department, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN U.S.A.; Department of Information Systems and Business Analytics, Debbie & Jerry Ivy College of Business, Iowa State University, Ames, IA U.S.A.; School of Strategy, Innovation and Technology, The University of Sydney Darlington, New South Wales 2006, Australia; Operations & Decision Technologies Department, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University Bloomington, IN U.S.A.
Abstract: Public service communication aims to raise awareness and change behaviors on critical public issues, such as health, safety, and the environment. Public service communication typically takes one of two forms: a public service announcement (PSA), such as a TV or radio advertisement that broadcasts information (a monologue), or a public service interaction (PSI), such as a meeting with officials that both provides and collects information (a dialogue). Celebrity involvement has traditionally been limited to PSAs due to cost and scalability challenges, but advancements in AI now enable the use of digital humans as scalable, interactive “celebrity-as-a-service” solutions. These AI-controlled digital celebrities mimic real people, enabling one-on-one celebrity interactions at scale. In an online experiment, we compared a digital celebrity to a non-celebrity digital human delivering a skin cancer awareness message in both a PSA and a one-on-one PSI. Results showed that both perceived celebrity (celebrity vs. non-celebrity) and interactivity (PSI vs. PSA) increased trustworthiness and enjoyment. Trustworthiness, in turn, increased the intention to comply with the public service message, while both trustworthiness and enjoyment increased the likelihood of sharing the message. We conclude that AI-controlled digital celebrities open the door to incorporating celebrities into one-on-one PSIs to drive more effective, scalable, and cost-effective public service communication.

Title: Detecting and Correcting Estimation Bias Caused by Content Deletion in User-generated Content Studies
Authors: Mengke Qiao, Qinglai He, Ke-Wei Huang
Affiliations: Department of Information Systems, Statistics, & Management Science Culverhouse College of Business, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL U.S.A.; Department of Operations and Information Management Wisconsin School of Business, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI U.S.A.; Department of Information Systems and Analytics, School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: User-generated content (UGC) platforms increasingly enable content deletion to manage the online environment and user-posted content, which contributes to missing data issues in empirical research involving UGC data. Such missingness may be correlated with the unobserved data, resulting in the most challenging missingness type–Missing Not at Random (MNAR), which can lead to biased estimates in empirical analyses. Despite its prevalence, limited scholarly attention has been given to the missing data challenges arising from content deletion, and researchers lack theoretical guidance for diagnosing and handling such missingness. In this study, we conduct an in-depth investigation of the reasons for content deletion across various UGC platforms and identify variables susceptible to the MNAR issue in empirical studies. We also develop a theoretical framework for diagnosing missingness mechanisms and selecting appropriate correction methods. Most importantly, we propose theoretical formulas to correct biased estimation in two MNAR scenarios for scale-level studies. Extensive simulations and sensitivity tests demonstrate that our proposed methods effectively reduce the estimation bias under scale-level MNAR compared to benchmark approaches. Collectively, our work advances the missing data literature and provides practical implications for empirical researchers.

Title: Intelligent Approach to Discovering a New Functional Model Quantifying the Long-Tail Distribution of Online Markets
Authors: Xian Yang, Zhijie Lin, Yuanfeng Cai
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, China University of Petroleum Beijing, China; School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University Beijing, China; Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College, City University of New York New York, U.S.A.
Abstract: Actual sales data are valuable but often inaccessible. Thus, researchers and practitioners rely on sales–sales rank relationship models, such as the power-law distribution, to infer sales information. However, these models often poorly fit the sales distribution of online markets due to the long-tail phenomenon, creating a need for a more precise functional model. This paper proposes a novel model discovery framework, genetic programming with two-phase pruning (GPTP), which combines genetic programming with a newly developed two-phase pruning method to automatically learn a functional model relating sales to sales rank. Through analysis of sales data from both offline and online markets for 203,994 product items in 148 categories, we discover a new natural-power-law model that outperforms the traditional power-law model and provides a more accurate mathematical means of quantifying the long-tail distribution in online markets. The findings demonstrate that the proposed GPTP framework can intelligently learn the generalized knowledge underlying large business datasets and precisely determine the universal functional relationship model across multiple product categories in a white-box manner. The new model will enable researchers and practitioners to more accurately predict actual sales and explore various marketing issues.

Title: Cross-Platform Links: Blessing or Curse?
Authors: Jianchao Sheng, Jianqing Chen
Affiliations: Faculty of Business for Science & Technology, School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui, China; Jindal School of Management, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, TX, U.S.A.
Abstract: In the digital-content industry, platforms compete to attract users and earn advertising revenue from content consumption. Conventional wisdom suggests that platforms should restrict cross-platform links to avoid user loss. However, practices of several platforms, such as TikTok—where content creators can include links in their profiles to competing platforms like YouTube—seem to contradict this notion, facilitating users’ exploration of preferred content elsewhere. In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model to examine two competing platforms’ strategies regarding cross-platform links. We find that the equilibrium strategies are driven by two opposing effects. On one hand, the cross-platform link causes users with high degrees of misfit to be redirected to the rival platform, resulting in a consumption-loss effect. On the other hand, the cross-platform link motivates the creator to enhance content quality, which not only attracts more users but also helps them find preferred content through the link. This quality-enhancement effect benefits the platform by increasing consumption from users who remain on the platform. The trade-off between these two opposing effects depends critically on the misfit between users and content, as well as the average advertising revenue generated from content consumption (i.e., the advertising rate). Our analysis shows that, in the presence of a regular creator, when the unit misfit cost is high, both platforms allow cross-platform links in equilibrium. When both the unit misfit cost and the advertising rate are low, both platforms ban the link in equilibrium. When the unit misfit cost is low and the advertising rate is high, both allowing and banning the link can be possible equilibrium outcomes. Furthermore, we show that the cross-platform link benefits both the creator and users, and both platforms opting to ban cross-platform links creates a prisoner’s dilemma even in terms of their revenues, warranting the attention of platform regulators.

Title: How Generative AI Transforms Questioning Behavior on Q&A Platforms: Evidence from a Natural Experiment with Pilot Usage of ChatGPT
Authors: Xinzhi Rao, Guohou Shan, Michael Rivera, Liangfei Qiu, Nan Wang
Affiliations: Department of Information Systems and Operations Management, Warrington College of Business, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL U.S.A.; Department of Supply Chain and Information Management, D’Amore-McKim School of Business, Northeastern University, Boston, MA U.S.A.; Department of Decision and Technology Analytics, College of Business, Lehigh University Bethlehem, PA U.S.A.; Department of Leadership and Organization Management, School of Economics and Management, Beihang University, Beijing, China
Abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has enabled the automated generation of answers, introducing new dynamics in user behavior related to question-asking on digital platforms. However, the impact of users’ experience with generative AI for answer generation on their questioning behavior remains unclear. On the one hand, the availability of generative AI tools may lead users to rely on these tools for formulating questions, potentially resulting in fewer but higher-quality inquiries. On the other hand, using generative AI may motivate users to ask more questions to enhance their knowledge and build social reputation within the community. We investigate how the use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, to generate answers affects users’ questioning behavior on Stack Overflow, one of the largest Q&A platforms. Leveraging a natural experiment involving the introduction and subsequent ban of ChatGPT on the platform, we apply a difference-in-differences (DID) estimation approach to assess the effects of generative AI usage on the quantity and quality of user-generated questions. We measure these outcomes through metrics such as the number of questions posted per week, question length, novelty, and the number of received upvotes. Our findings reveal that the use of generative AI to generate answers is associated with an increase in the number of questions, which feature longer, more novel content and receive more upvotes. We examine two mechanisms: complexity shift, where ChatGPT handles routine queries while more advanced queries remain for the community, and skill enhancement, where users learn from ChatGPT to ask clearer questions. We also test two moderators: answer volume (proxy for user experience) and platform reputation score (proxy for user reputation). Results show weaker effects among experienced answerers but stronger effects among high reputation users. These insights highlight how generative AI shapes engagement and can guide platform strategies for AI integration.

Title: Synthetic diversity: Racial depictions influence consumer responses to AI ‐generated models in advertising
Authors: Rhonda Hadi, Esther Uduehi, Felipe Thomaz, Andrew Stephen
Affiliations: Saïd Business School University of Oxford Oxford UK; Foster School of Business University of Washington Washington DC USA
Abstract: Abstract As brands seek to increase racial representation in their advertising, many are turning to AI‐generated images of humans (i.e., synthetic models) as a scalable solution. This research demonstrates that consumer reactions to synthetic models are asymmetric, depending on the racial identity being depicted. Across five studies, we demonstrate that disclosing the AI‐generated nature of models lowers firm evaluations when the featured models are from racially underrepresented groups (e.g., Black, Hispanic, and Asian models), but not when they are White. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions of the authenticity of the firm's inclusion efforts, which in turn elevate inferences of manipulative intent. Importantly, these negative effects can be mitigated when consumers are informed that the firm is owned by members of the depicted racial community, suggesting that credible signals of authentic community ties can neutralize the evaluative penalty of AI disclosure. Our findings extend research on racialized depictions in advertising by identifying synthetic depiction as a novel threat to the evaluative benefits of minority representation, and by theorizing why this threat operates asymmetrically by race. More broadly, our results highlight that technological innovations in advertising cannot be divorced from the social and historical contexts that shape their meaning.

Title: Investors' ideology and corporate symbolic and substantive climate actions
Authors: Chang Liu, Wei Shi
Affiliations: CUHK Business School Chinese University of Hong Kong Hong Kong China; Miami Business School University of Miami Coral Gables Florida USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Prior research suggests that institutional investors' liberalism is associated with firms' engagement in environmental sustainability, yet whether this association manifests in symbolic or substantive actions remains unclear. Taking a question‐driven approach, our analyses of Russell 3000 firms (2010–2020) reveal that investor liberalism, measured as the proportion of donations made to the Democratic Party, is positively associated with symbolic climate actions only from 2016 onward (a period when political polarization intensified), reversing a negative association during 2010–2015. Its positive association with substantive actions from 2016 onward, however, appears only among consistent Democratic donors (stronger liberal values), among dedicated investors, or in firms without CEO duality (greater investor influence). These findings indicate that liberal investor ownership may encourage, rather than deter, firms' environmental decoupling. Managerial Summary Liberal institutional investors tend to favor greater corporate environmental sustainability efforts, but are they associated with firms' symbolic or substantive climate actions? Our findings based on U.S. firms reveal that across the full 2010–2020 period, firms with more liberal investors, as indicated by their Democratic‐leaning political donations, do not exhibit more symbolic or substantive climate actions. From 2016 onward, as political polarization intensified, firms with more liberal investors exhibited more symbolic climate actions but not substantive ones. During this period, only investors with stronger liberal commitment (i.e., consistent Democratic donors) are associated with more substantive actions. Democratic‐donating investors are also associated with more substantive actions when they are dedicated investors or when firm CEOs do not chair their boards.

Title: Managing supply chain tensions: The strategic interaction between promoted listings and manufacturer encroachment
Authors: Yu Xia, Zheng Luo, Yunlong Yang
Abstract: The rapid expansion of private-brand products and the growing prevalence of manufacturer direct selling have intensified vertical competition in e-commerce marketplaces. To cope with the tensions with upstream manufacturers, e-commerce platforms increasingly adopt promoted-listing strategies. Specifically, platforms may either favor national-brand products or prioritize their own private-brand products. In this study, we develop a game-theoretical model to uncover the strategic role of promoted listings in shaping a platform's response to potential manufacturer encroachment. Our analysis identifies two distinct effects of promoted listings. The competition effect directly reshapes competition between national-brand and private-brand products by changing product visibility, whereas the strategic effect indirectly influences the manufacturer's encroachment decision. We show that the classical win-win outcome between the platform and the manufacturer exists only when consumers’ valuation of the private-brand product is sufficiently low. Under the competition effect, the platform promotes the national-brand product when private-brand valuation is low but the private-brand product when private-brand valuation is high. Under the strategic effect, which arises when the manufacturer's direct-selling cost is moderate, the platform promotes the national-brand product if manufacturer encroachment is beneficial and the private-brand product otherwise. Consequently, promoted listings serve not only as a marketing instrument for influencing product competition but also as a strategic tool for channel management, revealing their dual role in product promotion and channel strategy.

Title: A Mere Presence Effect of Asymmetric Information
Authors: Jiaqi Yu, Oleg Urminsky
Affiliations: The University of Hong Kong Assistant professor of marketing, Faculty of Business and Economics, , Hong Kong SAR; University of Chicago Booth School of Business Theodore O. Yntema Professor of Marketing, , Chicago, IL, USA, 60637
Abstract: Abstract Differences in discretionary disclosures of quantitative product attributes often result in asymmetric information across products. For example, one brand of milk may feature its protein content on the package label, while the other does not. How do such asymmetric product claims affect consumer choices? We predict that consumers will be sensitive to the mere presence of a quantified claim, judging a product that presents attribute quantity by the valence of the disclosed attribute (positive vs. negative) regardless of the quantity communicated (e.g., high vs. low value of a low-evaluability attribute). Across eight pre-registered studies, we find a robust mere presence effect, in which consumers judge products more (less) favorably when a positive (negative) quantitative quality-relevant attribute is presented, even when the quantitative information represents a relatively low level of quality. Our findings are consistent with an overgeneralized heuristic account, in which consumers rely on the valence of an attribute when it is present, instead of the quantity conveyed. Our findings demonstrate that when a quantitative attribute is salient but not evaluable, asymmetric information disclosure may impede, rather than facilitate, consumers’ judgments of product quality.

Title: How Private Equity Fuels Nonbank Lending
Authors: Sharjil Haque, Simon Mayer, Teng Wang
Affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; Tepper School of Business, Carnegie Mellon University; University of Texas at Arlington
Abstract: Abstract We demonstrate how private equity (PE) promotes nonbank lending by substituting for bank monitoring. Relative to non-PE-backed loans, PE-backed loans exhibit lower bank monitoring, smaller loan shares retained by lead banks, and larger shares held by nonbanks. The substitution is strongest when sponsors have greater incentives to engage with portfolio firms, is not associated with weaker loan performance, and persists during borrower distress. Our findings suggest that PE sponsors’ active engagement—through monitoring and support in distress—reduces banks’ need for monitoring and information production, enabling them to retain less skin in the game and sell loans to nonbanks.

Title: Optimal Information and Security Design
Authors: Nicolas Inostroza, Anton Tsoy
Affiliations: University of Toronto, Canada, and Finance Theory Group
Abstract: Abstract An asset owner designs an asset-backed security and a signal about its value. After experiencing a liquidity shock and privately observing the signal, he sells the security to imperfectly competitive buyers. With flexible information design, the security’s informational sensitivity is a blessing, not a curse. Among double-monotone securities, the issuer prefers to sell the asset in combination with an appropriate signal rather than design more complex securities. Within the class of monotone securities, live-or-die securities are optimal and strictly dominate asset sales. When signals are restricted to be sufficiently informative about the upside, debt and additional-tier-1 debt become optimal.

Title: Insurance and assurance: government interventions and depositor behavior in crisis
Authors: Sümeyra Atmaca, Karolin Kirschenmann, Steven Ongena, Koen Schoors
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Ghent University, Tweekerkenstraat 2, 9000 Ghent; Social Science, University College Roosevelt, Lange Noordstraat 1, 4331 CB Middelburg; Pensions and Sustainable Financial Markets, ZEW Mannheim, L7,1, 68161 Mannheim; Business and Economics, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Jakob-Welder-Weg 4, 55128 Mainz; Department of Finance, University of Zurich, Plattenstrasse 14, 8031 Zurich; Swiss Finance Institute, Banking Chair, Walchestrasse 9, 8006 Zürich, Switzerland; KU Leuven, Department of Accountancy, Finance and Insurance, Naamsestraat 69, 3000 Leuven, Belgium; NTNU Business School, Department of Finance, Klæbuveien 72, 7030 Trondheim, Norway; CEPR, Banking and Corporate Finance Programme, 77 Bastwick Street, London, EC1V 3PZ, United Kingdom
Abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention—explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization—shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. Stabilization is markedly stronger after the takeover by a financially strong private bank than during state ownership, despite unchanged statutory coverage. These patterns are inconsistent with a strong bailout-expectations view in which explicit insurance is largely irrelevant and instead point to credibility as a key determinant of depositor behavior. We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees. Overall, our findings highlight that the form and credibility of government backstops, rather than coverage levels alone, are central to retail deposit funding stability during crises.

Title: Disagreement and Bond PEAD
Authors: Yoshio Nozawa, Yancheng Qiu, Yan Xiong
Affiliations: University of Toronto, UTSC Management, Toronto, Ontario M1C 1A4, Canada; The University of Sydney Business School, Sydney, New South Wales 2006, Australia; Faculty of Business and Economics, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: This paper documents post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in corporate bond prices using transaction data. We find a counterintuitive relationship between the drift and trading volume: PEAD is more pronounced for more heavily traded bonds than for less frequently traded bonds. Across markets, PEAD is observed for credit default swaps but not for stocks. We explain these findings using a unified model that incorporates both debt and equity trading, where investors possess private information about the underlying firm’s cash flows and may hold differing opinions. Our empirical evidence supports the model’s prediction that payoff structures and investor disagreement account for the distinct price dynamics across asset classes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge research support from the Center for Investing at HKUST. Y. Xiong thanks the support by National Natural Science Foundation of China [NSFC 72422007] and the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Project 16501523]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07966 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance.

Title: Conditional and Lenient Drug Approvals
Authors: Chenxi Xu, Giuseppe Lopomo, David Ridley, Peng Sun
Affiliations: Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr. School of Business, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina 27708
Abstract: Firms are often allowed to sell new drugs based on preliminary efficacy evidence, with final approval contingent on confirmatory testing. We characterize optimal approval policies for a government agency that maximizes consumer welfare while considering the firm’s incentives. We assume that firms have private information about testing costs and the government’s payoff depends on the drug’s expected efficacy. The optimal policy may include partial conditional approval for drugs with low expected efficacy, and leniency in granting final approval below conventional standards. Our calibration suggests these tools can generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual social value. This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Funding: The authors received no external funding for this research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03836 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Martin Bichler, market design, platform, and demand analytics.
Area: market design, platform, and demand analytics

Title: Semibandit Learning for Monotone Stochastic Optimization
Authors: Rohan Ghuge, Zhengjia Zhuo, Arpit Agarwal, Viswanath Nagarajan
Affiliations: Department of Information, Risk, and Operations Management, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan–Ann Arbor, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400076, India

Title: Alert for Alerts: How Investment Price Tracking Alerts Affect Retail Investors1
Authors: Yanzhen Chen, Che-Wei Liu, Ming-Hui Wen
Affiliations: Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, School of Business and Management The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong, China; Department of Information Systems, W. P. Carey School of Business Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, U.S.A.; Department of Commercial Design and Management, School of Innovative Design and Management National Taipei University of Business, Taipei, Taiwan
Abstract: The burgeoning innovations in financial technology (fintech) are bringing powerful investment tools from Wall Street to Main Street. Among these tools, digital engagement practices (DEPs), such as price tracking alerts, have seen widespread adoption across online investment platforms. While the fintech industry positions these alerts as neutral, informational tools that enhance investor autonomy, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has raised concerns that such features may exploit behavioral biases and unintentionally harm retail investors. Motivated by this regulatory challenge, we introduce a regulation-centric framework (“what – why – who – how”) that explicitly links empirical analysis to the policy questions confronting regulators. This framework structures our analysis around four sequential questions: What is the effect of alerts on investor outcomes? Why do these effects arise—specifically, through which behavioral mechanisms? Who is most affected, based on investor characteristics and context? How should regulation respond in a targeted and enforceable manner? Using detailed account-level data from a major digital mutual fund platform, we found that alerts tend to reduce investor performance by increasing trading frequency and observed no evidence of increased risk-taking. With tracking alerts, investors are more likely to sell when prices rise with no corresponding change in selling when prices fall, a pattern consistent with the disposition effect. These effects were most pronounced among inexperienced and financially less literate investors, particularly when tracking volatile or unfamiliar assets. Our findings support a regulator-led model in which digital brokers are required to monitor, report, and refine DEPs under auditable, behaviorally informed standards. We offer evidence-based policy recommendations that balance investor protection with the continued advancement of fintech innovation.

Title: Competing against whom? Competitor identification and opportunity belief revision
Authors: Alex Tyulyupo, Balázs Kovács
Abstract: Entrepreneurship theories acknowledge that competitive conditions matter for opportunity beliefs, yet how entrepreneurs identify competitors and how this identification shapes venture concept development have received little theoretical or empirical attention. We develop a process account of how entrepreneurs identify competitors and revise opportunity beliefs and venture concepts in response. Unlike market demand or technological feasibility, competitors are strategic agents who can adapt in response to entry, and as the venture concept evolves, so does the set of competitors it faces. We theorize an adaptive cycle in which encountering a competitor prompts threat assessment, which raises perceived competitive pressure and lowers confidence in venture success while motivating venture concept adaptation that can partly restore perceived viability. A controlled experiment isolates the cycle's components and shows that identical competitive information produces widely divergent threat assessments. A behavioral simulation in which participants develop their own ventures and search for competitors shows that entrepreneurs starting from similar concepts identify largely non-overlapping competitor sets. Some reposition their ventures spontaneously in response to what they find, and adaptation attenuates the link between threat and perceived competitive pressure.

Title: Political Voice and (Mortgage) Market Participation: Evidence from the dilution of Voting Rights Act
Authors: Seongjin Park, Arkodipta Sarkar, Nishant Vats
Abstract: Using US Supreme Court’s narrow-decision on Shelby v. Holder as a shock that diluted voting rights of Black Americans in covered counties, we document the relationship between political voice and economic decision-making. We show fewer Black Americans buy homes after their de-facto disenfranchisement, reflected through lower mortgage applications. Among those who apply for mortgages, there is a flight to Black lenders. Leveraging individual-level survey data, we show confidence in government and financial institutions plays a significant role in driving these effects. Our findings demonstrate that the effects of disenfranchisement extend beyond the ballot box to fundamental economic decisions like homeownership.

Title: Ethnographic Theorizing in Human Resource Management: From Theory‐as‐Design to Theory‐in‐Use
Authors: Jaejin Lee, Nina Jörden
Affiliations: Saïd Business School, University of Oxford Oxford UK; Bennett School of Public Policy, University of Cambridge Cambridge UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT Research on human resource management (HRM) has generated influential frameworks for explaining the relationships between HR practices and organizational outcomes. Existing accounts offer less insight into how the frameworks informing those practices acquire meaning, authority, and practical traction in organizational settings. We conceptualize this as a gap between theory‐as‐design and theory‐in‐use and develop ethnographic theorizing as a mode of examining the use‐life of selected design‐oriented HRM frameworks. Our contribution is twofold. First, we specify how sustained immersion, temporal depth, embodied co‐presence, and relational obligation enable researchers to follow frameworks as they are enacted and negotiated. Second, we develop three recursively related analytic moves for theory development— Complement, Complicate, and Reframe —through which ethnographic evidence can elaborate, qualify, or revise existing theoretical accounts. We demonstrate this approach through two ethnographic studies of HR analytics in different organizations. The comparison shows how legitimacy work, identity negotiation, and meaning‐making shaped the enactment of data‐driven HRM in these settings. The paper thus offers a structured approach for studying how established HRM frameworks operate in use and for assessing when situated evidence warrants changes to their constructs, relationships, or boundary conditions. In addition, we discuss implications for HRM theory, research design, and practice.

Title: Extending the by-production approach: a shared inputs framework for modeling technologies with undesirable outputs
Authors: Shuqi Xu, Qingyuan Zhu, K Hervé Dakpo, Zhiyang Shen, Michael Vardanyan
Abstract: Modeling production in the presence of both desirable and undesirable outputs is a critical issue in productivity and efficiency analysis. The conventional by-production approach, which partitions inputs into strictly defined polluting and nonpolluting categories, offers theoretical consistency with the first two laws thermodynamics but may not fully capture the realities of shared resource usage in practice. This study proposes an extended by-production framework that relaxes the rigid input classification by treating total inputs as shared resources allocated across the interdependent sub-processes, called sub-technologies, comprising the by-production technology. The proposed shared inputs-based approach assumes that each input contributes independently to its respective output type and incorporates interactions between two sub-technologies – one producing desirable outputs and the other generating undesirable outputs. We develop a set of production axioms underlying the new framework and demonstrate that it satisfies the first two laws of thermodynamics. An empirical application using a sample from the power sector illustrates that the proposed approach provides more differentiated efficiency assessments than traditional by-production models.

Title: Dynamic capacity-constrained bin packing for capacity batching: a new framework for multi-stage steel production scheduling
Authors: Ziqing Zhu, Zhimin Lv, Pengju Xu, Haodong Zhang, Ri Jin, Huiyun Yang, Xing Zhao, Zihan Jin, Minghui Wang
Abstract: The capacitated lot-sizing problem (CLSP) arising in multi-stage steel production scheduling is commonly formulated as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) model. However, for industrial-scale systems with multiple processes, parallel equipment, time-varying capacity, and product–equipment compatibility requirements, such formulations often suffer from high-dimensional constraint coupling and computational intractability. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a dynamic capacity-constrained bin packing model (DCBPM) and develops a DCBPM-based scheduling framework for day-level capacity batching across continuous casting, hot rolling, pickling and tandem cold rolling, and continuous annealing. The proposed framework has three components. First, the DCBPM provides a structural reformulation of the CLSP by representing time-indexed equipment slots as bins with dynamically updated residual capacities and order–stage production segments as items. Second, a constraint-preserving decoder constructs feasible schedules by enforcing capacity, inter-stage precedence, category coexistence, and maintenance-related compatibility constraints during the packing process. Third, a non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II)-based optimization layer is used as a representative intelligent optimization procedure to generate order-priority sequences and explore trade-offs between order tardiness and equipment load variance. Experiments based on real production orders demonstrate the computational efficiency of the decoder, while the NSGA-II-guided framework identifies schedules with substantially lower equipment-load variance at the cost of increased tardiness relative to simple priority-based baselines. Detailed constraint verification further confirms schedule feasibility and practical applicability.

Title: Exact decomposition algorithms for the student clustering problem
Authors: Tunchan Cura
Abstract: The Student Clustering Problem (SCP), a decision problem that precedes the School Bus Routing Problem, involves the assignment of students to schools under multi-grade capacity constraints. As a variant of the Capacitated Clustering Problem, the SCP is NP-hard, and large-scale instances are typically addressed using metaheuristics due to the computational limitations of standard Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solvers. This study proposes, to the best of our knowledge, the first problem-specific exact decomposition algorithms for the SCP. Whereas earlier studies solved monolithic MILP formulations with general-purpose exact solvers, we develop dedicated algorithms that exploit the problem's decomposition structure, separating the combinatorial school selection (master problem) from the student assignment task (the Student–School Assignment Problem, SSAP). We show that the SSAP is solvable in polynomial time due to the total unimodularity of its bipartite constraint matrix, and we establish a partial-integrality property showing that the integrality gap arises solely from the selection variables. Building on these results, we present two exact methods that share a single-tree branch-and-check architecture and differ only in the cut returned by the subproblem: the first uses combinatorial (no-good) cuts to enumerate minimum-cardinality configurations, while the second is a branch-and-Benders-cut method that generates dual optimality cuts from the transportation subproblem. An attractiveness-based pricing phase guides the search in both. Both algorithms employ a lexicographic objective that prioritizes minimizing the number of selected schools, followed by total transportation distance. Computational experiments on 121 benchmark instances, including a real-world case study from Fortaleza, Brazil, show that both methods match or improve upon the standard MILP formulation and state-of-the-art metaheuristics such as GRASP, A-BRKGA, and Clustering Search, achieving better or equal objective values in all 484 pairwise comparisons. The two exact methods certify optimality on exactly the same 91 of the 121 instances, against 51 for the monolithic MILP, and return identical objective values on every instance they certify. This confirms what the structural analysis predicts: because the subproblem is totally unimodular, the dual Benders cut reproduces the bound the master relaxation already supplies and so adds no certification power. The two are complementary rather than interchangeable: the branch-and-Benders-cut method assumes nothing about the cost structure and so applies to the general formulation, whereas the combinatorial method exploits the lexicographic structure and, within that regime, returns the better incumbent where the time budget binds. The generality of the former is tested rather than asserted: with heterogeneous, non-dominating opening costs the branch-and-Benders-cut method certifies optima that open more schools than the minimum cardinality, and across three cost levels it is at no level significantly inferior in solution quality to the monolithic formulation. Overall, the proposed framework provides a robust and provably optimal approach for decision support in educational logistics and resource allocation.

Title: Expanding Markets or Capturing Share? The Competitive Effects of Subscriptions on Spending in Restaurant Delivery
Authors: Daniel M. McCarthy, Shin Oblander, Young-Hoon Park, Yeohong Yoon
Abstract: Subscription programs are increasingly central to platform strategy, but their effects on competitors and category demand remain unclear. The authors study restaurant delivery subscriptions using individual-level transaction data on Postmates Unlimited, the first widely available U.S. subscription program in the category, and DoorDash's later DashPass program. Using a matched, staggered difference-in-differences design, they find that signing up for Postmates Unlimited is associated with a 90.4% increase in spending at the focal firm, with no significant average change in competing-firm spending and no offsetting decline in adjacent food categories, consistent with category expansion. Competitive effects depend on customers' prior platform usage. For “singlehomers” (who only used Postmates prior to subscribing), subscribing is associated with increased spending at both the focal firm and competing platforms, even after cancellation. For “multihomers” (who had also previously used competing platforms), the focal-firm effect is larger, and competing-firm spending falls while customers remain subscribed; after cancellation, the focal-firm lift persists, but the decrease in competitor spending does not. DashPass results are broadly similar, but customers with prior Postmates subscription experience show little increase in category spending. Together, these findings suggest subscriptions can both expand markets and capture share, depending on prior platform usage and subscription experience.

Title: Improving operational performance through boarding time slack: Evidence from the U.S. airline industry
Authors: Chandrasekhar Manchiraju, Ashutosh Bhave, Milind G Sohoni
Affiliations: Michigan State University; University of Arkansas; The State University of New York
Abstract: Flight delays have a significant impact on airlines, passengers, and the U.S. economy. Airlines also use flight on-time performance (OTP)—a metric based on the proportion of delayed flights—to attract travelers by demonstrating service reliability. It is well established that adding buffers to flight time and ground time improves on-time arrivals. However, such buffers can impose significant costs. The flight and ground times comprise multiple activities, and prior research has primarily focused on studying the impact of aggregate buffers. In this article, we study the impact of increasing the buffer of a critical ground time activity, namely boarding time, potentially without increasing the aggregate ground time buffer, on flight delays. To do so, we use the context of Delta Air Lines’ recent policy changes wherein the airline increased the boarding time for domestic narrow-body flights by 5 minutes and started compensating flight attendants for pre-flight boarding. Using a difference-in-difference-in-differences framework, we analyze and quantify the impact of these policies on Delta’s flight delays. Our findings indicate a significant reduction in departure delays following the policy changes, with increased boarding time playing a critical role in improving on-time departures. Our analysis finds no evidence that boarding compensation contributed to the improvement in on-time departures. We show that the increase in boarding time can improve the likelihood of on-time departures, potentially without requiring additional total ground time or incurring additional scheduling costs. We observe that the benefit is more pronounced for longer flights, busier routes, and later departures in the day. Airlines are often criticized for relying on costly, ad hoc schedule buffering to improve OTP. However, our results demonstrate that carefully planning buffer time for critical activities can significantly improve operational performance.

Title: Assortment Optimization Given Basket Shopping Behavior Using the Ising Model
Authors: Andrey Vasilyev, Sebastian Maier, Ralf W. Seifert
Abstract: In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

Title: Technology-Mediated Services in Health Care: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
Authors: Kyuyeon (Jenny) Rhee, Xiao Liu, Suparerk Lekwijit, Pei-Yu Chen
Affiliations: Arizona State University, Information Systems, Tempe, Arizona, United States; Arizona State University W P Carey School of Business, Information Systems, Tempe, Arizona, United States
Abstract: This study examines how telehealth delivery models are associated with access to care and protocol adherence in underserved populations. While prior research reports mixed evidence on telehealth’s effectiveness, we argue that these inconsistencies arise because telehealth is not a single intervention but is implemented through distinct service configurations that address different barriers. Drawing on the theoretical framework of digital economics, we conceptualize telehealth as a technology-mediated service that can alter key economic frictions, including search and verification, transportation, tracking, and setup costs. We focus on two widely adopted models—specialist-facilitated telehealth and remote telehealth—and theorize that each addresses different subsets of these frictions, leading to distinct effects on care access and protocol adherence across settings. Using panel data from U.S. Community Health Centers on mental health services, we document three findings. First, adoption of the specialist-facilitated model is associated with increased access to mental health care, particularly in areas with greater clinical need. Second, remote telehealth is not associated with increased access on average but is associated with higher adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. These effects are consistent with improvements in screening and documentation processes rather than increases in utilization. Third, the estimated effects of both models vary across local cost environments. The access effects of specialist-facilitated telehealth are larger in areas where search and verification frictions are greater. In contrast, the effects of remote telehealth are attenuated where patient-side setup costs are high but are larger where transportation barriers and documentation frictions are greater. These findings advance a model-specific perspective on telehealth’s effects, extend the digital economics framework to technology-mediated services, and provide evidence that the estimated effects of digital health interventions vary with how delivery models interact with underlying cost environments.

Title: Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
Authors: Minghong Yuan, Wen Wen, Indranil Roy Bardhan
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Information Risk and Operations Management, Austin, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, McCombs School of Business, Austin, Texas, United States; The University of Texas at Austin, Information, Risk & Operations Management, Austin, Texas, United States
Abstract: What is the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on healthcare value? Does PE ownership reduce healthcare value, and if so, can its effect be mitigated using health information technologies (IT)? Given the significant investments by PE firms in the healthcare sector in recent years, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policy makers, care providers, and patients, to understand their likely impact and whether PE ownership is aligned with their interests. Because PE firms seek to improve efficiency and generate short-term financial returns, the cost-cutting strategies used to achieve these goals may come at the expense of care quality, leading to competing hypotheses on the impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. We argue that IT-enabled health information sharing capabilities can help PE-owned hospitals to better manage this cost-quality tension and achieve higher healthcare value. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach and data from US hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we estimate changes in healthcare value following PE acquisition and ownership. Overall, we find that PE ownership of hospitals reduces healthcare value. This decline is partially driven by reduction in clinical staffing following PE ownership. We further find that pre-existing, hospital health information sharing capabilities mitigate the negative impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. Specifically, such capabilities can strengthen the effect of PE ownership on cost reduction and, at the same time, mitigate PE-induced, care quality deterioration. Our results highlight the critical role of common data standards needed to promote IT-enabled information sharing between healthcare providers, which, in turn, can align the incentives of PE firms with the goals of value-based care.

Title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
Authors: Doug J. Chung, Dongkyu Chang
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Marketing, Austin, Texas, United States; City University of Hong Kong, Economics and Finance, Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

Title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
Authors: Yannick Exner, Jochen Hartmann, Ziqian Ding, Shunyuan Zhang, Oded Netzer
Affiliations: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Management, Munich, Germany; Technical University of Munich, Munchen, Germany; Carnegie Mellon University Tepper School of Business, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States; Harvard Business School, Marketing, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; Columbia University, Marketing, New York, New York, United States
Abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

Title: Gendered Effects of a Crisis-induced Work-from-Home Shock: A Time-Motion Study Using Digital Footprints
Authors: Kamalini Ramdas, Amalia Miller, Alp Sungu
Affiliations: London Business School, Management Science & Operations, London, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; University of Virginia, Economics, United States; University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, Operations, Information and Decisions Dept, Philadelphia, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: While organizations are adopting hybrid and even remote-first work schedules, the potentially gendered impact of work-from-home (WFH) on operational outcomes remains poorly understood. Methodology/results: To examine this question, we combine a crisis-induced shock (i.e., the Covid-19 lockdown) that forced a shift to WFH due to stay-at-home orders, with a novel methodology to gather contextualized digital trace data. We examine the online time allocation — akin to a time-motion study for white collars — of 1,094 individuals across various activities and industries, when in-person work related and leisure activities were abruptly curtailed by the pandemic, inducing a shift to home-based work and online activities. Analysis of over 30 million website visits reveals that overall, this crisis-induced WFH increased the time devoted to both work-related and leisure pursuits online. However, these gains are significantly larger for men, giving rise to new gender gaps. We observe notable disparities in online work and leisure activities, including on smartphones, suggesting that crisis-induced WFH reshapes workers’ daily activities differently across genders. These gender differences are amplified among parents — a pattern consistent with increased household obligations placing greater constraints on women’s ability to fully benefit from the flexibility offered by WFH. Furthermore, we observe a substantial relative decline in women’s job search activities after the WFH shock, also corroborated using a large, external dataset from a major online recruitment platform. Managerial implications: These results underscore how sudden WFH mandates as response to a major crisis can differentially affect women’s work, employment prospects and long-term career trajectories. Our findings call attention to the importance of factors outside of the office in determining the success of WFH arrangements. Even though WFH could lower facilities cost and carbon footprint and increase workers’ flexibility, gender-specific constraints — especially those related to household responsibilities — can produce uneven outcomes. These results highlight the need for organizations and policymakers to design WFH policies that effectively address gender disparities, particularly in environments where childcare and other domestic duties fall disproportionately on women.

Title: Operational Implications of Diagnostic Discrepancies: The Weigh-In of Focal and Related Physician Experience
Authors: Seokjun Youn, Yingchao Lan
Affiliations: University of Arizona, Management Information Systems, Tucson, Arizona, United States; University of Nebraska — Lincoln, Supply Chain Management and Analytics, Lincoln, Nebraska, United States
Abstract: Problem Definition: Diagnostic discrepancies, defined as mismatches between patients’ admitting and principal diagnoses, are common but heterogeneous claims-based markers. These discrepancies represent a misalignment in the diagnostic process, reflecting diagnostic updating, reprioritization, residual clinical complexity, documentation practices, or error, without establishing clinical preventability, and may signal latent operational burden in subsequent physician decision-making. We examine whether this retrospective operational flag identifies inpatient stays with larger adjusted resource-use differentials and whether those differentials vary with physician experience. Methodology/Results: Leveraging a patient-level dataset of 5.7 million emergency-department-origin inpatient stays from Florida hospitals, we examine the operational burden associated with diagnostic discrepancies, measured by total costs per hospitalization. Our results show that discrepancy-flagged inpatient stays have a 6.62% higher adjusted total cost after rich patient risk adjustment and high-dimensional fixed effects. The adjusted differential is smaller at higher focal experience (treating similar diagnoses) and larger at higher related experience (treating diverse diagnoses). The pattern remains qualitatively similar across alternative discrepancy definitions, richer diagnosis and service-line controls, risk-adjusted benchmarking, physician matching, alternative experience measures, and alternative samples. Exploratory analyses further show that flagged inpatient stays exhibit higher costs across multiple resource-use domains with varying intensity, higher diagnostic and procedural intensity, and longer adjusted time to first procedure. Managerial Implications: The discrepancy flag is most appropriately used for retrospective monitoring, benchmarking, and case-review triage, not as a direct measure of preventable error or as an automatic performance score. The physician experience patterns motivate prospective evaluation of assignment, consultation, training, and decision-support practices.

Title: Action-oriented Narratives. How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
Authors: Claudio Biscaro, Arvind Malhotra, Ann Majchrzak
Affiliations: Johannes Kepler Universität Linz, Institute of Leadership and Change Management, Linz, Austria; UNC at Chapel Hill, Kenan-Flagler Business School, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States; University of Southern California, Information Systems, Los Angeles, California, United States
Abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis, discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers – subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources – are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call ‘action-oriented narratives:’ simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting.

Title: Overcoming poverty and unemployment: The transfer dynamics of entrepreneurship training.
Authors: Janina Peschmann, Michael M. Gielnik, Michael Frese, Kim Marie Bischoff
Abstract: Our study examines the training transfer dynamics of action-oriented entrepreneurship training to understand when and how a positive impact on the alleviation of poverty and unemployment among young adults unfolds. We theorize about the training transfer dynamics in terms of absolute changes and developmental trajectories. To test our hypotheses, we conducted field experiments across seven countries with 6,257 university students who we randomly assigned to a training group or a nonintervention control group. We collected data before the implementation of an entrepreneurship training program (T1), directly after the training program (T2), as well as 9-18 (T3) and 19-32 months (T4) after the baseline, with a total number of 15,660 observations. Results from discontinuous growth curve modeling show that action-oriented entrepreneurship training can increase income and employment in the short and long term. We further demonstrate that training transfer dynamics can unfold in the form of a "catch-up" effect, which is characterized by nonsignificant or even negative short-term absolute changes but positive long-term developmental trajectories in economic effectiveness outcomes. Our results contribute to the literature on training transfer and hold important practical implications for policymakers regarding the evaluation of future entrepreneurship training interventions.
