Title: An exact aggregation–disaggregation method for a class of mixed-integer linear programs
Authors: Jiarui Zhang, Alessio Trivella, Xiaojie Luan
Abstract: Although aggregating items such as commodities, vehicles, or resources into groups is widely used in planning and operations, the structural conditions under which aggregation is exact have not been systematically characterized. In this paper, we provide a mathematical foundation for aggregation techniques using mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs). Specifically, we prove that a class of MILPs can be solved to optimality by aggregating certain sets of variables and constraints, solving a smaller model with fewer symmetries and the same linear relaxation value, and then disaggregating the solution in polynomial time. The method applies to MILPs with block-diagonal and coupling constraints in which variable vectors share identical coefficients in the objective and coupling constraints. The exactness of the aggregation holds when (i) the diagonal blocks are identical totally unimodular matrices with proportional right-hand sides, or (ii) their constraints represent the balance of network flows with the same source or same sink. This aggregation–disaggregation method has both theoretical and computational value. On the theoretical side, it formalizes the fundamental mechanisms underlying existing aggregation techniques, extends and/or strengthens the theory and applicability of several structure-based methods for MILPs, and establishes polynomial-time solvability for a class of MILPs. Computationally, we verify the effectiveness of the method on variants of the service network design, vehicle scheduling, and interval scheduling problems. Using Gurobi, we show that, compared to directly solving the original formulations, the method brings speedups of one to three orders of magnitude.

Title: Designing and adapting dropshipping virtual distribution networks
Authors: Thomas B. Cassidey, Emily C. Griffin, Burcu B. Keskin, Ozgur Satici
Abstract: The growth of e-commerce has seen the rise of dropshipping firms that do not carry inventory but maintain a network of suppliers from which they ship to satisfy customer demand. Some of these firms partner with major retailers to sell through their online channels but lack the physical distribution centers typical of retail supply chains and expected by major retailers’ ordering systems. We design a network of virtual distribution centers (VDCs) that allows the firm to sell through the website of its retail partner while protecting its supplier network from disintermediation. These VDCs allow the dropshipping firm to virtually aggregate inventories and display them at a centralized geographic location, with an associated lead time, which represents the combined inventories of all suppliers assigned to that VDC. If the expected lead time from this geographic location to the customer is unrealistic given current shipping carrier performance, we propose that the VDC network can be adapted by manipulating inventory visibility. We present novel randomized dual-guided clustering and branch-and-price solution approaches to solve these problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a large real-world dataset comprising over 200,000 orders, 5000 suppliers, and 5000 customer locations, and find performance gains of over 50% in late delivery reduction at a cost of approximately two percentage points in order fulfillment rate compared to the unadapted network, given optimization of the late delivery tolerance parameter.

Title: Strategic timing of buyer financing in supply chains with stochastic costs: The role of wholesale price-locking leadership
Authors: Wei Cheng, Xiangfeng Chen

Title: Measuring Measurement Error
Authors: N Aaron Pancost, Garrett Schaller
Affiliations: University of Texas at Austin , McCombs School of Business; Colorado State University , College of Business
Abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.

Title: CEO Ideologically (In)Congruent Activism and Investor Reactions: An Attribution of CEO Intentions Perspective
Authors: Miao Yun, Longwang Fu
Affiliations: City University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: Abstract The phenomenon of chief executive officers (CEOs) taking activism stances on contested sociopolitical issues is increasing, yet it remains unclear how observing investors discern CEO intentions behind activism engagements, thereby shaping their judgments and subsequent reactions. By relaxing the assumption that CEO activism is an unabashed expression of personal beliefs, we propose the concept of CEO ideologically (in)congruent activism and develop a framework wherein investors may attribute CEO intentions underlying incongruent (versus congruent) activism engagements as more organization‐driven (versus self‐driven) interest pursuits, thereby leading to more positive investor evaluations and reactions. Furthermore, we argue that the positive effect of CEO ideologically incongruent activism on investor reactions will be amplified when the CEO owns a higher level of stock ownership but weakened when the firm receives a greater corporate social responsibility (CSR) rating. We corroborate our propositions using a sample of CEO activism events for S&P 500 firms from 2012 to 2021. Our findings demonstrate the heterogeneity and critical influence of CEO intentions behind activism engagements and shed light on how investors integrate multi‐informational cues when evaluating and reacting to managerial incongruent behaviours.

Title: The Role of Digital Ad Clutter in Ad Viewership and Memory
Authors: Sean Melessa, Poet Larsen, Paul Hoban
Abstract: Advertisers face an increasingly cluttered digital ecosystem where customer attention matters. Despite this, the extent to which digital advertising clutter influences ad viewership remains unclear. This paper presents three separate eye-tracking experiments (subjects: N = 99, N = 250, and N = 575) using over a dozen custom-built web pages to better understand how digital ad clutter affects consumers’ viewing of digital ads. Across experiments, we show that increased clutter led consumers to allocate more attention to the overall advertising space and adjust how they distribute viewership across ad positions. A complementary survey revealed that clutter also reduced ad memory and recall for individual ads. We discuss the implications for advertisers and publishers regarding ad pricing and placement in crowded digital environments.

Title: Correcting omitted-variable bias without instruments: An ICA-based alternative to Gaussian copula methods
Authors: Rouven E. Haschka, Florian Dost
Abstract: This paper proposes an instrument-free correction for omitted-variable bias and overcomes a key limitation of Gaussian copula control function (GCCF) approaches. Omitted-variable bias is the most common source of endogeneity in marketing, and many articles apply GCCF to address it. Yet GCCF require a nonlinear regressor-error relation, whereas textbooks assume linear, additive relationships between regressors and omitted variables. The authors prove that GCCF is biased in classical omitted-variable settings. Extant articles that address omitted-variables with GCCF also show language cues implicitly assuming linear relationships, which invalidate the use of GCCF. The proposed endogeneity correction is tailored to this prominent case, utilizing independent component analysis (ICA). It assumes a latent normally distributed component that additively influences both the endogenous regressor and the error. This can be interpreted as the sum of omitted variables, which, according to the Central Limit Theorem, add up to a normal distribution. Through ICA, this component is identified and extracted from the endogenous regressor, rendering the regression model free of endogeneity and enabling causal inference. The paper proves that the model is point-identified despite endogeneity due to omitted variables, that the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and that Jackknife resampling yields valid standard errors.

Title: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
Authors: Amit Pazgal, David Soberman, Raphael Thomadsen
Abstract: Firms are often less differentiated than standard price-competition models predict. We explain this gap by showing how firms can use informative or reminder advertising to soften competition. When firms choose locations, advertising, and prices endogenously, they may choose to soften price competition through limited advertising rather than greater product differentiation, allowing them to locate closer together while limiting price competition. This outcome of low advertising and central collocation is especially likely when advertising costs are high. We also observe that partially-differentiated equilibria, with one firm locating centrally and the other at an edge, and full differentiation, can each emerge under certain conditions. Thus, firms endogenously choose a mix of advertising and product differentiation to moderate price competition. Further, the shape of travel costs influences the equilibrium outcome. If the disutility from distance is highly convex, such as occurs when consumer preferences exhibit satisficing, central collocation becomes the unique equilibrium when more consumers are concentrated at the edge locations. However, when the disutility from distance is linear, having more customers located towards the edge locations makes collocation less likely. Overall, the interaction of advertising costs, consumer preferences, and location choices help explain why firms often forgo product differentiation.

Title: Pricing and information provision in service platforms with heterogeneous customers
Authors: Xin Weng, Lijian Lu, Li Xiao
Affiliations: Fuzhou University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Macau
Abstract: Service platforms frequently employ virtual queues where customers have differing sensitivities to wait times and cannot see their precise positions in line. In these settings, providers often disclose waiting-time information to influence customers’ decisions on whether to join or balk. A natural benchmark is to report the long-term average waiting time, yet whether this deterministic disclosure policy is optimal remains unclear when both pricing and customer participation are endogenous. This study develops a stylized theoretical framework to explore the joint structure of pricing and waiting-time information disclosure for service providers managing diverse customers in a virtual queue. The provider decides on both the service price and the waiting-time disclosure policy within a rational-expectations framework. Our findings reveal that the optimal disclosure strategy is captured by scaled Rademacher distributions, meaning at most two distinct announcement values are required. This reduces a complex infinite-dimensional problem to a more manageable finite-dimensional optimization task. Leveraging this framework, we derive the optimal strategies for pricing and disclosure, identifying scenarios where variability in announced waiting times is beneficial. Our analysis shows that noise is advantageous when customers can handle uncertain wait-time signals or initially perceive the service as quick. The optimal level of noise correlates with system congestion, offering the greatest benefits when there is a notable disparity between perceived and actual congestion levels. This provides significant advantages when disclosing waiting times with noise. These findings offer actionable insights for service platforms, guiding them in creating cohesive strategies that encompass pricing, information disclosure, and service configuration, ultimately enhancing customer experience and operational efficiency.

Title: Response efficiency versus response customization: An examination of firms’ responses to platform-empowered group complaints
Authors: Zilong Liu, Xuequn Wang, Xin (Robert) Luo, Chaoqun Chu, Tingting Song
Affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics; University of New Mexico; Hong Kong Metropolitan University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: The rise of group complaints on digital platforms, where consumers can publicly voice collective concerns, presents significant challenges for firms’ service recovery operations. Prior research assessing service operations on digital platforms has focused primarily on individual complaints, and less is known about how firms respond to platform-empowered (PE) group complaints. We examine this question through the lens of a trade-off between response efficiency and response customization and argue that this trade-off evolves as group complaints develop over time. Based on a large-scale dataset from Tousu, a leading complaint platform in China, we find that group complaints paradoxically increase response time and decrease empathy and explanation in firms’ responses. Further analyses indicate that these effects depend on dynamic group size and dynamic need diversity. When dynamic need diversity is low, larger groups are associated with more standardized, efficiency-oriented responses, whereas when dynamic need diversity is high, larger groups are associated with slower but more customized responses. These findings extend research on service operations by showing how PE group complaints reshape firms’ complaint handling. Our study also provides operational guidance for managing group complaints more effectively.

Title: Multi-self presentation and knowledge contribution in platform operations: Evidence from a natural experiment
Authors: Yingpeng Zhu, Zike Cao, Gen Li, Yi Yang, Liangfei Qiu
Affiliations: University of Macau; Zhejiang University; Fudan University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Florida
Abstract: Operations of online user-generated content (UGC) platforms often involve tackling under-provision , wherein users lack motivation to contribute sufficient content. We study a novel design deployed to address this issue: the integration of a proprietary social feature that allows users to post casual free-form content (e.g., casual social content) alongside standard formal content on the platform. Leveraging a quasi-experiment on a large Chinese online knowledge-sharing platform, we assess the effects of integrating such a social feature on users’ formal knowledge contribution (i.e., writing answers to others’ questions ). Using difference-in-differences (DiD) analyses paired with various matching strategies, such as propensity score matching and look-ahead propensity score matching, we find that users who adopt and frequently use the feature (i.e., high adopters) show a stronger incentive to contribute answers without compromising quality. These results are further validated by a set of robustness checks. Further mediation analysis suggests that such a complementary effect might be because of two mechanisms related to the integrated social feature’s multi-self presentation function: first, the new feature increases high adopters’ engagement on the platform and leads them to consume more knowledge content, which in turn facilitates knowledge contribution; second, high adopters receive more social recognition benefits by building a more complete self through the integrated social feature, and such increased social recognition benefits further motivate more subsequent content contribution. Moreover, employing a text-mining approach to assess the semantic similarity between users’ casual social content and their formal knowledge contributions, we find that the complementary effect is amplified for high adopters whose casual posts remain more closely connected to their formal knowledge domain (i.e., are more semantically aligned with their formal knowledge). Our results have novel implications for platform design and operations to motivate users to contribute valuable content.

Title: Valuation bottlenecks: Why isn’t a better business enough for a higher market capitalization?
Authors: Shumpei Iwao, Vatsal Mitesh Tailor, Qi Wu
Affiliations: Keio University; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Case Western Reserve University
Abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market’s response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm’s weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

Title: From institutional expansion to exposure-driven co-evolution: Reinterpreting “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”
Authors: Yinghao Pan, Dingyi Tang, Jie Wu, Yuan Sun, Liangfei Qiu
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China; University of Florida; Modern Business Research Center & School of Business Administration (MBA) & School of Management and E-Business (Cross-Border E-Commerce College), Zhejiang Gongshang University, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: This paper builds on and reinterprets “Operations and Supply Chain Management in China”, which offers a comprehensive account of the rapid institutional, educational, and research development of Operations and Supply Chain Management (OSCM) in China. While the Institutional–Dynamic–Organizational (IDO) framework effectively captures domestic structural transformation, it under-theorizes a critical external driver of this evolution: international knowledge exposure and collaboration. To address this gap, we complement the domestic institutional perspective with a bibliometric study of published articles in Production and Operations Management from 1992 to 2026. The evidence shows that China's growing presence in OSCM research is overwhelmingly collaboration-mediated, with China–U.S. co-authorship constituting the dominant channel of integration. The rise of China in top-tier OSCM journals is therefore not primarily an autonomous national trajectory, but a structurally embedded phenomenon within global co-authorship networks. Our findings suggest that China's OSCM evolution cannot be fully explained by domestic institutional expansion, policy support, or educational scaling alone. Instead, it reflects a broader process of exposure-driven co-evolution within a globally integrated knowledge system. In this system, international collaboration is not merely a byproduct of scientific development but a central mechanism shaping the structure and trajectory of global OSCM knowledge production.

Title: Mind the cost of disturbance: Firm-level supply chain risk and the bank loan cost
Authors: Daxuan Cheng, Lei Gao, Yin Liao, Zheyao Pan
Affiliations: Macquarie University; George Mason University
Abstract: This study investigates whether and how supply chain risk, a core operational vulnerability, is priced in financial credit markets. Using a novel text-based firm-level measure, we show that elevated supply chain risk leads to higher loan interest spreads. Exploiting natural disasters as exogenous shocks to production networks, we provide causal evidence that shocks increase perceived supply chain fragility and, in turn, raise borrowing costs. These effects are amplified when lenders face greater private-information deficiency, and are further strengthened when external information production is more intensive—the former heightening lenders’ concern over supply chain exposure, the latter enhancing their capacity to recognize and price it. Critically, lenders treat supply chain fragility as a form of credit risk: firms with higher supply chain risk face increased default risk, and firms whose production networks are struck by supplier disasters face a higher probability of covenant violation and tighter covenant restrictions, signaling lenders’ anticipation of repayment difficulties. Our findings highlight a new financial consequence of operational risk, showing that supply chain disruption directly affects corporate financing outcomes.

Title: Branch-and-Price for the Team Orienteering Problem with Time Windows and Bivariate Time-Varying Profit
Authors: Yuning Hu, Xinggang Luo, Xiaojuan Jiang, Ran Yan, Zhongliang Zhang
Affiliations: School of Management, Hangzhou Dianzi University, Hangzhou 310018, China; School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
Abstract: Motivated by multiple real-world applications, this study investigates the team orienteering problem with time windows and bivariate time-varying profit (TOPTW-BTP), where the profit collected at each node is modeled as a nonlinear function of both the arrival time and the service duration. We model the problem on a time-expanded network and introduce the concept of the bivariate-time (BT) arc, proving that dominated BT arcs can be systematically eliminated to reduce the solution space. To capture diverse real-world temporal profit patterns, we consider three types of arrival-time profit functions, monotonic (typically decreasing), concave, and others (e.g., bimodal), and discuss tailored modeling approaches for each case to avoid unnecessary arrival-time discretization. Especially for the concave case, we propose a novel route extension method that exploits the structural properties of concavity to mathematically formalize the extension as direct functional additions, thereby achieving a compact representation. This method is also applicable to related problems such as vehicle routing with time windows and convex node costs. A branch-and-price framework is developed to solve the TOPTW-BTP. Computational experiments show that the proposed algorithm efficiently solves instances with up to 100 nodes across all three types of arrival-time profit function, with the theoretical simplification in the concave case naturally leading to a more streamlined implementation than the state-of-the-art approach. Title: Retail on Wheels: A Time-Sensitive Traveling Salesman Problem
Authors: Zhuolun Dong, Junyu Cao, Wei Qi
Affiliations: McCombs School of Business, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
Abstract: Rapid advancement in self-driving technology has brought mobile retail into the spotlight. Motivated by its potential, we present a model, theory, and insights into the operations of mobile retail, where a fleet of wheeled stores traverses a service region, selectively seeks locations in which to perch, and fulfills local customer demand. The goal of retailers is to strike a balance between perching and migrating to maximize total revenue. To dispatch such stores, retailers need to consider the following time-sensitive factors: (i) how busy the service is, (ii) how soon customers will arrive, and (iii) how quickly freshness decays. We propose and analyze a model that incorporates these factors into the classical traveling salesman problem (TSP), which we call the “time-sensitive TSP.” Using the continuous approximation approach, we derive the optimal revenue as well as the upper and lower bounds in the asymptotic regime as candidate locations increase to infinity. The tightness of the bounds is validated. Our analysis demonstrates that store mobility creates value by bringing proximity to customers. We further uncover the effects of these time-sensitive features on decision making. Specifically, the scaling relationship between revenue and fleet size is affected by customer tardiness and busyness. Busyness determines stores’ ability to expand their service, whereas tardiness affects how effectively stores can utilize the initial high-freshness period. These findings deepen our understanding of mobile retail operations. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: J. Title: Shipment Monitoring, Allocation, and the Impact on Food Waste
Authors: Tao Lu
Affiliations: School of Business, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut 06269
Abstract: Often advocated for the potential to reduce waste in fresh produce supply chains, sensor technologies enable firms to monitor the condition of each product unit and allocate them to markets at different transportation distances, thereby matching units with shorter shelf lives with closer markets. In this paper, we consider a firm purchasing and transporting a fresh produce product for sale in two destination markets. Postharvest processes cause a proportion of the product to be in risky condition, potentially becoming unsalable (“spoiled”) due to shelf-life deterioration during transportation. With monitoring technology, the firm first determines a purchase quantity and then decides how to allocate each unit (in either good or risky condition) between markets. We characterize the optimal allocation policies, which can be used to efficiently determine the optimal purchase quantity. Our analysis shows that such technology may inadvertently increase total waste by inducing larger purchase quantities; this increase is often, but not always, accompanied by a lower waste rate and improved distribution efficiency. As firms increasingly adopt monitoring technology for shipment allocation, additional policy and managerial attention may be required. Improvements in postharvest processes can strengthen the waste-reduction benefits of monitoring technology. Firms seeking to maintain their sustainability goals can capture most of the profit gains from monitoring by carefully moderating increases in purchase quantities. Title: Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data
Authors: Hyun-Soo Ahn, Mengzhenyu Zhang, Zijin Zhang
Affiliations: Stephen M. Ross School of Business, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; School of Management, University College London, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom; Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts 02467
Abstract: Making Better Decisions with Imperfect Historical Data Historical data can provide valuable information for online decision making, but its usefulness may be limited when the environment has changed. In “Online Decisions with (Biased) Offline Data,” Ahn, Zhang, and Zhang study how firms can combine potentially biased offline data with newly collected online observations in two canonical operations management problems: dynamic inventory decisions and dynamic pricing. The authors develop two online learning policies that balance the benefits of historical information against the risk of relying on data from a different distribution. The soft-switch policy automatically adjusts the reliance on offline and online data without requiring prior knowledge of the degree of bias. The hard-switch policy instead uses information about the magnitude of the distributional shift to determine when to rely primarily on online data. Both policies achieve optimal regret up to a logarithmic factor, whereas the analysis quantifies how the value of offline data depends on its size and bias.

Authors: Roman Słowiński

Title: Innovation adoption across regions: psychological openness and the early diffusion of digital platforms
Authors: Tobias Ebert, Martin Obschonka, Luca M. Aiello, Jeff Potter, P. Jason Rentfrow, Samuel D. Gosling
Abstract: Early regional adoption is crucial for platform-enabled innovations because their viability depends on enough people within a region adopting them to generate network effects. Existing research on regional innovation diffusion explains early adoption largely through demographic, economic, infrastructural, or institutional conditions, paying limited attention to regional population psychology. We conceptualize regional psychological openness as an invisible social infrastructure that is relevant for understanding early platform adoption. To test this idea, we introduce a newly curated dataset that allows us to trace the initial development of three major platform innovations (i.e., accommodation sharing platforms, ride-sharing platforms, social media platforms) across hundreds of U.S. metropolitan regions. Across all three platform types, regions differ markedly in early adoption. We link these adoption data to large-scale geo-referenced personality information from millions of U.S. residents ( N = 3,234,899). Results show that regional psychological openness consistently predicts earlier uptake even after accounting for demographic, socio-economic, social, infrastructural, geographical, and other psychological characteristics. In sum, the study advances a behavioral perspective on regional innovation adoption by integrating population psychology into explanations of platform diffusion.

Title: External collaboration and local knowledge divergence in regional knowledge spaces
Authors: Jisoo Hur, Dieter F. Kogler, Keungoui Kim
Abstract: This study investigates the association between regional collaboration structures and the semantic position of locally produced scientific knowledge. Drawing on the Regional Innovation Systems framework, it distinguishes between intra-regional and inter-regional collaboration as complementary dimensions of scientific knowledge production. Using over nine million Web of Science publications from European regions between 1998 and 2021, this study employs semantic text embeddings to measure local knowledge divergence, defined as the semantic distance between each publication and the established regional knowledge base. Within the same region–field–period, externally collaborated publication groups exhibit slightly higher average local knowledge divergence than internally collaborated groups. However, the estimated difference is substantively negligible and varies across periods. The principal pooled-sample finding is an inverted U-shaped association between external collaboration share and regional local knowledge divergence, with the fitted curve reaching its maximum at an external collaboration share of approximately 45%. The realised magnitude of this association is modest, and heterogeneity analyses show that it is most pronounced in life sciences and biomedicine and after 2010. These findings identify a context-dependent association rather than a causal or universally optimal collaboration structure, demonstrating how regional scientific collaboration portfolios relate to the evolution of publicly disclosed knowledge trajectories.

Title: Who Gains from creative destruction? Evidence from high-quality entrepreneurship in the United States
Authors: Astrid Marinoni, John Voorheis
Abstract: The question of who gains from high-quality entrepreneurship is crucial to understanding whether investments in innovative startup firms produce socially beneficial outcomes. Although entrepreneurship is widely viewed as a central driver of economic growth, recent research has raised concerns that it may also exacerbate inequality and other undesirable social outcomes. We bring new evidence to this debate by analyzing the impact of entrepreneurship on a variety of local economic outcomes, including income inequality, average incomes, and income mobility, using IRS and U.S. Census Bureau microdata. We find that entrepreneurship indeed increases income inequality, although this effect fades in the years after firm founding. While entrepreneurship produces statistically significant income gains across the distribution, the economic magnitude of these effects varies dramatically, with benefits concentrated among top earners. We also find that entrepreneurship can serve as a mobility tool for less well-off individuals, increasing their probability of rising to the top of the income distribution. These income and mobility gains, however, are uneven across demographic groups.

Title: Social Network Prediction Problems: Using Meta-Paths and Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Representation for Label Propagation
Authors: Negar Maleki, Balaji Padmanabhan, Kaushik Dutta
Affiliations: School of Information Systems and Management, Muma College of Business, University of South Florida, Tampa, Florida 333620; Decision, Operations & Information Technologies Department, Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742
Abstract: Graph representations for real-world social networks in the past have missed two important elements: (i) the multiplexity of connections and (ii) representing time. This paper presents a dynamic heterogeneous graph representation for social networks that includes time in every component of the graph, that is, nodes and edges, each of different types that captures heterogeneity. We illustrate the power of this representation by presenting four time-dependent queries and a multiclass classification problem that cannot easily be handled in conventional homogeneous graph representations. As a proof of concept, we present a detailed representation of a relatively new social media platform (Steemit), which we use to illustrate both the dynamic querying capability, as well as a prediction task using label propagation algorithm (LPA). We also present temporal social media meta-paths to generalize the LPA to dynamic heterogeneous graph structures, that is, Meta-paths + LPA. To validate and compare our proposed method, we conduct an experiment using three benchmark data sets and show that our proposed method outperforms almost all four state-of-the-art algorithms in category prediction task by at least 13.79% accuracy. Title: PPFL : A Personalized Federated Learning Framework for Heterogeneous Population
Authors: Hao Di, Yi Yang, Haishan Ye, Xiangyu Chang
Affiliations: School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China; W. P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona 85287
Abstract: Personalization aims to characterize individual preferences and is widely applied across many fields. However, conventional personalized methods operate in a centralized manner, potentially exposing raw data when pooling individual information. In this paper, with privacy considerations, we develop a flexible and interpretable personalized framework within the paradigm of federated learning, called population personalized federated learning (PPFL). By leveraging “canonical models” to capture fundamental characteristics of a heterogeneous population and employing “membership vectors” to reveal clients’ preferences, PPFL models heterogeneity as clients’ varying preferences for these characteristics. This approach provides substantial insights into client characteristics, which are lacking in existing personalized federated learning (PFL) methods. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between PPFL and three main branches of PFL methods: clustered FL, multitask PFL, and decoupling PFL, and we demonstrate the advantages of PPFL. To solve PPFL (a nonconvex optimization problem with linear constraints), we propose a novel random block coordinate descent algorithm and establish its convergence properties. We conduct experiments in both pathological and practical data sets, and the results validate the effectiveness of PPFL. Title: Solving Cutting Stock Problems via an Extended Ryan-Foster Branching Scheme and Fast Column Generation
Authors: Renan F. F. da Silva, Rafael C. S. Schouery
Affiliations: University of Campinas, Campinas, São Paulo 13083-889, Brazil
Abstract: We present a branch-cut-and-price framework to solve cutting stock problems with strong relaxations using set covering (packing) formulations, which are solved by column generation. The main contributions of this paper include an extended Ryan-Foster scheme, which allows us to use this powerful branching scheme even in nonbinary problems by using a conflict propagation lemma; a fast column generation process based on a diversification strategy; custom primal heuristics, enabling us to find optimal solutions for several open instances; and a technique to use a smaller feasibility tolerance in floating-point linear programming solvers, combined with numerically safe methods to produce stronger and safer lower bounds. Additional performance-improving strategies include a technique that controls the height of the branch-and-bound tree; a variable selection algorithm based on branching history; a new set of dual inequalities; insights to obtain a lean model; and the subset-row inequalities. By employing this comprehensive framework, we overcame the current state-of-the-art concerning the following problems: cutting stock, skiving stock, ordered open-end bin packing, class-constrained bin packing, and identical parallel machines scheduling with minimum makespan. Additionally, a new challenging benchmark for cutting stock is introduced. History: Accepted by Pascal Van Hentenryck, Area Editor for Computational Modeling: Methods & Analysis. Title: Demands Satiated or Not? A Psychology-Informed Deep Probabilistic Approach to Offline Store Recommendations
Authors: Jiangning He, Weikun Wu, Jiayi Guo, Xiao Fang
Affiliations: School of Information Management and Engineering, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai 200433, China; and Key Laboratory of Interdisciplinary Research of Computation and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai 200433, China; Lerner College of Business and Economics and Institute for Financial Services Analytics, University of Delaware, Newark, Delaware 19716
Abstract: Offline store recommendations have emerged as a powerful tool in the mall industry for enhancing the customer experience and boosting mall revenue. Existing research focuses on mining behavioral patterns but largely overlooks the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive store choice behaviors. To bridge this gap, our study is a pioneering work that incorporates demand satiation to enhance offline store recommendations. Informed by optimum stimulation level (OSL) theory, we propose a novel dynamic demand satiation model (DDSM) featuring two adaptive components: (1) the satiation decay component takes an exponential form to capture the decay of satiation over time, and (2) the intention adaptation component utilizes deep recurrent neural networks to account for diverse shopping intentions. Using a real-world offline shopping data set, we empirically demonstrate and analyze the superior performance of our method over several classic and state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we conduct an interpretability analysis to gain insights into the model’s recommendation mechanism. We also explore the role of demand satiation in enhancing the offline shopping experience through a user study. History: Accepted by Ram Ramesh, Area Editor for Data Science & Machine Learning. Title: Strong Partitioning and a Machine Learning Approximation for Accelerating the Global Optimization of Nonconvex Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Programs
Authors: Rohit Kannan, Harsha Nagarajan, Deepjyoti Deka
Affiliations: Grado Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, Virginia 24061; Applied Mathematics and Plasma Physics, Theoretical Division, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, New Mexico 87544; Massachusetts Institute of Technology Energy Initiative, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
Abstract: We learn optimal instance-specific heuristics for the global minimization of nonconvex quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQPs). Specifically, we consider partitioning-based convex mixed-integer programming relaxations for nonconvex QCQPs and propose the novel problem of strong partitioning to optimally partition variable domains without sacrificing global optimality. Because solving this max-min strong partitioning problem exactly can be very challenging, we design a local optimization method that leverages generalized gradients of the value function of its inner-minimization problem. However, even solving the strong partitioning problem to local optimality can be time consuming. To address this, we propose a simple and practical machine learning (ML) approximation for homogeneous families of QCQPs. Motivated by practical applications, we conduct a detailed computational study using the open-source global solver Alpine to evaluate the effectiveness of our ML approximation in accelerating the repeated solution of homogeneous QCQPs with fixed structure. Our study considers randomly generated QCQP families, including instances of the pooling problem, that are benchmarked using state-of-the-art global optimization software. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our ML approximation of strong partitioning reduces Alpine’s solution time by a factor of 2–4.5 on average, with maximum reduction factors ranging from 10 to 200 across these QCQP families. Title: Human-Algorithm Collaborative Truth Inference in Crowdsourcing
Authors: Xuan Wei, Mingyue Zhang, Qingpeng Zhang, Zhi Li, Daniel Dajun Zeng
Affiliations: Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200040, China; School of Business and Management, Shanghai International Studies University, Shanghai 201620, China; Musketeers Foundation Institute of Data Science, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China; and Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China; Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100045, China; and School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 101408, China
Abstract: Crowdsourcing has become a pivotal strategy in gathering large-scale, high-quality labeled data, particularly in data-intensive applications powered by artificial intelligence. To aggregate the noisy crowd efforts, many studies have considered learning a predictive algorithm based on the noisy human annotations and subsequently integrating the learned knowledge back into the data aggregation process. However, it is unclear how to design such hybrid systems that maximize the complementary strengths of humans and algorithms. In response, we analyze the patterns of human and algorithm intelligence and propose that the inductive bias of algorithms can effectively mitigate inconsistencies in human labeling, thus complementing human efforts. Building on this premise, we propose a human-algorithm collaborative framework (HAC) to combine human labels with algorithmic predictions. By proposing a metric called hybrid complementarity score (HCS) to quantify human-algorithm complementarity, our framework can dynamically adjust the weight of each algorithm based on its complementarity, significantly enhancing the overall efficacy of the human-algorithm integration. To validate the effectiveness of our framework, we first instantiate it with several algorithms, including a high-complementarity algorithm building upon the inductive bias of clustering-aware design. We then benchmark our framework against leading baselines across eight real-world tasks. Our results not only demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed framework but also affirm its robustness across different algorithm selections (e.g., types and number of algorithms) and hyperparameter configurations. This research not only delivers a feasible and effective solution for truth inference in crowdsourcing but also contributes to the burgeoning community of human-algorithm collaboration. Title: Quadratic Optimization Through the Lens of Adjustable Robust Optimization
Authors: Abbas Khademi, Ahmadreza Marandi
Affiliations: School of Mathematics, Statistics and Computer Science, College of Science, University of Tehran, Tehran 14174-66191, Iran; and School of Mathematics, Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM), Tehran 19395-5746, Iran; Department of Industrial Engineering and Innovation Sciences, Eindhoven University of Technology, 5612 AE Eindhoven, Netherlands; and Faculty of Management, University of British Columbia, Kelowna, British Columbia V1V 1V7, Canada; and Eindhoven Artificial Intelligence Systems Institute, 5600 MB Eindhoven, Netherlands
Abstract: Quadratic optimization (QO) has been studied extensively in the literature due to its applicability in many practical problems. Although practical, it is known that QO problems are generally NP-hard. Therefore, researchers developed many approximation methods to find good solutions. In this paper, we analyze QO problems using robust optimization techniques. To this end, we first show that any QO problem can be reformulated as a disjoint biconvex QO problem. Then, we provide an equivalent adjustable robust optimization (ARO) reformulation and leverage the methods available in the literature on ARO to approximate this reformulation. More specifically, we show that using a so-called decision rule technique to approximate the ARO reformulation is equivalent to using a reformulation-linearization technique on the original QO problem. Additionally, we design an algorithm that can find a close-to-optimal solution based on our new reformulations. Title: A Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for the Kidney Exchange Problem
Authors: Matteo Petris, Claudia Archetti, Diego Cattaruzza, Maxime Ogier, Frédéric Semet

Abstract: In this paper, we study a Kidney Exchange Problem (KEP) with altruistic donors and incompatible patient-donor pairs. Kidney exchanges can be modelled in a directed graph as circuits starting and ending in an incompatible pair or as paths starting at an altruistic donor. For medical reasons, circuits and paths are of limited length and are associated with a medical benefit to performing the transplants. The aim of the KEP is to determine a set of disjoint kidney exchanges of maximal medical benefit or maximal cardinality. Several solution methods are available in the literature to solve the KEP. However, they are usually most able to efficiently address instances with specific characteristics or of limited size. In this work, we propose an efficient method that stands out from the literature as it is able to report solutions of very good quality on large-size instances regardless of the characteristics (the type of objective function and the maximum length of circuits or paths). To do so, we consider a set-packing formulation for the KEP with exponentially many variables associated with circuits and paths, and develop a Branch-Price-and-Cut (BPC) algorithm to solve it. As a methodological contribution, the BPC algorithm features two novel heuristics to separate a well-known family of nonrobust inequalities, namely, the subset-row inequalities. The heuristics aim to detect such inequalities via an original transformation from violated clique and odd-hole inequalities. Extensive computational experiments have been performed on three sets of instances from the literature and on a newly generated set of challenging instances. Title: Eliminating Social Popularity Bias in Recommendation: Causal Inference-Based Social Graph Neural Networks
Authors: Huilin Xu, Ruina Yang, Ruibin Geng
Affiliations: School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China; and System Behavior and Management Laboratory, Philosophy and Social Sciences Laboratory of the Ministry of Education, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China; School of Management, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an 710072, China
Abstract: In the era of information overload, social recommender systems, which leverage the emergence of online social networks to perform personalized content filtering based on user preferences, have proven successful. However, social recommender models not only exhibit a well-known bias toward popular items but also have a social popularity bias that is often overlooked in existing research. Both biases can lead the model to learn inaccurate user representations, ultimately compromising the diversity and accuracy of recommendations. This paper focuses on integrating social networks into recommendations in an unbiased way. First, a new causal graph is proposed to understand how item and social popularity affect user representation and how user consistency preferences affect ranking scores. Next, to eliminate the adverse effects of popularity bias, we explore how to leverage backdoor adjustments to learn unbiased user representations and obtain accurate ranking scores through a counterfactual reasoning strategy. Finally, using the backdoor adjustment operator and the counterfactual reasoning strategy as key components, a causal inference-based social graph neural network is proposed. Evaluation results on four real-world data sets show that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in recommendation accuracy and diversity. Title: A Low-Rank ADMM Splitting Approach for Semidefinite Programming
Authors: Qiushi Han, Chenxi Li, Zhenwei Lin, Caihua Chen, Qi Deng, Dongdong Ge, Huikang Liu, Yinyu Ye

Abstract: We introduce a new first order method for solving the semidefinite programming (SDP) problem with a convex and differentiable objective based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and a matrix-splitting technique. Our algorithm has an advantage over the Burer–Monteiro (BM) approach as it involves much easier quadratically regularized subproblems in each iteration. Title: Construction of Value Functions of Integer Programs with Finite Domain
Authors: Yifei Huang, Junlong Zhang
Affiliations: Department of Management, Technology and Economics, ETH Zürich, 8092 Zürich, Switzerland; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
Abstract: Value functions play a central role in integer programming duality, and they are also used to develop solution methods for stochastic integer programs, bilevel integer programs, and robust optimization problems. In this paper, we propose a column-by-column algorithm for constructing the value functions of integer programs with finite domain over the set of level-set minimal vectors. The proposed algorithm starts with the first column and sequentially adds the rest of the columns one by one. Each time a column is added, a new set of level-set minimal vectors is generated based on the previous set, and the optimal objective values over the level-set minimal vectors are also computed. The advantage of the proposed algorithm is that no integer program needs to be solved in the algorithm for instances with nonnegative constraint matrices. Computational results on benchmark instances show that the proposed algorithm can achieve a speedup of up to three orders of magnitude compared with a state-of-the-art algorithm. We also extend the proposed algorithm to build value functions of integer programs with negative elements in the constraint matrix. Abstract: Over the last few years, there has been a surge in the use of learning techniques to improve the performance of optimization algorithms. Title: Estimation of Patient Recruitment Using Summary Data Aggregated Across Trials
Authors: Anh Ninh, Gregory J. Hunt, Diep Nguyen

Abstract: Accurate modeling of patient recruitment is critical for helping ensure operational efficiency of clinical trials. However, current methods to estimate key model parameters typically require granular center-level data, which can be challenging to obtain. We propose using summary-level data aggregated from publicly available historical trials to help ameliorate these problems. Specifically, we introduce an estimation framework that estimates Poisson-Gamma model parameters of phase III trials by leveraging data from multiple public trials using a maximum likelihood approach. Our framework has desirable theoretical properties in the objective function, which facilitate solution development. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach can accurately estimate model parameters in both simulations and real data case studies of hypertension and type 2 diabetes trials from ClinicalTrials.gov. Title: COMET: An Interactive Framework for Efficient and Effective Community Search via Active Learning
Authors: Jiawei Zhou, Kai Wang, Jianwei Wang, Kunpeng Zhang, Xuemin Lin
Affiliations: Antai College of Economics and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200030, China; School of Computer Science and Engineering, University of New South Wales, Sydney, New South Wales 2052, Australia; Department of Decision Operations & Information Technologies, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742
Abstract: In recent years, substantial advancements in query-dependent community search (CS) have been driven by growing demands in various downstream applications such as social network analysis, fraud detection, bioinformatics, and others. They require methods to identify structurally cohesive communities that are dependent on specific queries. Learning-based interactive CS (ICS) models the search process as multiround with human interaction, enhancing its practicality. Nonetheless, learning-based approaches for ICS face two challenges. First, current methods for narrowing the search space rely on either query information or fixed topological structures, resulting in insufficient robustness when querying communities on large-scale graphs. Second, there is an absence of an effective interaction strategy in ICS, where the algorithm should offer users choices of highly uncertain nodes to iteratively refine search quality. To address these issues, we propose COMET, an interactive community search framework designed for large-scale graphs. COMET consists of three key modules: First, it features a community-aware subgraph module tailored to each specific query based on Personalized PageRank (PPR), considering both query information and topological structure. Second, we conceptualize ICS as a series of binary classification tasks, employing a graph neural network (GNN) to propagate label information within the candidate subgraph in each round. Finally, a novel active learning–based node selection module uses entropy from GNN and PPR from the subgraph module to dynamically select the most crucial nodes for labeling in each round. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that COMET significantly outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based CS and ICS methods across eight real-world data sets. Title: Which to Trust: Extracting Collective Wisdom Based on Opinion Quality Rank Learning
Authors: Shuai Jiang, Yanhong Guo, Chuanren Liu, Hui Xiong

Abstract: Aggregating diverse human opinions in the digital era is essential in harnessing collective wisdom to unravel intricate management dilemmas. The aggregation process has significant hurdles to overcome due to the heterogeneity in the quality of individual opinions. This study introduces a CrowdRank machine learning architecture to provide an innovative solution to the central problem of opinion aggregation by learning to rank individual opinions. CrowdRank operates through two phases. (1) It leverages a BNN, pretrained on historical data, to conduct pairwise opinion comparisons. This network, designed to capture meaningful interactions between opinion features, adheres to key axiomatic principles to ensure a principled evaluation of opinion quality. (2) CrowdRank employs expectation propagation to synthesize these microassessments into a coherent global ranking of individual opinions. We validated the efficacy of our approach through a large-scale empirical investigation using real-world financial analyst forecasts. The validation results demonstrated the superiority of our approach over existing methods in accurately predicting both pairwise and aggregate opinion rankings. Importantly, CrowdRank significantly improves the objectivity and precision of collective financial analyst forecasts. Title: Exact MILP Models for Redundancy Allocation with Mixed Components
Authors: Jianguang Feng, Zhi-Long Chen, Ada Che, Chengbin Chu
Affiliations: School of Management, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an 710072, China; Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742; Univ Gustave Eiffel, ESIEE Paris and COSYS-GRETTIA, F-77454 Marne-la-Vallée, France
Abstract: The redundancy allocation problem (RAP) aims to find an allocation of redundant components that maximizes system reliability under resource constraints. In this paper, we consider the RAP for complex systems with heterogeneous components, which may have bridges or interconnecting subsystems and are generally more complicated in structure than commonly studied series-parallel systems. A major challenge of the RAP is that the reliability function is nonlinear. To tackle this, we develop six exact mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulations, which, to our knowledge, are the first of such formulations for the problem. The key idea is to use binary variables and big-M constraints to successively linearize each product term in the reliability function. In addition, we propose a novel tree representation of the reliability function to establish the interconnections between different product terms, which is then used to reduce the number of decision variables and constraints needed in the linearization. We also propose an alternative form of the reliability function that only involves the failure probabilities of subsystems, and leverage this to derive better variable bounds, smaller big-M constants, and simpler formulations. We compare the six MILP formulations by solving them directly using an MILP solver based on three sets of test instances of varying complexity. Results indicate that all formulations achieve optimal solutions quickly for the first set and within reasonable computation times for the second set. For the third set, two formulations can always be solved within a given time limit. Overall, the MILP formulation derived based on the alternative form of the reliability function and a specific type of tree representation scheme performs the best. We also demonstrate that our approach is more robust and scalable than a benchmark branch-and-bound method. Title: A Logic-Based Benders Decomposition for the Car Resequencing Problem with a Painted Body Storage
Authors: Xinyi Guo, Jean-François Côté, Canrong Zhang, Lixin Miao

Abstract: The cost of producing diverse cars depends on the sequence in which they are arranged in the body shop, paint shop, and assembly shop. Before entering the downstream assembly shop, the upstream car sequence shared by the body shop and paint shop is readjusted via the painted body storage, which consists of several first-in-first-out lanes. The car resequencing problem addressed in this paper requires determining the upstream and downstream sequences and the car-to-lane assignment to minimize the total cost of the three shops. In the second level, cars are rearranged by determining their configurations and downstream positions. A feasible assignment of cars to lanes is sought in the third level to respect this sequence change. We provide a mathematical formulation for each level and propose two shortest-path problem reformulations for the first level, where solving the first reformulation is equivalent to a k-shortest-path problem. The second reformulation is a shortest-path model restricted by demand constraints. A lower bound, valid inequalities, and a heuristic method are also proposed as enhancements. Title: Centrality of Shortest Paths: Algorithms and Complexity Results

Abstract: The centrality of a node is often used to measure its importance to the structure of a network. Some centrality measures can be extended to measure the importance of a path. In this paper, we consider the problem of finding the most central shortest path. We show that the computational complexity of this problem depends on the measure of centrality used and in the case of degree centrality, whether the network is weighted or not. We develop a polynomial algorithm for the most degree-central shortest path problem with the worst-case running time of [Formula: see text], where | V | is the number of vertices, | E | is the number of edges, and [Formula: see text] is the maximum degree of the graph. In addition, we show that the same problem is NP-hard on a weighted graph. Furthermore, we show that the problem of finding the most betweenness-central shortest path is solvable in polynomial time, whereas finding the most closeness-central shortest path is NP-hard, regardless of whether the graph is weighted or not. We also develop an algorithm for finding the most betweenness-central shortest path with a running time of [Formula: see text] on unweighted graphs and [Formula: see text] on graphs with positively weighted edges. Title: Solving the Multiagent Pathfinding Problem with Time-Expanded Networks
Authors: Tommaso Adamo, Roberto Baldacci, Gianpaolo Ghiani, Emanuela Guerriero
Affiliations: Dipartimento di Ingegneria dell’Innovazione, Università del Salento, 73100 Lecce, Italy; College of Science and Engineering, Hamad Bin Khalifa University, Doha 34110, Qatar
Abstract: The Multiagent Pathfinding Problem involves determining optimal, collision-free routes for a fleet of multiple autonomous vehicles from current positions to prescribed (goal) positions within a transportation or logistics facility such as a port terminal or a warehouse. This paper describes an exact algorithm for the problem, in which a sequence of reduced Mixed Integer Programming problems is solved iteratively on suitably defined time-expanded networks until an optimal solution is found. Computational results show that our approach outperforms a state-of-the-art solution algorithm on various medium- and large-sized instances. Additionally, we provide several managerial insights. Title: Stochastic Optimization Model with Exogenous and Decision-Dependent Uncertainty for Medical Evacuation
Authors: M. A. Lejeune, F. Margot, A. D. de Oliveira
Affiliations: Decision Sciences Department, George Washington University, Washington, District of Columbia 20052; Ecole Supérieure de la Santé, Lausanne, Switzerland; Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington 98052
Abstract: The timely and reliable medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) of injured soldiers on the battlefield is a primary concern for every military force. The objective is to design an evacuation network that maximizes the chance of survival and functional recovery of the wounded. We propose a chance-constrained MEDEVAC model that accounts for endogenous and exogenous uncertainty and show how decisions affect endogenous uncertainties. We develop a Boolean reformulation and expose its advantages over standard scenario-based reformulations. We design an algorithmic framework that includes a new convex integer relaxation, a multiterm convexification method, a tight bounding scheme, and the novel smallest domain branching rule. Results based on real-life data show the efficiency of our approach and provide suggestions for solving mixed-integer nonlinear problems. The study provides healthcare planners guidance about how to implement a reliable evacuation network and allows for a proper implementation of the Golden Hour doctrine. We design the value of endogenous uncertainty framework to assess the life-or-death benefits obtained by accounting for endogenous uncertainty. In congested networks, up to about 19% more soldiers can be evacuated with our model versus one disregarding endogenous uncertainty. We also show the importance to take into account the exogenous uncertainty in medical resources’ availability. Title: The Sensitivity of the U.S. Presidential Election to Coordinated Voter Relocation
Authors: Carlos Cardonha, David Bergman, Andre A. Cire, Leonardo Lozano, Tallys Yunes
Affiliations: Department of Operations and Information Management, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut 06828; Department of Management, University of Toronto Scarborough and Rotman School of Management, Toronto, Ontario M1C 1A4, Canada; Operations, Business Analytics & Information Systems, University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio 45221; Miami Herbert Business School, University of Miami, Coral Gables, Florida 33146
Abstract: U.S. presidential elections are determined by the Electoral College. In all but two states, a statewide winner-take-all system for electors can lead to decisive outcomes based on narrow victories in key states. Small groups of voters can significantly impact results, not only through turnout but also through a less-explored mechanism: the strategic relocation of a relatively small number of dedicated voters across state lines. The extent to which election outcomes are sensitive to such coordinated movements has not been thoroughly investigated. We introduce an analytical framework that integrates forecasting, simulation, and optimization to identify these pivotal voter shifts. Our findings show that small-scale relocations can meaningfully alter election probabilities under a range of parameter settings and polling data sources. Furthermore, we examine how the optimization-based recommendations align with actual election results, demonstrating that the suggested movements would have been beneficial in the 2024 U.S. presidential election—even when based on pre-election data. Given the remarkably small number of individuals required and the fact that electoral residency in many states can be established within about a month, our results have direct implications for policymaking and campaign strategy. Moreover, they highlight new opportunities for applying operations research methods to political science. History: Accepted by Alice E. Smith, Editor-in-Chief. Title: Decoupling Geometry from Optimization in 2D Irregular Cutting and Packing Problems: An Open-Source Collision Detection Engine
Authors: Jeroen Gardeyn, Greet Vanden Berghe, Tony Wauters
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, KU Leuven, 3001 Leuven, Belgium
Abstract: Addressing irregular cutting and packing (C&P) optimization problems poses two distinct challenges: the geometric challenge of determining whether an item can be feasibly placed at a certain position and the optimization challenge of finding a good solution according to some objective function. Until now, those tackling such problems have had to address both challenges simultaneously, requiring two distinct sets of expertise and a lot of research and development effort. One way to lower this barrier is to decouple the two challenges. In this paper, we introduce a powerful collision detection engine (CDE) for two-dimensional (2D) irregular C&P problems, which assumes full responsibility for the geometric challenge. The CDE (i) allows users to focus with full confidence on their optimization challenge by abstracting geometry away, and (ii) enables independent advances to propagate to all optimization algorithms built atop it. We present a set of core principles and design philosophies to model a general and adaptable CDE focused on maximizing performance, accuracy, and robustness. These principles are accompanied by a concrete open-source implementation called jagua-rs. This paper, together with its implementation, serves as a catalyst for future advances in irregular C&P problems by providing a solid foundation that can either be used as it currently exists or further improved upon. Title: Cluster Branching for Vehicle Routing Problems
Authors: João Marcos Pereira Silva, Eduardo Uchoa, Anand Subramanian
Affiliations: Departament of Production Engineering, Federal Fluminense University, Niterói, Rio de Janeiro 24210-240, Brazil; and National Institute for Research in Digital Science and Technology (Inria), 78153 Le Chesnay, France; Departamento de Sistemas de Computação, Federal University of Paraíba, João Pessoa, Paraíba 58051-900, Brazil
Abstract: This article introduces cluster branching, a novel branching strategy for exact algorithms solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs). Whereas branching is crucial for the efficiency of branch-and-bound-based algorithms, existing branching types such as edge branching, CutSet branching, and Ryan and Foster branching have their limitations. The proposed branching strategy aggregates multiple edge variables into higher-level decision structures corresponding to clusters of customers. Through extensive computational experiments on capacitated VRPs and VRPs with time windows instances, we demonstrate that cluster branching (CB) significantly enhances the performance of a state-of-the-art branch-cut-and-price algorithm, often improving branching quality and reducing the size of the search trees, which allows more instances to be solved. Beyond that, CB is also shown to have a robust performance over different instance types and may work well even for those with randomly positioned customers. Title: Exact Methods and a Two-Stage Iterative Heuristic for the Carrier-Vehicle Traveling Salesman Problem
Authors: Yantong Li, Shanshan Zhou, Jean-François Côté
Affiliations: School of Maritime Economics and Management, Dalian Maritime University, Dalian 116026, China; Centre Interuniversitaire de Recherche sur les Réseaux d’Entreprise, la Logistique et le Transport, Université Laval, Québec City, Québec G1V 0A6, Canada
Abstract: The carrier-vehicle traveling salesman problem (CVTSP) aims to optimize the routes of a larger, but slower, carrier and a smaller, but faster, vehicle to minimize the maximum completion time for visiting a set of targets. This paper introduces an enhanced formulation for the CVTSP using a set of new valid inequalities derived from structural properties. A logic-based Benders decomposition method is tailored to solve the problem by introducing various types of Benders cuts. In particular, a new analytical cut is developed based on valid bounds of the travel time between any two consecutive visited nodes. To handle practical instances, we design a simple, yet effective, two-stage iterative heuristic, which repeatedly solves a traveling salesman problem using an updated approximate travel time matrix. We conduct numerical experiments on 529 benchmark instances. Results show that the proposed formulation and exact method perform well, especially for the instances with small vehicle endurance and distant targets. The heuristic quickly achieves optimality for all instances with known optimal values. It finds new best solutions for most open instances, outperforming state-of-the-art heuristics in solution quality and efficiency. Title: Outlier Detection in Regression: Conic Quadratic Formulations
Authors: Andrés Gómez, José Neto
Affiliations: Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089; SAMOVAR, Télécom SudParis, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91120 Palaiseau, France
Abstract: In many applications, when building linear regression models, it is important to account for the presence of outliers, that is, corrupted input data points. Such problems can be formulated as mixed-integer optimization problems involving cubic terms, each given by the product of a binary variable and a quadratic term of the continuous variables. Existing approaches in the literature, typically relying on the linearization of the cubic terms using big-M constraints, suffer from weak relaxation and poor performance in practice. In this work we derive stronger second-order conic relaxations that do not involve big-M constraints. Our computational experiments indicate that the proposed formulations are several orders of magnitude faster than existing big-M formulations in the literature for this problem. In addition, we verify that exact solution of the mixed-integer optimization problems can lead to substantially better-quality solutions than simpler relaxations or heuristics commonly used in practice.
