Title: Note from the Editor
Authors: Alice Smith

Title: Editorial Board
Judge financial holdings and case outcomes: Evidence from judge financial disclosures
Authors: Tuhin Harit, Sunil Parupati, Jedson Pinto, Gil Sadka
Abstract: This paper examines the association between judges’ financial holdings and the outcome of legal cases. Using novel data on financial disclosures of judges and the civil case information of public firms across district courts in the United States between 2000 and 2021, we document multiple instances in which judges fail to recuse themselves from cases where they hold common stock in one of the parties. We find evidence that judges appear to rule more favorably when deciding over conflicted cases than when deciding over unconflicted ones. We also find that investors are positively surprised by these outcomes, as reflected by stock returns to case outcomes. The 2017 electronic disclosure reform, which made judicial financial holdings more accessible, significantly increases judges’ recusals and attenuates investor surprise. Collectively, our results provide the first large-scale evidence of the relation between judges’ financial holdings and case outcomes.

Title: Video-based deception detection and financial fraud
Authors: Binglei Duan, Danqi Hu, Hai Lu
Abstract: ABSTRACT Based on a comprehensive visual deception score constructed from China’s mandatorily disclosed IPO roadshow videos using computer vision and machine learning, we find that visual cues embedded in these videos predict IPO financial fraud. The predictive power is incremental to financial, textual, and audio indicators. Further analyses show that these cues are well grounded in psychology research and focusing on the psychology-based deception-cue-area features improves fraud predicting performance. Furthermore, decomposing each video into five topics, we find that only the deception score of the topic on financial performance is positively associated with financial fraud. We further show that insiders of firms with higher visual deception scores are more likely to sell shares shortly after lock-up periods expire, and these firms experience significantly lower subsequent stock returns. Our study demonstrates the feasibility and potential value of using video information for fraud detection in accounting and finance.

Title: Marketing misinformation in the age of AI
Authors: Gita Venkataramani Johar, Amna Kirmani
Affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University New York New York USA; Robert H. Smith School of Business University of Maryland College Park Maryland USA
Abstract: Abstract We shine a spotlight on marketing misinformation—claims about products and brands that contradict or distort verifiable facts. Misinformation may be created unintentionally or intentionally by companies, competitors, customers, or third parties seeking to harm companies or consumers. We focus on the role of AI in creating, obfuscating, and disseminating misinformation in the form of text, audio, images, and videos generated using large language models. This type of information can pose a substantial risk for brand safety. Consumers may be aware that AI can generate misinformation but may lack the ability to guard against it. We discuss how different stakeholders in the information ecosystem can help in the prevention and correction of misinformation and propose a future research agenda in this critical and fast‐growing area.

Title: Artificial intelligence and venture capital: Revisiting sourcing, selection, and nurturing activities
Authors: Gary Dushnitsky
Affiliations: Strategy & Entrepreneurship Area London Business School London UK
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Venture capital (VC) is an information‐intensive form of entrepreneurial finance conducted under extreme uncertainty. Investors must originate promising opportunities, select ventures with sparse and strategically disclosed information, and monitor and support firms after investment. Prior research documents both formal mechanisms (e.g., staged financing, syndication) and informal mechanisms built on referrals, reputation, and constant interaction. Geographic and social proximity enable these mechanisms by lowering the cost of obtaining contextual information and coordinating action. We develop a mechanism‐based account of how data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) reconfigure this established model. Our framework yields propositions on geographic dispersion in sourcing, portfolio selection, and the distinct effects of AI on monitoring versus value‐added support. It also identifies boundary conditions associated with institutional setting and heterogeneous AI adoption. Managerial Summary For venture capital firms, AI is not a single tool and adoption is not a binary choice. A fund may use data systems to identify founders, machine‐learning models to organize deal flow, generative AI to summarize diligence materials, or analytics to monitor portfolio companies. Each application changes a different part of the VC process. In sourcing, AI can widen the funnel beyond warm introductions and local ecosystems, especially in sectors such as software and e‐commerce where hiring, product, and customer signals are visible. In selection, AI can make diligence faster and more consistent, but models trained on past investments may favor ventures that resemble previously funded companies and may miss novel opportunities for which historical analogues are weak. In post‐investment activity, continuous operational data can partly replace physical presence for monitoring, while value‐add support such as customer introductions, recruiting, strategy advice, and founder coaching remain relationship‐intensive. The practical implication is a task‐level approach: automate codifiable search and processing, retain independent human judgment where uncertainty is fundamental, and use AI to strengthen rather than erode trusted investor–founder relationships. Funds also face organizational choices about building proprietary infrastructure, buying external tools, or combining the two. The appropriate configuration depends on data access, strategy, scale, and the activity in which the fund seeks advantage.

Title: Entrepreneurial theorizing with generative artificial intelligence
Authors: Sung Ho Park, Alex Murray
Affiliations: Department of Management, Lundquist College of Business University of Oregon Eugene Oregon USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

Title: Pet-owner synchrony: Operationalization, application, and implications
Authors: Sunhee Choi, Wesley Friske, Mayukh Dass
Abstract: Abstract Despite the pet industry’s significant economic and social importance, academic attention to this sector of the economy has been limited. Rather than focusing solely on the household demographics of pet ownership or the attitudinal components of the pet-owner relationship, we explore actual purchase decisions of pet owners. In this study, we examine pet-owner synchrony, a behavioral operationalization of pet-owner relationships that is grounded in attachment theory, anthropomorphism, and the extended self. Utilizing scanner data from 875,853 market baskets including 23 million transactions collected from a regional supermarket chain, we analyze cross-category co-occurrence patterns within shopping baskets. Our analysis reveals affinities, or parallels, in pet owners’ purchases of health and wellness products and hedonic products for both themselves and their pets, which we attribute to pet-owner synchrony. We identify two moderators that influence the strength of pet-owner synchrony: pet type (cat versus dog) and the presence of young children in the household. In addition, we evaluate how basket size, holidays, and price elasticities impact pet-owner synchrony. Our findings deliver useful insights into pet-owner relationships, have direct implications for retail and manufacturing managers, and yield recommendations for public policy.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: The ripple effects of customer orientation: Personal, vicarious, and temporal pathways to frontline employee well-being
Authors: Siddeeq M. Shabazz, Gabriel Gazzoli, Jin Ho Jung, Todd Arnold, Alex Zablah, Woo Gon Kim, R. L. Fernando Garcia
Abstract: Employee well‑being has declined globally, with frontline employees (FLEs) particularly affected. Drawing on conservation of resources (COR) theory, we examine (1) why and under what conditions customer orientation shapes FLE well‑being, (2) how well‑being influences customer‑oriented outcomes, and (3) how customer orientation operates within service encounters to shape well‑being. Two multi‑wave, multi‑source field studies in healthcare (USA) and hospitality (Philippines) reveal that customer orientation generates a set of ripple effects that shape FLE well‑being and, ultimately, customer outcomes. The first ripple is personal, linking customer orientation to well‑being via work meaningfulness. The second is vicarious: merely observing co‑workers engaging in customer‑oriented behaviors promotes FLE well‑being by strengthening the effect of the employee’s own customer orientation. An experiment then traces these across-encounter effects to their within‑encounter origin, showing that customer orientation shapes how strongly an interaction carries over into those that follow, the building block from which lasting well‑being accumulates. Our investigation underscores the dual benefits of customer orientation, a healthier frontline workforce alongside better service and improved customer outcomes.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Minimizing network development costs using reverse p-median models
Authors: Jaehwan Jeong, Joyendu Bhadury
Abstract: The reverse p-median problem seeks network modifications that improve the accessibility of predetermined facility locations subject to budget and network-design constraints. Solving this problem on general networks with discrete edge length choices is computationally challenging because shortest-path distances must be repeatedly recalculated across a large number of feasible network configurations. To address this challenge, we develop a globally optimal solution framework, called the Reverse p-Median Solver (RPM), which combines structured enumeration with two complementary search procedures to efficiently explore the feasible budget domain. A key feature of RPM is its ability to identify globally optimal networks over the entire feasible budget range and construct the corresponding Pareto-efficient frontier between network cost and investment budget, enabling decision-makers to systematically evaluate trade-offs between infrastructure investment and network performance. Computational experiments on illustrative electricity-grid examples and a large-scale transportation network case study in Virginia demonstrate the practical applicability and scalability of the proposed framework.

Title: A new perspective on multi-objective project scheduling problems: Evaluating with multiple reference profiles
Authors: Ziyang Tang, Tom Servranckx, Mario Vanhoucke, Zhengwen He
Abstract: This paper addresses the multi-objective resource-constrained project scheduling problem (MORCPSP) under a non-compensatory preference structure over conflicting objectives. From the decision maker’s perspective, objectives reflecting distinct stakeholder concerns (such as minimising project tardiness and minimising resource leveling cost) often exhibit a non-compensatory relationship, in which good performance on one objective cannot fully offset unacceptable performance on the other. This characteristic makes it difficult for decision makers to specify precise compensatory weights between objectives. Moreover, existing multi-objective heuristic algorithms (MOHAs) typically generate large sets of non-dominated schedules without using preference information during the search, thereby leaving decision makers with the burden of selecting from numerous alternative schedules. To address these limitations, we develop MOHA-EMP, a preference-guided framework that integrates the Evaluating with Multiple Reference Profiles (EMP) procedure into the fitness evaluation and selection of the evolutionary search. Computational experiments conducted on 2700 RanGen2 instances and 480 PSPLIB J30 instances show MOHA-EMP achieves higher preference satisfaction than its standard MOHA counterparts for five benchmarking MOHAs (NSGA-II, ECGA, NTGA2, bNTGA and MOEA/D), improving the average EMP-measure by 12.5%–27.1% while reducing the number of output schedules by 89%–95%. The sensitivity analysis further shows that the method remains robust under varying project sizes, deadlines, resource constraints and network structures. These findings indicate the broad applicability of preference-integrated evolutionary search for decision support in MORCPSP.

Title: Multi-visit truck-drone pickup and delivery problem with release dates and drone resupply
Authors: Shuang Liang, Yanru Chen, Bo Du
Abstract: This study addresses a novel integrated truck-drone routing and demand allocation problem that captures three underexplored real-world complexities simultaneously: item release dates, time windows, and simultaneous pickup and delivery. Unlike existing studies that rely on a single drone type, we introduce resupply drones as a distinct second type that delivers newly released items from depot to en‑route trucks. This combination of features, including release dates, time windows, simultaneous pickup and delivery, and dual drone type service, has not been jointly addressed in prior literature. Decisions include customer assignment to truck, drone, or locker service; truck and delivery drone routes; delivery drone launch and retrieval nodes; and resupply drone-truck matching and rendezvous coordination. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer bilinear programming model that captures payload- and waiting-dependent delivery drone energy consumption and truck load variations. To strengthen exact solution methods, we develop valid inequalities that reduce computational time by 37.53% on small instances. For large-scale problems, we develop a customized adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) with acceleration rules that exploit relationships among release dates, time windows, and delivery modes to prevent infeasibility, alongside a node-based feasibility test and efficient drone-scheduling mechanism that cuts waiting-induced energy use. On medium and large instances, the ALNS outperforms three benchmark algorithms, with reported average cost reductions of 37.87%, 54.75%, and 21.37%. Sensitivity analysis provides valuable managerial insights for logistics practitioners.

Title: Operations management for sustainable development and public policy making
Authors: Jan C Fransoo, Guan-Yuan Wang, Simone Balvers
Affiliations: Tilburg University
Abstract: Public policy making often faces challenges in implementation due to a lack of attention to operational realities. Operations management (OM) research, with its strong empirical component and focus on detailed model-based mechanisms, offers unique insights for successful policy execution. This paper explores the synergies between economics, development economics, and OM in addressing public policy implementation, arguing that OM’s process-level understanding, empirical rigor, and focus on operational feasibility can enhance policy design and evaluation. We illustrate this potential through examples from sustainability and social development, demonstrating how OM can bridge the gap between economic policy insights and operational execution.

Title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
Authors: Erdem Dogukan Yilmaz, Ivana Naumovska, Vikas A. Aggarwal
Affiliations: INSEAD, 77305 Fontainebleau, France
Abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy.

Title: Why Do We Discriminate? Directional Beliefs and Biased Information Processing
Authors: Markus Eyting
Affiliations: Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, 55128 Mainz, Germany; and Leibniz Institute for Financial Research Sustainable Architecture for Finance in Europe, 60323 Frankfurt am Main, Germany
Abstract: Identifying the cause of discrimination is crucial to designing effective policies and to understanding discrimination dynamics. This paper provides a potential link between existing models of taste-based and statistical discrimination by studying directional belief formation through biased information search and processing. By selectively acquiring and processing information, individuals form directional beliefs and consequently discriminate based on these beliefs. Through a series of experiments in which individuals endogenously acquire and process various signals, I document discrimination stemming from directional beliefs and demonstrate important differences in how it manifests compared with taste-based and statistical discrimination. Finally, I show that limiting individuals’ scope to interpret information reduces such discrimination. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Title: Systemically Important Banks and Loan Performance: Evidence from India
Authors: Shashwat Agrawal, Nishant Kashyap, Sriniwas Mahapatro, Prasanna Tantri
Affiliations: Department of Finance, Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Boston, Massachusetts 02467; Finance and Accounting Area, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, Vastrapur, Ahmedabad, Gujarat 380015, India; Department of Finance and Accounting, Saunders College of Business, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York 14623; Finance Area, Indian School of Business, Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Telangana 500032, India
Abstract: We examine whether designating banks as systemically important affects loan performance in an emerging-market setting where such banks are large domestic institutions and market imperfections make monitoring crucial for loan performance. Using loan-level data and the staggered designation of banks as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (DSIBs) in India, we find that loan performance deteriorates following DSIB designation. The evidence points to bank-level moral hazard as the underlying mechanism: DSIBs reduce postorigination monitoring and weaken loan recovery efforts. Borrowers respond accordingly, exhibiting poorer financial health and loan repayment, particularly on loans extended by DSIBs. This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03238 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Jan Bouwens, accounting.

Title: A Continuous-Time Model of Subscription and Repeat Purchase
Authors: Wee Chaimanowong, Tony Ke
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Marketing, Shatin, Hong Kong
Abstract: Problem definition: We present a continuous-time model of consumers’ joint decisions of membership subscription and repeat purchase. A consumer pays a flow membership fee; her valuation follows a Brownian motion, purchase needs arrive via a Poisson process, and she chooses whether to buy and when to unsubscribe. The model is analytically tractable thanks to the connection between consumer lifetime and hitting time of Brownian motions. Methodology/results: Consumers’ unsubscription decision solves an optimal-stopping problem with a closed-form valuation cutoff; purchase occurs when valuation exceeds the transaction price. These thresholds generate three fluid consumer modes—buyer, tracker, and churner. We find that consumers who are about to terminate subscription tend to purchase less frequently, and who are currently subscribing are more likely to continue subscription. This endogenous customer loyalty is captured by a one-parameter retention formula [Formula: see text], which can accommodate rapid early attrition and an asymptotic slow decay. Managerial implications: For empirical estimation, we cast latent-valuation filtering as a heat-diffusion problem and develop a kernel-iteration likelihood approximation with vanishing discretization errors. Three empirical studies that feature two distinct firm-customer relationships demonstrate that our model performs on par with or better than existing models. Based on the model estimates, firms can infer consumers’ latent engagement and churn risk from purchase histories and devise the optimal package of membership fee and transaction price.

Title: Operations Management in the Sharing Economy: Advances, Challenges, and Opportunities
Authors: Huan Cao, Liu Ming, Daehoon Noh, David Simchi-Levi, Tunay Tunca, Yi Xu, Weiming Zhu
Affiliations: Lyft Inc, Marketplace, San Francisco, California, United States; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzen, Business School, China; Korea University, Logistics, Service, and Operations Management, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Massachusetts Institute of Technology, OR Center, LIDS and IDSS, Massachusetts, United States; University of Maryland, DOIT, College Park, Maryland, United States; University of Maryland, DOIT, United States; Universidad de Navarra IESE Business School, Production, Technology and Operations Management, Barcelona, Catalunya, Spain
Abstract: The rapid growth of the sharing economy over the past decade has changed many industries in profound ways. The innovative business models that have emerged in the sharing economy present unique opportunities as well as challenges, which have attracted a significant amount of attention from researchers in the operations management field. In this paper, we discuss the advances, challenges, and opportunities for research on operations management in the sharing economy. We divide sharing economy into eight categories: Ride Sharing, Space Sharing, Bike Sharing, Vehicle Sharing, Group Buying, Crowdfunding, Freelancing, and Last-Mile Delivery. For each business category, we identify the gaps and current challenges in the existing literature, discuss emerging industry trends and research topics, and suggest several future research directions. Our goal is to stimulate discussion and ideas about future studies in this area.

Title: To Be or Not to Be (Aligned with Elites): Navigating Systemic Power within Informal Institutions
Authors: Christopher Sutter, Babita Bhatt, Israr Qureshi
Affiliations: University of Cincinnati; Queen’s University Belfast
Abstract: Social intermediaries play a critical role in addressing exclusion, but must navigate entrenched power relations within informal institutions. Drawing on comparative case studies of three social intermediaries, this study examines how intermediaries negotiate systemic power—manifested through domination and discipline—across intersecting caste–gender hierarchies. We identify three distinct approaches to elite engagement: elite delegation, elite co-optation, and creative accommodation. Each of these reflects a specific combination of communal positioning and power frame adopted by intermediaries. Elite delegation, grounded in a detached communal positioning and a zero-sum power frame, prioritizes rapid scaling but reproduces existing hierarchies. Elite co-optation, marked by pragmatic communal positioning and a conditional positive-sum power frame, fosters short-term cooperation yet achieves only partial inclusion. Creative accommodation, characterized by embedded communal positioning and a positive-sum power frame, enables social transformation by simultaneously empowering marginalized groups and constructively engaging elites. By demonstrating how communal positioning and power frames shape these approaches, the study advances understanding of how systemic power sustains exclusion and how it can be reconfigured from within. We contribute to research on informal institutions and inclusion by elucidating how intermediaries can leverage positive-sum engagements to reshape domination and discipline, fostering more equitable and enduring informal institutional change.

Title: How Mega-Threats Influence Workplace Cooperation: Effect of #BlackLivesMatter Salience on Cooperation among and between Black and White Coworkers
Authors: Steffen Keck, Christian Schumacher, Abhinav Gupta, Keith Leavitt
Affiliations: University of Vienna; Vienna University of Economics and Business; University of Washington; Oregon State University
Abstract: Mega-threats—public, shocking, and identity-relevant events involving violence or injustice—can disrupt organizational life. Yet, research has largely overlooked the fact that such events may create asymmetric identity-based threats for employees who share identities with victims versus those who share identities with perceived perpetrators, leading to divergent psychological responses and workplace cooperation within and between groups. We examine how the salience of a race-based mega-threat shapes cooperation between Black and White employees. Drawing on self-categorization theory and intergroup interaction research, we propose that mega-threat salience more strongly increases intra-racial cooperation among Black versus White employees, due to heightened in-group identification among the former. Conversely, we hypothesize that mega-threat salience more strongly reduces White employees’ willingness to initiate cooperation with Black colleagues, driven by perceptions of a morally tainted social identity and concerns about social rejection. We argue that this negative effect is attenuated when White employees hold relatively lower (vs. higher) professional status than their Black interaction partners. We find support for these predictions in over 124,000 dyadic interactions between Black and White players in the National Basketball Association during periods of heightened Black Lives Matter salience. Two experimental studies replicate these findings and provide evidence for the envisioned mechanisms.

Title: Tied In or Tied Up? The Contrasting Effects of Social Ties on Employee Turnover
Authors: Alessandro Iorio, Shad Morris
Affiliations: Bocconi University; Brigham Young University
Abstract: A key theoretical tension in organizational network research lies in understanding how interpersonal connections shape employee turnover. While extensive workplace networks can reduce turnover by granting access to valuable information and resources, they can also increase it by exposing employees to information overload, leading to cognitive strain and disengagement. Drawing on process theory, we bridge these two previously disconnected mechanisms—information access and information overload—to uncover how they jointly influence turnover. We propose that an intermediate number of instrumental workplace connections maximizes retention, as it balances the benefits of information access with the burdens of overload. Specifically, we theorize that information access exhibits diminishing marginal returns in mitigating turnover as additional connections provide less value, while information overload accelerates as employees struggle to process a growing volume of inputs, resulting in a U-shaped relationship between the size of an employee’s network and turnover. We test these arguments across four studies: two preregistered experiments and two field studies of employees in large organizations. Our findings challenge conventional wisdom that larger networks are universally beneficial, providing insights into how the structure of informal networks drives turnover dynamics.

Title: Are You Looking at Me? Orchestrating Voyeuristic Events to Add Value for Those Being Observed
Authors: Dean A. Shepherd, Vinit Parida, Sarah Chase, Joakim Wincent
Affiliations: University of Notre Dame; Luleå University of Technology and University of Vaasa; Hanken School of Economics and University of St. Gallen
Abstract: Voyeurism offers audiences a window into the private lives of others. Given the widespread appeal of voyeurism, it is unsurprising that organizations have sought to commercialize voyeuristic events across various industries. Prior research has focused on the audience’s role in voyeuristic experiences. However, those being observed (i.e., observees) play an essential role in shaping audiences’ voyeuristic experiences, making it crucial to explore how voyeuristic businesses strive to manage observees’ engagement. For this exploration, we used an inductive approach. We focused on the voyeuristic business of slum tourism and interviewed the observees (slum residents), audience members (tourists), and orchestrators (tour guides) in the Dharavi slum. We found that businesses attempt to orchestrate a voyeuristic event to ensure continued observee participation by scripting the event, claiming to improve the lives of those in the transgressed community, bounding audience behavior, personalizing the observees, and memorializing the voyeuristic experience. This orchestrated interaction can temporarily blur the traditional roles of audience and observee, with some observees momentarily taking on the perspective of the audience and the audience momentarily being observed. This temporary switching of roles can enhance the experience of the voyeuristic event for the audience and for some of the nonconsenting observees.

Title: When Women Stick Together: Network Dynamics and Shared Resources Following Disruptive Events
Authors: Yiftach Yarmar, Tiantian Yang, Marissa D. King
Affiliations: INSEAD; University of Pennsylvania
Abstract: Social networks play a role in exacerbating or ameliorating inequality. The persistence of network-based inequality is well documented. However, the mechanisms that disrupt this unequal access to resources remain poorly understood. This study investigates how structurally disruptive events, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&As), reshape gender homophily and resource sharing in networks. We examine how 59 M&As shape the evolution of 82,064 physicians’ referral and patient-sharing networks. We find that disruptive events enhance women’s access to resources by altering gender-homophily dynamics in formation, and maintenance. Specifically, acquisitions intensify men’s tendency to form ties with other men. In contrast, women are more likely to preserve ties with other women, with all-women dyads exhibiting greater resilience and higher maintenance rates than mixed-gender or all-men dyads. This dynamic results in richer networks for women, shielding them from the adverse effects of organizational disruption. These results highlight contrasting network behaviors following disruption: women winnow their networks, reinforcing stable, trust-based relationships with women, while men widen theirs, forming new distant ties with men. By demonstrating how gendered network dynamics evolve in response to disruptions, this study contributes to scholarship on gender inequality, network resilience, and conditions under which homophilous ties can mitigate disparities.

Title: Political Segregation in the Labor Market and the Persistence of Pay Gaps
Authors: Ray Tsai Fang, Felice B. Klein, Chi Nguyen, Jeff Lingwall, Alexander Lewis
Affiliations: University of Washington at Tacoma; Boise State University; Oklahoma State University; University of Texas at San Antonio
Abstract: Many scholars assume that initiatives to promote gender and racial pay equality are largely performative, helping firms appear socially responsible while making little progress. However, the extent to which such initiatives are genuinely supported may depend on the ideological leaning of the field in which they occur. We propose that the higher the ratio of liberals in an industry or occupation, the more its members will be guided by logics that support the equal distribution of resources between gender and racial groups. Using large-scale archival samples of U.S. employees and recent data on U.S. firms and nonprofit organizations, we find support for our theory. The results indicate that membership in liberal-leaning industries and occupations is associated with stronger support for the use of pro-equality practices. Liberal-leaning industries and occupations also showed greater progress toward gender and racial pay equality over time. Notably, we controlled for various alternative explanations, such as demographic and geographic differences between fields. Thus, this paper suggests that the political composition of a field may give rise to logics and norms that shape how efforts to promote group equality are understood and pursued.

Title: Who’s Behind the Red Suit? Exploring Role Prototypicality within Calling Enactment among Professional Santas
Authors: Christina B. Hymer, Bethany S. Cockburn, Borbala Csillag
Affiliations: University of Tennessee; Northern Illinois University; Oregon State University

Title: Care-Full Reviewing at Academy of Management Journal : Celebrating Our Reviewers and Putting Care Front and Center in the Review Process
Authors: Madeline Toubiana, Fadel K. Matta, Jamie J. Ladge, Tine Köhler, David Kryscynski, Charlotte Cloutier, Benjamin M. Cole
Affiliations: University of Ottawa; University of Georgia; Boston College; University of Melbourne; Rutgers University; HEC Montreal; Fordham University

Title: Contested credibility: Public perceptions of scientists as experts
Authors: Anders Broström, Cornelia Lawson, Mabel Sanchez-Barrioluengo
Abstract: Science is widely embraced as an important prerequisite for innovation, and there is widespread support for public investment in science on that basis. However, it remains more contested whether and when science is recognized as a relevant source of expertise in contemporary debates beyond the academic sphere. Drawing on nationally representative survey panels from two European countries (the United Kingdom and Sweden), we investigate whether scientists are perceived as more credible senders of messages regarding societal challenges compared with attribution to other types of expert groups (government, businesspersons, and issue advocates). Evidence from a conjoint analysis paints a rather bleak picture: scientists’ credibility is only superior to that of government officials, but not businesspersons or issue advocates. We furthermore find that scientists are more credible when communicating technological issues than non-technological ones. This pattern can be traced back to three types of perceived sources of distrust (vested interest, partisanship and irrelevance) that are activated more strongly for non-technological issues. The same three sources of distrust also underpin the general credibility disadvantage of scientists as experts. Implications for our understanding of the social contract of science are discussed.

Title: Event System Theory: A Decade of Progress and a Future of Potential
Authors: Frederick P. Morgeson, Terence R. Mitchell, Dong Liu
Affiliations: Michigan State University; University of Washington; Georgia Institute of Technology

Title: Does Global Slowing Explain Age Effects in Inhibitory Control?
Authors: Jacob Sellers, Han Zhang, John Jonides, Taraz G. Lee
Affiliations: Department of Psychology, University of Michigan
Abstract: A long-standing debate in the study of cognitive aging centers around the issue of whether aging results in a selective deficit in inhibitory control beyond general slowing of cognitive processing. Previous studies have obtained mixed findings, in part because the typical free-response-time paradigm lacks the specificity required to disentangle component processes underlying inhibitory control. Here, we apply a forced-response paradigm and computational model to test whether aging results in overall speed differences or a selective deficit in inhibitory control. Across two experiments, over 200 older adults and younger adults completed a forced-response arrow-flanker task. We found strong evidence that older adults demonstrate a global slowing of processing without any selective deficit in inhibitory control in this task. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global slowing is sufficient to explain the mixed findings in previous free-response-time studies. Overall, these results argue against a selective inhibitory-control deficit in older adults.

Title: Dancing to multiple tunes: Establishing legitimacy with first‐time and repeat backers in crowdfunding campaigns
Authors: Stephanie Hepp, Alexander Vossen, Lien Denoo
Affiliations: Entrepreneurship in Context University of Siegen Siegen Germany; Jheronimus Academy of Data Science Tilburg University ‘s‐Hertogenbosch The Netherlands; Department of Strategy & Entrepreneurship Tilburg University Tilburg The Netherlands
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Using 14,108 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns, we examine three strategies to gather support from first‐time versus repeat backers: narrative distinctiveness aligning with backers' expectations of novelty, endorsement from Kickstarter staff, and campaign leadership's reciprocity of funding other campaigns. Staff endorsement is more strongly associated with support from first‐time backers, while campaign leadership's reciprocity is associated primarily with repeat backers. Differences between first‐time and repeat backers are evident in evaluating narrative distinctiveness: narratives distinct from past campaigns correlate positively with repeat backers and greater funding but negatively with first‐time backers. Narratives distinct from live campaigns correlate positively with first‐time backers but are associated with lower funding amounts. Our findings conceptualize differences between first‐time and repeat backers that shape the associations between campaign legitimization strategies and backer support. Managerial Summary This work examines how Kickstarter campaigns should be designed to attract both new people and get support from existing community members. We test whether differences between these two target groups exist in evaluating commonly established “success factors” of campaigns: An endorsement from Kickstarter, the involvement of the campaign founder on the platform, and a campaign text highlighting the campaign's novel contributions. We find differences in all three between both groups and conclude with insights on how managers should design crowdfunding campaigns based on long‐term goals and objectives. We also offer some implications for crowdfunding platforms, such as Kickstarter, in supporting content creators in attracting new backers, which aids with overall platform growth.

Title: Learning to innovate: How and when firms transform intellectual capital into exploratory and exploitative innovation
Authors: Gholamhossein (Amir) Mehralian, Arash Sadeghi, Ralf Wilden
Affiliations: University of Exeter Business School Exeter UK; University of Leicester School of Business Leicester UK; Macquarie University Innovation, Strategy and Entrepreneurship (ISE) Research Centre Macquarie Business School Sydney Australia
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Corporate entrepreneurship (CE) requires firms to pursue both exploratory and exploitative innovation, yet limited research explains how intellectual capital (IC) is translated into these distinct outcomes. We develop a contingency model that specifies how and when IC drives exploration and exploitation. We theorize that a firm's capacity for learning and transformation (CLT) functions as a firm‐level learning and transformation capability through which IC can be translated into either exploratory or exploitative innovation. Knowledge breadth strengthens the indirect effect of IC on exploratory innovation via CLT, whereas knowledge depth amplifies the indirect effect on exploitative innovation. We test the model in two complementary field studies. Study 1 employs a time‐lagged design with objective archival data, and Study 2 replicates the findings using survey data. Results consistently support the proposed theoretical model. Managerial Summary Firms operating in fast‐changing and uncertain environments often struggle to balance developing new products with improving existing ones. Our study shows that simply having strong knowledge resources is not enough. What matters is how effectively firms learn from and use that knowledge. We find that firms perform better when they build strong learning capabilities that help them adapt, recombine, and apply knowledge over time. Importantly, the type of knowledge a firm holds shapes this process: broad knowledge supports new product development, while deep, specialized knowledge strengthens improvements to existing products. For managers, this means focusing not only on acquiring knowledge but also on building systems and practices that continuously translate knowledge into action and innovation.

Title: It's a match! Similarity in personality traits in the business angel–founder dyad and follow‐on funding
Authors: Angela Altmeier, Christian Fisch
Affiliations: Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust (SnT) University of Luxembourg Luxembourg Luxembourg
Abstract: Abstract Research summary We assess how personality alignment in investor–founder dyads is associated with the likelihood of follow‐on funding, a vital outcome for early‐stage ventures. Using machine learning to infer the Big Five personality traits from Twitter data for 9497 business angel–founder dyads, we find that similarity in conscientiousness and agreeableness is associated with a higher likelihood of follow‐on funding, while similarity in neuroticism is associated with a lower likelihood. We attribute these patterns to the trait‐specific benefits of supplementary (conscientiousness and agreeableness) and complementary (neuroticism) fit. Robustness checks and additional analyses support and nuance the conclusion that personality fit matters for venture outcomes, highlighting the strategic role of personality fit in the investor–founder relationship. Managerial summary We show that personality similarity between business angels and founders is associated with whether a venture secures follow‐on funding. Similarity in conscientiousness (being organized and reliable) and agreeableness (being cooperative and trusting) is linked to a higher likelihood of securing follow‐on funding, while similarity in neuroticism (emotional instability) is linked to a lower likelihood. We interpret these patterns as collaboration dynamics: similarity can help through supplementary fit (e.g., shared work style and cooperation), but differences can help through complementary fit (e.g., one partner's emotional stability offsets the other's emotional instability). Practically, founders and business angels should develop self‐awareness and consider personality fit alongside other characteristics when forming partnerships. Policymakers and incubators can support better matches and strengthen collaboration by promoting awareness of interpersonal dynamics.

Title: Issue Information
From critique to catalyst: How academic entrepreneurs transform negative feedback into pivots and performance
Authors: D. Carrington Motley, Michael Leatherbee, Riitta Katila
Affiliations: Tepper School of Business Carnegie Mellon University Pittsburgh Pennsylvania USA; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile Santiago Chile; Department of Management Science & Engineering Stanford University Stanford California USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary This study examines how academic entrepreneurs refine business ideas in response to external critique and how these responses relate to performance. We develop a framework that links feedback (critique), business‐idea changes (pivots), and performance, and test it using detailed data on external stakeholder feedback, changes to the business idea's core and periphery, and commercialization outcomes in 316 academic‐led teams. We find that academic entrepreneurs frequently modify their business idea's core in response to negative feedback, and that core changes—rather than peripheral ones—are positively associated with commercialization. Challenging the idea that all entrepreneurs are inertial, we find that academic entrepreneurs both actively embrace and benefit from changes to the business idea's core. By tracing the feedback‐response dynamics of business idea components, our study adds granularity to research on pivoting. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs often face a choice between reworking the core of a business idea and making changes to its periphery. Analyzing 316 academic‐led teams seeking to commercialize technologies using the Lean Startup Method, we find that academic‐led teams frequently change their idea's core in response to negative feedback—and that only core changes, rather than peripheral changes, are linked to improved commercialization outcomes. Overall, the results show the effectiveness of the Lean Startup Method and demonstrate that focusing feedback on the core of the business idea is an effective way to provide feedback to academic entrepreneurs.

Title: The signal of institutional governance in early‐stage financing for university spinoffs
Authors: Andrea Belz, Alexandra Graddy‐Reed, Fernando Zapatero
Affiliations: Information Sciences Institute and Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Viterbi School of Engineering University of Southern California Los Angeles California USA; Sol Price School of Public Policy University of Southern California Los Angeles California USA; Richard D. Cohen Professor in Finance Questrom School of Business, Boston University Boston Massachusetts USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary University spinoffs (USOs) translate scientific advancement to economic gains, but the role of the university's governance as a public or private institution is infrequently explored. With a novel dataset of academic entrepreneurs with National Science Foundation I‐Corps training, we examine institutional governance as a fundraising signal. We demonstrate how angel investors and venture capitalists (VCs) show a preference for private USOs. However, with different investment objectives, the groups conduct distinct sensemaking that weighs this cue differently. For angels, industry moderates the effect such that they prefer private university life science firms to public USOs. However, industry mediates the effect for VCs, who prefer life sciences to engineering. We describe this variation as mixed salience—when a signal yields differences in decision‐making for distinct audiences. Managerial Summary University spinoffs (USOs) are important for economic growth, but little is known about differences between USOs from public and private universities. We study how angel investors and venture capitalists (VCs) fund USOs of public and private schools. These two investor groups make funding decisions with different priorities and approaches. Both groups appear to prefer private universities. A deeper look reveals that angel investors prefer private university life science teams to the public university counterparts. On the other hand, VCs prefer life sciences teams to engineering teams—and life sciences teams are more likely to come from private schools. Evidently, the two investor audiences respond to the public/private distinction in different ways.

Title: Public support and VC financing in academic startups
Authors: Maud Thys, Maikel Pellens, Hanna Hottenrott, Marius Berger
Affiliations: Department of Management, Strategy, and Innovation KU Leuven Leuven Belgium; ECOOM – Expertise Center for R&D Monitoring KU Leuven Leuven Belgium; ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research Mannheim Germany; TUM School of Management Munich Germany
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We investigate public support and venture capital (VC) investment in academic startups. Government support may enable follow‐on investment by providing a quality signal to investors. This signal is especially important for academic startups, which face large funding gaps due to their complexity, cutting‐edge nature, and uncertainty regarding the founders' management capabilities and commitment. Using a panel of startups in Germany, our analyses confirm that academic startups are more likely to obtain follow‐on VC investment after receiving public support than non‐academic startups. Further, this effect is limited in time, lasts longer for academic startups, is concentrated in high‐tech manufacturing firms, and is stronger for investments from business angels. Our findings have implications for policymakers seeking to foster academic entrepreneurship through policy programs and VC investment. Managerial Summary Obtaining seed and growth capital is essential for potentially highly innovative startups. We show that startups that obtain public support are more likely to receive VC funding and that this effect is stronger for startups with academic founders, approximately twice as large. We further show that this benefit is limited in time, concentrated in the high‐tech manufacturing industry, and more salient for business angel financing than for investment by independent VC funds or corporate VCs. For founders of academic startups, our results imply that acquiring public support might enhance the chances of attracting follow‐on financing.

Title: Micro‐transitions and work identity: The case of academic entrepreneurs
Authors: Marouane Bousfiha, Henrik Berglund
Affiliations: Unit for Innovation and Entrepreneurship, Department of Economy and Society, School of Business, Economics and Law University of Gothenburg Gothenburg Sweden; Division of Entrepreneurship and Strategy, Department of Technology Management and Economics Chalmers University of Technology Gothenburg Sweden
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper examines how academic entrepreneurs—scientists who found research‐based startups while remaining in academia—construct and sustain their professional identities amid frequent transitions between academic and entrepreneurial roles. Drawing on 27 interviews with Swedish academic entrepreneurs, we show that hybrid identities are not simply the result of reconciling abstract role categories but are shaped through the material and practical organization of everyday work. We introduce the concept of professional micro‐transitions as a key site of identity formation and argue that material artifacts and routines play a central role in this process. This study contributes to the literatures on identity work, role transitions, and academic entrepreneurship by offering a granular, materially grounded account of how hybrid identities are enacted and sustained in practice. Managerial Summary This article investigates how academic entrepreneurs—university scientists who create startups to commercialize research results while remaining in academia—manage to build a hybrid professional identity when frequently switching back and forth between their jobs as academics and for‐profit entrepreneurs. The findings reveal how they creatively find cross‐fertilizing effects between their academic and entrepreneurial work tasks. This in turn allows them to reevaluate and extend their professional identity. For universities, incubators, and policymakers, this study suggests that supporting academic entrepreneurship is not just about funding or IP policies. It also requires recognizing the practical identity work involved and creating flexible environments that allow scientists to integrate both roles in meaningful ways.

Title: Determinants and Consequences of Auditors’ Consultations with the National Office
Authors: Matthew G. Sherwood, Miguel Minutti-Meza, Aleksandra B. Zimmerman
Affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst; University of Miami; Florida State University
Abstract: ABSTRACT Audit teams may consult with their firm’s national office to obtain specialized expertise, satisfy regulatory and quality control requirements, and demonstrate due professional care. We describe the consultation process based on PCAOB standards, firm methodologies, and auditor interviews. We explain different types of consultations and highlight differences in the determinants and usefulness of mandatory versus voluntary consultations. Using PCAOB inspection data, we show that formal consultations are largely predictable based on engagement characteristics and, on average, are not associated with audit quality. However, two subsets of formal consultations that focus on accounting issues and occur earlier in the engagement process are associated with greater regulatory compliance and higher audit quality. Hence, an increasing reliance on all types of consultations does not automatically translate into higher audit quality. Collectively, our findings deepen our understanding of auditors’ use of national office consultations and their implications for audit practice. Data Availability: Audit engagement data from the PCAOB are proprietary; other data are from public sources. JEL Classification: M4.

Title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
Authors: Andy Wu, Ronald Wang
Affiliations: Strategy Unit, Harvard Business School Harvard University Boston Massachusetts USA; Department of Management Science and Engineering Stanford University Stanford California USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

Title: Structural concentration in weighted networks: A class of topology-aware indices
Authors: L. Riso, M.G. Zoia
Abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for measuring concentration in weighted systems embedded in networks of interactions. While traditional indices such as the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index quantify the dispersion of node weights, they ignore the topology of the relationships among the corresponding units. To address this limitation, we introduce a family of topology-aware concentration indices that jointly account for weight distributions and network structure. At the core of the framework lies a baseline Network Concentration Index (NCI), defined as a normalized quadratic form that measures the fraction of potential weighted interaction realized through the observed network. Building on this foundation, we develop a flexible class of extensions obtained by modifying either the interaction matrix or the normalization benchmark, including weighted, density-adjusted, null-model, degree-constrained, transformed-data, and multi-layer variants. The proposed framework preserves key properties such as normalization, invariance, and interpretability, while providing a common representation for topology-aware concentration measures under different interaction structures. Its general formulation allows alternative notions of interaction, including higher-order relationships or tail dependence, to be incorporated through an appropriate specification of the interaction matrix. Theoretical results establish the main properties of the proposed indices and clarify their relationship with classical concentration measures and standard network statistics. Simulation studies and empirical applications demonstrate that systems with identical weight distributions may exhibit substantially different levels of structural concentration depending on their network topology, highlighting the additional information captured by the proposed framework. The methodology is broadly applicable to economic, financial, and complex systems in which weighted entities interact through networks.

Title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
Authors: Brant E. Christensen, Nathan G. Lundstrom, Nathan J. Newton
Affiliations: Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA; University of Kansas Lawrence Kansas USA; Florida State University Tallahassee Florida USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

Title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
Authors: Michele Bisceglia, Alessio Piccolo, Jan Schneemeier
Abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

Title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
Authors: Benedikt Roder, Jochen Hartmann
Affiliations: Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany; Technical University of Munich, Munchen, Germany
Abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

Title: Comment Letters, Connected Investors, and Corporate Bond Issuance
Authors: Yi Ding, T. J. Wong, Ray Zhang, Tianyu Zhang
Affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Shenzhen 518172, China; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089; Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, British Columbia V5A 1S6, Canada
Abstract: Using a proprietary data set that documents corporate bond issuances in China, we find that bond regulators’ comment letters (CLs) on issuers’ public disclosures generally target opaque firms and reduce bond issuance success. We also find, however, that connected investors—financial institutions with prior business relationships with the issuers—purchase a relatively larger share of bond issuances from CL recipients than from non-CL recipients, and this greater participation contributes to overpricing. Further analysis shows that connected investors support CL recipients because they possess superior private information and obtain private benefits from their connections. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: R. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant 31-R833984]. Supplemental Material: The internet appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07607 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting.

Title: Competition for Customer Attention is Creating Oversupply Pockets in US Micromobility
Authors: Hale Erkan, Ashish Agarwal, Kumar Muthuraman, Ioannis Stamatopoulos
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, IROM, Austin, Texas, 78705, United States; The University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, IROM, Austin, Texas, United States; University of Texas at Austin Red McCombs School of Business, Information, Risk, and Operations Management, Austin, Texas, 78705, United States
Abstract: We present analytical and empirical arguments that competition over a nearly homogeneous service forces operators to oversupply scooters in urban centers. First, using deployment and ride data from operator APIs and city transportation departments, as well as telemetry data from one of the top three U.S. operators, we estimate average daily scooter utilization across nine major U.S. cities at 3.9%—half the 7.7% minimum utilization target set by transportation departments. Second, using a parsimonious game-theoretic model, we argue that if riders choose among available scooters roughly at random (e.g., the closest one), then in equilibrium all operators need to inflate their fleet sizes to preserve their market shares. Third, using granular data on riders’ choice sets and choices from Kansas City, MO, we provide evidence that these choices are indeed roughly random. Fourth, using our structurally estimated game-theoretic model, we find that in Kansas City, MO: (i) there is a 406% oversupply of scooters, (ii) the interaction between rider choice and competition accounts for 81% of this oversupply, and (iii) if the transportation department issued one more operator permit, oversupply would increase by an additional 82 pp. We conclude that transportation departments should be frugal with the number of permits they issue, and should welcome the consolidation of the scooter market.

Title: Learning Optimal Classification Trees Robust to Distribution Shifts
Authors: Nathan Lawrence Justin, Sina Aghaei, Andres Gomez, Phebe Vayanos
Affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089-0001, United States; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, United States; University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States; University of Southern California Viterbi School of Engineering, Industrial & Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States
Abstract: We consider the problem of learning classification trees that are robust to distribution shifts between training and testing/deployment data. This problem arises frequently in high stakes settings such as public health and social work where data is often collected using self-reported surveys which are highly sensitive to e.g., the framing of the questions, the time when and place where the survey is conducted, and the level of comfort the interviewee has in sharing information with the interviewer. We propose a method for learning optimal robust classification trees based on mixed-integer robust optimization technology. In particular, we demonstrate that the problem of learning an optimal robust tree can be cast as a single-stage mixed-integer robust optimization problem with a highly nonlinear and discontinuous objective. We reformulate this problem equivalently as a two-stage linear robust optimization problem for which we devise a tailored solution procedure based on constraint generation. We evaluate the performance of our approach on numerous publicly available datasets, and compare the performance to a regularized, non-robust optimal tree. We show an increase of up to 12.48 percentage points in worst-case accuracy and of up to 4.85 percentage points in average-case accuracy across several datasets and distribution shifts from using our robust solution in comparison to the non-robust one.

Title: Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming for Log-linear Autoregressive Uncertainty in the Right-hand Side
Authors: Christian Füllner, Steffen Rebennack
Affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Germany; Karlsruher Institute of Technology (KIT), Institute of Operations Research, Karlsruhe, Germany
Abstract: We consider the generation of cuts in stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) for multistage stochastic linear programming problems with stagewise dependent uncertainty in the right-hand side described by a nonlinear autoregressive process. We first derive cut formulas for the general nonlinear autoregressive process. For these general cuts, the computational tractability becomes a major challenge for SDDP-type algorithms. We are, however, able to develop tractable closed-form cut formulas for the special case of log-linear autoregressive processes. The obtained cuts are in general non-convex in the history of the stochastic process, but still linear in all decision variables, and thus can be directly incorporated into the subproblems in SDDP without compromising their linearity. If solvers do not allow for this, our formulas can be used to adapt the intercept of a given cut to a scenario at hand in a computationally tractable way. In this sense, cuts generated for one specific scenario are shared with other scenarios. Our findings are supported by a computational study of a hydrothermal scheduling problem, which demonstrates a favorable performance of our proposed version of SDDP compared to approaches from the literature.

Title: Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation
Authors: Chen Chen, Xuyuanda Qi
Affiliations: New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China
Abstract: When Sharing the Same Information Is Optimal Should a school advisor tailor recommendation letters to different employers or share the same information with everyone? Similar questions arise in start-up fundraising and biotech partnerships. In “Optimality of Public Persuasion for Single-Good Allocation,” Chen and Qi study how a sender can strategically disclose information when allocating an indivisible good to at most one self-interested receiver. The sender may send tailored private messages to individual receivers or publicly broadcast the same information to everyone. Surprisingly, the authors show that, when the sender has a known preference ordering over receivers, public persuasion is optimal even if receivers can subsequently communicate and share information. The optimal public mechanism can be derived from a simpler first-best allocation problem subject only to receivers’ participation constraints. The authors also develop a dual approach to characterize the structure of optimal mechanisms when the good’s characteristics are captured by a one-dimensional variable and all receivers’ utility functions are linear in this variable and reveal an intriguing decoupling structure.

Title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
Authors: Weixiao Huang, Carlos Morel Figueroa, Arjun Venat, Sarah E. Stanlick, Yunus D. Telliel, Alexander Teytelboym, Jennifer A. Pazour, Andrew C. Trapp
Affiliations: Business School, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180; Department of Computer Science, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Integrative and Global Studies, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Humanities & Arts, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, Massachusetts 01609; Department of Economics, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 3UQ, United Kingdom; and Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, New York 12180
Abstract: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

Title: Multicomponent biogas membrane separation by superstructure optimization
Authors: Bernardetta Addis, Veronica Piccialli, Christophe Castel
Abstract: This study addresses the challenge of membrane separation for biogas upgrading in a multicomponent system containing a small fraction of N 2 . The final product of the process is biomethane, which is the biogas after separation and purification, where all species in addition to methane have been removed. The minimal purity of CH 4 that allows transport and use is generally 98%. We aim to design a system that meets this purity requirement while maximizing biomethane recovery from the feed gas. To achieve this, we employ a superstructure optimization approach that balances performance with industrial feasibility and robustness. The problem is formulated as a Mixed Integer Non-Linear Programming (MINLP) model, incorporating cubic equality constraints derived from discretized differential equations governing membrane physics. Furthermore, the model allows to enforce industrial operability requirements (no small flows, reduced number of splits). Due to the difficulty of general solvers to tackle the resulting MINLP, we propose an ad-hoc solution procedure. After enumerating all viable industrial configurations, a global optimization algorithm determines the optimal design parameters and operating conditions to maximize recovery without compromising the purity threshold of 98% CH 4 . The advanced MEMSIC module is used for numerical simulation to evaluate the practical feasibility of optimized solutions. The numerical results highlight the increased complexity of the three-gas system compared to simpler two-gas scenarios, underscoring the need for sophisticated modeling and optimization techniques.

Title: Disagreement of disagreement
Authors: Christian L. Goulding, Campbell R. Harvey, Hrvoje Kurtović
Abstract: We show that leading investor disagreement proxies have near-zero cross-correlation – making disagreement pricing inferences challenging. We develop a frictionless model that generates overpricing from latent disagreement, jointly rationalizes major proxies, and generates new testable predictions. Equilibrium interrelationships motivate a new disagreement measure, DIS, which is more predictive of returns cross-sectionally than major proxies and more consistently predictive across macroeconomic regimes. We provide evidence that the friction-based channel of Miller (1977) and a frictionless mechanism coexist and are empirically separable. DIS also provides a micro-founded, disagreement-based account of the IVOL puzzle, absorbing IVOL’s predictability while revealing its regime and friction dependence.

Title: How do audit committee members' and audit partners' communication styles jointly influence client managers’ negotiation behavior?
Authors: Abhijit Das, Soon-Yeow Phang
Abstract: Auditor-client negotiations over contentious accounting issues can shape reported financial outcomes, yet little is known about how communication dynamics between audit committee (AC) members and auditors influence client negotiation behavior. We conduct an experiment in which experienced financial executives, assuming the role of chief financial officer, negotiate a disputed inventory obsolescence allowance with a simulated audit partner in the presence of an AC member; the AC member's distributive communication style (offensive vs. defensive) and the audit partner's reflective empathy (high vs. low) are manipulated between participants. Drawing on relational framing theory in interpersonal communication, we predict and find that a distributive-offensive AC communication style leads clients to establish their reporting positions and concede less to the auditor's proposed adjustment, unless it is accompanied by high reflective empathy from the audit partner, which neutralizes this resistance. This pattern emerges in the client's initial negotiation position and persists through the final negotiated allowance. Our findings suggest that auditors can use empathetic communication as a strategic tool to defuse the competitive posture that an assertive governance signal may provoke. Overall, our results provide insights into how AC members' and auditors' communication styles jointly shape client negotiation behavior, highlighting the importance of communication strategies in achieving effective audit negotiation outcomes.

Title: Training and productivity in micro-firms
Authors: Marco Rispoli, Federico Tamagni
Abstract: This paper examines the effect of training on productivity of micro-firms, defined in official statistics as firms with less than 10 employees. While training may represent a crucial mode of knowledge accumulation in micro-firms, which usually lack resources or structure to devote to formal innovation activities, the specificities of micro-businesses suggest that training may even be detrimental to productivity of this category of firms.
