Yet, the received wisdom that training should foster their productivity, as it does in larger firms, remains un-tested, mainly due to difficulties in previous literature to analyze micro-firms separately from the wider groups of small or small-medium enterprises. Exploiting a unique administrative panel dataset that records training expenses of a large sample of micro-firms located in three Italian regions, we address whether micro-firms which train enjoy a productivity premium vis-a-vis micro-firms that do not. Our main finding, controlling for endogeneity of training via Inverse Probability Weighted Regression Adjustment methods, combined with firm fixed-effects, is a positive and sizable average treatment effect of training, stable across a series of robustness checks and heterogeneity analysis.

Title: Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
Authors: Trent M. Davis, Yifei E. Chen, Wilma A. Bainbridge
Affiliations: Department of Psychology, University of Chicago; Institute for Mind and Biology, University of Chicago; Neuroscience Institute, University of Chicago
Abstract: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered—or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem’s predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

Title: Exploitation in the marketplace: A consumer behavior perspective
Authors: Jingxuan Liu, Vicki G. Morwitz
Affiliations: Columbia Business School Columbia University New York New York USA
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines exploitation in the marketplace from a consumer behavior perspective. We define marketplace exploitation as occurring when one party leverages structural and/or situational resource asymmetries to extract disproportionate value in ways that undermine fairness or autonomy, even when exchanges appear voluntary and mutually beneficial. We distinguish marketplace exploitation from related concepts including fairness, deception, and discrimination, arguing that it centers on the morally problematic use of contextual advantage. Adopting a dual lens, we develop conceptual frameworks for both firm‐to‐consumer exploitation (e.g., price gouging, dark patterns) and consumer‐to‐firm exploitation (e.g., free trial abuse, exploiting firm mistakes). These frameworks delineate how structural and situational asymmetries give rise to objective exploitative acts, when such acts are perceived as exploitative, and how they shape emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses. We synthesize a research agenda and outline methodological approaches for studying the antecedents, perceptions, and consequences of exploitation. This work contributes to consumer psychology by conceptualizing marketplace exploitation as both a subjective psychological experience and a strategic marketplace behavior, with implications for theory, policy, and ethical firm practices.

Title: New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new GenAI firms
Authors: Kathleen M. Eisenhardt, Xilan Zhang
Affiliations: Department of Management Science and Engineering Stanford University Stanford California USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics —Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.

Title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
Authors: Rahul Kapoor, Manav Raj
Affiliations: The Wharton School University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

Title: Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of AI ?
Authors: Christoph Zott, Raphael Amit
Affiliations: IESE Business School Barcelona Spain; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.

Title: Single machine optimistic bilevel scheduling problems with selection: State-of-the-art and new results
Authors: Vincent T’kindt, Alessandro Agnetis, Federico Della Croce
Abstract: We consider bilevel optimization for machine scheduling problems where two agents, the leader and the follower, take decisions on the same jobset. We survey the somewhat limited relevant literature, and thereafter we present a large set of new complexity results, focusing on single machine bilevel scheduling in the context of optimistic setting. Here, the leader acts first with the aim of selecting a subset of jobs to optimize his/her own objective function. Next, the follower schedules these selected jobs in order to optimize a given criterion. The optimistic setting is such that, among all his/her optimal solutions, the follower returns the one that is minimum for the leader’s objective function. We consider several basic scheduling criteria for both the leader and the follower and establish the complexity of the corresponding problems.

Title: Integrating response time and attention duration in Bayesian preference learning for multiple criteria decision aiding
Authors: Jiaxuan Jiang, Jiapeng Liu, Miłosz Kadziński, Xiuwu Liao, Jingyu Dong
Abstract: We propose a multiple criteria Bayesian preference learning framework incorporating behavioral cues for decision aiding. The framework jointly considers pairwise comparisons, response time, and criterion-level attention duration as complementary sources of information for representing preferences. Unlike traditional multiple criteria decision aiding methods that rely solely on holistic judgments, the approach treats behavioral signals as conditionally informative observations linked to a preference representation constructed within a given decision context. An additive value function is adopted, and posterior inference over individual preferences is performed using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We validate the approach through a laboratory experiment involving 102 participants selecting mobile phone contracts, using a dedicated application with time-, eye-, and mouse-tracking. Results indicate that incorporating behavioral cues leads to improved out-of-sample agreement with subsequently elicited judgments, compared to baseline methods that rely solely on pairwise comparisons. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a computational approach to integrating diverse behavioral data into preference elicitation and inference, with the potential to support more coherent and robust decision aiding in the multiple criteria decision aiding context.

Title: A two-stage optimization framework for maintenance depot location and technician allocation in urban rail transit systems
Authors: Guojian Hu, Yu Zheng, Siqi Qiu
Abstract: The strategic configuration of maintenance resources is essential for ensuring the efficiency and reliability of urban rail transit systems, requiring coordinated decisions on depot location and technician capacity allocation. However, existing studies have paid limited attention to the joint consideration of heterogeneous maintenance demand, response efficiency, and service-capacity adequacy under stochastic demand. To address these gaps, this study develops a two-stage optimization framework for maintenance resource sharing in urban rail transit networks. In the first stage, a depot location model is formulated to minimize the weighted maintenance response distance, incorporating heterogeneous station-level maintenance demand. In the second stage, a technician allocation model, formulated in both aggregate-capacity and generalized skill-compatible forms, maximizes system reliability subject to workforce budget constraints, enabling the framework to accommodate different levels of data granularity. For the aggregate-data computational implementation, a local search-based heuristic and a marginal benefit-based greedy algorithm are developed for the location and allocation models, respectively, while an exact integer linear programming reformulation provides allocation benchmarks. Experiments on networks derived from the Shanghai Metro show that the location heuristic obtains optimal or near-optimal layouts and the allocation algorithm matches the exact benchmark objective values in all tested instances. The combined heuristic process also substantially reduces total computation time relative to exact optimization. Sensitivity analysis reveals diminishing marginal benefits from depot and technician investments. It further shows that, under a limited workforce budget, increasing the number of depots improves response efficiency but may reduce system reliability because of capacity dilution.

Title: Repricing the green transition: market reactions to COP26 among MNCs diversified in pollution havens
Authors: Noman Shaheer, Kijong Kim, Fanshu Li, Rui Yang, En Xie
Abstract: Este estudio examina cómo el endurecimiento de las regulaciones ambientales globales afecta la valoración de mercado de las corporaciones multinacionales (MNCs) diversificadas en refugios de contaminación. Conceptualizamos la diversificación internacional en refugios de contaminación (ID-PH, por sus siglas en inglés) como una forma distintiva de diversificación geográfica mediante la cual las multinacionales han aprovechado las diferencias entre países en materia de regulación ambiental para obtener ventajas de costos. Sin embargo, la creciente atención internacional a los estándares ambientales puede redefinir el valor estratégico de la diversificación internacional en refugios de contaminación al amplificar los costos asociados al cumplimiento normativo, desafiando a las multinacionalesa adaptarse a las crecientes expectativas de los inversionistas en cuanto a sostenibilidad ambiental. Aprovechando la Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre el Cambio Climático de Glasgow de 2021 (COP26) como un choque exógeno de política global que transformó compromisos climáticos voluntarios en compromisos internacionales vinculantes, encontramos que las multinacionales con una mayor exposición a la diversificación internacional en refugios de contaminación experimentaron rendimientos anormales de las acciones significativamente más negativos tras la COP26. No obstante, las multinacionales que poseían sólidas capacidades ambientales y digitales pudieron mitigar la caída en su valoración, demostrando una capacidad de adaptación superior bajo un mayor escrutinio regulatorio. Al integrar la heterogeneidad de las políticas ambientales en la lógica de la diversificación internacional, este estudio contribuye a comprender cómo los choques de política global redefinen la valoración de las carteras internacionales de las multinacionales Estos hallazgos también ofrecen implicaciones prácticas para directivos y formuladores de políticas públicas, al demostrar que las inversiones en capacidades ambientales y digitales pueden ayudar a las multinacionales a afrontar de manera resiliente las transiciones regulatorias relacionadas con el cambio climático. Cette recherche examine comment le durcissement des réglementations environnementales mondiales influe sur la valorisation boursière des entreprises multinationales (Multinational Corporations - MNCs) diversifiées à travers les paradis de pollution. Nous conceptualisons la diversification internationale à travers les paradis de pollution (International Diversification across Pollution Havens - ID-PH) comme une forme distinctive de diversification géographique par laquelle les MNCs ont exploité les différences entre pays en matière de réglementation environnementale pour obtenir des avantages en termes de coûts. Cependant, l'attention croissante portée aux normes environnementales à l'échelle internationale pourrait redéfinir la valeur stratégique de l’ID-PH en amplifiant les charges liées à la mise en conformité, ce qui obligerait les MNCs à s'adapter aux attentes accrues des investisseurs en matière de durabilité environnementale. En utilisant la Conférence de Glasgow sur le climat de 2021 (COP26) comme un choc politique mondial exogène ayant transformé les engagements climatiques volontaires en engagements internationaux contraignants, nous constatons que les MNCs ayant un degré plus élevé d’ID-PH ont enregistré des rendements boursiers anormaux nettement plus négatifs après la COP26. Néanmoins, les MNCs dotées de solides capacités environnementales et numériques ont réussi à atténuer la baisse de leur valorisation, démontrant ainsi une capacité d'adaptation supérieure dans un contexte de surveillance réglementaire accrue. En intégrant l'hétérogénéité des politiques environnementales dans la logique de la diversification internationale, cette recherche approfondit la compréhension de la manière dont les chocs politiques mondiaux redéfinissent la valorisation des portefeuilles transnationaux des MNCs.

Title: Buying Data from Consumers: The Impact of Monitoring in U.S. Auto Insurance
Authors: Yizhou Jin, Shoshana Vasserman

Title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Impact of Immigration: Evidence from German Establishments
Authors: Agostina Brinatti, Nicolas Morales

Title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
Authors: John Gallemore, Vincent Giese
Affiliations: University of North Carolina; University of Mannheim
Abstract: ABSTRACT We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

Title: Would a Balanced PCAOB Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
Authors: Yoon Ju Kang, M. David Piercey
Affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst Amherst Massachusetts USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

Title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
Authors: Tobias J. Moskowitz, Chase P. Ross, Sharon Y. Ross, Kaushik Vasudevan
Abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

Title: Toward a (More) Comprehensive CPA Framework: A Reply to “Beyond Statically Motivated, Rational, and Atomistic Actors”
Authors: Pouyan Tabasi-Nejad, Yuval Deutsch
Affiliations: University of Manitoba; York University

Title: Organizational Zemblanity: How Organizational Learning Can Reinforce Rigidity, Error, and Misalignment
Authors: Marco Balzano, Christian Busch, Thomas Roulet
Affiliations: University of Trieste; University of Southern California; University of Cambridge
Abstract: Organizational learning can help organizations improve and adapt, but it can also reinforce error and misalignment. These negative outcomes are often interpreted as implementation problems or as signs of incomplete learning. We instead examine the possibility that dysfunction can arise from learning processes themselves, even when those processes operate as intended. We review 290 articles to identify recurring assumptions in the literature and the conditions under which they do not hold. We then identify three mechanisms that can turn learning systems into sources of rigidity and misalignment, and conceptualize the self-reinforcing trajectory produced by their interaction as learning-based organizational zemblanity. Our review shows how organizational learning can generate both adaptive and dysfunctional trajectories and outlines a research agenda on identifying and interrupting negative learning trajectories.

Title: Charitable capital allocation: Evidence from private foundations
Authors: Zhongjin (Gene) Lu, Steven Malliaris
Abstract: We examine how private foundations allocate charitable capital in response to recipient need. Using financial shocks to peer foundations (who fund the same recipients), we isolate exogenous changes in the marginal value of grants. Foundations respond to need by reallocating grants across recipients, particularly for scientific causes and longer donor–recipient relationships. However, their annual grantmaking budgets show little intertemporal flexibility, instead prioritizing capital preservation. Among governance characteristics, founder involvement predicts both cross-sectional responsiveness and intertemporal conservatism. Our findings highlight a tension: founders’ charitable intent supports effective allocation, but their inclination toward capital preservation can hinder impact maximization.

Title: Unemployment in later life: The effects of a job search skills training intervention and development orientations on job search and reemployment of older job seekers.
Authors: Sarah M. van den Hee, Edwin A. J. van Hooft, Greet Van Hoye, Barbara Nevicka
Abstract: Late-career unemployment has a demonstrated negative impact on individuals and society. Yet little is known about the mechanisms through which policy programs operate to support older unemployed individuals in finding reemployment. The present study aimed to provide more insight into how a job search skills training program facilitates older job seekers in their reemployment process and who benefits most from the program. Using a two-group field experimental design among 4,625 unemployed job seekers aged over 50, we examined the effects of the job search skills training intervention on participants' job search knowledge and self-efficacy, job search behaviors, and reemployment status and speed. In addition, the study examined whether the effects of job search skills training on job search knowledge and self-efficacy depend on older job seekers' development orientations (i.e., future time perspective and learning goal orientation). Job search skills training was found to increase older job seekers' job search knowledge and self-efficacy, and in turn their job search process quality, which then enhanced their chances and speed of finding reemployment. The positive effects of job search skills training on job search knowledge and self-efficacy appeared to be stronger for older job seekers with lower development orientations. The current findings advance training and job search theory by uncovering the explanatory mechanisms of a job search skills training program and by showing that individual attributes influence learning outcomes. Our findings also have important implications for the design, implementation, and evaluation of future policy programs aimed at older unemployed individuals and career counseling practice. Title: (Re)Entering the workforce after imprisonment: A new perspective on voluntary disclosure of criminal history and job-search assistance.
Authors: Lawrence Houston, Brett H. Neely, Timothy G. Kundro, Horatio D. Traylor
Abstract: = 493). Our results contribute to the theory on the reputational implications of criminal records, impression management, and employment discrimination. Additionally, our findings have implications for policies and practices intended to promote successful reintegration. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Roadblocks: Evaluating the impact of fines-related driver’s license suspension on work-related outcomes for socioeconomically disadvantaged workers.
Authors: Maura J. Mills, Matthew J. Dolliver, Russell A. Matthews, Leah Nelson, Peter A. Jones, Marshall L. White
Abstract: = 879), evidencing a positive association between license suspension and unemployment, and indicating that this relationship is mediated by compromised access to transportation. License suspension was also positively associated with turning toward the informal shadow economy for employment, with some individuals reporting turning to sex work and crime to make ends meet. Data bore out a number of employment- and well-being-related consequences of nonpayment policies, and suggested that effects may function differentially by race, with Black individuals experiencing disproportionately negative effects. In Study 2, archival data indicated that enforcement of license suspensions is likely to result in a net loss to state revenue, incentivizing policy revision. Collectively, our data suggest that fine and fee imposition, and associated driver's license suspension, are likely to have a number of negative effects for individuals, employers, and society alike. We offer policy and practice implications related to reevaluating license suspension for nonpayment of court-ordered legal financial obligations. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: The effects of food insecurity on work outcomes.
Authors: Jason H. Moy, Ussama Ahmad Khan, Wei Jee Ong, Christopher M. Barnes
Abstract: Food insecurity-insufficient access to safe and nutritious foods-is one of the most crucial societal grand challenges the world faces today. It affects 2.3 billion people globally, and addressing it is one of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals of 2030 (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations et al., 2025). Despite its prevalence and importance, the field of applied psychology has ignored this problem with the implicit assumption that food insecurity is not an issue relevant to the workplace. Contrary to this view, we hypothesize and demonstrate that food insecurity is detrimental to the three core work outcomes: task performance, work engagement, and organizational citizenship behaviors. To test our hypotheses, we employed a multimethod design across three empirical studies: (a) an experimental recall study, (b) a within-person diary study, and (c) a field experiment. Our findings consistently demonstrate that food insecurity leads to higher anxiety, which subsequently has a negative effect on task performance, work engagement, and organizational citizenship behavior. In our field experiment, we further demonstrated that providing food to those experiencing food insecurity can improve work outcomes. This research highlights that food insecurity is a significant issue with important implications for the workplace that requires greater attention from both researchers and business leaders. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Family socioeconomic status and job search: Pathways to job quality improvement for young adults without college degrees.
Authors: Le Zhou, Borbala Csillag, Connie R. Wanberg, Xuan Liu, Abdifatah A. Ali
Abstract: Improving job quality through job transitions is crucial in early adulthood. However, young adults without college degrees, particularly those from lower socioeconomic status (SES) families, can struggle to break out of lower quality jobs. Integrating socioeconomic and psychological perspectives, this research examines how family SES impacts job quality improvement through job search among young adults without college degrees when they transition from one job to another. We develop and test a model that explicates how family SES influences job quality improvement through constraints and resources for job search and self-regulated job search processes. Partnering with a Midwest state government agency, we collected data from young job seekers without college degrees through four longitudinal surveys over 6 months. Our findings revealed that job seekers from lower (vs. higher) SES families faced more basic needs constraints and had fewer college degree holders in their job search networks. These factors, in turn, influenced job seekers' wage increase goals and their job search metacognition. We also found that job seekers with higher wage increase goals achieved larger wage improvement between their previous and new jobs, and those who engaged in more job search metacognition were more likely to secure improvements in benefits, find new jobs with promotion opportunities, and perceive improvements in working conditions. These findings extend the literature on job quality, job search, socioeconomic mobility, and inequality and provide practical implications for multiple stakeholder groups. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: The cost of coping with infertility: Extending theory on stressor appraisal.
Authors: Natasha Poularikas, Alexiss Jeffers, Seoin Yoon, Joel Koopman, Nikolaos Dimotakis
Abstract: = 192]), we triangulate tests of our hypotheses and find support for our arguments. We discuss implications for transactional stress theory and illustrate how scholars can expand their conceptualization of coping to consider its potential toxicity. We further call attention to the critical societal and public policy implications of our findings, and we provide a roadmap with clear and actionable solutions. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: How policy implementation impacts employee suffering at work: An exploration of medical leaves of absence.
Authors: Liza Y. Barnes, Christina N. Lacerenza, Ashley E. Hardin
Abstract: Existing work offers rich theory on how work-life policies increase autonomy and balance and reduce work-life conflict. However, in moments when life is not merely imbalanced but severely upended, such as during times of severe illness or injury, this focus on balance and autonomy may be less relevant. We explore these moments of suffering by examining an often-overlooked work-life policy: medical leaves of absence. Through a qualitative grounded theory approach, we draw on the perspectives of 48 individuals (leave-takers and leave coordinators) to offer a comprehensive understanding of how medical leave policy implementation influences employee suffering at work. We first shed light on the elements of health-related suffering in the workplace and then introduce a healing-centered implementation approach. This dedicated examination of medical leave expands theoretical conversations by situating medical leave under a distinct category of policies, suffering-related policies. For these policies, suffering is the driver of policy use, and healing is a critical outcome for determining policy effectiveness. We also build a specific framework for concretely understanding the multidimensional nature of suffering in the workplace, which enables us to illuminate more precise implementation techniques that explicitly address each of the four elements of suffering in ways that existing constructs do not. Finally, we offer recommendations for how policy is written and implemented: offering paid medical leave, separating family and medical leave, eliminating the 1-year eligibility period, employing leave coordinators, cross-training employees to prepare for sudden outages, and offering additional suffering-related policies. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Industrial-organizational science that matters: Social impact and policy implications in the Journal of Applied Psychology.
Authors: Wendy J. Casper, Stephanie Brooke Escudero, Lillian T. Eby, Tianjun Sun, Talya N. Bauer, Bryan D. Edwards, Allison S. Gabriel, Jia Jasmine Hu

Title: The New Rules of Brand Visibility in AI Search
Authors: Shahper Richter, Alla Lvovich, Wietske Van Osch, Alex Richter
Abstract: As LLM-driven search grows, brands are facing two distinct challenges: visibility and accuracy. For AI search, SEO is now entwined with GEO, generative engine optimization. As zero-click LLM responses replace direct links on search result pages, new metrics are replacing traditional traffic analytics. New research suggests ways leaders can ensure that their brands become more visible, more accurately represented, and more competitively positioned over time.

Title: Increased scheduling flexibility for multi-league sports scheduling
Authors: Miao Li, David Van Bulck, Dries Goossens
Abstract: The multi-league sports scheduling problem involves scheduling a double round-robin tournament for each league, with the goal of minimizing venue capacity violations that may occur when teams from different leagues share the same venue. Due to the large number of matches that must be considered simultaneously, the problem is known to be particularly challenging, and hence several simplifying assumptions have been proposed in the literature and in practice. This paper examines the potential reduction in venue capacity violations by relaxing these assumptions and thereby introducing more scheduling flexibility. In particular, we relax the common assumption that a feasible home away pattern set must be given, allow that leagues are interrupted once started, and consider schedules that use more rounds than strictly needed (i.e. time-relaxed schedules). To overcome the computational challenges that come with increased scheduling flexibility, we propose an improved integer programming formulation as well as a Benders’ decomposition approach based on first-break-then-schedule. We compute (near) optimal solutions for instances with up to ten leagues. Our computational experiments show that introducing interruptions at the league level results in an average reduction of venue capacity violations of about 30%, whereas introducing home away pattern set flexibility results in an average reduction of up to 60%. Time-relaxed scheduling eliminates venue capacity violations almost entirely, offering a viable and substantially cheaper alternative to investing in additional infrastructure.

Title: Trustworthy AI and risk-aware planning for global supply chains: A probabilistic framework with knowledge graph constraints
Authors: Malka N. Halgamuge, Babak Abbasi, Vinh Thai, Kamrul Ahsan, Vanessa Cooper, Matthew Warren
Abstract: Global artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled supply chains (SCs) face AI-induced risks, such as bias in AI-driven decisions and the resulting erosion of trust. Despite extensive research on mitigation of AI-related risks using digital twins, Bayesian risk models, and graph optimization in isolation, the literature lacks a unified framework for jointly modelling and mitigating interconnected AI-induced risks. To this end, we propose an integrated framework underpinned by a knowledge-graph (KG)-constrained generative probabilistic planning approach that incorporates a risk-aware reward function and supply-chain trust propagation while leveraging a digital twin for cascading-failure stress testing. Using DataCo data comprising 180,519 transactions across 43 countries, we compare the proposed framework against six benchmarks: static, Bayesian, digital-twin, pure reinforcement learning (RL), component-isolation RL, and robust risk-averse. The results show that the proposed approach delivers the lowest overall weighted objective and lowest critical-failure rate across all evaluated policies. The findings offer three managerial insights: (i) adaptive, probabilistic risk-mitigation approaches outperform fixed rules as AI-driven risk and trust conditions shift in global supply chains; (ii) incorporating trust into decision rules helps managers decide when AI actions can proceed automatically and when human review is required; and (iii) monitoring disparity indicators, such as differences in delivery-risk exposure across regions or customer groups, allows fairness considerations to be assessed alongside operational performance.

Title: The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice
Authors: Steffen Altmann, Anita M Glenny, Robert Mahlstedt, Alexander Sebald
Affiliations: University of Würzburg, Germany; University of Copenhagen and IZA@LISER , Denmark; Danish Agency for Labor Market and Recruitment (STAR) , Denmark; University of Copenhagen and IZA@LISER; Copenhagen Business School , Denmark
Abstract: Abstract We study how online job search advice affects job search behaviour and labour market outcomes of unemployed workers. In a large-scale field experiment embedded in the online platform of the Danish public employment service, we provide job seekers with vacancy information and occupational recommendations. Using a two-stage randomized design with regionally varying treatment intensities, we examine both direct effects of advice and treatment spillovers. We find that advice significantly increases employment and earnings when provided to a limited share of job seekers. As treatment intensity rises, these effects diminish and eventually disappear. The decline is driven by negative spillovers among treated job seekers, consistent with increased congestion in the occupations towards which job seekers redirect their search. Spillover effects on untreated job seekers are heterogeneous and depend on how advice alters occupation-specific competition in local labour markets.

Title: The effect of the mandatory disclosure of corporate tax returns on reporting bias
Authors: Eric J. Allen, Henry L. Friedman, Aydin Uysal
Affiliations: UC Riverside; UCLA Anderson School of Management; Former Director of Equity Research at the Charles Schwab Corp. Deceased.
Abstract: ABSTRACT How do investor reactions to the mandatory disclosure of firm tax information influence managers' reporting choices? To answer this question, we build a structural model of reporting bias, which we test with a unique data set of Turkish firms that have been mandated to publicly disclose their tax returns since 2009. We find that both book and tax income numbers are informative to investors. Structural estimates are consistent with disclosure of the tax report reducing both market incentives to manage book earnings and investor uncertainty about underlying firm value. Tax disclosure is associated with higher reported tax income, though the increase is not statistically significant. Counterfactual estimates suggest that book‐tax‐conformity could change financial and tax reporting biases, but lead to a lower quality information environment relative to the separate disclosure of book and tax reports.

Title: Can Facebook Ads Prevent Malaria? Two Field Experiments in India
Authors: Dante Donati, Nandan Rao, Victor Orozco-Olvera, Ana Maria Muñoz Boudet
Affiliations: Columbia Business School, New York, New York 10027; Virtual Lab and Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, Philomath, Oregon 97370; Development Impact Group, The World Bank, Washington, District of Columbia 20433; Gender Department, The World Bank, Washington, District of Columbia 20433
Abstract: Two field experiments evaluate a nationwide Facebook malaria prevention campaign in India, finding effects concentrated in urban, more advantaged populations.

Title: From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market
Authors: Stephen J. Anderson, Pradeep K. Chintagunta, Rupali Kaul, Naufel J. Vilcassim
Affiliations: Mays Business School, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas 77843; Booth School of Business, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; INSEAD, Singapore 138676; London School of Economics and Political Science, London WC2A 2AE, United Kingdom
Abstract: Using a field experiment with 550 Rwandan firms, we show marketing analytics causally enhances entrepreneurs’ cognition and raises firm sales and profits.

Title: The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
Authors: Stijn Bruers, Erwin Ooghe, Erik Schokkaert
Affiliations: Department of Economics, KU Leuven, 3000 Leuven, Belgium; and CESifo, 81679 Munich, Germany
Abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and two coupons for a plasma donation. Informing donors about the existing rewards increases plasma donations by 4.6% during the nine-month information period, although this effect fades with repeated reminders. Rewarding plasma donors with an extra coupon raises plasma donations by an additional 7.1% during the six-month reward period; this effect grows during the reward period but disappears immediately afterward. We also document a substitution effect; the plasma reward reduces blood donations by 3.3%. Survey evidence suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts eliciting reciprocity and that our findings may extend to volunteering decisions more broadly. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, Behavioral Economics and Decision Analysis. Funding: This paper is based on research funded by the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders; the content reflects solely the views of the authors and not those of the Red Cross. Title: Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems
Authors: Benjamin Legros
Affiliations: SKEMA Business School, Université Côte d’Azur, 92150 Paris, France

Title: Heterogeneous beliefs, asset prices, and business cycles
Authors: Saki Bigio, Dejanir Silva, Eduardo Zilberman
Abstract: We develop a complete-market production economy in which heterogeneous beliefs about productivity growth affect both asset prices and real activity. Firms must hire workers before productivity is realized, so operating leverage increases the exposure of profits to productivity risk. Because the firm’s discount factor depends on a wealth-weighted aggregation of investor beliefs, shifts in optimism compress risk premia and raise employment, while reversals trigger contractions. This mechanism generates an equilibrium feedback between asset prices, hiring, and risk exposure. A taxonomy of belief systems shows that only extrapolative beliefs produce amplification and endogenous risk build-up. Disciplined by survey expectations, the model jointly matches key asset-pricing, trading-volume, and business-cycle moments.

Title: Global Working Hours
Authors: Amory Gethin, Emmanuel Saez
Affiliations: Development Research Group, World Bank; University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: Abstract This article uses labor force surveys from 160 countries to build a new microdatabase on hours worked covering 97% of the world population in cross section. We also construct time series spanning over 20 years in 86 countries. Hours worked per adult slightly decline with GDP per capita but are weakly correlated with development overall. Hours worked by the young (aged 15–19) and elderly (aged 60+) fall with development, driven entirely by growing school attendance and public pension coverage. Hours worked among prime-age adults (aged 20–59) are stable with development but undergo a great gender reshuffling: falling hours per male worker have been exactly offset by increases in female labor force participation in many countries. Labor income taxes are strongly negatively related to hours worked across countries. This correlation is attenuated when controlling for social spending and disappears when further controlling for working hours regulations. Both social spending and working hours regulations are associated with lower hours worked.

Title: What Jobs Come to Mind? Stereotypes About Fields of Study
Authors: John J Conlon, Dev Patel
Affiliations: The Ohio State University; Brown University
Abstract: Abstract We test for stereotyping—the exaggeration of representative traits—in a high-stakes economic environment. Using surveys administered among undergraduates at the Ohio State University as well as large-scale nationally representative data, we measure how U.S. first-year students perceive the relationship between college majors and occupations. We show that students greatly overestimate the likelihood that majors lead to their representative jobs (e.g., counselor for psychology, journalist for journalism). Using an implicit association test, we show that students associate majors with their representative careers and that these associations strongly predict belief biases, in line with a stereotyping mechanism. A simple equilibrium model of the labor market predicts that stereotyping reduces welfare by increasing misallocation, which we corroborate with correlational evidence on job/major mismatch. In a field experiment, we test a light-touch policy to reduce stereotyping and find significant effects on students’ intentions about what to study as well as the classes and majors they enroll in.

Title: Beliefs About the Economy Are Excessively Sensitive to Household-Level Shocks: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
Authors: Dmitry Taubinsky, Luigi Butera, Matteo Saccarola, Chen Lian
Affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, and National Bureau of Economic Research; Copenhagen Business School; University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: Abstract We study how people’s beliefs about the economy covary with household-level events, using a unique link between Danish administrative data and a large-scale survey of consumer expectations. We find that compared to actual inflation, people’s inflation forecasts covary much more strongly (and negatively) with both recently realized household income changes and measures of expected future household income changes. We formally establish that these findings are stark deviations from the Bayesian rational expectations benchmark. Similar results hold for perceptions of past inflation (backcasts), suggesting that imperfect recall is a key mechanism for biased forecasts. Building on this, a series of additional tests, some of which use data on adverse health events, suggests that the forecast biases are at least partly due to affect-cued recall. That is, negative (positive) household-level events cue negative (positive) recollections, which lead to pessimistic (optimistic) forecasts.

Title: In Their Shoes: Empathy Through Information
Authors: Marianne Andries, Leonardo Bursztyn, Thomas Chaney, Milena Djourelova, Alex Imas
Affiliations: University of Southern California, United States; and Centre for Economic Policy and Research; University of Chicago and National Bureau of Economic Research; University of Southern California and National Bureau of Economic Research, United States; and CESifo; University of Chicago Booth School of Business and National Bureau of Economic Research
Abstract: Abstract We explore the mechanics of empathy. We show that information about an outgroup can activate and magnify empathy when presented in conjunction with an experience simulating their struggles. This response increases the willingness to help the struggling group. We provide evidence for this effect in an immersive virtual reality experiment where participants (witnesses) experience a simulation of the struggle of unauthorized migrants (protagonists), then replicate these results in a series of controlled lab experiments. We show that information enhances the witnesses’ empathetic response and drives them to engage in more prosocial behavior when it increases their perceived interpersonal similarity, or relatability to the protagonist—an effect we trace to attention: eye-tracking data reveal that information provision concentrates witnesses’ gaze on the struggles of the protagonist instead of searching through peripheral elements of the scene. Conversely, only information packages that strengthen perceived relatability—an effect that can vary across subgroups with heterogeneous attributes—magnify empathy. Together, our evidence suggests that the ability to put oneself in the shoes of another person or group can be enhanced by activating empathy through simple, targeted, information provision.

Title: Who Pays for Unions?
Authors: Samuel Dodini, Anna Stansbury, Alexander Willén
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas; MIT Sloan School of Management; Norwegian School of Economics
Abstract: Abstract If unions raise worker wages, who pays? We provide a comprehensive assessment of firm responses to increased unionization, using changes in the tax deductibility of union dues in Norway as a quasi-exogenous source of variation in firm-level union density. In the average private sector firm, higher union density raises labor costs and leads firms to contract employment and production, lowering profits without increasing the labor share. The incidence is shared: consumers bear part of the cost through higher prices, shareholders through lower profits, and the remainder is offset by productivity improvements. The total wage bill falls, with losses concentrated among less attached “outsider” workers. Firm responses vary systematically by the degree of market competition. In manufacturing, where firms operate in less competitive product and labor markets, the response is reversed: the average firm expands employment and production, reduces labor markdowns, and does not experience profit declines. Instead, higher labor costs are largely passed on to consumers through higher prices, with the remainder offset by productivity gains. Workers benefit as both wages and employment rise. These patterns suggest that unions can offset employer monopsony power and that firm responses—and therefore who ultimately bears the cost—depend importantly on market structure. Overall, unionization in this setting primarily redistributes from consumers rather than shareholders and has effects that differ sharply across firms, including a reallocation toward larger and more productive firms. We rationalize these patterns using a partial-equilibrium model of union bargaining with product- and labor-market power.

Title: Can green innovations enhance competitive advantage?
Authors: The Hoa Mai, Satheesh Seenivasan, David Sugianto Lie, Dinesh K. Gauri
Abstract: Abstract Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: Optimization under uncertainty for energy infrastructure planning: A synthesis of methods, tools, and open challenges
Authors: Rahman Khorramfar, Aron Brenner, Lara Booth, Ana Rivera, Ruaridh Macdonald, Priya Donti, Saurabh Amin
Abstract: Energy infrastructure planning under uncertainty has become increasingly complex as electrification, interdependence between energy carriers, decarbonization, and extreme weather events reshape long-term investment decisions. This paper surveys recent advances at the intersection of generation and transmission expansion, and optimization under uncertainty, with a focus on stochastic programming, robust optimization, and distributionally robust optimization. We then categorize modeling needs along the axes of modeling fidelity, uncertainty characterization, and solution methods to identify dominant modeling features and trace research gaps. We further examine emerging directions at the interface of optimization and machine learning, including forecasting, scenario generation, and learned surrogates and discuss how these tools can be embedded within infrastructure planning models.

Title: Trust builder or defensive moat? Blockchain adoption and incentive mechanisms in a food supply chain with asymmetric competition
Authors: Xiaofei Gao, Bin Liu, Chunqing Chang
Abstract: Recurring food safety incidents have severely eroded consumer trust. While blockchain may mitigate this problem, its strategic adoption under asymmetric competition remains underexplored. We develop a three-stage game-theoretic model with an e-commerce platform and two asymmetric manufacturers to investigate adoption equilibria, platform preferences, and welfare effects. Our analysis shows that blockchain-enabled credible traceability can create a trust-based differentiation opportunity for the weaker manufacturer. Under the baseline conditions, this opportunity is endogenously covered because the dominant manufacturer also has an incentive to adopt, so weaker-manufacturer-only adoption does not survive on the equilibrium path. Within a stricter parameter region, universal adoption emerges even though both manufacturers earn higher profits under mutual non-adoption; we refer to this outcome as the Defensive Transparency Paradox. Weaker-manufacturer-only adoption can re-emerge under specific departures from the baseline assumptions. We also uncover an incentive misalignment between manufacturers and the platform and show that a conditional subsidy mechanism can reshape equilibrium adoption and surplus allocation. Finally, within the common feasible region, universal adoption maximizes consumer surplus, whereas dominant-manufacturer-only adoption can yield higher total welfare over an intermediate range of implementation costs.

Title: Competing digital money
Authors: Jon Frost, Jean-Charles Rochet, Hyun Song Shin, Marianne Verdier
Affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) , Basel; Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAF) , Cambridge; Toulouse School of Economics (TSE) , Toulouse; Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, CRED (TEPP), Paris, France
Abstract: Abstract We study competition between two payment instruments: bank deposits and digital platform tokens. Using a Hotelling model that integrates the theory of two-sided markets and payment economics, we assess how this competition is affected by a public payment infrastructure that makes private payment instruments interoperable. We show that interoperability, whether implemented as a fast payment system or a central bank digital currency, may eliminate payment access exclusion and increase trade volumes and social welfare, but at the cost of some disintermediation. When new payment service providers (PSPs) enter and compete for consumers, they soften competition for merchants: incumbent intermediaries then charge merchants higher fees and earn higher profits. This contrasts with the entry of PSPs on the merchant side, which instead disciplines incumbent fees.

Title: The judgment-based approach to entrepreneurship: The uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus
Authors: Nicolai J. Foss, Peter G. Klein, Carmen Elena Dorobat, Matthew McCaffrey, Mark D. Packard
Abstract: The judgment-based approach (JBA) has emerged as an important contemporary perspective in management and entrepreneurship research. The JBA offers a distinctive theoretical account of entrepreneurship, centered on the formation and implementation of subjective theories of value creation under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, which highlights resource ownership, heterogeneous capital structure, organization and the firm, institutions, uncertainty, and the overarching need to appraise and coordinate all these factors using judgment. We present and develop the JBA by articulating the uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus, in which the joint presence of fundamental uncertainty and heterogeneous resources gives rise to the need for entrepreneurial judgment and makes its exercise economically consequential. Because judgment is subjective, tacit, and difficult to communicate or contract upon, entrepreneurs must rely on ownership and residual control rights to create value, linking judgment to the combination and deployment of resources, profit and loss, and organizational structure. The purpose of this article is threefold. First, we provide a systematic statement of the JBA as a theoretical framework, clarifying its core constructs, causal mechanisms, and domain of application. Second, we engage with key critiques and distinguish the JBA from related approaches, including opportunity-based, effectuation, and bricolage perspectives. Third, we outline directions for future research that build on the JBA's emphasis on judgment, ownership, and the organization and deployment of heterogeneous resources under uncertainty. By integrating these elements, we position the JBA as a coherent and distinctive theory of entrepreneurship with broad implications for research in management, organization, and strategy.

Title: Building Better Information: Reporting Technology, Internal Information Frictions, and Investment Efficiency
Authors: Philip G. Berger, Feng Li, Lisa Yao Liu, M. H. Franco Wong
Affiliations: The University of Chicago; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Columbia University; University of California, Irvine
Abstract: ABSTRACT We assess how firms use spending on reporting infrastructure to improve managerial reporting quality (MRQ) and whether doing so improves investment efficiency. Using the Sarbanes-Oxley Act’s internal control provisions (SOX 404) as a shock to MRQ demand, we find that treated firms increase reporting infrastructure spending, including for information technology and communications. We next examine variation across segments in the benefits and costs of improving reporting infrastructure. Segments increase spending more when facing larger internal moral hazard frictions and when they are less likely to have voluntarily improved MRQ before SOX (including segments insulated from competition, facing difficulty obtaining enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, or lacking internal control personnel). Finally, we find that treated firms improve investment efficiency post-SOX 404, with larger gains among firms with higher spending on reporting infrastructure. Our findings indicate that regulatory mandates can improve investment efficiency by inducing reporting infrastructure improvements that enhance MRQ. JEL Classifications: D83; G15; G18; G38; L15; M41; M42.

Title: Social Media Toxicity and Capital Markets
Authors: Elizabeth Blankespoor, Jedson Pinto, Kirti Sinha
Affiliations: University of Washington; The University of Texas at Dallas
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper asks about the existence, determinants, and implications of toxic content in financial social media. Using machine learning algorithms to measure toxicity in Seeking Alpha articles and comments, we find measurable toxicity concentrated primarily in user-generated comments rather than articles. Comment toxicity is greater for firms with more investor attention or uncertainty. We document three key results about toxicity in capital markets. First, toxicity displays a feedback loop in platform participation: past toxicity is associated with more future toxic contributors for a given firm. Second, firms receiving more toxic comments have greater retail trading volume but less informative retail trades, especially when comments disagree. Third, toxicity is associated with slower price discovery around earnings announcements. Our findings suggest that financial social media toxicity relates to both user behavior and market outcomes and raise important considerations for platform governance in financial markets. Data Availability: The Seeking Alpha articles and comments used in this study were obtained directly from Seeking Alpha under a data-sharing arrangement and are proprietary; we are not permitted to redistribute them. These data may be requested from Seeking Alpha. Compustat, Execucomp, CRSP, and New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) Trade and Quote (TAQ) data are available through Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS) to subscribing institutions. JEL Classifications: G14; G41; D83; D91.

Title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
Authors: Divya Anantharaman, Elizabeth Chuk, Tonni Shijun Xia
Abstract: Abstract We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.

Title: Leveraging 0–1 linear programming for partitioning and sampling in simulation-based optimization: The case of nested partitions
Authors: Tommaso Schettini, Fausto Errico, Jorge E. Mendoza, Carolina Osorio
Abstract: Discrete Simulation-based Optimization (DSO) problems typically involve highly complex stochastic systems such as urban road networks or electric grid networks. For such problems, computing the value of the objective function requires computationally intensive simulations. Many solution methods rely on iteratively sampling and partitioning the feasible space to progressively concentrate the sampling effort on its most promising portions. To boost the effectiveness of such methods, it is fundamental to quickly identify which portions of the feasible space are relevant to explore through an effective partitioning scheme. In this paper, we focus on binary DSO problems and introduce Nested Clusters, an enhancement of Nested Partitions that leverages the mathematical formulation of the feasible space to construct auxiliary 0–1 linear programming formulations for partitioning and sampling. Additionally, we expand Nested Clusters by introducing a biasing technique that improves the average quality of the sampled solutions, boosting the overall performance. Finally, we apply Nested Clusters to a simulation-based charger location problem for an autonomous fleet of ride-hailing taxis in New York City, which serves as our primary benchmark. We conduct further controlled synthetic tests on four binary simulation–optimization problems spanning different combinatorial structures and stochastic evaluators. On the tested ride-hailing charger-location instances, both proposed partitioning and biased sampling strategies independently improve solution quality relative to Nested Partitions; combining them yields an average 2.2% improvement in the best solutions found.

Title: Competitive distribution channel strategies in three-tier supply chains with horizontal product differentiation
Authors: Junsong Bian, Chenchen Yang, Suzhen Liang
Abstract: This study examines three-tier distribution channel strategies for competing manufacturers under price competition and quantity competition. Our results reveal that backward integration is always better than forward integration for the manufacturers. In the absence of channel competition, backward integration generates a higher profit margin for the manufacturer than forward integration by controlling the supply of product inputs, although both lead to the same retail price. Moreover, under channel competition, while both forward and backward integration reduce the effect of double marginalization, backward integration tends to increase product demand and reduce product prices more than forward integration. Furthermore, with the possibility of full (both forward and backward) integration, the competing manufacturers’ distribution channel strategies can be backward and/or full integration, depending on the level of horizontal product differentiation. Specifically, when the products are sufficiently substitutable, backward integration arises as an extra equilibrium channel choice as it leads to less market competition compared to full integration. Consequently, backward integration can be a win-win equilibrium outcome compared to full integration.

Title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
Authors: Juan Pablo Atal, José Ignacio Cuesta, Morten Sæthre
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and NBER; Stanford University and NBER; Norwegian School of Economics(NHH)
Abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

Title: The depositary of last resort
Authors: Pamfili Antipa, Kilian Rieder
Affiliations: Department of Economic History, London School of Economics and Political Science , London, WC2A 2AE; Economics and Research Department, Oesterreichische Nationalbank (Eurosystem) , Vienna 1090; Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) , London EC1R 5HL
Abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel microdata on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recourse to central bank deposits was heterogeneous and persisted well beyond the panic, reflecting easy access, low opportunity costs, and positive network externalities. At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits.

Title: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
Authors: Elena Bocchi, Adam Eric Greenberg, Zachary Estes
Abstract: Abstract Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a collecting mindset shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.

Title: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
Authors: Poornima Vinoo, Grant E. Donnelly, Mathew S. Isaac, Aaron R. Brough
Abstract: To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a lifestage bias in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying usage simulation mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

Title: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
Authors: Guillaume Roels, Ludo Van der Heyden
Affiliations: INSEAD
Abstract: While many business situations relevant to production and operations management (POM), such as supply chain coordination or sustainable operations, involve some form of collective action; managerial frameworks for collective action rarely appear in POM contexts. Valuable insights may thus be missed, reducing the effectiveness and implementability of the proposed POM solutions. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a framework for collective action that has its roots in the organizational behavior literature. We formalize it mathematically not only to offer definitional clarity, but also to relate it to common POM modeling approaches. We then illustrate its relevance to POM by mapping it to case studies in supply chain coordination and sustainable operations. The proposed framework, named the Strategy–Operations–People (SOP) framework, is structured in three levels, comprising three elements, two elements, and one element, respectively. First, the Strategy level induces and enforces solidarity among all team members by specifying common goals, shared values, and well-defined rules. Second, the Operations level organizes the decentralized execution of collective action in autonomous subgroups through a detailed specification of roles and processes. Third, the People level requires the individual commitment of all team members to the proposed collective action program, since a team’s performance rests on the individual contributions of its members. The framework thus addresses the common, subgroup, and individual dimensions of collective action. The SOP framework also contributes to the broader fields of team leadership and organizational behavior in two ways. First, its mathematical formalization brings operational clarity on the defining scope of the framework’s elements. Second, mapping the framework to two problems in supply chain management and sustainable operations illustrates its broad applicability, moving beyond collective action within organizations, to guide collective action taking place across organizations.

Title: Stationary Coupled-Flow Approximation for Time-Varying Retrial Queues
Authors: Ömer Schmiel, Benjamin Legros, Raik Stolletz
Affiliations: Chair of Production Management, 68161 Mannheim, Germany; School of Knowledge Economy and Management Business School, Université Côte d’Azur, 92156 Suresnes, France
Abstract: Although stationary queueing models, such as Erlang-C and Erlang-A, are widely used for performance evaluation in service systems, they do not account for time dependence and retrials, which limits their applicability. Building on stationary [Formula: see text] formulas and point-wise stationary approximations (PSAs), this paper proposes the stationary coupled-flow (SCF) approximation. The method partitions the time horizon into intervals, models each as an [Formula: see text] in steady state, and iteratively determines the arrival rate, accounting for new customers and retrials. This yields an approximation of long-run performance metrics of retrial queues with stationary or time-varying arrivals. We prove that the SCF approximation converges to a finite limit for constant and cyclic arrival rates. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the high accuracy of the SCF approximation. Furthermore, SCF outperforms PSA, particularly during peak periods. Therefore, SCF provides a fast, transparent tool for planning and staffing in services with retrials. It remains reliable when the exact distribution of retrials is uncertain, enabling day-to-day scheduling and scenario testing under time-varying demand. We find that the retrial probability plays a stronger role than the retrial-time distribution. The impact of retrials in time-varying queues is driven by two effects: the state at the abandonment epoch and the cycle length-retrial time interaction. We posit that as retrial times increase, the first effect dampens congestion feedback, whereas the second effect can amplify or smooth fluctuations. Under sufficiently high variability in retrial times, the cycle length-retrial time interaction becomes negligible, leaving the system governed by the abandonment-epoch state.
