Title: Impact of Short-Form Videos on Screentime and Sleep: Evidence from TikTok
Authors: Saharsh Agarwal, Uttara M. Ananthakrishnan
Affiliations: Information Systems Department, Indian School of Business, Hyderabad, Telangana 500032, India; Information Systems Department, Foster School of Business, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington 98195
Abstract: Short-form video platforms have become central to debates about digital overuse and sleep disruption, yet causal evidence on their behavioral impacts remains limited. We study the effects of adopting short-form video in the context of TikTok, which pioneered the format and accounts for a large share of global short-form video consumption. Using granular smartphone touchstream data from a large opt-in panel of U.S. Android users, we track app usage, screen time, and inferred sleep behavior before and after TikTok adoption. We employ a difference-in-differences framework leveraging a high-frequency app usage data set from nearly 7,000 TikTok adopters. Our findings reveal a significant increase in overall screen time—averaging 221 minutes per week for heavy TikTok users—following TikTok adoption, alongside notable declines in usage of other social media and gaming apps, suggesting a strong substitution effect. The screen time effects are highest during late night hours. We also observe shifts in sleep patterns, including delayed bedtimes and a moderate reduction in sleep duration, among high-intensity users. We observe no effects for low-intensity users, who engage minimally with TikTok postadoption. Our findings show that short-form video adoption expands total digital attention rather than merely reallocating it, with important implications for platform design, regulation, and digital well-being. As a side result, our analysis provides clear evidence of substitutability between TikTok and traditional social media platforms, which has important implications for competition policy. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08260 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems.

Title: The Sooner, the Better? Optimal Vaccination Policy with Limited Vaccine Supply
Authors: Miao Bai, Qi (George) Chen, Cuihong Li
Affiliations: University of Connecticut, Operations and Information Management, Storrs, Connecticut, United States; London Business School, Management Science and Operations, London, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; University of Connecticut, School of Business, Storrs, Connecticut, United States
Abstract: We study the optimal single-dose vaccination policy during an infectious disease outbreak, considering both limited vaccine supply and imperfect efficacy, which provides partial immunity to each vaccinated individual. The inclusion of imperfect efficacy introduces an additional compartment to the celebrated Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered (SIR) model, giving rise to an infinite horizon nonlinear optimal control problem. We derive a closed-form expression for the optimal vaccination policy under infinite administrative capacity and establish theoretical structures of the optimal policy under finite capacity. Our results suggest that delaying the start of the vaccination process may be optimal, especially when the vaccine is less effective, the vaccine supply is more limited, and the disease is more infectious. We identify key terms as an integral part of the analysis that characterize the individual-level benefit of vaccination and, importantly, provide insights into the intuition behind vaccination delay. Building on these theoretical findings, our numerical study verifies these insights based on sensitivity results. We demonstrate the significant benefit of delay in reducing the total number of infections compared to policies without delay. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to alternative model dynamics and objective functions, confirming that our key findings remain robust and our methodology applicable across different settings. Additionally, we develop a general framework and provide guidance for applying the methodology to broader epidemic settings. Our study contributes to the methodological framework to analyze optimal vaccination policies for infectious disease control, and uncovers an important policy structure — vaccination delay — that has been overlooked in the literature but has important implications for practice.

Title: Diffusion Approximation Error for Queueing Systems with General Primitives
Authors: Anton Braverman, Ziv Scully
Affiliations: Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208; School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853
Abstract: How Accurate Are Diffusion Approximations for Queues with General Distributions? Diffusion approximations are widely used to analyze complex queueing systems, but their accuracy is often best understood when arrival and service times follow exponential distributions. Braverman and Scully study what happens when these assumptions are relaxed. Their paper, “Diffusion Approximation Error for Queueing Systems with General Primitives,” develops a framework for quantifying steady-state approximation error across a broad class of arrival and service distributions. Examining several canonical queueing models, the authors show that the error naturally separates into interior and boundary components. The interior error can generally be controlled using only the first three moments of the underlying distributions, whereas boundary effects require more model-specific analysis. Methodologically, the paper extends Stein’s method to piecewise-deterministic Markov processes, providing new tools for analyzing systems with general renewal processes and broadening the range of queueing models for which rigorous diffusion-approximation guarantees can be obtained.

Title: Phantom Networks: Window on Agency in Social Mechanisms
Authors: Ronald Burt, Ray Reagans, Sonja Opper
Affiliations: Bocconi University Department of Management and Technology, management and techn, Milano, Milano, 20136, Italy; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Sloan School, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 02139-4307, United States; Bocconi University Department of Management and Technology, management and techn, Milano, Lombardia, Italy
Abstract: Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience — what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure-in-action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work

Title: Intergenerational Transmission
Authors: Trevor Israelsen, Innan Sasaki, Nadia Maamoun
Affiliations: Penn State University; Warwick Business School

Title: Toward a Framework of Social Marginalization: An Integrative Review and Research Agenda
Authors: McKenzie Preston, Y. Lillian Kim
Affiliations: New York University

Title: Who will I be? Refugee entrepreneurship and founder identity
Authors: Eunki Ro, E. Erin Powell, Ted Baker
Abstract: We conducted a 27-month field study of 23 North Korean Defector (NKD) founders. Founders responded in three different ways to the disparaging default social identities they encountered by self-categorizing into three “avowed” social identities, which served as aspirations for how they would build their ventures. Founders generated sensemaking narratives that explained their behavior – to themselves and to others – by anchoring on the past, present, or future circumstances and claiming individual capabilities to build their ventures. The resulting ventures were characterized by distinctive missions, branding, and hiring preferences and therefore by patterned differences in the roles founders played. We contribute to scholarly understanding of refugee entrepreneurship by showing that the ways in which refugee founders respond to being in a new country and constructing new identities is more varied – because it is embedded in their responses to local social evaluations – than prior research has portrayed. We contribute to the development of founder identity theory (FIDT) by expanding prior understanding of how social identities drive founder role creation. Overall, we show the extension of refugee founder agency as they move from self-categorizing into avowed social identities to embedding themselves in the concrete social relations required to perform a role.

Title: The revenue halo effect: How revenues and expenses asymmetrically affect perceptions of profitability
Authors: Maria Giulia Trupia, Franklin Shaddy
Abstract: There are two primary ways to boost profits: increase revenues or decrease expenses. For example, whether a company increases revenues by $1 million or decreases expenses by $1 million, its profits will increase by $1 million (all else equal). But how do people subjectively evaluate such changes to revenues and expenses, and what inferences do they draw as a result? Across nine experiments ( N = 6045), an archival data analysis, and four supplemental studies, we document a robust “revenue halo” effect: increases in revenues, relative to equivalent decreases in expenses, lead to more positive perceptions of profitability, in both the short and long run, and result in more favorable overall impressions of financial strength, performance, potential, and trajectory. Consequently, managers who propose ideas for increasing revenues (vs. decreasing expenses) are viewed as more competent; consultants who develop such strategies are more likely to be rehired; and companies that report higher revenues are more attractive to investors. We furthermore propose that the revenue halo effect can be explained, in part, by the belief that strategies for increasing revenues are more innovative than strategies for decreasing expenses. Finally, to underscore the real-world relevance of our account, we analyze approximately 13 million financial news articles, finding that when firms reported increased revenues (vs. decreased expenses), they subsequently rose in Fortune 's “World's Most Admired Companies” rankings (the following year). This research identifies a novel asymmetry in judgments of organizational performance, with implications for managerial decision-making, corporate communication, and capital allocation.
Journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

Title: Reframing Top‐Down and Bottom‐Up Dynamics in Sustainability Research: A Multilevel Framework for OB / HRM Scholars
Authors: Chidiebere Ogbonnaya, Tiffany Trzebiatowski, Hannes Leroy
Affiliations: King's College London; Colorado State University; Erasmus University Rotterdam
Abstract: Abstract Sustainability has emerged as an important priority for organizations navigating social, economic, and environmental uncertainty. We define sustainability as the ongoing process through which organizations balance objectives across these three domains while creating long‐term value for current and future stakeholders. Yet much of the existing research continues to focus on macro‐level considerations such as organizational commitments to corporate social responsibility (CSR) and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) initiatives and pays less attention to the experiences of people within organizations. This editorial introduces a thematic collection that advances a multilevel, person‐centred perspective on how macro‐, meso‐, and micro‐level organizational dynamics interact to shape sustainability. Drawing on selected articles published in the Journal of Management Studies between 2010 and 2026, the collection identifies four research clusters that demonstrate how formal sustainability commitments are shaped by social processes and individual experiences across organizational levels. Together, these articles underscore the central role of people management processes in explaining how and why sustainability goals are translated into organizational action. We conclude by outlining directions for future research that examines sustainability as a multilevel process shaped by the interaction between top‐down and bottom‐up dynamics.

Title: Turn Energy Efficiency Into Strategic Advantage
Authors: Ina Sebastian, Thomas Haskamp, Daniel Woerner, Lukas Falcke, Stephanie Woerner
Abstract: Rising fossil fuel costs are squeezing corporate margins. Researchers have found that companies can lower costs, hedge against price volatility, and create new value for customers by making energy consumption visible across operations, redesigning processes to cut waste, and embedding efficiency into their products.

Title: Flow Diversification
Authors: Sunil Wahal, Albert Y. Wang
Affiliations: Arizona State University W.P. Carey School of Business; Auburn University
Abstract: Abstract We measure flow diversification in mutual funds using the cross-sectional correlation of daily flows across investor clienteles. Greater flow diversification is associated with lower future flow volatility, smaller subsequent outflows, and lower cash holdings. We decompose flow correlation into predictable and unexpected components. Unexpectedly low flow correlation is associated with higher post-outflow fund returns, mitigating outflow-induced externalities on incumbent shareholders. Flow diversification also dampens the higher flow-performance sensitivity of illiquid funds, partially offsetting strategic complementarities that can generate fragility.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Resolution Design and Investment in Banking Groups – CORRIGENDUM
Authors: Albert Banal-Estañol, Gyöngyi Lóránth, David Pothier
Affiliations: Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Barcelona School of Management, Barcelona School of Economics, and City St George’s, University of London; University of Vienna
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: The Issuance and Design of Sustainability-Linked Loans
Authors: Aleksander A. Aleszczyk, Maria Loumioti, George Serafeim
Affiliations: New York University; The University of Texas at Dallas; Harvard University
Abstract: ABSTRACT We explore the contract design of sustainability-linked loans (SLLs), a rapidly growing form of ESG-labeled debt that ties loan pricing to firms’ sustainability performance. Using a global SLL sample issued between 2017 and 2023, we examine whether SLLs are structured to discipline borrowers with weak ESG performance through stringent sustainability-linked provisions. We find no association between borrower ESG performance and the rigor of SLL provisions, suggesting that SLLs are generally not designed as incentive contracts. Instead, SLL contract design aligns more closely with ESG branding and credit-product-expansion motives: borrowers leverage SLLs to enhance legitimacy and visibility and to attract additional capital, whereas lenders can convey their ESG commitment, cater to investor demand for ESG-labeled debt, and expand their credit product offering. Overall, our evidence suggests that SLLs function primarily as symbolic labels rather than credible mechanisms for driving meaningful improvements in firms’ sustainability outcomes. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M14; M41; G21; G32; Q56.

Title: CEO Tax Lock-In and Share Pledging
Authors: Jonathan Underwood, Benjamin P. Yost
Affiliations: Texas State University; Boston College
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study how CEOs’ personal tax incentives shape their share pledging decisions and firms’ restrictions on the practice. Pledging shares entails using company stock as collateral for personal loans, enabling executives to obtain liquidity without making a taxable sale of appreciated shares. Using pledging data from 2006 to 2024, we find a robust positive relation between CEOs’ unrealized capital gains tax liabilities, or tax burdens, and share pledging. This relation is weaker when interest rates are high, consistent with CEOs’ trading off tax benefits against borrowing costs. After Institutional Shareholder Services discouraged share pledging in 2012, firms with high-tax-burden CEOs were slower to adopt antipledging policies and, when they did adopt, chose less restrictive policies. Firms that adopted strong antipledging policies subsequently increased CEO cash pay and stock awards. Our evidence suggests that share pledging helps executives manage personal tax lock-in and that firms consider this benefit when restricting pledging. Data Availability: Data are available from the public and subscription sources identified in the text, subject to applicable data-use restrictions. JEL Classifications: G30; H24; J33; M52.

Title: Growing sentimental value through object usage
Authors: Daniel M. Grossman, Ryan Rahinel, John Lancaster
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Entrepreneurship, Ed G. Smith College of Business University of Missouri‐St. Louis St. Louis Missouri USA; Department of Marketing, Lundquist College of Business University of Oregon Eugene Oregon USA
Abstract: Abstract Consumers often protect their sentimentally valuable possessions by storing them away, which precludes them from being used. Across five studies, we show that usage of sentimentally valuable objects increases their sentimental value. Process evidence suggests one reason this happens: Repeatedly using a sentimentally valuable object makes the association held by the object (i.e., the source of its sentimental value) salient more frequently. This leads one to believe that such an association is more closely integrated into their self‐concept, which cyclically enhances the sentimental value of the object. We conclude by discussing the contribution of these findings to the literature, providing recommendations to marketers and consumers, and elaborating on directions for future research.

Title: Startup multihoming in enterprise software ecosystems: The role of skill breadth and organizational learning
Authors: Vijayaraghavan Venkataraman, Marco Ceccagnoli, Chris Forman
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore Bengaluru Karnataka India; Scheller College of Business Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta Georgia USA; Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management, Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Cornell University Ithaca New York USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary We investigate startup decisions to multihome to another platform. We develop a theory that shows startup engagement with the initial platform leads first to exploratory learning and later a shift toward exploitation, leading to an inverted U‐shape relationship between duration of platform partnership and the likelihood of multihoming. This tradeoff is shaped by the breadth of the startup's skill base. Startups with a broader set of skills initially face slower learning, but over time skill breadth provides greater adaptability that better positions them for multihoming. We test our theory using a novel dataset on SAP partners' multihoming decisions, examining the implications of Oracle acquisitions that increased the expected benefits of multihoming. Our empirical findings are consistent with our hypotheses. Managerial Summary The growth phase forms an important part of any startup's evolution, particularly when engaging with digital platform ecosystems, where expansion often depends on the ability to multihome. Startups' accumulated experience with a platform shapes how they respond when opportunities to expand to another platform arise. Startups with moderate levels of prior platform experience are most likely to expand, while longer relationships can create dependencies that reduce flexibility. Importantly, the breadth of a startup's skill base changes this trajectory. Startups with diverse skills are better able to avoid lock‐in and remain flexible, even after long partnerships. Evidence from the enterprise software ecosystem shows managers should see platform partnerships as both opportunity and risk, investing in broad skill sets to balance deep collaboration with the ability to grow across platforms.

Title: Multi-stakeholder market shaping for sustainability: effort types and enactment pathways in B2B markets
Authors: Kaisa Koskela-Huotari, Suvi Nenonen, Chelsey Jo Huisman, Hans Kjellberg
Abstract: Abstract Marketing scholarship has primarily focused on influencing consumer behavior towards sustainability, yet many sustainability challenges require market-level changes across multiple stakeholders. Addressing this gap, we examine how heterogeneous stakeholders collectively shape markets for sustainability. We conduct a multi-case study of B2B markets whose impact on climate change and biodiversity is actively contested. Drawing on institutional field theory, we conceptualize market shaping for sustainability as linked to issue fields where diverse stakeholders engage to influence market trajectories. Our abductive analysis identifies four types of multi-stakeholder market-shaping efforts pursuing markedly different—at times opposing—market-level outcomes: status quo maintenance, targeted reform, infrastructure reform, and market contraction. To explain this variation, we delineate four pathways through which stakeholders enact sustainability-related issues—two for challengers and two for incumbents. By linking these pathways to intended market-level outcomes, we advance theory on market-based sustainability interventions and offer actionable insights for navigating multi-stakeholder market-shaping processes.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: A new cut-and-solve-based approach for the single-source capacitated facility location problem
Authors: Guilherme Barbosa de Almeida, Marcone Jamilson Freitas Souza, Elisangela Martins de Sá, Sérgio Ricardo de Souza
Abstract: The Single-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problem involves locating facilities so that each customer’s demand is met by a single facility and capacity constraints are not violated. This paper focuses on developing an exact algorithm to handle this problem. In this sense, we propose an algorithm that uses four strategies: (i) strengthening the problem formulation through a cutting-plane procedure; (ii) exploiting partial linear relaxations to obtain good lower bounds; (iii) applying a heuristic to obtain a good upper bound; and (iv) applying a Cut-and-Solve-based scheme to construct a binary search tree. We evaluate and select cutting-plane generation procedures that differ from those previously used for the problem and propose a new heuristic procedure. The results of the computational experiments showed that the proposed algorithm found a greater or equal number of optimal values with lower runtime than the state-of-the-art exact algorithm in 22 out of 26 subsets, and than the CPLEX solver in 19 out of 26 subsets.

Title: Strategic cooperation: Winning in live-streaming e-commerce with key opinion leaders
Authors: Peng He, Henry Xu, Zhongyi Huang, Helen Cai, Victor Shi
Abstract: In live-streaming e-commerce, brands, Key Opinion Leaders (KOLs), and social platforms must make complex decisions about collaboration structures, balancing sales incentives against the risk of long-term reputation loss. Using differential game theory, this paper investigates three cooperation modes in a three-echelon social e-commerce supply chain: the independent-KOL mode, the brand-signing KOL mode, and the platform-signing KOL mode. Our findings indicate that when the live-streaming promotion effect is relatively strong, a higher KOL commission rate enhances brand goodwill when the reputation loss effect is relatively weak, but diminishes brand goodwill when the reputation loss effect is relatively strong. Moreover, the brand-signing mode enhances brand goodwill and KOL influence when both platform and KOL commission rates are relatively low. Conversely, when these rates exceed certain thresholds, the platform-signing mode becomes more advantageous and expands market demand. Additionally, signing a KOL accelerates profit growth for the signing parties, while non-signing members can also benefit from others' cooperative arrangements. Finally, the brand- or platform-signing KOL modes yield higher total cooperative profit than the independent-KOL mode when live-streaming efficiency is lower, whereas the opposite holds when efficiency is higher. These results offer strategic guidance for brand managers and platform operators in optimizing partnership structures and mitigating the dynamic risks inherent in KOL live-streaming.

Title: Commentary on Han et al.’s meta-analytic work on high-investment human resource practices: through the 3P lens for workforce management
Authors: Riki Takeuchi, He Huang, April Ye Zhou, Hwayoung Kim, Zelu Zhang
Abstract: Abstract Han, Kang, Allen and Pan’s (2026) meta-analysis integrates human capital resources (HCR) theory and institutional theory to examine how educational systems and labor market institutions jointly influence the effectiveness of high-investment human resource practices (HIHRPs). Contrary to their theoretical prediction, low–low educational system and labor market configurations relate to firm performance as positively as high–high configurations do, and that puzzle remains unresolved. This combination describes the institutional profile of many host economies, which makes it an international business problem: should multinational enterprises transfer their HIHRPs abroad or adapt to local practice? This commentary outlines substitution effects, drawn from the institutional voids literature and organizational support theory, as an alternative mechanism that may better account for its effect. We reflect that theoretical parsimony, while elegant, could oversimplify and obscure complex phenomena that span multiple levels of analysis, the types of topics that strategic international human resource management (SIHRM) aims to research. We then propose a people–places–practices (3P) lens to note the theoretical directions Han et al.’s work addresses and those it leaves for future work. The commentary illustrates how deliberate theory integration, guided by the specific research question and institutional context, can enhance explanatory power in SIHRM research.

Title: Partisanship, Information, and Punishment for Misconduct at Work
Authors: Vivek Pandey, Joanna S. Wu, Yuanzhe Zhang
Affiliations: University of Rochester
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether firms apply partisan standards when responding to employee financial misconduct. Using detailed individual‐level data on financial advisers, we find that advisers who are in the political minority at their firm (political minority advisers) are no different from their colleagues at the same firm and time in the incidence and severity of misconduct, yet following misconduct, they are significantly more likely to depart—a pattern we term “partisan punishment standards.” This pattern is especially pronounced at firms with lower internal information quality (IIQ), proxied with (1) lower external reporting quality (for public firms only), (2) private firms (relative to public firms), and (3) not hiring an independent public accountant to create an internal control report (for both public and private firms). We also document “partisan reporting standards”: Firms are more likely to publicly disclose misconduct by political minority advisers while remaining relatively silent in other cases. Firms that exhibit partisan punishment practices subsequently experience slower growth.

Title: Estimating the Private Value of Financial Statement Statistics
Authors: Russell Lundholm, Xin Zheng
Affiliations: University of British Columbia Vancouver British Columbia Canada
Abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a method for estimating the private value of knowing the future realization of some financial statistics, and then we apply the measure to the familiar ratios from the DuPont decomposition of return on equity. The estimation is grounded in the standard rational expectations model, adapted to accommodate relative risk aversion, and determines an investor's willingness to pay for information denominated in units of a riskless asset (e.g., money). The method can accommodate different levels of investable wealth, multiple assets, and any information system regarding those assets. We use this method to document several interesting contrasts. An investor with $1 million in wealth who already knows all the current DuPont ratios, as well as the most recent analyst forecast, would be willing to pay $2861 to know all of next year's ratios. This amount increases to $3158 for firms below the median size. We find that the value of financial information is higher in periods of high sentiment and for firms that are hard to value or hard to arbitrage (i.e., firms with high sentiment exposure). In practical terms, this suggests investors prioritize their information search to small, young, loss‐making, high‐growth, low book‐to‐market, non‐dividend‐paying, and illiquid firms. In terms of the DuPont components, we find that knowing next year's operating profit margin alone is worth $1226, whereas knowing next year's leverage is worth only $170 and knowing next year's sales growth is worth only $184. In practical terms, this suggests that investors allocate more attention to forecasting profitability and less attention to forecasting sales growth. Finally, we demonstrate that the estimated value of financial statistics increases substantially when we assume the investor can trade in the firm asset and can also hedge using an industry exchange‐traded fund (ETF). This result suggests that professional investors integrate their information search with their hedging behavior.

Title: Between Play and Reason: Integrating Sensible Foolishness Into Strategy‐Making Workshops
Authors: Rebecca Lu, Gary T. Burke, Omid Omidvar, David J. Carrington
Affiliations: Loughborough University; University of Bristol; Warwick Business School; Aston Business School
Abstract: Abstract Sensible foolishness through play can offer a valuable escape from prevailing dogmas and rational models of intelligence, affording actors freedom to explore, imagine, and create without constraint. Yet the value of sensible foolishness, and the vital interplay between play and reason, remains underexplored in strategy scholarship. Drawing on a qualitative experimental study of three SMEs, we examine how high‐stakes strategic challenges can be addressed through sensible foolishness. Our analysis shows how the interplay between play and reason gains generative momentum during strategy‐making workshops, as actors co‐create playful atmospheres and shift into more expressive, embodied ways of being. We identify three transitional modes – deliberate , dialectical , and dwelling – through which actors integrate play and reason and co‐produce moments of strategic insight and value. We develop a process theory of integrating sensible foolishness into strategy‐making, showing how attuned facilitation and atmospheric shifts enable its enactment as a collective, affectively sustained mode of strategizing. This extends debates in strategy and serious play scholarship by advancing a practice‐based view of sensible foolishness as a complementary instrument of collective strategic intelligence.

Title: The Double-Edged Offline Touchpoint: How Self-Pickup Stations Reshape Pure-Play E-Commerce Transactions
Authors: Jingcun Cao, Zhiqi Li, Chenxi Liao, Ying Xie
Abstract: Click-and-collect services through self-pickup stations have gained popularity as an alternative to traditional home delivery in e-commerce. This fulfillment option can increase customer purchases by enhancing post-purchase convenience and reducing transaction costs. However, increased hassle costs for customers and exposure to offline competition make the net impact uncertain. This study utilizes a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) approach to analyze individual-level transaction data from an online shopping platform in Asia. Self-pickup station openings are found to have a positive net effect on customer spending and shopping frequency on the platform, without cannibalizing home delivery. A closer examination of customer dynamics reveals that station openings stabilize the platform’s user base by reducing customer churn and deepening engagement among existing shoppers, rather than driving new user acquisition. Furthermore, these positive effects are moderated by: station accessibility, level of nearby offline competition, and product attributes. Specifically, this paper provides the first empirical evidence that the positive effect of pickup stations can be reduced, if platforms locate them close to major offline retail alternatives. These findings provide important implications for e-commerce platforms regarding self-pickup station benefits, product suitability, and location strategy to reduce the risk of customer loss to offline retailers.

Title: How Can We Research Social Mobility in Entrepreneurship?
Authors: Elsa T. Chan, Steven A. Brieger, Ngoc Luu, Marii Paskov, Mirela Xheneti
Affiliations: University of Sussex, UK; NEOMA Business School, France; University of Bristol, UK
Abstract: Social mobility is a central concern in contemporary societies, yet its dynamics within entrepreneurship remain insufficiently understood. This paper’s purpose is to facilitate research on entrepreneurial social mobility by making three key contributions: first, we examine the distinct conceptual and methodological challenges related to capturing social mobility in entrepreneurship and provide strategies for solving them; second, we introduce multidimensional social mobility measures that move beyond the predominant focus on income-based metrics in existing quantitative research; third, we demonstrate how alternative quantitative and qualitative methods can produce more holistic evidence for understanding social mobility among entrepreneurs.

Title: Learning to price under competition with reference price effects
Authors: Yongge Yang, Jiannan Ke, Cong Shi
Affiliations: Wuhan University; Business School of Science and Technology, Wuhan University, Wuhan, Hubei, China; University of Miami
Abstract: This article studies the algorithmic design of price competition in oligopolistic markets, with a focus on long-run market dynamics under reference price effects. We consider a sequential price competition framework with multiple sellers operating over a finite horizon, each lacking prior knowledge of the demand functions. Consumer demand depends not only on current prices but also on a reference price, defined as a weighted average of past prices that shapes consumer expectations. We characterize market stability through the concept of a stationary Nash equilibrium (SNE), where no seller has an incentive to deviate unilaterally and the reference price remains stable. To operate under incomplete demand information and limited observability of competitors’ prices, we propose a Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation with Callbacks (SPSAC) policy. Despite the lack of a monotonicity condition, which is typically required for convergence in online games, we show that this policy achieves a last-iterate convergence rate of O ( 1 / T ) for both prices and reference prices toward the SNE, along with a dynamic regret of O ( T ) over T periods. We further consider three extensions. In the first extension, when sellers have access to first-order feedback, the convergence rate improves to O ( 1 / T ) , highlighting the value of demand information in simplifying sequential price competition. In the second extension, where prices have long-term effects on the reference price and demand evolves as a nonstationary stochastic process, and in the third extension, where each seller maintains its own reference price, our policy continues to guarantee O ( 1 / T ) convergence and O ( T ) dynamic regret.

Title: The role of post-purchase communications on product returns and downstream consequences in online apparel retail
Authors: Punya Chatterjee, Susana Jaramillo, Ganga S Urumutta Hewage, Gretchen R Ross
Affiliations: University of Memphis; Texas Christian University
Abstract: The expansion of online apparel retail has introduced a persistent challenge: subtle mismatches between consumer expectations about a product and the reality—particularly regarding attributes like color or texture—often leading to dissatisfaction and costly returns. While prior research has primarily focused on pre-purchase solutions such as virtual try-ons or detailed product descriptions, these tactics are not always effective and are often inaccessible to small- and medium-sized apparel sellers—who comprise the vast majority of firms in the apparel sector—due to resource constraints. In this article, we explore a low-cost alternative: strategic post-purchase messaging—seller-initiated communications designed to reassure consumers of the product's quality, acknowledge potential concerns that the product may not be as expected, explain potential discrepancies, and offer recovery strategies and additional product-related guidance after a purchase is complete. Across three empirical studies we find that when consumers experience minor expectation-reality gaps, post-purchase messages sent at the time of delivery can reduce product return intentions and enhance positive downstream consequences, including, satisfaction, word-of-mouth, and repurchase intentions. A follow-up mixed-method survey conducted with small- and medium-sized online sellers supports the empirical findings that sending such messages is logistically and financially feasible. We identify perceived seller trustworthiness as the psychological mechanism driving this effect. Product reputation (based on consumer reviews) and post-purchase message content are explored as two theoretically derived moderators of the effect. Our findings make theoretical contributions and offer practical guidance—particularly for small- and medium-sized online apparel sellers seeking scalable, cost-friendly ways to manage product mismatches and strengthen consumer engagement in the absence of high product reputation.

Title: Agile approaches for gaming software development
Authors: Joohyun Kim, Monica Johar, Vijay Mookerjee
Affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas
Abstract: Online games increasingly operate as continuously evolving live services enabled by agile and continuous integration/continuous deployment-based development. In such environments, release timing is no longer a downstream scheduling choice but an operational control variable that interacts directly with functionality growth, error accumulation, and system complexity. This article develops a multi-release optimal control framework that endogenizes release timing and user-facing value. Extending the functionality and error dynamics structure from prior work, we embed repeated release decisions directly into the development process and characterize how construction effort, debugging effort, and cadence jointly determine long-run value creation. Within this framework, we analyze two structured release regimes widely observed in practice: a time-based release policy, with fixed sprint duration, and a functionality-based release policy, with fixed feature scope. We show that incremental release value declines endogenously as integration complexity increases. Under time-based policies, the number of new features delivered per release decreases over time. Under functionality-based policies, maintaining fixed feature bundles requires progressively longer development intervals. In both regimes, effort shifts systematically from construction toward debugging as the system matures. We further introduce a hybrid release policy as a supplementary benchmark, allowing the firm to switch between time-based and functionality-based policies subject to a switching cost. This benchmark identifies conditions under which policy flexibility improves release performance while preserving the operational structure of the two release regimes. The results provide an operations-based theory of release cadence under endogenous complexity growth in software systems with repeated deployment.

Title: How Awareness of Media Slant Affects Reaction to News: Field and Experimental Evidence from Microblog Users
Authors: Yihong Huang, Juanjuan Meng, Xi Weng
Affiliations: Guanghua School of Management, Peking University
Abstract: This paper investigates whether news consumers react strategically to media slant. Using data from Microblog users and an online experiment that varies whether sources and stances are disclosed, we find that users are more likely to repost news consistent with their own attitudes, yet they also exhibit a higher propensity to repost news inconsistent with the reporting outlet’s general stance. Evidence suggests that this latter behavior reflects strategic inference: users recognize the outlet’s tradeoff between popularity and stance, and thus infer greater popularity for inconsistent news. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that users with stronger Bayesian updating and level-k reasoning abilities display larger strategic reactions. Finally, we show that simply reminding users of media slant can serve as an effective nudge to foster more strategic responses. This paper was accepted by John Beshears, behavioral economics and decision analysis.
