Title: An IV Hazard Model of Loan Default with an Application to Subprime Mortgage Cohorts
Authors: Christopher J. Palmer
Abstract: ABSTRACT I develop a control function methodology robust to endogenous or mismeasured regressors in hazard models. Applying the estimator to the subprime mortgage crisis, I quantify what caused the foreclosure rate to triple across the 2003 to 2007 subprime cohorts. To identify the elasticity of default to housing prices, I use various home price instruments including historical variation in home price cyclicality. Loose credit played a significant role in the crisis, but much of the increase in defaults across cohorts was caused by price declines unrelated to lending standards, with a 10% price decline increasing subprime mortgage default rates by 50%.

Title: Appearance-Based Legitimate Distinctiveness: Founder Attractiveness, Gender, and Venture Evaluations
Authors: Henrik Lekkas, Torben Antretter, Ivo Blohm, Charlotta Sirén, Joakim Wincent
Affiliations: University of St.Gallen, Switzerland; Hanken School of Economics, Finland
Abstract: This study proposes a way to reconcile the beauty premium and beauty-is-beastly arguments by suggesting that founder appearance is processed through two separable and countervailing channels: perceived legitimacy and perceived distinctiveness. We further theorize that in startups, the relationship is gendered, because women do not fit the entrepreneurial prototype, limiting their perceived legitimacy. A field study of 359 founders supports our theorizing that male founders are evaluated best when moderately attractive, while female founders see no significant attractiveness effects. A preregistered experiment with 771 participants, using AI-manipulated attractiveness, does not confirm these patterns but supports our theorizing about both mediators.

Title: Assortment Optimization in the Presence of Context Effects
Authors: Reza Yousefi Maragheh, Shuai Li, Tiancheng Zhao, Xin Chen, James Davis, Jason Cho, Sushant Kumar, Kannan Achan
Affiliations: Wal-Mart.com USA LLC, Personalization, Sunnyvale, California, United States; Georgia Institute of Technology, H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Atlanta, Georgia, United States; Saint Louis University, Operations & Information Technology Mgmt, St. Louis, Missouri, United States; University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Industrial and Enterprise Systems Engineering, Urbana, Illinois, United States; Flexport, Inc, San Francisco, California, United States
Abstract: Problem definition. We study choice modeling and assortment optimization under context effects, where an item’s perceived attractiveness depends on the other items displayed alongside it. Methodology. We study the Contextual Multinomial Logit (CMNL) model, in which each item’s utility adjusts linearly with the presence of other items, yielding a pairwise (second-order) approximation to general context-dependent choice while preserving a structure that is simple to estimate and optimize. CMNL encompasses classical phenomena such as attraction, compromise, and similarity effects. Results. Theoretically, we establish strong hardness and inapproximability results for CMNL-based assortment optimization, yet identify practically motivated regimes that admit polynomial or pseudo-polynomial algorithms. On the estimation side, we prove the log-likelihood function is concave and provide necessary and sufficient identifiability conditions, enabling scalable and well-posed fitting. Empirically, on large SKU-level transaction data, CMNL improves predictive accuracy over standard benchmarks and converts these gains into a measurable revenue lift. We also provide an exact MILP formulation and practical heuristics for general instances. Managerial implications. CMNL provides a parsimonious, estimation-friendly framework that captures salient context effects and enables tractable and high-quality assortment decisions at scale, delivering not only superior predictive fit but also measurable revenue gains.

Title: Cost Learning and Strategic Inventory: Who Should Carry Inventory in a Vertical Supply Chain?
Authors: Ganesh Balasubramanian, Benny Mantin, Sachin Jayaswal
Affiliations: Dubai Business School, University of Dubai, Emirates Road, Dubai 14143, United Arab Emirates; Department of Engineering, Department of Economics and Management, University of Luxembourg, Esch-sur-Alzette 4365, Luxembourg; Operations and Decision Sciences, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, Ahmedabad 380015, India
Abstract: Problem definition: In a decentralized supply chain, the downstream retailer (he) may strategically carry inventory to induce lower future wholesale prices, triggering the upstream manufacturer (she) to raise the early-period wholesale price to deter such behavior. In the presence of cost learning, where future production cost declines with cumulative early-period production, the manufacturer faces a key trade-off. To accelerate cost learning, should she lower the early-period wholesale price to encourage larger retailer orders and downstream inventory carryover, or should she instead overproduce in the early period and hold inventory herself, bearing the holding cost? Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretic model to capture such supply chain interactions in the presence of the manufacturer’s cost learning and the retailer’s strategic inventory. We characterize the conditions for different inventory-holding patterns in the supply chain, where only the manufacturer, only the retailer, both, or neither carries inventory. Countering the established notion that a manufacturer should hold inventory to enhance cost learning when her holding cost is low, our research reveals that she should abstain from holding any inventory, even at zero holding cost, when the retailer’s holding cost is sufficiently low. Further, we show that the manufacturer should completely refrain from holding inventory as an instrument to accelerate learning, irrespective of the retailer’s holding cost, when there is no uncertainty associated with cost learning or when the learning benefits are realized continuously. Managerial implications: Our results guide manufacturers experiencing cost learning to determine their inventory decisions based on cost-learning features and the retailer’s holding cost. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2022.0178 .

Title: Reducing the Filtering Effect in Public School Admissions: A Bias-aware Analysis for Targeted Interventions
Authors: Yuri Faenza, Swati Gupta, Aapeli Vuorinen, Xuan Zhang
Affiliations: Columbia University, IEOR, New York, New York, United States; Georgia Institute of Technology, ISyE, Atlanta, Georgia, United States; Columbia University, Dept of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, New York, New York, United States; Facebook Inc, Core Data Science Group, Menlo Park, California, United States
Abstract: Problem definition: Traditionally, New York City’s top 8 public schools have selected candidates solely based on their scores in the Specialized High School Admissions Test (SHSAT). These scores are known to be impacted by socioeconomic status of students and amount of test preparation received in middle schools, leading to a massive filtering effect in the education pipeline. The classical mechanisms for assigning students to schools do not naturally address problems like school segregation and class diversity, which have worsened over the years. The scientific community, including policymakers, have reacted by incorporating group-specific quotas and proportionality constraints, with mixed results. The problem of finding effective and fair methods for broadening access to the education pipeline is still unsolved. Methodology/results: We take an operations approach to the problem different from most established literature, with the goal of increasing opportunities for students with high economic needs. Using data from the Department of Education (DOE) in New York City, we show that there is a shift in the distribution of scores obtained by students that the DOE classifies as “disadvantaged” (following criteria mostly based on socioeconomic factors). We model this shift as a “bias” that reflects an underestimation of the true potential of disadvantaged students. We analyze the impact this phenomenon has on an assortative matching market. We show that centrally planned interventions can significantly reduce the impact of bias through scholarships or training, when they target the segment of disadvantaged students with average performance. Managerial implications: To make these interventions incentive compatible and individually-fair, we propose a randomized policy for allocation of training resources to students, which is targeted more towards average performers. Our results challenge the existing notions of scholarships, asking for a closer look into resource allocation to students for a better access to education pipelines.

Title: Online Demand Fulfillment in Highly Asymmetric Markets
Authors: Hailun Zhang, Zhen Xu, Jiheng Zhang, Rachel Q. Zhang
Affiliations: School of Economics and Business Administration, Chongqing University, Chongqing, China; Management School, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom; Department of Industrial Engineering and Decision Analytics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Tsingshan Institute for Advanced Business Studies and School of Management, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: Problem definition: We study online demand fulfillment with limited flexibility in highly asymmetric markets, where some locations represented by the set [Formula: see text] have moderate to high market shares, whereas others have very low shares. Xu et al. was the first to establish that a positive generalized chaining gap (GCG) is a necessary and sufficient condition for bounded performance, which is defined as the expected lost sales as the total market size grows. Although a high GCG signals a better performance, the presence of high market asymmetry results in a low GCG and a larger performance bound, making the bound less useful for assessing actual system performance. Therefore, understanding system performance in highly asymmetric markets remains an important question. Methodology/results: We introduce a network condition called [Formula: see text]-connectivity, which ensures that after removing the markets with very low shares, the markets in [Formula: see text] are still connected through the available suppliers. We prove that [Formula: see text]-connectivity is both necessary and sufficient for maintaining bounded performance in highly asymmetric markets. This is achieved through a carefully designed online fulfillment policy that utilizes network partitioning and advanced analyses of mean-reverting processes using probability methods in an asymptotic context. Additionally, we offer strategies for network design to reduce the risk of [Formula: see text]-disconnectivity. Managerial implications: Our findings indicate that even the well-known long-chain structure may not ensure bounded performance in highly asymmetric markets, especially when low-demand markets are dispersed throughout the network. Instead, a “hub-and-spoke” network configuration with a shorter embedded long chain can help reduce the risk of [Formula: see text]-disconnectivity and enhance system performance. Funding: This research was supported in part by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72671048 and 72192805] and the Hong Kong Research Grants Council [Grants 16200617, 16200821, 16200019, and 16500225]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.1002 .

Title: Integrating Upstream and Downstream Planning to Increase Biomanufacturing Profitability
Authors: Mirko Schoemig-Beissner, Martin Grunow
Affiliations: TUM School of Management, Technical University of Munich, 80333 Munich, Germany; TUM School of Management, Munich Data Science Institute, Technical University of Munich, 80333 Munich, Germany
Abstract: Problem definition: Biomanufacturing uses biological systems, such as living cells, to produce an increasing number of products, including biopharmaceuticals. Industrial large-scale production occurs in two stages: the upstream fermentation process, where the product is formed in a nonlinear and stochastic manner, and the downstream purification process, where specialized resins are used but exhibit stochastic capacity decay. Despite their operational interdependence, both stages are often managed separately, neglecting the tradeoffs between upstream production and downstream purification capacity and their impact on profitability. Methodology/results: We develop a stochastic optimization model that integrates upstream harvesting, downstream purification, and resin replacement decisions using available process information. The problem is formulated as a discrete-time, infinite-horizon Markov decision process that maximizes long-term profitability. Exploiting the sigmoidal structure of product formation, we analytically characterize the optimal policy and show that there exist control-limit structures with intuitive bounds. We further compare integrated and separate decision-making and identify the economic conditions under which integration creates value. Numerical results for large-scale insulin production show that the integrated policy increases profits by approximately 4% compared with a condition-based but separate approach. Managerial implications: The optimal policy can be implemented as threshold-based rules using standard process measurements. Our results show that profitability requires coordinated decision-making across upstream fermentation and downstream purification and that focusing solely on upstream productivity or batch yield can lead to suboptimal outcomes. The value of integration is particularly high in low-margin environments, such as biosimilar production, where purification costs become economically critical. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.1395 .

Title: Flock Management for Solar Grazing
Authors: Vincent Slaugh, Linwei Xin, Shane Henderson
Affiliations: SC Johnson College of Business, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853; School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14853
Abstract: Problem definition: To control vegetation, solar asset owners employ farmers to graze sheep on solar sites. Whereas earning grazing revenue, farmers also provide agricultural value through raising and selling sheep. By accounting for flock dynamics of births, deaths, and sales, we model the operational economics of solar grazing for farmers and focus on key flock management decisions. Methodology/results: We model solar grazing operations as a finite-horizon linear program that jointly optimizes initial procurement decisions and subsequent sales decisions subject to age-structured flock dynamics and a target flock-size constraint. During the flock growth phase, the breed-versus-buy decision involves weighing the up-front costs and anticipated revenue from lamb and sheep sales against the heightened costs of vegetation management when the flock size is below its target level. By analyzing this trade-off, we demonstrate that the farmer’s total profit function is piecewise linear and concave in the number of sheep initially purchased externally. Beyond the flock growth phase, we prove that an optimal steady-state solution exhibits a maximum lifetime structure: ewes are retained up to a maximal age, and sales are restricted to lambs and final-year ewes. Finally, we extend the model to incorporate stochastic births and deaths, showing that a linear programming approach yields a tight bound on achievable performance in the stochastic model for large flocks and long horizons, and provide a practical policy that performs strongly in numerical examples. Managerial implications: Our results help small-scale farmers, renewable energy developers, and policymakers understand how solar grazing enhances the environmental benefits of solar farms, preserving agricultural value on land converted to solar use. In partnership with a solar-grazing platform that supports solar grazers and connects them with site owners, a spreadsheet implementation of our model has helped dozens of farmers make procurement decisions, predict cash flows, and even secure financing to purchase a flock. Funding: This work was partially supported by the National Science Foundation [Grant OAC 2410950]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2025.0305 .

Title: “Clean” Meat? Regulatory Entrepreneurship and Jurisdictional Contestation in a Nascent Industry
Authors: Cheng Gao, Alicia DeSantola, Nina Guilbeault
Affiliations: University of Michigan, USA; University of Washington, USA; Former Lecturer, UC Berkeley, USA
Abstract: In nascent industries, uncertainty about which regulatory agency has jurisdiction is often a major challenge for pioneering ventures. Yet, much of the literature on new ventures’ nonmarket strategy takes for granted the existence of a designated regulator. How do ventures manage regulatory jurisdictional uncertainty? We conduct an inductive, multi-case research study on how entrepreneurial organizations pioneering the nascent cell-cultivated-meat industry navigated such uncertainty in the United States between 2015 and 2019. Drawing on extensive semi-structured interviews and archival data, we uncover stratagems and processes that organizations employ across three phases of regulatory jurisdictional uncertainty: jurisdictional void, contestation, and convergence. Our resulting theoretical framework distinguishes two overarching strategies— complementary and oppositional —and unpacks their underlying mechanisms, theorizing how they enable organizations to influence jurisdictional uncertainty. Our study uniquely elucidates the rich dynamics among the disparate actors that compose nascent technology-enabled industries: new ventures, nonprofits, incumbents, investors, and regulators. More broadly, it provides a fresh perspective on how entrepreneurial organizations shape the regulatory architecture of the industries they are striving to create.

Title: Designing for unanticipated uses: How product attributes shape community‐led exaptation
Authors: Shi‐Ying Lim, Tian Heong Chan
Affiliations: School of Computing, National University of Singapore Singapore; Goizueta Business School, Emory University Atlanta Georgia USA
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Users often discover new uses for products that firms may later commercialize, which we call community‐led exaptation. We examine how product attributes shape users' discovery of new functions versus new functionalities. Using 1925 IKEA product hacks, we find that modularity increases the likelihood of new functions. This effect strengthens when product components are compatible across product lines but weakens when esthetic product variants exist. Visual simplicity, conversely, increases the likelihood of new functionalities. These findings suggest that firms can structure the opportunity space for discovery through product design. Exploratory analysis of archival data and interviews further illustrates how IKEA responds to these discoveries. We contribute to exaptation, user innovation, and design research by showing how product attributes shape the types of new uses communities discover. Managerial Summary How can firms design products to facilitate community‐led exaptation? We find that product attributes can shape what users discover. Modular products enable users to find new functions (i.e., applications), while visually simple products enable users to find new functionalities (i.e., new product capabilities). Firms' decisions to offer components that are compatible across product lines and esthetic product variants can influence the likelihood of new functions. Additionally, firms can capitalize on these new uses by showcasing promising community‐discovered functions on official channels or incorporate them as complements to existing product lines. However, functional modifications can raise safety concerns and may require additional development. Firms should therefore design for intended use, and for the kinds of new uses they are willing to seed and commercialize.

Title: Correction to “Revisiting Zuckerman's (1999) categorical imperative: An application of epistemic maps for replication”
Forbearance and the cost of credit
Authors: Pedro Gete, Andrey Pavlov, Athena Tsouderou, Susan Wachter
Affiliations: IE University Department of Finance, , Madrid, Spain; and Department of Finance, Durham University Business School, Durham; Beedie School of Business, Simon Fraser University Department of Finance, , Burnaby, British Columbia; University of Miami Business School, University of Miami Department of Finance, , Coral Gables, Florida; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania Real Estate and Finance Departments, , Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
Abstract: Abstract Using novel data from the GSE Credit Risk Transfer (CRT) market and the enactment of the 2020 CARES Act as a natural experiment, we study the ex ante pricing of mortgage forbearance. We show that private investors demanded higher compensation for bearing mortgage credit risk following the introduction of federal mortgage forbearance. The increase in CRT spreads was larger for securities with greater exposure to judicial foreclosure regimes, lower expected house price growth, higher house price volatility, and riskier borrowers. These patterns suggest that investors priced heightened uncertainty regarding future collateral values and recovery outcomes. We find little evidence that the response was driven by broader financial market conditions, prepayment risk, servicer liquidity concerns, or strategic forbearance take-up. Our findings show how borrower-protection policies are transmitted to mortgage markets through the pricing of mortgage credit risk.

Title: Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the Metco Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
Authors: Elizabeth Setren
Affiliations: Tufts University and NBER
Abstract: Abstract School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts, to relatively wealthier and predominantly white suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher-achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower-performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

Title: Option Value of Auditing: Evidence from Post-Audit Career Advancement
Authors: Jingwen Yang
Affiliations: The Pennsylvania State University
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies the career trajectories of individuals who exit auditing. Using individual-level employment data, I document that ex-auditors transition into a range of positions, especially in accounting and finance, and that ex-auditors who transition into accounting or finance roles are more likely to be promoted than peers in the same roles without an auditing background. These results suggest that auditing experience is not only associated with varied career options but also with advancement in those options. These promotion advantages are more pronounced for ex-auditors who obtained relevant industry or regional exposure through auditing, who were affiliated with Big N audit firms or with audit offices with greater market share or task complexity, who have three to five years of audit tenure, or who transitioned into positions with greater skill overlap with auditing. Together, this paper provides large-sample descriptive evidence that sheds light on the option value of auditing. Data Availability: Data are available from the commercial data providers identified in the paper. JEL Classifications: J24; J62; M42.

Title: From global to local? Designing optimal climate-linked industrial policy for global supply chains under sustainability gaps
Authors: Yifan Cao, Xiaoyan Xu
Abstract: In developed countries, local sourcing is typically more expensive than global alternatives due to sustainability gaps in supplier carbon intensity. Climate policies seek to promote cleaner inputs through incentives such as consumer tax credits, but their effectiveness on economic efficiency and climate externalities remains uncertain. To address this, we develop a game-theoretical model of a local original equipment manufacturer (OEM) that allocates orders between a less sustainable, cost-efficient global supplier and a more sustainable, costlier local supplier, subject to a government-imposed eligibility threshold that conditions consumer tax credits. Our analysis reveals a non-decreasing, three-zone structure for the optimal threshold: it starts at zero in emerging markets, rises gradually in transitional markets, and maximizes in mature markets. Complete localization arises only when the sustainability gap is narrow, while wider gaps restrict thresholds to an interior value to avoid disengagement. Stricter thresholds always increase economic surplus, but emission reductions occur only in intermediate-scale markets, especially when supplier sustainability differs substantially. Extending the model to competitive settings, we find that under global competition, localization policies take effect sooner but reach the maximum value more slowly, while local competition accelerates both the initiation and finalization of the localization process. Competition also alters economic and environmental effects: economic efficiency initially declines with market growth before recovering, and stricter thresholds fail to reduce emissions due to either policy exemptions or reduced output responsiveness. These results underscore that effective climate policy must be adaptive and aligned with market maturity, competition, and supplier characteristics.

Title: Competitive implications of spectrum subleasing on pricing, quality and sourcing decisions
Authors: Manish Tripathy, Hans Sebastian Heese, Tim Kraft
Abstract: In the last decade, a new class of service providers, known as Mobile Virtual Network Operators (MVNOs), has emerged in the cellular market. MVNOs minimize infrastructure investments by subleasing bandwidth from traditional Mobile Network Operators (MNOs). In this paper, we study a duopoly cellular service market in which two MNOs compete on price and quality while potentially subleasing spectrum to an MVNO. The MNOs decide the price for their own service as well as the quality level and wholesale price to offer the MVNO. We consider two MNO pricing cases: (i) No Anticipation, where the MNOs ignore the MVNO's potential entry in setting retail prices, and (ii) Anticipation, where they account for the MVNO's entry. The MVNO decides where to source from and the price to set for its service. Using a vertically differentiated spatial model of product positioning, we examine how service quality, price, and market structure change with the presence of an MVNO. We find that the MVNO never sources from only the low-quality MNO. Instead, the MVNO chooses between sourcing from the high-quality MNO or from both MNOs based on the benefits of bundling spectrum and the MVNO's reputation. If the interaction of the two significantly enhances the MVNO's quality, the MVNO sources from both; otherwise, it sources only from the high-quality MNO. We find that all firms can coexist in the No Anticipation case; however, the low-quality MNO can be pushed out of the market under the Anticipation case if the MVNO's reputation is sufficiently high.

Title: Deep reinforcement learning for aging cheese inventory management under correlated prices
Authors: Alexander Pahr, Paula Krumm, Anna Kolemesina, Martin Grunow
Abstract: In aging cheese inventory management, producers must jointly consider auto-correlated and cross-correlated prices for raw milk and age-differentiated cheese products. Issuance flexibility arises because the cheese age label specifies a minimum maturation time, allowing deliberate target-age excess. We develop a generic Markov decision process model for ameliorating inventory systems that captures auto-correlated and cross-correlated purchase and sales prices. Because state and action spaces grow exponentially in the number of age classes, we use deep reinforcement learning (DRL). However, standard actor-critic DRL algorithms struggle with the high-dimensional action spaces induced by issuance flexibility. For a reduced two-period hedging problem, we prove that the value of issuance flexibility declines with purchase-price auto-correlation. Building on this result, we develop two dimensionality reduction approaches. The first curtails issuance flexibility, whereas the second retains it via actor pipelining, with issuance actions determined by simple decision rules. On average, actor pipelining provides the best trade-off between policy quality and computational effort. Further, full factorial experiments reveal that, in contrast to prior work, the benefit of issuance flexibility is limited under cheese-specific price processes. It becomes substantial only in highly volatile, fast mean-reverting environments and can be omitted entirely in highly correlated settings. Additionally, we show that multi-agent actor designs provide limited value at substantially higher computational cost. Our DRL policies outperform a rolling-horizon planning benchmark by 16.7% on average. Moreover, modeling cheese-specific price dynamics yields a 7.1% profit improvement over simplified price assumptions.

Title: How Does Wage Inequality Affect the Labor Movement?
Authors: Barbara Biasi, Zoë Cullen, Julia Gilman, Nina Roussille
Affiliations: Yale University School of Management and National Bureau of Economic Research; Harvard Business School and National Bureau of Economic Research; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Massachusetts Institute of Technology and National Bureau of Economic Research
Abstract: Abstract This article provides evidence on how wage inequality among workers affects the labor movement, drawing on three complementary research designs: a vignette experiment with union organizers, a natural policy experiment that increased wage inequality among Wisconsin school teachers, and an information intervention during the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike. Across all studies, we find that inequality undermines union strength through multiple channels. First, among workers, those with high individual bargaining power are more likely to withdraw support in unequal environments, preferring individual over collective bargaining. Second, among union organizers, those facing hypothetical choices strategically respond to inequality in ways that may preserve membership but limit redistribution, such as shifting their campaign away from wages and choosing smaller, more homogeneous bargaining units.

Title: Catch Me if You Can! The Economic Analysis of Geofencing
Authors: Yi-Jen (Ian) Ho, Xiangjing (Olivia) Chen, Shengjun Mao
Affiliations: Harbert College of Business, Auburn University, Auburn, Alabama 36849; Rawls College of Business, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas 79409; Faculty of Business and Economics, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China
Abstract: Geofencing is widely used to reach nearby consumers, but our research shows that proximity alone should not determine where advertisers target. Using a game-theoretic model, we identify when geofencing is preferable to mass advertising and how businesses should configure it based on product attractiveness, consumer awareness, and location. When awareness is low, geofencing improves returns by concentrating advertising on the consumers most likely to respond. As awareness becomes uneven across locations, however, the best geofence may not be centered on the business itself. We introduce flexible geofencing, which allows advertisers to target a distant market when local consumers already know the business, but remote consumers do not. This strategy can generate higher advertising returns than traditional store-centered geofencing and, in most cases, increase consumer surplus and social welfare. The findings offer practical guidance for restaurants, retailers, parks, museums, healthcare providers, and public agencies seeking to allocate advertising budgets more efficiently. For policymakers, the analysis also highlights a potential exception: Remote targeting can sometimes reduce consumer surplus by overlooking uninformed local consumers, suggesting a role for initiatives that maintain local awareness.

Title: Attention Trap? How Visual Motion Shapes Children’s Screen Time and Engagement on Video Platforms
Authors: Sumeet Kumar, Madhu Viswanathan, Ravi Bapna
Affiliations: Indian School of Business, Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Telangana 500032, India; Leavey School of Business, Santa Clara University, Santa Clara, California 95053
Abstract: Children spend considerable time watching online video, yet we know relatively little about which features of video content shape their engagement. This research examines one measurable feature: visual motion. Analyzing more than 32,000 videos from popular children’s channels on YouTube, we find that videos with greater visual motion receive more views, even after accounting for other visual, audio, and content characteristics. A randomized YouTube advertising experiment using professionally produced educational videos confirms this relationship; adding motion to the background increased view rates by about 2% at essentially no additional cost. An eye-tracking study with children aged 6–10 helps explain why. Visual motion does not prevent children from looking away. Instead, it reduces the duration of longer attentional lapses by bringing their gaze back to the screen more quickly. The additional attention is directed primarily toward the moving background rather than the instructor. The findings show how a measurable design feature can shape children’s attention and provide creators and platforms with a way to assess and design children’s video content more systematically.

Title: Thank You, Now What? How Donors Respond to Calls to Action
Authors: K. Sudhir, Hortense Fong, Yonat Zwebner, Subroto Roy
Affiliations: Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut 06520; Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Reichman University, Herzliya, Israel 4610101; University of New Haven, West Haven, Connecticut 06516
Abstract: We study whether thank-you communications that charities send to past donors should include a call to action and show that the answer depends on whether the donor has already given in the current giving cycle.

Title: The Power of Data: Assessing Primary Care Performance Using Routinely Collected Emergency Department Data
Authors: Nicos Savva, Sandra Sülz, Mark Kinirons, Emer Sutherland, Richard Leach
Affiliations: Management Science & Operations, London Business School, London NW1 4SA, United Kingdom; Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management, Erasmus University, 3062 PA Rotterdam, Netherlands; Guy’s and St. Thomas’ National Health Service Foundation Trust and Kings College London, London SE1 7EH, United Kingdom; King’s College Hospital, London WC2R 2LS, United Kingdom
Abstract: This paper develops and validates an approach to assess the impact of individual primary care practices (PCPs) on demand for emergency department (ED) services. Using operational data from two geographically adjacent EDs in England, we focus on attendances for ambulatory care-sensitive (ACS) conditions, which are more appropriately and cost-effectively treated outside the ED. We employ a variance-decomposition approach that controls for observed and unobserved heterogeneity and explicitly accounts for socioeconomic differences. The analysis shows that approximately 52% of the variation in ACS attendance proportions is attributable to systematic differences across PCPs and that these differences are operationally meaningful. Using this methodology, we construct a PCP-level measure of systematic variation in ACS attendances and show that it correlates with patient feedback from National Health Service surveys, Quality and Outcomes Framework scores, and PCP staffing decisions. This measure outperforms existing metrics based on ACS admissions in identifying PCP-level variation and is robust to alternative modeling choices. The modular nature of the approach allows it to be applied to data from one or multiple hospitals, providing policymakers with a practical tool to evaluate PCP-level interventions and their downstream effects on ED demand. This paper was accepted by Carri Chan, healthcare management. Title: The Asymmetric Nature of Social Hierarchies: Unpacking the Dynamic Relationship Between Power and Status
Authors: Rebecca L. Mitchell, James G. Matusik, Nicholas A. Hays
Affiliations: Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, Colorado 80304; Terry College of Business, University of Georgia, Athens, Georgia 30602; Broad College of Business, Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan 48824
Abstract: Scholars and practitioners alike have long presumed that power and status, two foundational bases of social hierarchy, share a symmetric, mutually reinforcing relationship. However, support for this presumption has largely taken the form of theoretical accounts due to the prevalence of static research designs and a dearth of dynamic methodology in organizational research. Drawing on the Dual Perspective Model, we propose that one’s status is more likely to drive changes in one’s power than vice versa because status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status. Using data from two studies involving project teams and a contemporary methodology from developmental psychology for modeling dynamic relationships (bivariate dual change score models), we illustrate that there is indeed a mutually reinforcing relationship between power and status over time, but this relationship is asymmetric. In three additional experiments, we find that perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry. We also find similar effects whether power is formal—attached to a position or role—or involves control over informal resources. Across all studies, we find that the path from status to changes in power is stronger than the path from power to changes in status.

Title: What can macro-active bond funds tell us about monetary policy change?
Authors: Claire Yurong Hong, Jun Pan, Shiwen Tian
Abstract: This paper focuses on actively managed bond mutual funds, whose performance is most sensitive to monetary policy shocks. We document significant and persistent FOMC-day outperformance by macro-active bond funds, which is particularly pronounced during periods of heightened macroeconomic disagreement and attention. Consistent with their forecasting ability, these funds’ pre-FOMC portfolio duration adjustments can predict FOMC-day monetary policy shocks beyond the information offered by economic data and asset returns. Furthermore, we show that this macro-investing skill extends to GDP and CPI announcements and is consistently shared across various fund styles within fund families.

Title: Timeless: Karl Weick's Enduring Influence on Management Studies
Authors: Joep Cornelissen, Johann Fortwengel
Affiliations: Erasmus University; University of Liverpool Management School; King's College London; University of Pretoria
Abstract: Abstract The essay by Patriotta and Weick (2026) constitutes one of the last scholarly contributions by Karl Weick. In this Introduction, we position the essay vis‐à‐vis Weick's broader scholarship, and we outline how the ideas articulated in this piece complement theorizing on sensemaking. We also reflect on the more general influence of Weick on scholarship in management studies, including work published in JMS . We develop the argument that Weick's enduring legacy is not only confined to the introduction and articulation of some core and highly influential ideas to the field, but that his distinct ways of thinking, writing, and interpretation of what it means to be a scholar will have an at least equally lasting impact on present and future generations. In particular, in the age of artificial intelligence and the acceleration of academia, we propose that we have much to learn from Weick's mode of scholarship. In this sense, Weick's influence will be timeless and enduring; spanning concepts, the idea of having a distinct voice, and a model of scholarship.

Title: Heavy Time: Sensemaking and the Temporal Experience
Authors: Gerardo Patriotta, Karl E. Weick
Affiliations: University of Bath; University of Michigan

Title: Direct and Indirect Effects of Transparency Regulation
Authors: Matthias Breuer, Patricia Breuer
Abstract: We examine the direct and indirect effects of transparency regulation on economic activity. Using two distinct sources of regulatory variation—the varying extent of financial-reporting requirements and the staggered introduction of electronic business registers in Europe—, we find that direct exposure to transparency regulation tends to hurt focal firms’ economic activity (e.g., production and employment). By contrast, we find that indirect exposure to transparency regulation imposed on other related firms tends to help focal firms’ economic activity. In terms of relative magnitudes, we find that the negative direct and positive indirect effects tend to be of similar size, almost perfectly offsetting each other. Collectively, our evidence suggests that transparency regulation appears to primarily reallocate economic activity from more toward less regulated markets rather than help or hurt aggregate economic activity.

Title: Analyst visibility and earnings forecast quality
Authors: Qiang Cheng, Tian Deng, Sterling Huang, An-Ping Lin
Abstract: Abstract This study examines how a reduction in analysts’ visibility, resulting from brokerages’ switch to anonymous forecasts on Eikon, affects earnings forecast quality. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that treatment analysts respond by issuing more accurate forecasts in the post-anonymization period. Treatment analysts who improve forecast quality the most can sustain visibility, as reflected in their coverage by the financial media, enhance their likelihood of being voted as star analysts, and induce greater client trading. These results are consistent with analysts’ incentives to offset the reduced visibility so as to advance their careers and increase trading commissions for their brokerages. We further show that treatment analysts use a set of visibility-enhancing strategies, including issuing broader and more frequent forecasts and setting bolder target prices. Our findings suggest that reduced visibility can prompt analysts to respond strategically in ways that can improve information quality.

Title: When the market moves: How stock market fluctuations shape risk-related behaviors at work.
Authors: Joseph Kichul Kim, Joel Koopman, Kyoung Yong Kim, Ran Ahn, Youngduk Lee
Abstract: How employees' personal stock holdings perform during the day has become increasingly visible and accessible, yet research has rarely examined how fluctuations in those holdings shape employees' experiences at work. Integrating cross-domain spillover and regulatory focus theories, we propose that morning fluctuation in personal stock holdings spills over into the workplace by influencing employees' risk propensity-their willingness to take or avoid risks-and, in turn, their risk-related workplace behaviors. Specifically, drawing from regulatory focus theory, we propose that a more positive (vs. negative) fluctuation in personal stock holdings than usual is associated with subsequent increases (vs. decreases) in employees' willingness to engage in risk. In a 10-day experience sampling study of full-time employees who personally invest in the South Korean stock market, a more positive morning fluctuation in stock holding value than they typically experience predicted higher state risk propensity, which subsequently led to greater risk-taking behavior and voice. These indirect effects were moderated by long-term orientation, such that employees lower (vs. higher) in long-term orientation showed greater sensitivity to morning fluctuation in stock holding value. We then conducted two complementary experiments that supported the theorized regulatory focus mechanism by demonstrating that more positive fluctuation in personal stock holdings elicited promotion focus, whereas more negative fluctuation heightened prevention focus, and that these motivational states subsequently shaped employees' willingness to engage in risk. Together, these findings highlight employees' personal stock holdings as an overlooked source of daily behavioral variability at work. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

Title: Universal Portfolio Shrinkage
Authors: Bryan Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Mo Pourmohammadi, Fabio Trojani
Affiliations: Yale School of Management, AQR Capital Management, and NBER , the; Swiss Finance Institute and EPFL , Switzerland, and , London; CEPR , Switzerland, and , London; Yale School of Management , the; University of Geneva and Swiss Finance Institute
Abstract: Abstract We introduce a nonlinear covariance shrinkage method for building optimal portfolios. Our universal portfolio shrinkage approximator (UPSA) is built from closed-form basis portfolios, is cheap to implement, and improves on existing shrinkage methods. Rather than uniformly penalizing all principal components of returns or discarding low-variance ones, UPSA instead reweights components to explicitly optimize expected out-of-sample portfolio performance. In empirical applications using a large cross-section of anomaly factors, it delivers robust improvements over alternative shrinkage methods in the literature.

Title: Affordable Housing, Unaffordable Credit? Concentration and High-Cost Lending for Manufactured Homes
Authors: Sebastian Doerr, Andreas Fuster
Affiliations: Bank for International Settlements , Switzerland, and CEPR; University of Zurich and Swiss Finance Institute , Switzerland, and CEPR
Abstract: Abstract This paper shows that high market concentration in the U.S. manufactured home loan market allows lenders to charge markedly higher interest rates than in the mortgage market for site-built homes. Borrowers in counties with higher lender concentration face significantly higher rates, and evidence from bunching at a regulatory rate threshold, an instrumental variable analysis, and a difference-in-differences analysis suggests a causal link. Integrated lenders, which play an outsized role in this market, charge particularly high rates, and we provide evidence suggesting that these lenders exploit their market power over borrowers. We discuss factors that may explain limited lender entry.

Title: Original Sin Redux: Role of Duration Risk
Authors: Carol Bertaut, Valentina Bruno, Hyun Song Shin
Affiliations: Federal Reserve Board; American University and NBER, the United States, and CEPR; Bank for International Settlements
Abstract: Abstract We highlight the role of duration and exchange rate risks on portfolio flows by using a unique and comprehensive database of U.S. investor flows into emerging market government bonds denominated in local currency. Borrowing long-term mitigates rollover risk but amplifies valuation changes that further interact with currency movements. Our analysis highlights the double-edged nature of long-term borrowing and draws attention to market stress dynamics due to strategic complementarities among mutual fund investors.

Title: Book Review: Ilana Redstone. The Certainty Trap: Why We Need to Question Ourselves More—and How We Can Judge Others Less RedstoneI. (2024). The certainty trap: Why we need to question ourselves more—and how we can judge others less. Pitchstone Publishing. 248 pp. ISBN 9781634312561.
Authors: Rellie Derfler-Rozin
Affiliations: Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland, College Park, MD
Abstract: To state that we live in troubled and deeply polarized times in the United States and other countries has become almost a cliché.The underlying conditions that give rise to this observation remain pressing: Political and social discourse increasingly oscillates between extremes, hate crimes are on the rise (Farrell & Lockwood, 2023), and trust in institutions (Brady & Kent, 2022), including educational institutions, has eroded over time. 1 As a scholar who has researched and taught negotiation and conflict resolution for more than a decade, I found this book to be particularly timely.Research on dialogue and conflict resolution has largely emphasized the importance of civic discourse (e.g., Weaver et al., 2023), perspective-taking (e.g., Longmire & Harrison, 2018), and understanding the moral foundations underlying political disagreement (Graham et al., 2013).Several of these approaches, particularly Moral Foundations Theory and the emphasis on moral humility, intersect with arguments advanced in Redstone's book.At the same time, the book departs in important ways from dominant assumptions in the literature.Redstone contends that encouraging respectful discourse, while necessary, is insufficient for conflict resolution.Instead, she advocates engaging in deeper introspection, with particular emphasis on cultivating comfort with uncertainty.This emphasis on uncertainty represents a notable departure from scholarship on the motivation for resolving and reducing uncertainty (e.g., FeldmanHall & Shenhav, 2019).Redstone's argument is compelling: The contexts in which uncertainty feels most intolerable-discussions of highly charged social and political issues-are precisely those in which embracing uncertainty is most essential.A related departure from existing research is her claim that combating misinformation and disinformation, while important, should not be the primary focus of efforts to reduce polarization.Instead, she suggests that learning to live with uncertainty addresses the deeper source of the problem and may, as a secondary effect, enhance individuals' ability to evaluate and discern information.Redstone uses examples from both the political right and left, coupled with her insistence that no group holds moral superiority.She emphasizes the shared responsibility of recognizing the certainty trap and taking steps to avoid it.Redstone articulates the certainty trap through three interrelated fallacies: the settled question fallacy, the fallacy of equal knowledge, and the fallacy of known intent.The settled question fallacy refers to the tendency to treat complex issues as though they have already been conclusively resolved.Resisting this fallacy requires the ability to ask questions openly without being demonized (p.11).Importantly, Redstone emphasizes that rejecting the settled question fallacy does notBook Review 1488839A

Title: Generative Search: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
Authors: Shuang Zheng, Yuting Zhu, Xin Ye, Liang Shen
Affiliations: School of Business, Renmin University of China, Beijing 100086, China; and DUT School of Economics and Management, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian City 116024, China; and Meituan, Beijing 100102, China; NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119245; DUT School of Economics and Management, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian City 116024, China; Meituan, Beijing 100102, China
Abstract: Generative search is an emerging search paradigm that integrates Generative AI (GenAI) into traditional search engines by presenting users with AI-generated responses before conventional search results. Whereas keyword-based search requires consumers to translate their underlying needs into effective keyword queries, generative search lets users express those intentions directly in natural language, a shift made possible by GenAI’s new mode of information presentation. This shift moves the consumer-search engine interaction upstream to the stage of problem formulation, rendering empirically observable a previously hidden phase of search behavior: the mapping from problem formulation to keyword articulation. Yet, it remains empirically unknown whether generative search increases consumer purchases and how search behavior changes when it can begin from expressed intent rather than keywords. Using a large-scale field experiment conducted on Meituan, a leading Chinese technology platform, this paper provides empirical evidence on the effectiveness of generative search. We find that generative search significantly increases consumer purchases. Further analysis reveals that generative search facilitates more effective and diverse keyword queries and reduces exploratory browsing and clicking, while concentrating evaluation within relevant categories and merchants. The empirical evidence is most consistent with a mechanism in which AI-generated answers provide information about consumers’ underlying needs, while also expanding awareness of relevant attributes and shifting attention toward more relevant categories. These findings provide empirical insights for future consumer search models that allow search to originate at the intention-expressing stage. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing.
