Title: Structural Estimation of Intertemporal Externalities with Application in ICU Admissions
Authors: Yiwen Shen, Carri W. Chan, Fanyin Zheng, Gabriel Escobar
Affiliations: School of Business and Management, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Clear Water Bay, Kowloon, Hong Kong; Decision, Risk, and Operations, Columbia Business School, New York, New York 10027; Imperial Business School, Imperial College London, London SW7 2BX, United Kingdom; Division of Research, Kaiser Permanente, Oakland, California 94612
Abstract: Problem definition: In many service systems, the system manager needs to balance between addressing the needs of current customers and ensuring the system’s ability to serve future customers. Such balancing behavior is particularly important in capacity-constrained systems with heterogeneous service levels, in which the manager needs to decide which level of service to provide to the current customer, taking into account the intertemporal externalities of their decisions. Methodology/results: We develop a dynamic discrete choice model to describe the decision-making process in a gatekeeper system with multiple classes of servers and customers. The discount factor in the model captures how much the decision maker internalizes the intertemporal externalities of their customer routing decisions. In contrast to most empirical studies in the literature that use a prespecified discount factor, we establish joint identification of the discount factor and the utility parameters from data. We then apply the model to empirically study the intensive care unit (ICU) admission decisions for emergency department (ED) patients. Using a large hospitalization data set, we find that there is large heterogeneity in the estimated discount factors across hospitals. Via counterfactual simulations, we show that understanding the balancing behavior from data are important for hospitals to manage their ICU congestion. Managerial implications: Our results suggest that it is important to understand how the decision maker internalizes the intertemporal externalities from data. In addition, the balancing behavior regarding current customers and future available capacity provides a potential channel for improving system performance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/msom.2024.0891 .

Title: Two-Sided Pricing and Learning with Buyer Choice: A Generalized SGD Method
Authors: Meichun Lin, Woonghee Tim Huh
Affiliations: Lee Kong Chian School of Business, Singapore Management University, Singapore 178899; Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia V6T 1Z4, Canada
Abstract: Learning to Price in Two-Sided Markets Many two-sided platforms set purchase prices for sellers and selling prices for buyers. In “Two-Sided Pricing and Learning with Buyer Choice: A Generalized SGD Method,” Lin and Huh study how platforms can make these decisions when responses on both sides are uncertain and must be learned from limited data. They first show that, when supply and demand models are known, simple fixed-price policies that match expected supply and demand can be asymptotically optimal. Building on this insight, the authors develop a novel generalization of classical stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for learning a fixed-price policy. Unlike standard SGD, their method does not require the construction of a strongly convex objective function. This flexibility allows it to accommodate demand interactions arising from buyer choice. The resulting learning algorithm is near-optimal when the planning horizon is large.

Title: Robust extensible bin packing and a convex knapsack problem
Authors: Noam Goldberg, Michael Poss, Yariv N. Marmor
Abstract: We study a robust extensible bin packing problem, under a budget uncertainty model where item sizes lie in the intersection of a box with a one-norm ball. We design an algorithm based on the column-and-constraint generation framework, which alternates between solving a master robust bin-packing problem with a finite uncertainty set and solving a separation problem. We show that the separation is strongly NP-hard given solutions to the continuous relaxation of the master problem. Then, focusing on the separation problem for the integer master problem, we show that this problem becomes a special case of the continuous convex knapsack problem, which is known to be weakly NP-hard. Next, we prove that our special case remains NP-hard. We develop a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program (DP) and a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for our special case whose running times match those of the binary knapsack problem. Finally, our computational study shows that the DP can be significantly more efficient in practice compared with solving the problem with specially ordered set (SOS) constraints using advanced mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers. Our experiments also demonstrate the application of our separation problem method to solving the robust extensible bin packing problem, including separating based on approximate master solutions in intermediate iterations. We further enhance the algorithm by proposing custom symmetry breaking inequalities, valid when bins have identical costs per unit of excess capacity. Finally, a case-study, based on real elective surgery data, demonstrates the potential advantage of our model compared with the actual schedule and optimal nominal schedules.

Title: Sustainable organizations
Authors: Thomas Geelen, Jakub Hajda, Jan Starmans
Abstract: We develop a theory of stakeholder governance examining how green stakeholders influence organizations. Conflicts of interest arise from heterogeneous green preferences and intensify as they diverge. Changes in green preferences can generate unexpected outcomes by shifting control rights: greener stakeholders may reduce organizational sustainability, while browner ones might enhance it. We show that a top-down approach consistently improves organizational sustainability, while a bottom-up approach can harm it. We also uncover an asymmetry in compensation and delegation decisions between green and brown principals, driven by the public good nature of social payoffs. These findings have implications for manager–employee, investor–entrepreneur, and board–CEO relationships.

Title: Bankruptcy lawyers and credit recovery
Authors: Brian Jonghwan Lee
Abstract: I study how bankruptcy law firm advertisements affect household credit, exploiting the borders of local TV advertisement media markets. I document a significant advertising effect on filing rates and subsequently show that ad exposure is associated with better financial outcomes. I then characterize how ad-induced filers are different from existing filers in terms of case, financial, and credit variables. I find that ad-induced filers are more likely to receive a discharge, file with lawyer representation, and be first-time filers. I interpret these findings as evidence that bankruptcy law firm advertisements help mitigate frictions in the bankruptcy decision.

Title: Old and connected versus young and creative: Networks and the diffusion of new scientific ideas
Authors: Wei Cheng, Bruce A. Weinberg
Abstract: The adoption of new ideas is essential for progress and involves innovators, potential adopters, and their networks. We apply natural language processing, network analysis, and a novel fixed effects strategy to study how career age affects idea adoption in coauthorship networks in biomedical science. At short network distances (≤3 steps away), young innovators' ideas are adopted the most while, at greater distances, mid-career innovators' ideas have the highest adoption. The main reason for this contrast is that young potential adopters are disproportionately likely to adopt new ideas introduced by nearby young innovators. Simulations show that the aging of innovators and of potential adopters have comparable effects on the adoption of important new ideas.

Title: Platform development in incumbent firms: The interplay of data and actor interests in adding platforms to existing businesses
Authors: Jack Fraser, Elizabeth J. Altman, Pinar Ozcan
Affiliations: Imperial Business School Imperial College London London UK; Manning School of Business University of Massachusetts Lowell Lowell Massachusetts USA; Saïd Business School University of Oxford Oxford UK
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite growing interest in platform transitions, limited research examines how firms navigate challenges of building platform businesses alongside existing products. Through a longitudinal case study of a financial services firm launching a platform, we develop a process model revealing how data bottlenecks shape platform development. These bottlenecks arise from the interplay of technological limitations and control tensions over data aggregation, sharing, and usage. We identify five sequential bottlenecks, where resolving one reconfigures constraints, giving rise to the next. We theorize how data heterogeneity, variation in strategic sensitivity, and actors' absorptive capacity create opportunities for platform sponsors to capture value without competing with complementors. We extend resource dependency theory by showing how peripheral units overcome power imbalances by demonstrating value creation potential with limited data. Managerial Summary When established firms launch platforms alongside existing product businesses, they face significant data‐related obstacles. Drawing on a four‐year study of a financial services firm building a platform connecting SMEs with lenders, we show how firms must navigate challenges in collecting data from internal units and customers, making incompatible data sources work together, and persuading partners to share and use data in new ways. We find that these obstacles emerge in sequence, where resolving one creates the conditions for the next. We also find that not all data is equally useful to all partners, and that these differences can open market segments the platform sponsor can serve without competing with its own partners. Managers can maintain momentum by combining short‐term data workarounds with longer‐term structural solutions.

Title: Political Connections, Financial Constraints, and Corporate Taxation
Authors: Ke Na, Terry Shevlin, Youan Wang, Zigan Wang
Affiliations: Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business; University of California Irvine; Xiamen University; Zhejiang University Tsinghua University
Abstract: Abstract We find that the effect of political connections on tax planning depends on firms’ financial conditions. After increased political connections, financially unconstrained firms increase tax planning and spending on tax services, as documented in prior studies, whereas constrained firms decrease tax planning and spending on tax services. Moreover, decreases in tax planning are only present for constrained firms that obtain new bank loans and public debt and when the connected politicians serve on banking-related committees. Our results suggest that by facilitating access to external financing, political connections reduce financially constrained firms’ use of tax planning as an internal financing tool.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Connected Social Media
Authors: Zhiqian Jiang, Baixiao Liu, Yuchen Xu, Bohui Zhang
Affiliations: Xiamen University School of Management; Peking University HSBC Business School; University of New South Wales UNSW Business School; The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-Shenzhen), School of Management and Economics and Shenzhen Finance Institute
Abstract: Abstract We examine whether and how firms use connected social media outlets to counteract negative coverage in traditional media. Employing a sample of Chinese listed firms with ties to social media outlets, we find that connected outlets portray firms more favorably than unconnected ones. Following unfavorable coverage in traditional media, connected outlets shift attention toward long-term prospects and promote favorable narratives, consistent with an optimism-shifting mechanism. The effect is more pronounced when firms have stronger incentives to stabilize stock prices and when managers face heightened career concerns. Our findings highlight the role of connected social media outlets in shaping corporate narratives.
Journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

Title: Fast but reliable? Consistency of preference elicitation with ranking and rating for multicriteria decision analysis in Real‑World cases
Authors: M. Kuller, P. Beutler, J. Lienert
Abstract: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) methods require stakeholder preference elicitation, but standard approaches like Swing weight elicitation can be time-consuming and cognitively demanding for practical applications. This study investigated whether fast preference elicitation methods—direct ranking and rating of objectives—can effectively substitute for rigorous Swing weight elicitation in real-world public decision-making contexts. Data were collected from three case studies involving flood early warning system development in West Africa and wastewater management transitions in two Swiss rural communities. Individual stakeholder preferences for objectives were elicited through ranking, rating, and Swing weight methods across multiple workshops. Consistency between ranking and rating was high for most stakeholders (median γ-values around -0.9). Weights derived from objectives ranking correlated better with Swing weights than rating weights, particularly in the largest case study. When aggregated across stakeholders, fast elicitation methods implemented in MCDA produced nearly identical rankings of alternatives compared to Swing weights (Kendall's τ > 0.84), with no rank reversals in top-5 alternatives between weights derived from objectives ranking and Swing. However, holistic, direct ranking of alternatives showed poor correlation with MCDA-calculated rankings (τ < 0.5), supporting value-focused thinking principles. These findings demonstrate that fast ranking of objectives can approximate Swing weight elicitation outcomes while significantly reducing time and cognitive burden, offering a practical approach for consensus-seeking in resource-constrained public decision processes.

Title: Agency vs. resale: Selling format choice on competing platforms with asymmetric suppliers
Authors: Benrong Zheng, Guoxuan Huang, T.C.E. Cheng
Abstract: This study investigates how competing online platforms choose between agency and resale selling formats when sourcing from exclusive suppliers with differing cost efficiencies. Utilizing a game-theoretic framework, we analyze how supplier cost asymmetry and platform competition influence equilibrium selling strategies, firm profitability and consumer welfare. Our findings reveal a key trade-off: the resale model mitigates competition through double marginalization, while the agency model enables more cost-efficient suppliers to exploit their advantages via aggressive pricing. Platforms adopt the resale-resale (RR) strategy when supplier cost differences are minimal and the commission rate is low. As cost asymmetry or the commission rate increases, the equilibrium shifts toward agency-based or asymmetric formats: high commissions induce the agency-agency (AA) equilibria, whereas sufficiently large cost asymmetry leads to asymmetric equilibria, with RA arising under low commissions and AR under high commissions. Notably, we identify an agency trap, a prisoner's dilemma outcome where platforms choose the AA equilibrium even though both would earn higher profits under the RR model. This outcome arises when the commission rate is sufficiently high and supplier cost asymmetry is either low or lies within a narrow high-asymmetry range. Welfare analysis indicates that agency-dominated models (AA or AR) tend to maximize consumer surplus and social welfare, albeit at the expense of supplier profits. These findings remain robust across various extensions, including platform-side asymmetry, service competition, and endogenous commissions. These results suggest that platforms should align their selling format choices with supplier cost asymmetry and market competition, rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all strategy.

Title: Audit culture: how indicators and rankings are reshaping the world
Authors: Christiaan Röell

Title: Infinite-Scrolling vs. Pagination: The Impact of Interface Layouts on Product Returns
Authors: Huitian Zhang, Lei Su, Jaideep Sengupta
Abstract: Interface layout, although a fundamental and prominent aspect inherent to online interfaces, has received limited attention in consumer research. This paper explores how the two major types of interface layout (infinite scrolling and pagination) influence consumers’ product return behavior in the context of free returns, a standard policy on e-commerce sites. Across five studies featuring real websites, we show that an infinite-scrolling (versus paginated) layout increases consumers’ tendency to return purchased products. This effect occurs because infinite scrolling dampens consumers’ perceived navigational control over the website, which impairs their choice closure after making decisions, thereby increasing product return intentions. We also identify both theoretically relevant and managerially important moderators and interventions to mitigate this adverse effect of infinite scrolling, such as incorporating navigational aids (e.g., displaying sequence numbers alongside), providing affirmative feedback, and accounting for the cost of product returns. This research not only contributes to the literature on interface effects, website navigation, and product returns but also provides applied insights for marketing practitioners.

Title: The Humanizing Power of Accents in Voicebots: When Accent-Based Humanization Increases User Engagement
Authors: Hesam Ghasemi, Amir Sepehri, Cait Lamberton
Abstract: Given that consumers often exhibit resistance toward algorithmic systems, firms face challenges in encouraging engagement with voicebots. In this paper, we find that users’ engagement with voicebots may be enhanced by endowing these tools with non-standard accents that deviate from “standard” pronunciation. Across a range of accents, languages, genders, and contexts, our data suggest that voicebots communicating with non-standard accents make the concept of human diversity salient in the users’ minds. As a result, voicebots communicating with non-standard accents are more readily anthropomorphized. This effect translates into greater preference for the non-standard accented voicebot in customer service settings, stronger support for startups leveraging accented vs. unaccented voicebots, higher willingness to pay for monthly subscriptions, and a greater likelihood of opting in to receive future updates and communications. Consistent with our theory, however, these effects do not hold when the anthropomorphism effect is either overridden by other cues or is undesirable for the consumer. Together, this work highlights the benefits of accented speech in improving human-AI interactions. We also hope that it sparks further investigation into factors that make technology more readily accepted by consumers.

Title: First In, First Out? Birth Order and Next-Generation Engagement in Family Firms
Authors: Mohamed Genedy, Lucia Naldi, Karin Hellerstedt
Affiliations: House of Innovation (HOI), Stockholm School of Economics, Sweden; Jönköping International Business School, Centre for Family Entrepreneurship and Ownership (CeFEO), Jönköping University, Sweden; IE University, Spain
Abstract: Research shows that next-generation engagement in the family business is important for the business’s long-term survival. However, the literature has neglected how differences among children could explain their career choices in the family business. We address this gap by drawing on birth order theory to examine differences in three career choices of the next-generation: joining the family business, holding a managerial position, and leaving the family business. Using a sample from Sweden, we employ family-stratified hazard models and show that later-borns are more likely to join the family business as their initial career choice compared to earlier-born siblings. However, when the next-generation joins the family business, later-borns are less likely to hold managerial positions in the family business and more likely to leave the family business. We conduct several mechanism tests explaining our hypotheses and run additional robustness tests to support our results. This study advances the research on next-generation engagement in family firms.

Title: Single versus variable pricing under uncertainty with limited capacity
Authors: Chunlin Wang, Huaqing (Mike) Wang, Haresh Gurnani, Saibal Ray
Affiliations: University of New Mexico; Palm Beach Atlantic University; Stony Brook University; McGill University
Abstract: This paper studies a firm’s pricing strategies under joint uncertainty in costs and demand (market size), with potential capacity constraints. We organize four pricing strategies along a single dimension: the amount and type of realized information a firm commits its pricing rule to use, ranging from none, under single pricing , to both cost and demand , under the most flexible strategy; between these extremes, demand-based pricing conditions price on realized demand alone, and cost-based pricing conditions price on realized cost alone. We examine the implications of this informational flexibility for three stakeholders: the firm, consumers, and society. We note that, across all capacity levels, the firm’s profit is maximized by the most flexible pricing strategy, namely, pricing based on both cost and demand realizations. In contrast, the pricing strategy that maximizes consumer surplus and social welfare depends on the severity of the capacity constraint. Under tight capacity, demand-based pricing and pricing based on both cost and demand realizations dominate. However, when capacity is sufficiently large (i.e., an uncapacitated setting), cost-based pricing maximizes consumer surplus and social welfare. Interestingly, for intermediate capacity levels, single pricing might be the best option for both consumers and society, even though it commits the firm to using the least information. The above results are robust to both discrete and continuous demand distributions. We further show that when costs and demand are positively correlated, single pricing still might be socially optimal. Overall, the paper shows how the information a pricing rule commits to use interacts with capacity constraints to shape the profit and welfare effects of pricing flexibility, offering guidance on when each strategy is likely to be favorable for the stakeholders.

Title: Gain by letting go: Environmental investments and profitability of benefit corporations
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Yiyuan Ruan, Luyi Gui, Nan Zhang
Affiliations: South China University of Technology; Lingnan University; University of California Irvine
Abstract: Benefit corporation is a new legal status of for-profit companies, which requires statutory commitment to public benefit purposes. The adoption of benefit corporation rather than a traditional C corporation is generally regarded as a tradeoff: a benefit corporation is believed to invest more in responsible business practices at the expense of profit compared to a profit-maximizing C corporation counterpart. In this article, we examine the validity of this perspective from a supply chain perspective, focusing on a consumer goods brand that pledges to reduce total emissions as its public benefit purpose. We develop parsimonious models of the brand’s emission reduction investment and product distribution decisions when it sells to consumers directly, indirectly via a retailer, or both. Through a comparison of the optimal decisions when the brand is incorporated as a benefit corporation versus a profit-maximizing C corporation, we show that converting to a benefit corporation intensifies the rebound effect associated with carbon footprint reduction, and thereby may reduce the brand’s investment in such reductions when it strongly emphasizes total emission abatement in its objective. A moderate focus on profit can mitigate this problem and enhance a benefit corporation’s investment in carbon footprint reduction especially under dual distribution channels. Furthermore, the brand can be more profitable as a benefit corporation than as a profit-maximizing C corporation under dual distribution channels, as the benefit corporation status increases channel differentiation and softens competition. Our study indicates that profit and public benefit objectives may reinforce each other. A well-balanced corporate goal can lay plausible grounds for mitigating profit concerns and shareholder pushback to the benefit corporation status, as well as for increasing environmental investment incentives derived from that status. In addition, policies that help benefit corporations access market through differentiated dual channels can be pathways to improve their financial viability and public benefit impacts.

Title: Pay transparency and inequality concerns: Productivity and job satisfaction
Authors: Lin Chen, Antoine Désir, Guillaume Roels
Affiliations: The University of Hong Kong; Technology and Operations Management, INSEAD; Technology and Operations Management, INSEAD, Fontainebleau, France
Abstract: Although pay transparency is generally effective at reducing the gender gap, it is not without downsides, sometimes leading to reduced productivity and lower job satisfaction due to inequality concerns. Yet, workers could have different objects of comparison: income, utility, or rewards. Across these different types of inequality concerns, when does pay transparency result in both higher output and fair outcomes? We consider a model of moral hazard involving a principal and two agents of heterogeneous abilities who are averse to inequalities between each other. We study three bases of comparison: income, utility, and reward. Anticipating the agents’ change in behavior as a result of pay transparency, the principal adjusts the terms of their output-sharing contract with them. We find that pay transparency under income comparison never benefits the principal and might give rise to feelings of guilt and envy—thus reducing agents’ utility. In contrast, under reward comparison, it is always beneficial to the principal and results in fair outcomes. Under utility comparison, it lies somewhere in between, offering a higher payoff and fair outcomes when agents are not so heterogeneous, but hurting them without changing the principal’s payoff otherwise. In sum, we find that pay transparency has the potential for increasing productivity without negative feelings of fairness. However, the object of comparison matters. Therefore, it is paramount for organizations to contextualize income information to shift employees’ concerns away from income to either utility or reward considerations by adopting process transparency in addition to outcome transparency.

Title: Returnless Partial Refunds: A Large-Scale Field Experiment in E-Commerce
Authors: Lu Fang, Chunhua Wu, Zhe Yuan, Kaifu Zhang
Affiliations: School of Management, Zhejiang University of Finance and Economics, Hangzhou 310018, China; and Laboratory for Human-AI Collaboration and Digital Intelligence Innovation, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058, China; UBC Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia V6T 1Z2, Canada; Center for Research of Private Economy, School of Economics, Future Regional Development Laboratory, and Academy of Financial Research, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058, China; Partner Company
Abstract: A large-scale field experiment shows AI-enabled returnless partial refunds increase customer value and reduce operating costs while raising strategic-behavior risks.

Title: Superstition Everywhere
Authors: Jeffery (Jinfan) Chang, Huancheng Du
Affiliations: School of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Shenzhen, Guangdong Province 518172, People’s Republic of China; School of Finance, Central University of Finance and Economics, Beijing 102206, People’s Republic of China
Abstract: In Chinese culture, the digit 8 is considered lucky and the digit 4 unlucky. We find that this numerological superstition has a significant impact across China’s stock, bond, foreign exchange, and commodity futures markets, affecting asset prices in both the primary and secondary markets. The superstition effect, that is, asset prices ending in a lucky (unlucky) digit are far more (less) frequent than expected by chance, is prevalent across finance markets. We show that this phenomenon is driven by two mechanisms: sophisticated investors’ reliance on superstition as an anchor to manage ambiguity, and the overoptimism of unsophisticated investors. While the superstition effect does not lead to any systematic mispricing for assets traded primarily by sophisticated investors, it is closely associated with overpricing for assets heavily traded by unsophisticated investors. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: J. (J.) Chang received financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72573148]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01449 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance.

Title: Near-Optimal Mechanisms for Resource Allocation Without Monetary Transfers
Authors: Moïse Blanchard, Patrick Jaillet
Affiliations: H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332; Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139
Abstract: Aligning Incentives Without Opening the Wallet Many organizations must repeatedly allocate scarce resources—computing capacity, scientific equipment, school seats, or food-bank supplies—when monetary payments are impractical or undesirable. Blanchard and Jaillet show how future allocations can serve as rewards and penalties, inducing strategic agents to report their values truthfully while keeping welfare close to the full-information ideal. Their mechanisms use the promised utility framework and apply to general utility distributions in both finite-horizon and discounted infinite-horizon settings. The key insight is geometric; performance depends on the shape of the attainable-utility frontier. When agents often have similar values for the resource, the planner can shift allocations at little welfare cost and align incentives more effectively. The paper establishes universal convergence guarantees, faster rates for smooth utility distributions, and even exponentially small welfare losses in some discounted settings with frequent ties. The results provide a unified, quantitative framework for deciding when nonmonetary allocation can nearly match mechanisms that use payments.

Title: Commons without borders: How entrepreneurs can engage local actors into collective action for the governance of supra-local common-pool resources
Authors: Coline Serres, Christina Hertel, Sophie Bacq
Abstract: Based on 41 interviews across three UK-based commons enterprises, this study addresses one of the most pressing challenges of our time: encouraging local actors to contribute to the sustainable governance of supra-local common-pool resources (CPRs)—shared resources whose use and impacts extend beyond community boundaries. While existing research has focused on locally bound natural CPRs, we lack understanding of how entrepreneurial ventures can mobilize the members of local communities to govern resources that span multiple jurisdictions. Our findings reveal a two-step process through which entrepreneurs first embed their commons enterprises in the local community, using asset locks and diversified engagement strategies to involve citizens, local businesses, and public authorities. Building on this embedding, three commoning practices emerge: collective learning about the CPR, collective action and capacity building for CPR stewardship, and collective institutionalization of CPR governance. Around these practices, a community of commoners emerges that is nested within the local community and increasingly sustains collective action independently of the entrepreneur. These practices anchor the supra-local CPR within the local community through three mechanisms: resource proximization, local conditionality, and bonding as a selective incentive, thereby overcoming the collective action barriers arising from lacking resource proximity and perceived responsibility. Our study contributes to research at the intersection of entrepreneurship and the commons by demonstrating the strategic role of common property regimes, shifting attention from the resource to the commoning practices and communities that form around it, and specifying the mechanisms that enable local collective action for supra-local CPR governance.

Title: Connective Resource Mobilization: A Relational Approach to Movement Continuity in Transnational Activism
Authors: Pamela P. Tsui
Affiliations: University of Toronto
Abstract: Social movement studies have long centered social movement organizations (SMOs) as the primary vehicles of mobilization. Yet contemporary movements are increasingly decentralized and digitally mediated, challenging SMO-centric frameworks such as resource mobilization theory (RMT). As contention becomes more individualized and non-conventional, organization- and event-centered approaches struggle to explain how movements persist, evolve, or dissolve under shifting conditions. Drawing on RMT and economic sociology, this article advances a relational resource mobilization framework through four propositions: resource mobilization (1) is historically contingent; (2) translates into tactics differently across organizational configurations; (3) is relational; and (4) provides an analytic for examining movement continuity across time and space. Within this framework, I introduce the model of connective resource mobilization to theorize how digitally mediated movements generate strategic capacity through personalized earmarking practices across borders and phases of contention. Based on 179 interviews and observation at 187 events in Hong Kong and Canada, I trace how the Hong Kong Pro-Democracy Movement evolved from its 2019 protest peak through its subsequent downturn across domestic and diasporic contexts. The analysis demonstrates how a relational approach to resource mobilization can illuminate divergent trajectories of movement continuity across historical, geographic, political, and socio-technological contexts.

Title: The wisdom of the diverse crowd(funders)
Authors: Hadar Gafni, Lars Bo Jeppesen
Abstract: Crowdfunding platforms aim to democratize entrepreneurial finance by creating ecosystems that elicit the ‘wisdom of crowds’—aggregating the judgments of individual and often amateur funders. However, there is limited evidence on whether crowds can effectively apply their collective wisdom on these platforms. We address this gap by analyzing MyC4, a crowdlending platform that connects Western lenders with borrowers in developing countries. We examine whether lenders effectively screen borrowers, identify platform attributes that influence lenders' screening accuracy, and uncover the underlying mechanisms driving these effects. Empirically, we leverage platform-initiated ‘top-up’ funding by MyC4 administrators, which allows us to observe the counterfactual repayment performance of loans that would otherwise have remained unfunded, enabling us to evaluate lenders' screening ability against an otherwise unobservable benchmark. Our results indicate that crowdlenders can effectively screen creditworthy borrowers, but only when financial information about borrowers is made available. Lenders' screening effectiveness diminishes substantially for prosocial loans, as many funders converge on similar, socially motivated decisions. These findings provide novel evidence on crowdlenders' performance, highlighting key trade-offs for crowdfunding platforms and offering actionable insights for their administrators.

Title: Firms' board diversity and radical innovation: mediation mechanism of firms' attention to digital transformation
Authors: Wan Cheng, Jingyu Li, Li Liu
Abstract: This study integrates board information processing theory with the attention-based view to examine how board diversity affects radical innovation through an organizational attention pathway. We argue that board diversity shapes firms' attention to digital transformation (FADT), which in turn promotes radical innovation, and that industry competition conditions this process by heightening the urgency of attending to digital opportunities. Using longitudinal data from 2556 publicly listed Chinese firms from 2008 to 2019, we find that board diversity has an inverted U-shaped relationship with FADT and that FADT positively affects radical innovation. FADT thus mediates the inverted U-shaped relationship between board diversity and radical innovation, producing an inverted U-shaped indirect effect. Industry competition strengthens the relationship between board diversity and FADT, making this indirect effect more pronounced in competitive environments. These findings clarify how board diversity contributes to radical innovation by directing organizational attention toward digital transformation and show why moderate diversity is especially valuable when firms face strong competitive pressure.

Title: Effects of a Theory-Based Smartphone Intervention to Decrease Neuroticism in the General Public
Authors: Amanda J. Wright, Peter Haehner, Rosalie Andrae, Till Lubczyk, Christopher J. Hopwood, Wiebke Bleidorn
Affiliations: Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences, Texas A&M University; Department of Psychology, University of Zürich; Faculty of Health and Sports, HMU Health and Medical University
Abstract: Many people wish to be less neurotic, and such decreases could have far-reaching benefits, but evidence on nonclinical interventions and change mechanisms is limited. Using a German-speaking, adult sample ( N = 446), we conducted a 6-week, smartphone-based randomized controlled intervention to test effects of theory-based strategies targeting different neuroticism levels and aspects. Across groups, there were significant self-report effects ( d effect = −0.22 to −0.37) that persisted through a 2-month follow-up ( d effect = −0.16 to −0.33), and follow-up peer-report effects for one of two measures ( d effect = −0.18 to −0.30). Treatment-group comparisons indicated that state-level strategies fostered larger immediate (albeit shorter-lasting) effects, whereas habit-level strategies led to smaller initial declines that strengthened over time. Behavior-focused strategies, for states and especially habits, yielded particularly strong effects across assessment methods, both independently and incrementally. Our findings demonstrate that neuroticism can be changed within 6 weeks and provide insight into effective mechanisms of change.

Title: Disillusionment With Meritocracy During the Transition to Adulthood: Longitudinal Change in Belief Systems and Depression in China
Authors: Shuming Fan, Oliver P. John, Filip De Fruyt
Affiliations: Department of Developmental, Personality and Social Psychology, Ghent University; Department of Psychology, University of California, Berkeley
Abstract: Meritocracy —the belief that individual effort rather than structural advantages drives success—has long shaped societal narratives but now faces growing skepticism. Using four waves of China Family Panel Studies, we examined changes in meritocratic and nonmeritocratic beliefs among 524 participants from early adolescence (ages 10–13 in 2012) to emerging adulthood (ages 18–21 in 2020) and assessed their concurrent associations with depression trajectories. Meritocratic beliefs declined significantly in both college ( d = −0.56) and noncollege ( d = −0.30) groups. Only college students increased in nonmeritocratic beliefs ( d = 0.72), and these changes were associated with steeper increases in depression. College students’ recognition of structural barriers to success is associated with heightened psychological costs, although causality cannot be inferred.

Title: Navigating new accounting standards: Implications for firms and their auditors
Authors: Will Anding
Abstract: I examine the consequences of implementing new accounting standards on financial reporting quality. While prior research suggests that standards generally achieve their regulatory objectives, recent literature identifies firms’ significant technical accounting capacity constraints, motivating the need to explore the broader consequences of accounting standards adoption on financial reporting quality. Using a novel AI-based approach to identify firms affected by new accounting standards, I find a decrease in financial reporting quality when firms implement new standards. Evidence suggests the impaired financial reporting quality is in accounting areas unrelated to the new standards, consistent with a distraction effect. Results are more pronounced when firms face other concurrent accounting-related challenges, when accounting standards are more complex, and when auditors have resource constraints. These findings provide evidence of the unintended consequences of new accounting standards and shed light on potential ways to mitigate these costs.

Title: Through thick and thin? When sustainable packaging design increases consumer waste generation
Authors: Lyndsay Loomer, Sarah C. Whitley
Abstract: Abstract Packaging decisions involve a complex balance of cost, functionality, efficiency, branding, and sustainability initiatives. One promising sustainability strategy that also reduces costs is lightweighting, a manufacturing practice aimed at reducing raw material usage. In reducing raw material use, lightweighting results in structural changes to the packaging, specifically a reduction in packaging density, which has downstream consequences on consumer disposal. When assessing packaging for disposability cues, we show packaging density drives perceptions of its quality, value, and associated feelings of waste aversion. While lightweighting reduces firms’ waste, this work finds that once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging. However, prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness. This work highlights that even sustainable firm practices can result in unintended and unsustainable consequences.
Journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

Title: When manufacturer encroachment backfires: Effects of cross-selling in Internet of Things product supply chains
Authors: Rui Hou, Yongjiao Ruan, You Zhao
Abstract: This paper studies a supply chain in which a manufacturer sells an Internet of Things (IoT)–enabled product through an e-commerce platform and may also open a direct channel (i.e., encroachment). The manufacturer endogenously chooses the IoT functionality level, while the platform and the manufacturer benefit from cross-selling of consumables enabled by IoT data, regardless of the sales channel. We examine how the presence of cross-channel externalities affects the manufacturer's encroachment and investment strategies. We develop a game-theoretic model includes a subscription-based charging mode for IoT service. Contrary to prior research, we show that higher platform cross-selling revenue can discourage the manufacturer from investing in IoT functionality under encroachment. We also find that encroachment can increase wholesale prices rather than reduce them when the platform lacks pricing power. Surprisingly, even when channels are equally efficient, encroachment may harm the manufacturer while benefiting the platform. Our results highlight that cross-selling externalities can distort investment incentives and decouple encroachment from profit gains. Manufacturers should reconsider encroachment when platforms extract disproportionate value via cross-selling. Platforms, in turn, can shape channel outcomes through pricing structures and IoT fee designs, and may even subsidize encroachment to boost ecosystem-level monetization.

Title: Firm Balance Sheet Liquidity, Monetary Policy Shocks, and Investment Dynamics
Authors: Priit Jeenas
Abstract: I study the role of firms' balance sheet liquidity in the transmission of monetary policy to investment. I develop a heterogeneous firm macroeconomic model with financial constraints, debt issuance costs, and differential returns on firms' cash and borrowing. The model matches key novel moments from U.S. firm-level data on liquid asset holdings, debt issuance activity, and investment responses to identified monetary shocks. Counterfactual analysis shows that the rise in U.S. firms' liquid asset holdings over recent decades has significantly increased the relevance of balance sheet liquidity and the behavior of liquid asset returns in monetary transmission.

Title: How Do Forward‐Looking Estimates of Credit Losses Affect the Judgments of Financial Statement Users?
Authors: Lisa Koonce, Cassie Mongold, Laura Quaid, Jennifer Winchel
Affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin Austin Texas USA; University of Illinois Urbana‐Champaign Champaign Illinois USA; Independent Researcher; University of Virginia Charlottesville Virginia USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Financial accounting standard setters recently changed the accounting for estimates involving credit risk. The change shifted the accounting from an incurred‐loss model (ILM), which is based on credit‐risk conditions that exist at the time of the estimate, to a model based on expected credit losses over the life of the asset in question (ELM), which considers expectations of future conditions. Our paper is based on the theoretical premise that ELM will reduce surprise via its Day 1 forewarning, which, in turn, should lessen the potential for hindsight bias (i.e., Monday‐morning quarterbacking) and judging management as having made a poor quality lending decision if an actual credit loss later occurs. Three experiments support this premise, revealing when ELM accounting should have a differential impact relative to the prior accounting.

Title: Is the Gene‐ie Out of the Bottle? The Problems and Perils of Genetics Research in Management
Authors: Jean Clarke, Joep Cornelissen, Mark P. Healey
Affiliations: emlyon business school; Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Manchester
Abstract: Abstract In recent years, the field of management research has witnessed the emergence of a stream of research that seeks to identify the genetic determinants of managerial, entrepreneurial, and organizational behaviour. We challenge the reductionist epistemology underpinning this genetic perspective in management research and highlight the inherently weak inferences about human behaviour that follow from its prevailing methods and explanatory models. We further examine the ethical implications that arise from its underlying assumptions and potential future applications. We then propose recasting the role of genetics as part of a broader phenomenon‐driven approach towards studying and explaining human behaviour in management research and outline a conceptual framework aimed at generating stronger and contextually grounded explanatory models of managerial, entrepreneurial, and organizational behaviour.

Title: Beyond Good and Bad: Understanding the Contradictory Effects of Positive Leadership Behavior and Negative Leadership Behavior
Authors: Haoying (Howie) Xu, Xing Wang, Daan van Knippenberg
Affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology; Colorado State University; Rice University
Abstract: Organizational scholarship has long focused on leadership behavior, largely assuming that “good” and “bad” leaders can be distinguished by distinct sets of behaviors that can be organized into constructs with an inherent positive or negative valence (e.g., transformational, ethical, abusive). This assumption has guided extensive construct development and generated a substantial body of evidence consistent with each leadership construct’s expected valence. Yet, emerging research has documented the “dark side” of positive leadership and the “bright side” of negative leadership, revealing effects that contradict these expectations—effects that we call leadership contradictory effects. Despite growing interest in this line of research, the literature remains fragmented, with limited clarity regarding its scope and little theoretical integration explaining why, how, and when such effects occur. This motivates our review, which synthesizes these fragmented findings into a cohesive theoretical account organized around shared themes that cut across leadership constructs. First, we define leadership contradictory effects and review major approaches to operationalize them. Then, we advance an integrative framework that delineates three major theoretical themes, their associated theories, and three categories of boundary conditions to explain why, how, and when leadership contradictory effects arise. Finally, we propose paths forward, including suggestions to guide future research in this emerging domain. Overall, our work reorients scholars and points them beyond valence-based assumptions about leadership effects as a means to explore a broader range of consequences.

Title: Learning Capacity Constraints with Convex Neural Networks in Lot-Sizing Problems
Authors: David Tremblet, Simon Thevenin, Alexandre Dolgui
Affiliations: HEC Montréal, Montréal, Quebec H3T 2A7, Canada; IMT Atlantique, LS2N-CNRS, 44307 Nantes, France
Abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for integrating convex neural networks into mixed-integer linear programs. We introduce a mixed-integer linear programming formulation that employs the Maxout activation function, and our experiments show that this network type outperforms rectified linear unit–based networks. Additionally, we propose a novel formulation for convex networks that does not require auxiliary variables. We show that such reformulation can be solved efficiently using Lagrangian relaxation and branch-and-cut approaches. These methods are generic enough to be readily adapted to a wide range of problems and significantly simplify the integration of convex networks into mathematical programs. We evaluate these approaches on multi-item capacitated lot-sizing problems in which capacity constraints are replaced by neural networks translated into linear programs. Numerical experiments involving lot-sizing problems suggest that our methodology outperforms approaches that integrate lot-sizing and scheduling. Our methodology yields better solutions than conventional approaches regardless of whether both problems are solved in an integrated or hierarchical fashion. In particular, the proposed Lagrangian relaxation algorithm returns high-quality feasible solutions quickly, and the branch-and-cut approach efficiently solves lot-sizing models with large convex neural networks, making these two approaches attractive for solving large-scale instances. History: Accepted by Andrea Lodi, Area Editor for Design & Analysis of Algorithms–Discrete. Funding: The present work was conducted within the project ASSISTANT ( https://assistant-project.eu/ ) funded by the European Commission [Grant 101000165], H2020–ICT-38-2020, artificial intelligence for manufacturing. The authors also thank the region Pays de la Loire for financial support.
