The complete IJOC Software and Data Repository is available at https://informsjoc.github.io/ .

Title: Social Networks as Information Conduits for Online Credit Supply and Demand
Authors: Linda Allen, Lin Peng, Yu Shan
Affiliations: Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College/CUNY, New York, New York 10010; Whitman School of Management, Syracuse University, Syracuse, New York 13244
Abstract: We study how intercommunity social networks influence loan demand and supply on fintech lending platforms. Demand for online loans rises following increases in online borrowing activity in geographically distant but socially connected areas. On the supply side, borrower area social proximity to deposit-rich regions increases funding likelihood and is associated with better ex post loan performance. We establish causality with shift-share instrumental variables (SSIVs) obtained from natural disasters (demand side) and financial adviser misconduct (supply side). Social connectedness expands both loan demand and supply in disadvantaged communities without increasing delinquency rates. Intercommunity social networks raise awareness of alternative lending platforms and transmit hard-to-obtain information that mitigates community-level information asymmetry. This paper has been accepted by Will Cong for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06050 .
Accepting Editor: This paper was accepted by Will Cong, Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance.
Area: special issue on the digital finance

Title: Erratum: “Dynamic Pricing and Matching for Two-Sided Queues”
Authors: Sushil Mahavir Varma, Pornpawee Bumpensanti, Siva Theja Maguluri, He Wang
Affiliations: School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332; Amazon, Bellevue, Washington 98004
Abstract: Corrections to the Publication “Dynamic Pricing and Matching for Two-Sided Queues” In the context of two-sided queues, Theorem 2 of the paper [Dynamic Pricing and Matching for Two-Sided Queues. Operations Research 2023;71(1):83–100] establishes optimality guarantees for the two-price policy combined with the max-weight matching policies. As stated, this theorem is not valid. In this erratum, we show that the conclusions of Theorem 2 hold under a slight modification of the max-weight policy, which does not use some of the edges in the graph to match. Moreover, we point out some technical issues in this paper and outline how to resolve them.

Title: Mobilizing ecosystem support for architectural innovation: Broker-mediated expectation formation
Authors: Sean (Tsuhsiang) Hsu, Susan K. Cohen, Yaoyi Jing
Abstract: Architectural innovators must mobilize coordinated ecosystem support to commercialize unproven technologies, yet research has paid limited attention to how prospective ecosystem participants become convinced that a not-yet-existent ecosystem is likely to emerge. We address this problem by theorizing broker-mediated expectation formation as a mechanism of ecosystem emergence. Rather than simply connecting firms or transferring information, brokers assemble alliance portfolios whose visible pattern of commitments provides evidence that the complementary conditions necessary for ecosystem success are beginning to take shape. We argue that brokers with related technological experience and multiparty alliance experience are better able to assemble alliance portfolios with broad adoption-chain coverage, making distributed commitments more visible to prospective ecosystem participants. As adoption-chain coverage expands, ecosystem members become more willing to ally with the innovator. We test our arguments in the context of Qualcomm's effort to commercialize its unproven CDMA architecture between 1989 and 1999, a preparadigmatic period characterized by substantial uncertainty regarding technological feasibility, ecosystem coordination, and adoption-chain support. Using event-history analysis of alliance formation, we find that broker technological experience and multiparty alliance experience increase adoption-chain coverage, which subsequently increases the likelihood prospective ecosystem members form alliances with Qualcomm. Our findings suggest that prospective ecosystem participants use the visible commitments represented in broker alliance portfolios to infer whether ecosystem-specific commitments are accumulating across the adoption chain, identifying broker-mediated expectation formation as a mechanism through which ecosystem support for architectural innovation broadens.

Title: Who are my people and what can I do? Community remapping for entrepreneurial venturing after forced migration
Authors: Todd W. Moss, Trenton Alma Williams, Kurian George, Maria Minniti
Abstract: Scholarship on post-disruption adaptation largely assumes conditions of partial disruption—situations where despite losing access to one or multiple domains, other important domains remain intact. Yet wholesale disruptions pose a qualitatively different challenge for entrepreneurship. We explore how experiences of wholesale disruption shape actors' reconstruction of their contextual structure, perceived scope of their entrepreneurial possibility space, and the long-term trajectory of their ventures. We conduct an inductive study of the venturing efforts of refugees following their wholesale disruption caused by forced migration to the USA. We develop a grounded theoretical model of community remapping for venturing after wholesale disruption that explains why some refugees enact dynamic, growing ventures while others enact more stable, static ventures and eschew growth aspirations. Our findings and theorizing contribute to literatures on venturing in response to wholesale disruptions and on refugee entrepreneurship.

Title: Machine-learning about ESG preferences: Evidence from fund flows
Authors: George O. Aragon, Shuaiyu Chen
Abstract: We construct Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) scores for U.S. active equity mutual funds using roughly 500 metrics across ESG issues and rating agencies. Under a revealed-preference framework, we use machine learning to identify issues driving fund flows and generate ESG-driven flows as proxies for ESG performance. We estimate expected benchmark-adjusted returns using ex-post realized returns and ex-ante measures. Better-ESG funds attract larger subsequent flows and face fewer redemptions after poor performance, yet have lower expected returns, indicating flows reflect investor ESG preferences rather than high-return beliefs. Investors effectively pay $48 million more annually for a top-ESG fund.

Title: Debt and assets
Authors: Efraim Benmelech, Nitish Kumar, Raghuram Rajan
Abstract: Prior studies imply that a majority of US corporate debt by value is cash-flow based and only a small fraction is asset backed. Because corporations often prefer to keep assets unencumbered until creditors insist on security, much unsecured cash-flow-based debt is also implicitly asset backed. Moreover, the degree of asset backing varies with a firm’s condition and the economic environment. Asset values thus affect both the amount and the price of unsecured borrowing, with effects amplified in adverse conditions—consistent with financial accelerator theories. Because all corporate debt is supported by future cash flows as well as asset values, with the relative support shifting with firm-specific and economy-wide conditions, we find that the industry practice of classifying debt as “asset based” or “cash flow based” is overly categorical, especially for long-term corporate bonds.

Title: Related exposures to distressed borrowers and bank lending
Authors: Sumit Agarwal, Ricardo Correa, Bernardo Morais, Jessica Roldán, Claudia Ruiz-Ortega
Abstract: We study how banks’ exposure to a large set of related and suddenly-distressed borrowers impacts their commercial lending and risk taking. Using Mexican credit registry data, we examine the effect of the 2014 collapse in energy prices. After this shock, energy-exposed banks—regardless of their ex-ante financial health—raise further their exposure to the energy sector by expanding lending at looser credit terms to borrowers with higher expected losses, while recapitalizing through retained earnings. The shock is transmitted to non-energy firms—despite price controls on retail-energy products—via a contraction in bank lending, especially to bank-dependent borrowers.

Title: Issue information
American Finance Association
ANNOUNCEMENTS
The Equilibrium Effects of Eviction Policies
Authors: Boaz Abramson
Abstract: ABSTRACT I propose a dynamic equilibrium model of rental markets that endogenously gives rise to defaults on rents and evictions. In the model, eviction protections make it harder to evict delinquent renters, but higher default costs to landlords increase equilibrium rents. I quantify the model using micro data on evictions, rents, and homelessness. I find that stronger eviction protections exacerbate housing insecurity and lower welfare. The key empirical driver of this result is the persistent nature of risk underlying rent delinquencies. Rental assistance reduces housing insecurity and improves welfare because it lowers the likelihood that renters default ex ante.

Title: Twin Defaults and Bank Capital Requirements
Authors: Caterina Mendicino, Kalin Nikolov, Juan Rubio‐Ramirez, Javier Suarez, Dominik Supera
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine optimal capital requirements in a quantitative general equilibrium model with banks exposed to nondiversifiable borrower default risk. Contrary to standard models of bank default risk, our framework captures the limited upside, but significant downside risk of loan portfolio returns. This helps to reproduce the frequency and severity of twin defaults : simultaneously high firm and bank defaults. Hence, the optimal bank capital requirement, which trades off a lower frequency of twin defaults against restricting credit provision, is higher than under default risk models which underestimate the impact of borrower default on bank solvency.

Title: Learning to Navigate a New Financial Technology
Authors: Emily Breza, Martin Kanz, Leora Klapper
Abstract: ABSTRACT We present results from a field experiment that introduced digital payroll accounts to unbanked factory workers to examine how inexperienced consumers learn to use a new financial technology. We find that exposure to payroll accounts leads to increased account use, accelerated learning, and avoidance of common consumer protection risks. Those receiving electronic wage payments gradually build trust in the technology, learn to use accounts without assistance, and avoid illicit fees. Using experimental variation in assignment to bank versus mobile money accounts, we show that these impacts are concentrated in mobile money accounts, the newer, more complex, and less trusted financial technology.

Title: Can artificial intelligence accelerate technological progress? Researchers' perspectives on AI in manufacturing and materials science
Authors: John P. Nelson, Olajide E. Olugbade, Philip Shapira, Justin B. Biddle
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) raises expectations of substantial increases in rates of technological progress, but such anticipations are often not connected to detailed ground-level studies of AI use in innovation processes. Accordingly, it remains unclear how and to what extent AI can accelerate innovation. To help to fill this gap, we explore and assess results from 32 interviews with U.S.-based academic manufacturing and materials sciences researchers experienced with AI and machine learning (ML) techniques. We found that AI was primarily used for modeling of materials and manufacturing processes, facilitating cheaper and more rapid search of design spaces for materials and manufacturing processes alike. Benefits included cost, time, and computation savings in technology development. However, AI/ML tools were unreliable outside design spaces for which dense data were already available; they required skilled and judicious application in tandem with older research techniques; and concerns were raised about the potential to detrimentally circumvent opportunities for disruptive theoretical advancement. Based on these results, we suggest there is reason for optimism about acceleration in sustaining innovations through the use of AI/ML; but that support for conventional empirical, computational, and theoretical research is required to maintain the likelihood of further disruptive advances in manufacturing and materials.

Title: Research grant effects across funding modes and industry collaboration
Authors: Stefano Baruffaldi, Felicia Jorzick, Cornelia Lawson
Abstract: The impact of public research funding remains debated, with limited evidence on how effects differ across funding modes. In this paper, we provide causal evidence on the impact of a major UK funder and use this setting to explore how its effects vary across institutional features. We implement a regression discontinuity design using novel data on more than 2000 applications evaluated by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC). We study the causal effect and examine differences between open, investigator-initiated schemes—characterised by greater researcher autonomy in defining research questions—and directional, funder-initiated schemes—which direct efforts toward predefined priorities. We further explore heterogeneities in how industry collaboration interacts with these funding modes. Our results show that investigator-initiated grants are associated with stronger subsequent performance advantage for funded researchers, but only when projects remain academically embedded. Directional grants, instead, exhibit more positive effects when combined with industry collaboration. While on average research grants have a substantial positive impact in our setting, their effects vary across key features, informing debates on the design of public science funding systems and highlighting the need for further research on the interplay between different funding characteristics.

Title: How to craft a mission? A Theory of Action for the strategic public management of mission-oriented innovation policy
Authors: Iacopo Gronchi
Abstract: This paper explores the role of strategic public management within mission-oriented innovation policy. While recent scholarship has emphasised multiple aspects of missions, the distinct relevance of strategic public management in their implementation remains under-explored. To address this gap, the paper performs two complementary tasks. First, it uses a qualitative meta-synthesis of the relevant innovation literature to articulate a new Theory of Action for the analysis of missioncraft: namely, the institutional work public managers perform to create or maintain (disrupt) institutional logics supporting (hinder) their effective implementation. Second, it leverages a pre-study of the extant literature to illustrate the Theory of Action with three historical vignettes showing how the ToA can be applied at different scales and under different institutional logics (US' DARPA; China's NEV Plan programme; and EU's RIS3). Overall, the paper argues that the implementation of mission-oriented innovation policy requires public managers to adopt three critical strategic roles: i) enabling strategic learning across the public sector organisations leading the mission; ii) enabling dynamic accountability in the portfolio of projects supported by the mission; and iii) enabling collaborative innovation among the societal actors partaking the mission. By shifting the focus on the micro-foundations of mission implementation from structural underpinnings (i.e., legal, organisational, managerial) to agentic functions (i.e., strategic roles), the paper provides a new diagnostic lens for innovation policy research and practice – reflecting whether and how public managers can support mission-oriented innovation policy in light of the context-specific opportunities and constraints they face in their institutional work.

Title: Seek and Ye Might Not Find: The Effects of Contract Framing on Knowledge Sharing and Knowledge Seeking
Authors: Ta‐Tung (Stephanie) Cheng, Xi (Jason) Kuang, Brian Vansant, Suyun (Sue) Wu
Affiliations: University of Wyoming Laramie Wyoming USA; Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta Georgia USA; Auburn University Auburn Alabama USA; The University of Texas at El Paso El Paso Texas USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We conduct two experiments to examine whether and how the framing (bonus vs. penalty) of a target‐based incentive contract affects knowledge sharing and knowledge seeking. In the first experiment, we predict and find that penalty‐framed contracts increase employees' stress due to the fear of potential loss, which in turn reduces their willingness to share knowledge. Additionally, consistent with loss aversion, employees under penalty‐framed contracts are more likely to seek knowledge than those under bonus‐framed contracts. The second experiment corroborates our theoretical arguments by demonstrating the crucial role of stress in reducing knowledge‐sharing behavior. The results show that, when stress is alleviated through an informal control mechanism, penalty‐framed contracts no longer reduce knowledge sharing. The implications of our findings for research and practice are discussed.

Title: Common Ownership and Auditor Sharing
Authors: Young Hoon Kim
Affiliations: George Mason University Fairfax Virginia USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether common ownership by institutional investors is associated with auditor sharing among their investee companies. Auditor sharing can enhance audit quality through facilitated monitoring and improve financial reporting comparability—two benefits that enable common owners to internalize externalities across their portfolio firms (i.e., to reduce negative spillovers from audit failures and to capture positive spillovers from improved comparability across commonly owned peer investees). Using same‐industry company pairs in the United States, I find that common ownership is positively associated with the likelihood of sharing the same audit firm, and this association is stronger when co‐owners have longer investment horizons or more aligned incentives. A quasi‐experimental test leveraging BlackRock's acquisition of Barclays provides consistent evidence. Additional analyses indicate that shared board members serve as a potential channel through which auditor sharing arises. Finally, commonly owned, auditor‐sharing companies exhibit higher audit quality and are more likely to collectively dismiss auditors following revealed failures, consistent with improved oversight. These findings contribute to the literature on shared auditors, auditor choice, and common ownership by showing how a noncontractual relationship induced by common ownership shapes auditor sharing across companies and influences the shared auditor's incentives.

Title: Regulatory Intermediation in Times of Crisis: The Impact of Independent Oversight on the Functioning of Professional Accounting Bodies
Authors: Brendan O'Dwyer, Roel Boomsma, Chris Humphrey
Affiliations: Alliance Manchester Business School Manchester UK; University of Amsterdam Business School Amsterdam the Netherlands; UNSW Business School Sydney Australia; University of Sydney Business School Sydney Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT The rise of independent oversight of the accounting profession has attracted considerable research attention. Much of this research has studied how professional accounting bodies and the Big 4 firms have shaped the mandate and capabilities of independent oversight bodies. Less is known about how independent oversight has affected the workings of professional accounting bodies, particularly their capacity to simultaneously govern and represent their members. This paper advances our understanding of this dynamic through a longitudinal, interpretive case study of how the Dutch professional accounting body, the NBA (the Royal Netherlands Institute of Chartered Accountants), adapted and developed its regulatory intermediary role during a lengthy period of intense oversight by the Dutch regulator, the AFM (the Authority for the Financial Markets), and shifting levels of Big 4 firm discord. Drawing on extensive archival materials and insights gained from in‐depth interviews with key participants, the study advances existing theorizations of the work of regulatory intermediaries by highlighting both their functional variability and fragility. In responding to recurring crises and critique, the NBA's intermediary role shifted from facilitation to curation and ultimately to orchestrating the Big 4 firms' regulatory response. Such shifts were neither smooth nor predictable—characterized by a sense of “role limbo” as the NBA battled to bolster its identity and authority when sidelined by the AFM or dictated to or impeded by the Big 4 firms. In examining such shifting intermediation and contesting levels of influence, the NBA's governance and representation functions emerge as more symbiotic than oppositional, with the NBA using its fulfillment of one as a means of strengthening its execution of the other. Overall, the paper's analysis uncovers the functional fragility of the NBA, which questions whether repeated calls for professional accounting bodies to rediscover their public interest mandate have adequately appreciated the complex, contested nature of the regulatory environment in which they operate.

Title: SEC Attention, A to Z
Authors: Lorien Stice‐Lawrence
Affiliations: University of Southern California Los Angeles California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT I use downloads of regulatory filings by SEC employees as a measure of SEC attention and find that SEC employees are disproportionately less likely to review the filings of firms with names later in the alphabet. Additional tests show that alphabetical order determines a firm's priority when the SEC follows up on common shocks among peer firms and that the strength of the SEC's alphabetical bias does not vary with the intensity of resource constraints. Further, the SEC appears to be more surprised by the restatements of end‐of‐the‐alphabet firms. These results are consistent with a cognitive bias that leads SEC employees to pay more attention to firms at the top of alphabetically sorted lists. Last, using shocks to alphabetical order caused by firm name changes, I find that alphabetically induced increases in SEC attention are linked with lower future noncompliance, suggesting that the regulatory effects of alphabetical order are material. Overall, this study highlights the “human” element of regulatory attention.

Title: Analysts' Cultural Long‐Term Orientation and Their Information Production
Authors: Shuping Chen, Jay Heon Jung, Sonya S. Lim, Yong Yu
Affiliations: McCombs School of Business University of Texas at Austin Austin Texas USA; Bayes Business School, City St George's University of London London UK; Driehaus College of Business DePaul University Chicago Illinois USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study how analysts' inherited cultural attitudes to time orientation affect their production of long‐term information and the profitability of their stock recommendations. We find that analysts from long‐term‐oriented cultures exhibit a longer forecast horizon and issue more long‐term forecasts. They also produce more accurate long‐term forecasts and ask more long‐term‐focused questions during conference calls, eliciting greater long‐term disclosure from managers. In addition, they are more likely to use discounted valuation models that explicitly incorporate expectations about firms' long‐term prospects. Further, their stock recommendations are more profitable, consistent with their production of long‐term information enhancing valuation. Our findings highlight the role of cultural long‐term orientation in shaping analysts' information production in capital markets.

Title: Product Market Threats: Implications for Future Performance and Use by Market Participants
Authors: Marcus Kirk, Zhenhao (Jeffery) Piao, Diana L. Weng
Affiliations: Fisher School of Accounting, Warrington College of Business, University of Florida Gainesville Florida USA; School of Accountancy, Trulaske College of Business University of Missouri‐Columbia Columbia Missouri USA; Lynn Pippenger School of Accountancy, Muma College of Business University of South Florida Tampa Florida USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether competition in the form of emerging threats from rivals' overlapping product strategies has explanatory power for future performance and volatility, beyond existing competition measures and firm life cycle proxies. We proxy for emerging threats using product market fluidity, which captures competitive pressures and instability arising from rivals' evolving product overlap. Specifically, higher fluidity (i.e., higher product market threats) is negatively associated with future profitability and operating cash flows and positively associated with the variability of future profitability and operating cash flows. We also find fluidity is negatively associated with future asset turnover, margins, and expenses, and only moderately positively associated with future sales, shedding light on the mechanisms through which product market threats manifest in future performance. However, capital market participants do not fully incorporate this information, leading to predictable future stock returns and analyst forecast errors. Overall, our findings suggest that the dynamism and fluidity in a firm's product market space convey valuable and distinct information to capital market participants.

Title: The Questioning of Special Items During Conference Calls: High Quality or Highly Questionable?
Authors: Jiajia Fu, Yuan Ji, James Potepa
Affiliations: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley Edinburg Texas USA; The University of Texas at Arlington Arlington Texas USA; American University Washington DC USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Accounting standards require firms to distinguish recurring revenues and expenses from nonrecurring gains and losses, which are often referred to as special items. However, not all special items are genuinely nonrecurring. Exploiting the setting of earnings conference calls, we explore whether analysts can identify opportunistic special items, as evidenced by asking for more information about them. We find evidence that managers' discussions of special items more often relate to predicted special items, whereas analysts have more questions about potentially opportunistic special items. Managers adopt a relatively more negative tone and use more words when answering questions about potentially opportunistic special items. Finally, we find that analysts who question potentially opportunistic special items have fewer opportunities to speak in the subsequent call, consistent with managerial retaliation.

Title: Cost Information, Insider Trading, and Product Market Equilibrium
Authors: Dingwei Gu, Hanwen Sun
Affiliations: School of Management Fudan University Shanghai China; School of Management University of Bath Bath UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study how insider trading based on private cost information affects product market outcomes when firms differ in cost variance. In our model, managers exploit firm‐specific cost information to pursue short‐term trading gains, leading them to adjust output decisions and reshape product market competition. We show that trading opportunities have heterogeneous effects on firms' production and value: firms with high cost variance overproduce, whereas those with low cost variance underproduce; correspondingly, the value of firms with high cost variance rises, while that of firms with low cost variance declines. These results demonstrate how heterogeneous costs and private cost information create real economic consequences by linking insider trading incentives to distortions in product market competition and firm value.

Title: Does Mobile Communication Technology Have Capital Market Consequences? Evidence From Worldwide Launches of 3G Networks
Authors: Jinshuai Hu, Yongtae Kim, Siqi Li, Yibing Wu
Affiliations: Xiamen University Xiamen China; Santa Clara University Santa Clara California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Exploiting the staggered rollout of third‐generation (3G) mobile broadband networks across 40 countries between 1999 and 2012, we examine how technological progress affects capital markets. We find that the introduction of 3G networks is followed by a reduction in bid‐ask spreads and an increase in price informativeness. These effects are more pronounced among firms with lower institutional ownership, indicating that information access through mobile broadband networks disproportionally benefits retail investors. We further show that these effects are concentrated in countries with well‐functioning markets, as characterized by transparent accounting information, broad investor participation, and strong legal protections for investors. Taken together, our findings suggest that mobile broadband connectivity reduces information frictions and improves price informativeness. They further highlight the institutional conditions under which these benefits materialize.

Title: Behind Closed Doors: Interaction Rituals and the Building of Social Ties in Private Company‐Investor Meetings
Authors: Per Ahblom, Carl Henning Christner, Andrea Mennicken
Affiliations: Norwegian University of Science and Technology Trondheim Norway; Stockholm School of Economics Stockholm Sweden; King's College London London UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines private meetings between company managers and institutional investors as part of the broader financial reporting environment. Using direct observations of 39 such meetings across four large, listed companies—complemented with the study of preparatory work and internal documents—the paper investigates how these meetings help build and maintain relationships between companies and investors. The analysis shows that the importance of these meetings lies not primarily in the exchange of new information but in the creation of familiarity, focused engagement, and exclusivity, which strengthen social ties and reinforce participants' positions in the capital market. Drawing on interaction ritual theory, the paper identifies three forms of ritual work through which these outcomes are produced: assembly work, conversational work, and bodily work. The study contributes to research on the social embeddedness of capital markets and suggests that private reporting meetings should be understood not only as informational events but also as relational mechanisms that shape access, trust, and network persistence.

Title: Issue Information
Abstract: une étude historique sur la conception de l'utilité de la comptabilité/The Epistemic Rise of Accounting Research in Financial Economics: A Historical Study on the Conception of the Usefulness of Accounting PIER-LUC LAJOIE and YVES GENDRON.......

Title: Better Together? Facial Expressions as a Mechanism Shaping Enjoyment During Shared Experience
Authors: Argaman Bell Meir, Liron Amihai, Daniel Toledano, Inbal Ravreby, Yaara Yeshurun
Affiliations: School of Psychological Sciences, Tel-Aviv University; Sagol School of Neuroscience, Tel-Aviv University
Abstract: We explored the impact of shared experiences on enjoyment, focusing on the role of facial expressions. Participants ( N = 190, aged 18–35, recruited in Israel) listened to humorous audio clips with a friend or alone, while their facial expressions were recorded via Zoom. Our primary analysis showed that friend presence influenced enjoyment in a content-dependent way, enhancing enjoyment for knock-knock jokes and reducing it for stand-up. Across both types of humor, friend presence amplified the intensity of happy facial expressions. Complementing these findings, a post hoc mediation analysis revealed that these happy expressions partially accounted for shared experiences’ effect on enjoyment, suggesting they are a key mechanism linking social context to affective responses. Friends also exhibited facial-expression synchronization, reflecting communicative responsiveness to one another. Notably, these effects were reduced when participants could not see each other. These findings suggest that facial expressions actively shape enjoyment during shared experiences, offering insight into how people connect and experience the world together.

Title: Why Design Thinking Needs a Responsibility Reboot
Authors: Pietro Micheli Micheli, Jatinder Jit (J.J.) Singh, Minu Kumar, Neil Goldberg
Abstract: User-centered design methods focus on giving users what they seem to want. But approaches like design thinking can lead practitioners to ignore potential harms or fail to adequately consider ethical design principles. Companies can be innovative while minimizing such risks by putting mission and values at the forefront of the design process, being mindful of how KPIs or other incentives may influence design choices, and pausing to consider a product’s potential broad impact before scaling.

Title: Auditor-Employed Tax Experts and Audit Quality
Authors: Andrew M. Bauer, Miguel Minutti-Meza, Saad Siddiqui, Aleksandra B. Zimmerman
Affiliations: University of Waterloo; University of Miami; The University of Texas at Austin; Florida State University
Abstract: ABSTRACT Using PCAOB data, we examine variation in auditor-employed tax experts’ involvement to assist the audit team. Tax expert hours average 5 percent of total audit hours and are positively associated with several proxies for the complexity of tax estimates. Greater tax expert involvement correlates with a higher detection rate of tax-related internal control material weaknesses (ICMWs) and a greater frequency of subsequent tax-related restatements. However, earlier tax expert involvement is associated with fewer ICMWs, although it is not significantly associated with subsequent restatements. Overall, our findings provide new evidence on how the timing and intensity of tax expert involvement relate to audit outcomes. Although involving tax experts is a typical response to auditing complex estimates, their involvement alone does not fully mitigate restatement risk. Importantly, timely coordination between the audit team and tax experts plays a critical role in ensuring high audit quality. Data Availability: Audit engagement data from the PCAOB are proprietary; other data are from public sources. JEL Classifications: M4.

Title: Financial Statement Audits of Private Firms and IRS Enforcement Outcomes
Authors: Michele S. Mullaney, Bridget Stomberg, Brian Williams
Affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington
Abstract: ABSTRACT Using IRS tax return data for private C corporations, we examine the relation between GAAP audits and IRS enforcement outcomes. Among IRS-audited tax returns, we find that those with audited GAAP financial statements have fewer and smaller proposed deficiencies. These effects persist after controlling for tax preparers. Furthermore, we estimate that the explanatory power of audited GAAP financial statements is comparable to that of external debtholders. Audited GAAP financial statements are also associated with a higher likelihood of unagreed proposed deficiencies, more detailed tax return disclosures, and fewer IRS audit hours, all of which are consistent with more defensible tax positions. Tax returns with audited GAAP financial statements exhibit greater initial voluntary compliance and generate smaller proposed deficiencies per IRS audit hour. These results inform private firms as they weigh the costs and benefits of financial statement audits and the IRS as it allocates enforcement resources. Data Availability: The IRS provided confidential tax information to Michele S. Mullaney pursuant to an agreement under the Intergovernmental Personnel Act of 1970 through the Statistics of Income Division’s Joint Statistical Research Program. JEL Classifications: H25; H26; M41; M42; M48.

Title: Temporal grammars of novelty: How carbon removal entrepreneurs frame new technologies
Authors: Ioana Sendroiu
Affiliations: Sociology, Management and Strategy University of Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR China
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper assesses the ways in which carbon dioxide removal ventures frame their work. Drawing on George Herbert Mead's philosophy of the present, it conceptualizes temporal grammars of novelty as a framing strategy that involves connecting two points in time, namely present and future, to elaborate novelty. Dictionary, dependency parsing, and large language model approaches trace the use of temporal grammars of novelty across the websites of carbon removal companies in the market, and connect this to venture sales volumes. Analyses show that ventures deploying newer technologies and using temporal grammars of novelty have higher sales. In contrast, explicitly causal language does not prove beneficial. This paper addresses a fundamental problem in conceptualizing novelty by arguing that it is referential without being causal, and shows this with reference to the framing strategies deployed by environmental entrepreneurs. Managerial Summary Carbon removal entrepreneurs must convince buyers that novel, often unproven technologies are credible. This paper shows that how they talk about time matters. Analyzing website language and sales across carbon removal ventures, it finds that firms using more speculative technologies sell more when they link present action to future possibility: what they are designing, building, or deploying now, and what this will make possible later, at scale. By contrast, causal language—detailed claims about why or how specific features will produce outcomes—is not helpful and is negatively associated with sales. When framing novelty, pairing present action with future promise is more credible than over‐specified causal certainty.

Title: From accidents to assets—The value pathways of patents for serendipitous inventions
Authors: Christoph Grimpe, Karin Hoisl, Myriam Mariani, Wolfgang Sofka
Affiliations: Department of Strategy and Innovation Copenhagen Business School Frederiksberg Denmark; Mannheim Business School University of Mannheim Mannheim Germany; Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition Munich Germany; Department of Management and Technology and ICRIOS Bocconi University Milan Italy; Strategy, International Business and Entrepreneurship Group (SIBE) University of Liverpool Management School Liverpool UK
Abstract: Abstract Research Summary Firms often celebrate accidental inventions that lead to major breakthroughs, yet little is known about how the value of serendipitous inventions materializes. Using data from 8530 patented inventions across 23 countries, our research shows that these inventions differ from planned R&D outcomes. Serendipitous inventions are less likely to have a strong technological impact, be turned into marketable products, or serve as effective blocking tools in patent strategy. However, they are more likely to generate value through licensing, indicating that while they may not fit the originating firm's strategy, they can succeed elsewhere. Hence, serendipitous patented inventions represent “option‐like” assets that offer external channels to capture value rather than relying on internal use. Managerial Summary Accidental breakthroughs like microwaves, penicillin, or Velcro are often celebrated, but their potential to create value in practice remains unclear. Analyzing data from 8530 patented inventions across 23 countries, we find that such serendipitous inventions differ fundamentally from planned R&D outcomes. They are less likely to yield major technological impacts, products, or strategic patents but more likely to generate value through licensing, functioning as “option‐like” assets that are valuable externally more than internally. Thus, relative to planned inventions that benefit from downstream complementary assets, serendipitous patented inventions pay off more for firms with strong licensing or technology‐selling capabilities.

Title: Retail investor trading and market reactions to earnings announcements
Authors: Henry L. Friedman, Zitong Zeng
Abstract: We examine whether retail investor trading enhances or impedes the market’s processing of earnings information. To address the endogenous nature of retail trading decisions, we exploit brokerage outages as plausibly exogenous shocks to retail trading during earnings announcement windows. Our findings show that retail trading significantly enhances price responses to earnings news. Exogenous reductions in retail trading weaken earnings response coefficients and slow price adjustment. These results are driven by investors at traditional broker platforms providing liquidity; the impact of Robinhood-only outages is statistically insignificant. Distinguishing between the broad retail population and Robinhood traders helps reconcile prior mixed evidence on the role of retail traders in impounding earnings news into price. Our outage-based tests find limited evidence that retail trading reduces post-earnings announcement drift. Overall, our results demonstrate that retail investors enhance earnings-related price discovery through liquidity provision while revealing important heterogeneity across trading platforms.

Title: Surge pricing and multi-agency interaction in humanitarian logistics: An equilibrium approach
Authors: Mojtaba Salarpour
Abstract: In this paper, we develop a network model for hurricane relief logistics in which multiple agencies choose pre-positioned stock and response shipments while sharing depots and freight lanes. The pre-positioning decision carries a procurement or reservation cost and is limited by available depot storage. After landfall, agencies ship relief supplies through lanes whose freight prices increase with total use. We formulate both a centralized planner model and a decentralized agency model on the same physical network using a variational inequality framework. The model also includes time-based shortage penalties, service balance across demand zones, and a budgeted expected-shortage hedge. Numerical examples calibrated to a U.S. Gulf Coast setting examine lane expansion, early shortage costs, service balance, expected-shortage protection, coordination surcharges, and stochastic planner-GNE comparisons. Replicated sample average approximation checks and independent out of sample evaluations are used to support the stochastic comparisons. The results show that, among the tested individual stresses, the increase in demand has the largest effect on cost, that local lane expansion has diminishing returns when congestion shifts to other lanes, and that decentralized decisions can create service gaps even when total cost gaps are small.

Title: Platform contracts for emission-reducing smart products with consumers’ privacy concern
Authors: Prasenjit Mandal, Debashree Ray, Abhishek Chakraborty, Tania Saha, Ou Tang
Abstract: IoT-enabled smart home devices, such as smart thermostats, can help reduce household carbon emissions through data-driven energy optimization. However, their reliance on continuous data collection poses significant consumers’ privacy concerns, creating a fundamental tension between sustainability benefits and privacy risks. This paper studies a supply chain where a manufacturer sells smart home devices via an online platform that chooses an optimal contract: the reselling or agency contract. The manufacturer invests in emission-reducing technologies. Given that consumers are emission-sensitive and privacy-concerned, and consumer data has a significant monetizable value for the platform, we examine how these factors influence smart product pricing, emission reduction efforts, and stakeholders’ contract preferences. Our results reveal that higher emission sensitivity does not always lead to greater emission reductions, particularly when investment costs in emission reduction are high. Next, under the reselling model, a higher marginal value of consumer data incentivizes the manufacturer to increase emission reduction, while the product price response depends on the cost of emission reduction. In contrast, under the agency model, the equilibrium outcomes are unaffected by data value. Further, our results indicate that the platform chooses the reselling contract when the data value is significantly high or very low, whereas the agency model is preferable for intermediate data values. Moreover, under specific market conditions, both contracts can lead to ‘win-win-win’ outcomes for the manufacturer, the platform, and the consumers. Most importantly, we also show that our key findings on ‘win-win-win’ outcomes are robust to alternative leadership structures, including manufacturer-led contract choice.

Title: Decision-focused learning for distributionally robust multi-agent dynamic vehicle routing in e-commerce last-mile delivery
Authors: Ruowei Liu, Yuhao Ma, Rongfei Ma
Abstract: E-commerce last-mile delivery requires coordinated vehicle routing under uncertain demand, travel times, and dynamically arriving orders. We develop DFL-DRO-DVRP, a sequential decision architecture that integrates regret-based learning, samplewise adversarial robustification motivated by Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, and best-response coordination among delivery agents. The architecture first trains the predictor with a robustified SPO+ objective and then adjusts deployed routes through agent-level best responses. A nested formulation makes these interfaces explicit, while a conditional error decomposition separates prediction, perturbation, and centralized deployment terms. Across four benchmark settings, DFL-DRO-DVRP attains the lowest total cost on Solomon, distribution-shift, and multi-agent instances, improving on the data-driven hybrid ALNS baseline by 1.5%, 1.4%, and 2.5%, respectively; on the nominal e-commerce benchmark, its 0.5% cost difference is not statistically significant. Under demand, time-window, and travel-time shifts, the method limits cost increases to 6.1%, 8.7%, and 5.2%, compared with 6.8%, 9.5%, and 5.8% for the strongest competing baseline. These results show that the proposed composition remains competitive under nominal conditions and provides its clearest advantages when distributional robustness and decentralized coordination are operationally relevant.

Title: Cross-border cooperation among securities regulators and supply chain collaboration: evidence from U.S.-listed foreign firms
Authors: Xiaoqi Chen, Liangliang Jiang, Yuqi Wang
Abstract: Las cadenas de suministro internacionales son esenciales para conectar los mercados globales, pero enfrentan desafíos persistentes. Si bien los marcos regulatorios son cruciales para respaldar las operaciones comerciales internacionales, la supervisión fragmentada entre jurisdicciones a menudo socava la resiliencia de las cadenas de suministro. Examinamos cómo la cooperación entre los organismos reguladores de los mercados de valores a través de la adopción del Memorando Multilateral de Entendimiento (MMoU, por sus siglas en inglés) afecta la contratación dentro de las cadenas globales de suministro. Utilizando un modelo de diferencias en diferencias apilado ( stacked difference-in-differences ), encontramos que, en comparación con las empresas nacionales, las empresas extranjeras que cotizan en los Estados Unidos experimentan aumentos tanto en nuevos contratos como en nuevos clientes provenientes de países signatarios del Memorando Multilateral de Entendimiento después de que sus países de origen suscriben el acuerdo. Este efecto positivo es más pronunciado entre las empresas que enfrentan mayores costos de agencia y restricciones financieras más estrictas, así como en países con mayores barreras para el cumplimiento de contratos. El Memorando Multilateral de Entendimiento fortalece la capacidad de financiamiento de los proveedores y prolonga la duración tanto de las relaciones comerciales en la cadena de suministro como de los contratos. Además, mostramos que la expansión de la contratación dentro de las cadenas de suministro es impulsada principalmente por clientes de países miembros del Memorando Multilateral de Entendimiento distintos de los Estados Unidos. En conjunto, nuestros hallazgos demuestran que la cooperación regulatoria transfronteriza genera externalidades positivas para el desarrollo de las cadenas globales de suministro. 国际供应链是连接全球市场的重要纽带，但面临着持续的挑战。尽管监管框架对于支持国际商业运营至关重要，跨司法辖区的碎片化监管往往削弱供应链韧性。我们研究了证券监管机构之间的合作如何通过采纳《多边谅解备忘录》（MMoU）影响全球供应链缔约。采用堆叠双重差分模型，我们发现，相对于国内公司而言，在美国上市的外国公司在其母国签署该协议后，来自MMoU签署国的新合同和新客户数量均有所增加。这一正向效应在面临较高代理成本和更严格财务约束的公司中，以及在合同执行障碍较大的国家中更为显著。MMoU增强了供应商的融资能力，并延长了供应链关系与合同的存续期。我们进一步表明，供应链缔约的扩张主要由来自非美国MMoU成员国的客户所驱动。总体而言，我们的研究结果表明，跨境监管合作在促进全球供应链方面产生了正向溢出效应。 Global supply chains are crucial for connecting markets worldwide but face challenges due to the complexity of international business. These networks depend on effective financial systems for transparency and trust. However, firms must navigate different regulations and economic conditions across countries. This study explores how the Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MMoU), introduced by the International Organization of Securities Commissions in 2002, impacts global supply chain relationships. The MMoU facilitates information-sharing and cooperation between securities regulators, potentially influencing business activities beyond capital markets.This article investigates whether the MMoU affects the formation of supply chain relationships between U.S.-listed foreign firms and customers in countries that have adopted the MMoU. The study uses a stacked difference-in-differences regression framework to analyze data from U.S.-listed foreign firms whose home countries signed the MMoU, comparing them to domestic firms. The research examines how the MMoU reduces information asymmetry and financial risks, making it easier for firms to establish supply chain ties. The study uses data from the FactSet supply-chain link database and considers various factors like firm size, leverage, and country-level economic indicators. The analysis shows that the MMoU significantly increases the formation of new supply chain relationships, especially for firms facing higher agency costs and financial constraints. The results indicate that the MMoU enhances firms' ability to form supply chain relationships by improving information transparency and reducing financial risks. The study finds that the MMoU leads to increased capital investment, external financing, and

Title: Markup Estimation Using Production and Demand Data: An Application to the U.S. Brewing Industry
Authors: Jan De Loecker, Paul T Scott
Affiliations: KU Leuven , and , UK; CEPR , and , UK; MIT , USA
Abstract: Abstract We compare and combine two distinct approaches to estimating market power in the U.S. brewing industry—one based on production data, the other on demand. Both methods produce similar estimates of average markups and reveal a recent upward trend. We then combine the two approaches in two ways. First, we replace conventional instruments in demand estimation with a moment involving a production-based markup estimate, yielding similar results. We then evaluate the common (but controversial) assumption that retail markets operate competitively, finding that demand-based markups recovered with the assumption of competitive retail markets align with production-based estimates, as long as downstream costs are accounted for.

Title: Justice Good as Random?
Authors: Niklas Hüther, Kristoph Kleiner
Abstract: ABSTRACT The random assignment of judges promotes fairness and underpins causal identification across the social sciences. Analyzing Chapter 11 bankruptcies, we find sophisticated parties “judge‐shop”: relative to secured hedge fund creditors, cases involving unsecured hedge fund creditors and equity holders are assigned judges with lower past conversion rates and higher unsecured recovery rates. Experienced legal counsel similarly influences assignment. Because judges are not assigned consecutive large cases, knowledgeable parties can judge‐shop by timing the filing date. We develop a method to measure the resulting bias and demonstrate the need for controls and bounded instrumental variable specifications in judge/examiner designs.

Title: The Relational Dynamics of Multiparty Alliances: An Interdependence‐Based View
Authors: Wenqian Wang, Jiabei Hu, Fabrice Lumineau
Affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University; Purdue University; The University of Hong Kong
Abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing relevance of multiparty alliances, existing research remains fragmented and predominantly organized around functional purposes or structural forms, overlooking the relational dynamics among alliance partners. Such an omission prevents a systematic understanding of what fundamentally distinguishes multiparty alliances from their dyadic counterparts and how different types of multiparty alliances vary from one another. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic review of research from leading management journals published between 1990 and 2025. Adopting an interdependence‐based view, we offer two main insights. First, the presence of more than two partners introduces three categorically distinct features compared to dyadic alliances: a change in membership, a change in reciprocity patterns, and the emergence of faultlines. Each of these features poses distinct challenges. Second, and more importantly, we show how pooled, sequential, and reciprocal forms of interdependence shape the emergence, evolution, and consequences of these relational features, thereby explaining systematic variations across multiparty alliances. Building on these insights, we develop an integrative framework that clarifies the distinctiveness of multiparty alliances and identifies key mechanisms and boundary conditions. This framework informs a future research agenda to redirect scholarly attention to the unique relational dynamics within and across multiparty alliances.

Title: Passing on Talent: A Generativity Perspective on the Effects of Perceived Overqualification Among Older Employees
Authors: Jia Yu, Deshani B. Ganegoda, Chao Ma
Affiliations: China State Shipbuilding Corporation Limited; Renmin University of China; Melbourne Business School, The University of Melbourne; Xi’an Jiaotong University
Abstract: Drawing on generativity theory, we examine the positive effects of perceived overqualification among older employees. Specifically, we argue that perceptions of overqualification in older employees are positively associated with a core generativity motive—that is, a desire to support and guide the next generation and be needed by them. Further, we argue that generativity motive predicts prosocial attitudes and behaviors in the form of prosocial meaning of work for future generations and helping behavior. Additionally, we identify mature-age practices—that is, human resource practices tailored to address older employees’ needs—as a key contextual factor that strengthens the indirect pathway between perceptions of overqualification in older employees and their prosocial attitudes and behaviors. We test and find support for our hypotheses in two independent field studies—a three-wave field study of older employees (Study 1, N = 261) and a dyadic three-wave field study of employees of various ages and their respective supervisors (Study 2, N = 274 dyads). Theoretical and practical implications of our study are discussed.

Title: When small costs make big impacts: Vertical contracts with menu costs
Authors: Ciwei Dong, Xi Li, Xiutian Shi
Affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law; University of Hong Kong; Nanjing University of Science and Technology
Abstract: Retailers incur price-adjustment costs called menu costs when changing the prices of their products over time. These products are often sourced from upstream suppliers, who endogenously determine wholesale prices, which have cascading effects on retail prices. In this paper, we consider the pricing strategies of supply chain members in the presence of menu costs. Our analysis suggests that even a minuscule menu cost can substantially affect pricing strategies and the equilibrium outcome. Upstream manufacturers always benefit from a menu cost whereas downstream retailers benefit from only a moderate menu cost and are hurt by both high and low menu costs. Meanwhile, menu costs always alleviate the issue of double marginalization, thereby improving supply chain profits, consumer surplus, and social welfare. This study provides channel members with guidance on how to set prices in the presence of menu costs. It also recommends retailers to optimally maintain a moderate menu cost.

Title: Code and Data Repository for A novel and efficient formulation and solution approach for the region coverage problem with identical circles
Authors: Qinghua Wu, Minxuan Li, Xiangjing Lai, Jin-Kao Hao, Yuzhuo Qiu
Abstract: The software and data in this repository are a snapshot of the software and data that were used in the research reported on the paper A novel and efficient formulation and solution approach for the region coverage problem with identical circles by Q.H. Wu, M.X. Li, X.J. Lai, J.K. Hao, and Y.Z. Qiu.

Title: From Data–Model Fit to Model–World Fit: A Framework for Integrating Domain Knowledge into Artificial Intelligence
Authors: Arturo Castellanos, Monica Chiarini Tremblay, Roman Lukyanenko, Jeffrey Parsons, Veda C. Storey
Affiliations: Raymond A. Mason School of Business, William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia 23185; Raymond A. Mason School of Business, College of William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia 23187; McIntire School of Commerce, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22903; Faculty of Business Administration, Memorial University of Newfoundland, St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador A1B 3X5, Canada; Computer Information Systems Department, Georgia State University, Atlanta, Georgia
Abstract: Machine learning (ML)–based artificial intelligence (AI) systems often perform well in controlled settings but fail when deployed in the real world. These failures stem from a fundamental problem: ML/AI models optimize data–model fit by increasing statistical performance on training data, whereas real-world deployment demands a new paradigm in ML/AI: model–world fit that preserves domain semantics and contextual understanding. We propose a machine learning model–world fit framework that provides both a conceptual structure for understanding how domain knowledge shapes ML/AI systems and a research road map for investigating these relationships. The framework identifies how domain knowledge can be integrated into the ML/AI development process via external knowledge representations, such as data, value, process models, or domain ontologies. Incorporating external knowledge representations can help overcome three types of knowledge deficiencies in AI: know-what, know-how, and know-why. To illustrate the framework, we apply it to a child welfare placement case, a domain in which contextual understanding is critical and statistical accuracy is an insufficient evaluation criterion. Our insights lead to several directions for scholars working at the intersection of machine learning, design science, and knowledge representation. History: Ahmed Abbasi, Senior Editor; Min Zhao, Associate Editor. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0031 .

Title: Improving Competitiveness: A Freelancer-Centric Approach for Recommending Reskilling Strategies
Authors: Haoxin Liu, Shuo Yu, Stephen He, Wen Wen, Yidong Chai
Affiliations: School of Management, Faculty of Business for Science & Technology, International Institute of Finance, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China; Area of Information Systems and Quantitative Sciences, Rawls College of Business, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, Texas 79409; Department of Marketing, Alvarez College of Business, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas 78249; Department of Information, Risk & Operations Management, McCombs School of Business, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Department of Information Systems, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong 999077, China; and School of Management, Hefei University of Technology, Hefei 230009, China; and Business Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, City University of Hong Kong, Dongguan 523808, China
Abstract: As new technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly reshape labor markets and the value of different skills, workers increasingly need to decide which skills to acquire to remain competitive. Yet most online labor platforms focus on helping employers find workers or workers find jobs, offering limited guidance on how workers can strategically reskill to improve their market competitiveness. We address this gap by developing an AI-enabled freelancer-centric skill advisor (FESA) that recommends skills based on freelancers’ desired tasks and supports both exploration (exploring new skills) and exploitation (deepening existing expertise) reskilling strategies. Using real-world data from a major online labor market, we show that FESA substantially outperforms existing approaches in identifying skills that improve freelancers’ competitiveness. A controlled experiment further shows that users are more motivated to pursue FESA’s personalized recommendations than generic popular-skill recommendations. Importantly, our experimental results reveal a key design lesson for AI-powered skill recommendation systems: More information is not always better. Revealing freelancers’ low market rankings can reduce their motivation to reskill, particularly under exploration reskilling strategies. Our study offers practical guidance for online platforms, workforce-development programs, and policymakers designing digital tools to support reskilling in rapidly changing labor markets.

Title: Communicating Corporate Culture in Labor Markets: Evidence from Job Postings
Authors: Allen H. Huang, Joseph Pacelli, Terrence Tianshuo Shi, Yuan Zou
Affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Kowloon, Hong Kong; Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163; UCLA Anderson School of Management, Los Angeles, California 90095
Abstract: We examine how culture information in job postings influences firms’ hiring outcomes. We utilize machine learning methods to measure five core values present in job postings and demonstrate that culture information helps attract job seekers, as it is associated with higher worker inflows. The effect strengthens when job seekers value culture in their job searches and face frictions in learning about culture from other sources. Additional analyses indicate that individual cultural dimensions in job postings are more salient to job seekers when they have heightened preferences for that particular value. Finally, culture information is associated with a higher likelihood that interviews result in offers, and greater acceptance of those offers. Overall, our results suggest that culture information in job postings helps job seekers sort into culturally aligned firms. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Title: Motivated Procrastination
Authors: Charlotte Cordes, Jana Friedrichsen, Simeon Schudy
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munich, 80539 Munich, Germany; Institute of Economics and CESifo, Kiel University, 24098 Kiel, Germany; Institute of Economics and CESifo, Ulm University, 89081 Ulm, Germany
Abstract: This study provides a rigorous empirical test for motivated memory as a cause for procrastination. In a longitudinal experiment over four weeks, individuals had to complete a cumbersome task of unknown length and receive noisy signals about their assigned workload. Varying scope for motivated memory results in more optimistic beliefs among workers who receive negative signals but not among those who receive positive ones. This suppression of negative news through motivated memory causes individuals to defer more work to the future. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis.
